# Sophicly Table of Techniques — Reference

_Generated from the Table of Techniques prototype (304 techniques). Do not edit by hand — regenerate with `build-techniques-md.js`._

Each entry gives the technique’s definition, worked examples, and effect on the reader (Focus / Feel / Think / Act). Some carry expanded collections (e.g. the Coming-of-Age archetypal journeys, or Want vs Need goals).

## Story Archetypes & Plot

### Antihero `Az`

An antihero is a main character who lacks some of a hero's qualities, such as goodness, honesty or courage. Even so, the antihero leads the story, and the reader keeps following them. Some antiheroes do terrible things, and others are only proud, selfish or weak. An antihero is different from a villain, who is the hero's enemy: the antihero is the person whose story we follow, even when that person does villainous things.

**The concept:** An antihero is a main character readers do not fully approve of, so following one makes readers ask why they still read on. When we are shown a character's thoughts and reasons, we start to see the world as that character does, even when the actions are wrong. In Frankenstein, Victor Frankenstein tells the story himself, so we understand his ambition, yet he runs out of the room when the creature he has made comes to life. When you write about any antihero, say which qualities of a hero the character lacks, why the reader keeps following them, and what the writer wants us to understand.

**Examples:** “I am in blood / Stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more, / Returning were as tedious as go o'er” — Macbeth, who has already killed King Duncan and had his friend Banquo killed, says he has gone so far into blood that turning back would be as hard as going on — Macbeth; “Are there no prisons?” — Scrooge, the main character, says this to two men who are collecting money to help the poor, so we meet a hero who lacks kindness — A Christmas Carol; “I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society” — Pip, who tells his own story, admits this about teaching Joe, the kind blacksmith married to his sister, so we see from inside how ashamed of Joe he has become — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We stay with a main character we cannot fully approve of, and watch what their faults cost. · Feel: We feel uneasy, because we are drawn to someone we know we should judge, and we may recognise ourselves in them. · Think: We ask why we keep taking the side of a flawed main character, and what the writer wants us to see about human weakness. · Act: We notice when films, news stories or people online win our sympathy while doing wrong, and ask why we forgive them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any antihero, a main character who lacks a hero's goodness yet still leads the story. 1. Which hero's qualities does this character lack, such as kindness, honesty or courage? 2. What keeps the reader following them: do we hear their thoughts, enjoy their cleverness, or share their cause? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand about following someone we do not approve of? Try the questions on Richard III by Shakespeare. Richard, Duke of Gloucester, lacks kindness and loyalty: he plots to turn his brother Clarence and the king against each other. We follow him because he speaks his plans straight to the audience, and his cleverness is entertaining. After he persuades Lady Anne to accept him beside the coffin of King Henry VI, whom he killed, he asks the audience “Was ever woman in this humour woo'd?”, which means: was a woman ever courted in such a mood? Shakespeare may want us to notice that we can enjoy a man we should condemn, and to ask why.

**How to create it:** Choose one hero's quality your protagonist lacks, such as kindness, honesty or courage. Show the lack in what they do early on, so the reader sees it before being told. Give the reader a reason to stay with them, such as their thoughts, their humour or a cause the reader shares. Check that a friend can say what the protagonist does wrong and why they still want to read on; if they cannot say one of these, make that part clearer.

**Related:** The Rebel, The Outsider, The Shadow, The Hero, Foil

### The Everyman `Ev`

An Everyman is an ordinary main character, with a plain home, family and way of life that many readers share. Unlike a hero with special gifts, the Everyman begins with none, so readers can imagine themselves in the character's place. The story often puts the Everyman into an extraordinary situation, such as a journey, a danger or a hard choice. An Everyman need not be ordinary in every way: the character can still have a strong mind or a clear fault.

**The concept:** An Everyman lets readers feel that an extraordinary event could happen to them, because the main character is like them. The word comes from Everyman, an English play of about the year 1500, in which the main character stands for every human being. When a character's life looks like ours, we share the character's fears and hopes more easily. In Jane Eyre, Jane, a governess, tells her employer Mr Rochester that she is “poor, obscure, plain, and little”, yet has feelings like his. When you write about any Everyman, say what is ordinary about the character, what extraordinary event tests them, and what the writer wants readers to see.

**Examples:** “Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do” — Alice is an ordinary girl, bored on a riverbank, before she follows the White Rabbit down a hole — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; “Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle Henry, who was a farmer” — Dorothy's home is a plain farm, before a cyclone carries her house away to the Land of Oz — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz; “my father kept the Admiral Benbow inn” — Jim Hawkins, who tells the story, is the son of an innkeeper, and he is drawn into a hunt for pirate treasure — Treasure Island

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the everyday details of a main character's life, and find we are standing inside them. · Feel: We feel close to the character, so we share their fear when something extraordinary happens, because they are like us. · Think: We ask what the writer wants ordinary people to understand about courage, choice or change, since the story could happen to us. · Act: We notice when stories, adverts and news reports use an ordinary person to speak for us, and ask what they want us to do.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any Everyman, an ordinary main character in whose place readers can imagine themselves. 1. What is ordinary about this character: their home, family, work or worries? 2. What extraordinary event or choice does the story put in front of them? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand through an ordinary person facing it? Try the questions on Peter Pan. Wendy Darling lives in an ordinary London house: her father goes to an office and talks about stocks and shares, and her mother keeps the household accounts. Peter Pan comes to her bedroom and takes her to the Neverland, where she becomes a mother to the Lost Boys, a group of boys who live without a mother. Later Wendy decides to go home, and she grows up. J. M. Barrie may want readers to see that an ordinary girl can have a great adventure, and still choose to go home.

**How to create it:** Choose three plain details about your character's life, such as their street, their job and one small worry. Show these in the opening, so a reader with a similar life can see themselves there. Then put one extraordinary event in front of the character, and show them reacting in an ordinary way, such as hesitating or asking for help. Ask a friend to name one ordinary detail about your character; if they cannot, add one.

**Kinds of Everyman** — The ordinary figure the reader stands beside — told many ways, each a different reason we see ourselves in them.

- **Kinds of everyman** — Why the reader identifies with this ordinary figure
  - **The Reluctant Witness** — An ordinary person drawn into events far larger than themselves. _(e.g. “What have we done, Phil?” — the friend who only stood and watched is the one who finally asks the question — DNA)_
  - **The Moral Anchor** — The plain, decent centre against which other characters are judged. _(e.g. “I got the conch... I got a right to speak” — the plain rule he keeps repeating becomes the measure of everyone who breaks it — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **The Overlooked Hero** — An unremarkable figure who proves quietly, decisively brave. _(e.g. “I will go to Platform 1 and get on the train and then I will get off at Paddington” — a boy everyone treats as helpless plans the journey step by step, then makes it alone — The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time)_
  - **The Everyman in Extremis** — A normal person tested past their limits by extreme circumstance. _(e.g. “The world, that understandable and lawful world, was slipping away.” — an ordinary boy feels the rules he grew up inside stop holding — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **The Representative Victim** — One ordinary life made to stand for the suffering of many. _(e.g. “millions and millions of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us” — one dead girl is turned into a name for everyone the system uses and discards — An Inspector Calls)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Underdog `Ud`

An underdog is a main character who begins with less power, money, strength or status than the people or forces they face. The underdog is a kind of hero who starts with big disadvantages, and most readers hope the underdog will succeed, or at least will not give up. An underdog can be poor, young, small or looked down on, yet still have courage, cleverness or determination. An underdog does not always win: a story may end in victory, in defeat, or somewhere in between.

**The concept:** An underdog, a character who starts with big disadvantages, makes readers hope that the underdog will win. When the disadvantages are clear, we take the underdog's side, and each small step forward feels important. In the Bible story of David and Goliath (1 Samuel 17), David, a young shepherd, faces Goliath, a huge enemy soldier, with only a staff, a sling and five smooth stones. When you write about any underdog, say what disadvantages the character has, what the character uses to face them, and what the story shows about people with less power.

**Examples:** “Please, sir, I want some more.” — Oliver, a hungry workhouse boy chosen by lot to ask, goes up to the master, who has all the power, and asks for another helping of food — Oliver Twist; “she had no bed to lie down on, but was made to lie by the hearth among the ashes” — the girl is made to do the hard work by her father's new wife and the wife's two daughters, so she begins with the least power in the house — Cinderella; “Wicked and cruel boy!” — Jane, a ten-year-old orphan living in her aunt's house, says this to her cousin John Reed, who is four years older, large and stout, after he throws a book at her — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the gap between the character and the opponent, and notice each small step the character takes. · Feel: We feel hope for the weaker side, mixed with fear that the opponent will win, because we can see how much is against them. · Think: We ask who or what has put the character at a disadvantage, and whether courage and cleverness can matter more than power. · Act: We notice who is the underdog in sport, at school and in the news, and ask whether the disadvantages they face are fair.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any underdog, a main character who begins with less power than the people or forces they face. 1. What does the character lack compared with the opponent, such as power, money, size or status? 2. What does the character use against the opponent, such as courage, cleverness, help from others or determination? 3. Does the character win, lose or end somewhere between, and what does the writer want readers to understand about people with less power? Try the questions on Hansel and Gretel. The two children are poor and small, and their stepmother wants to leave them in the forest because the family has too little food. The first time they are left in the forest, Hansel uses white pebbles to find the way home. The second time, a witch locks Hansel in a stable and plans to eat him. Later Gretel pushes the witch into her own oven and shuts the door. The children win and go home with the witch's jewels, so the tale shows that small, hungry children can beat a stronger enemy by being clever.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character lacks, and make it clear early, such as money, strength or a place in the group. Show one person or force with much more power standing in the character's way. Let the character use a skill or a friend, so that each step forward has a reason. Check that your reader can say what the disadvantages are in one sentence; if not, state them more clearly.

**Kinds of Underdog** — The disadvantaged figure we root for — told many ways, each a different disadvantage overcome or exposed.

- **Kinds of underdog** — The disadvantage faced, and whether it is overcome
  - **The Social Underdog** — Held down by class or poverty, striving upward against it. _(e.g. “how come you got everything... an’ I got nothin’?” — the question is not really about his friend; it is about the class he was born into — Blood Brothers)_
  - **The Overlooked Talent** — Dismissed by those around them until their worth is proven. _(e.g. “Give not this rotten orange to your friend” — she is thrown away in public on no evidence, and the play spends the rest of itself proving him wrong — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **The Physical Underdog** — Outmatched in strength, winning through wit or sheer will. _(e.g. “a man can be destroyed but not defeated” — he loses the fish to the sea and still will not call it a defeat — The Old Man and the Sea)_
  - **The Doomed Underdog** — The disadvantage proves too great, and the world too cruel. _(e.g. “George raised the gun and his hand shook” — the kindest thing left to do for him is also the worst — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **The Rising Many** — The powerless combine to challenge the powerful. _(e.g. “Beasts of England” — a song is the first thing the powerless own together — Animal Farm)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Orphan `Or`

An orphan is a main character who has lost their parents, or been left or cast out by their family. The loss can come through death, or through being abandoned, sent away or rejected. With no parent to look after them, an orphan who is the hero of a story often has to look after themselves and look for a place where they belong. An orphan does not always find a family: some are taken in, some build one from friends, and some stay alone.

**The concept:** An orphan story shows a character with no parent to turn to, so the character often has to learn to look after themselves. Without a parent, dangers and kindnesses can matter more, because there may be nobody else to give help. In Jane Eyre, Jane, a ten-year-old orphan living in her aunt's house, says “I have no father or mother, brothers or sisters”. When you write about any orphan, say what the character has lost, how this changes what they do, and what the writer wants readers to understand about belonging.

**Examples:** “As I never saw my father or my mother” — Pip, who tells his own story, says this in the first lines of Great Expectations, so one of the first facts we learn about him is that he has no parents — Great Expectations; “I was dependent on none, and related to none” — the creature, whom Victor Frankenstein made and then ran away from, says, while he thinks about the books he has read, that he has no one to depend on and no relatives — Frankenstein; “Dorothy, who was an orphan” — the book tells us this about Dorothy, who lives on a Kansas farm with her Uncle Henry and Aunt Em, the relatives who look after her — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice what the character has lost, and who is missing when the character needs help. · Feel: We feel protective and sad for a character with no parent to turn to, and we admire their strength when they cope. · Think: We ask how losing a family shapes the character, and what the writer shows about belonging and who takes care of us. · Act: We notice people around us who have no family close by, and think about how we can include them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any orphan, a main character who has lost their parents or been cast out by their family. 1. Who has the character lost, and how did the loss happen? 2. How does the loss change what the character does, such as looking after themselves, trusting few people or looking for a home? 3. Does the character find, build or lack a family by the end, and what does the writer want readers to understand about belonging? Try the questions on Oliver Twist. Oliver's mother dies soon after he is born, and he grows up in a workhouse, a place where poor people must work for food and a bed. With no one to protect him, he is sent to work for others, and he runs away to London, where Fagin's gang of thieves give him a place to stay. By the end Mr Brownlow, a kind gentleman, adopts Oliver as his son. Dickens may want readers to see that a child with no family needs care from the people around him.

**How to create it:** Decide how your character lost their family, and show the loss in one clear scene. Show one habit that comes from it, such as hiding food, trusting nobody or leaving a room before anyone else. Give the character one person who offers care, and let the character hesitate to accept it. Check that a friend can say what your character misses most; if not, show it again in a small action.

**Kinds of Orphan** — The parentless figure seeking belonging — told many ways, each a different absence shaping the child.

- **Kinds of orphan** — How the lost parents shape the child left behind
  - **The Seeker of Belonging** — The orphan searches for a family or a place to call home. _(e.g. “a new forever family” — the kind words the adults use for the thing the child is still looking for — My Name Is Leon)_
  - **The Self-Made Orphan** — Deprivation forges independence and moral steel. _(e.g. “I resisted all the way: a new thing for me” — the first time the orphan fights back is the moment her character starts — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The Chosen One** — The orphan's lost origins conceal a special destiny. _(e.g. “I can never be sorry, father” — the foundling learns her real family are gentry, and chooses the poor man who raised her — Silas Marner)_
  - **The Hardened Orphan** — Neglect curdles into resentment or cunning. _(e.g. “Why should I do anything for you? You never do anything for me” — the coldness she was raised on is handed straight back — A Taste of Honey)_
  - **The Haunted Orphan** — The absent parents shape the child as an open wound. _(e.g. “You! Why didn’t you give me away!” — the grown man screams at his mother that the wound is which child she kept — Blood Brothers)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Lost Soul `Ls`

A lost soul is a main character who pulls away from other people and from ordinary life, often after a hurt. The hurt may be a loss, a betrayal or a shame, and the character often keeps apart because company feels too painful. Unlike an orphan, who has lost their family, a lost soul may still have people nearby and keep away from them. A lost soul can be the hero of a story, and may come back to other people by the end, or may stay alone.

**The concept:** A lost soul shows what a hurt can do to someone who keeps it hidden: hiding away can stop the hurt from healing. When a character avoids other people, the reader sees the pain underneath and wants to know what caused it. In Jekyll and Hyde, Dr Jekyll writes to his friend Utterson that he will lead “a life of extreme seclusion”, which means a life apart from other people. When you write about any lost soul, say what hurt the character, how they keep away from others, and what the writer wants us to understand about being alone.

**Examples:** “secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster” — the narrator describes Scrooge, who keeps everyone at a distance, and the Ghost of Christmas Past later shows him as a lonely boy left at school over Christmas — A Christmas Carol; “I shunned the face of man” — Victor Frankenstein, weighed down by guilt after the deaths of his young brother William and of Justine, a servant in his family's house, says he avoided other people — Frankenstein; “lost all my mirth, forgone all custom of exercises” — Hamlet tells two old friends that he has lost all his cheerfulness and given up his usual activities, after his father's death and his mother's marriage to his uncle Claudius — Hamlet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the distance the character keeps from other people, and look for the hurt behind it. · Feel: We feel unease and then pity, because the character's loneliness looks like a way of coping with pain. · Think: We ask what hurt the character, and whether keeping apart protects them or stops the hurt from healing. · Act: We notice people who stay quiet and apart, and ask whether they are hurting, instead of judging them as unfriendly.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any lost soul, a main character who pulls away from other people and from ordinary life. 1. What loss, hurt or shame has the character suffered? 2. How does the character keep away from others, and where do they hide? 3. Does the character come back to other people, and what does the writer want us to understand about being alone? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. At the start of the play Romeo is hurt because Rosaline, the woman he loves, has sworn never to love anyone. His father, Montague, says that Romeo “Shuts up his windows, locks fair daylight out” and stays in his room, and Benvolio, Romeo's cousin, says Romeo hid in a wood when he came near. Romeo does come back to other people: Benvolio persuades him to go to the Capulets' feast, where he meets Juliet. Shakespeare may want us to see that a hurt like this can end when something new matters to the person.

**How to create it:** Decide what hurt your character, and keep the cause hidden at first. Show how they keep away from others, such as eating alone, refusing visitors or staying in one room. Let one other person try to reach them, and show the character pushing that person away. Ask a friend if they can tell there is a hurt behind the distance; if not, add one small sign, such as a locked drawer or an old letter.

**Kinds of Lost Soul** — Writers show lost souls in different ways. Some are shut out by the people around them. Some lose their faith or their purpose, and some do wrong until little good is left in them. Some are held still by grief. Some are cut off for good, and their own choices caused it. When you write a lost soul, decide what the loss was and what caused it.

- **Kinds of lost soul** — what the character has lost, and what has left them cut off from other people
  - **Shut out by society** — The people around the character treat them as an outsider. They are shut out because of who they are and not because of anything they have done. _(e.g. “You call me misbeliever, cut-throat dog, / And spit upon my Jewish gaberdine” — Shylock, a Jewish money-lender, tells Antonio how Antonio has insulted him and spat on his clothes — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **Adrift after losing faith or purpose** — The character no longer believes in what they used to trust. With nothing to aim for, they drift from place to place. _(e.g. "phoney" — Holden Caulfield, a teenager who has left his school, uses this word for the people around him as he drifts through New York — The Catcher in the Rye)_
  - **Slowly hollowed out by wrongdoing** — The character does wrong things, and each one takes something good out of them. In the end very little of the person they once were is left. _(e.g. "a tale told by an idiot" — Macbeth says that life is like this, a story full of noise that means nothing, when he hears that his wife has died after he killed to become king — Macbeth)_
  - **Frozen in the past by grief** — A great loss holds the character in one moment of time. They cannot move on, so their own life stops while the world goes on. _(e.g. “the bride within the bridal dress had withered like the dress” — Pip describes Miss Havisham, who was left by the man she was to marry and still wears her wedding dress years later, with her clocks stopped at the time she was left — Great Expectations)_
  - **Cut off for good, and to blame for it** — The character is shut out from any hope of rescue. They chose this themselves, and there is no way back. _(e.g. “I wear the chain I forged in life... I made it link by link, and yard by yard” — Marley's ghost tells Scrooge that his heavy chain was made by his own actions in life, so nobody else punished him — A Christmas Carol)_

### The Rebel `Rb`

A rebel is a character who refuses to obey, or tries to remove, a rule, an order or a ruler that they think is unfair. The refusal can be loud or quiet, and it often costs the rebel something. A rebel may be a hero, a villain or both, because a fair cause can be fought for cruelly, and an unfair one peacefully. A rebel is not the same as an outsider, who only stands apart from a group: the rebel acts against the group's rules.

**The concept:** A rebel lets readers look at a rule from the side of someone who refuses it, and decide whether the refusal is fair. When a character risks losing safety, freedom or even life by refusing, we see how strongly the character believes they are right. In Romeo and Juliet, Lord Capulet orders his daughter Juliet to marry Count Paris, and when she refuses, he tells her she can “hang, beg, starve, die in the streets”. When you write about any rebel, say what the character refuses, why they think it is unfair, and what the refusal costs.

**Examples:** “I am not deceitful: if I were, I should say I loved you; but I declare I do not love you” — Jane, aged ten, says this to her aunt, Mrs Reed, after hearing what Mrs Reed said about her to a visitor — Jane Eyre; “I am not to be intimidated into anything so wholly unreasonable” — Elizabeth Bennet says this to Lady Catherine, a rich and powerful noblewoman, who demands that she promise never to marry Mr Darcy — Pride and Prejudice; “That is my message to you, comrades: Rebellion!” — Old Major, an old boar, tells the animals of the farm that they should overthrow the human beings who own them — Animal Farm

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at what the character refuses to accept, and who has the power to punish them. · Feel: We feel admiration for someone who says no, mixed with fear of what the refusal may cost them. · Think: We ask whether the rule is fair, and whether the character's way of fighting it helps others or only themselves. · Act: We notice rules around us that people question, and ask whether each rule is fair before we obey or refuse it.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any rebel, a character who refuses to obey, or tries to remove, a rule, an order or a ruler they think is unfair. 1. What does the character refuse, and who holds the power over them? 2. How does the character act against it, and what does it cost them? 3. Does the writer treat the rebel as right, wrong or both, and what does the writer want readers to understand? Try the questions on Julius Caesar. Brutus, an honoured Roman, fears that Caesar, who holds great power in Rome, “would be crown'd” as king. He joins a plot against Caesar, and the plotters kill him. Civil war follows, and Brutus ends his own life with his sword. Antony, Caesar's friend, says “This was the noblest Roman of them all”, and adds that the other plotters acted from envy but Brutus acted for the common good. The play lets us see a rebel who is honoured and who also kills.

**How to create it:** Decide what rule, order or ruler your character thinks is unfair, and show one scene where it hurts someone. Give the character one way of acting, such as a spoken no, a hidden act or a plan made with others. Show what the action costs them, so the reader feels the risk. Ask a friend whether your rebel is right, wrong or both; if they cannot say, show one result of what the rebel does.

**Kinds of Rebel** — The figure who defies the established order — told many ways, each a different order refused.

- **Kinds of rebel** — The order defied, and the cost of defiance
  - **The Political Rebel** — Rises against tyranny or an unjust regime. _(e.g. “This island’s mine, by Sycorax my mother, / Which thou tak’st from me” — he answers his ruler with a claim about who was there first — The Tempest)_
  - **The Moral Rebel** — Defies a corrupt norm for the sake of conscience. _(e.g. “these girls aren’t cheap labour — they’re people” — she contradicts her own father in his own dining room — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **The Romantic Rebel** — The brooding outsider who scorns all convention. _(e.g. “That is my wife” — the brooding master’s defiance of the law is finally dragged into the light — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The Doomed Rebel** — Defiance is crushed by the power it challenges. _(e.g. “Then I defy you, stars!” — he shouts his defiance at fate, and the same hour destroys him — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **The Self-Serving Rebel** — Rebellion masks ambition, not principle. _(e.g. “All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others” — the rule that began the revolution is edited by the ones it made powerful — Animal Farm)_

**Related:** Dramatic Situations, Nemesis, The Hero, Antihero

### The Explorer `Ex`

An explorer is a character driven by curiosity, or by a wish to go beyond what is known, such as a new place or idea. The explorer is often the hero of a story, and often leaves home or crosses a limit that other people accept. The journey can bring wonder, danger, loss, or all three. An explorer may be a traveller, a scientist or a child, and may be looking for something or running from something.

**The concept:** An explorer story lets readers go beyond what they know, through a character who cannot stop wondering what lies further on. Curiosity pulls the character and the reader forward, and the unknown can bring wonder and danger together. In Frankenstein, Robert Walton, a ship's captain, writes to his sister that he is sailing towards the far north, hoping to see “a part of the world never before visited”. When you write about any explorer, say what limit the character wants to cross, what drives them, and what the journey brings them.

**Examples:** “a power of vision which might overpass that limit” — Jane, who works as a governess, stands on the roof of Thornfield Hall and longs to see beyond the hills, to towns and places she has only heard about — Jane Eyre; “burning with curiosity, she ran across the field after it” — Alice, bored on a riverbank, sees a White Rabbit with a watch and runs after it, so her curiosity takes her to a strange new world — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; “my insatiable desire of seeing foreign countries” — Gulliver, home after his first voyage, stays only two months with his wife and family because this wish, which is never satisfied, will not let him stay — Gulliver's Travels

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look past the edge of what the character knows, and feel the pull of what lies beyond it. · Feel: We feel the excitement of the unknown, mixed with fear of what the journey may cost the character. · Think: We ask what the character hopes to find, and what the writer says about the value and the risk of curiosity. · Act: We follow our own curiosity into new places, subjects and people, and ask what we might gain or risk.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any explorer, a character driven by curiosity to go beyond what is known. 1. What limit does the character want to cross, and what lies beyond it? 2. What drives the character: curiosity, ambition, escape or something else? 3. What does the journey bring the character, and what does the writer want readers to understand about curiosity? Try the questions on Robinson Crusoe. The limit is his father's advice, which is to stay at home in the “middle station” of life, a safe place between the rich and the poor. Crusoe is driven by a wish for the sea: he says he “would be satisfied with nothing but going to sea”. A shipwreck later leaves him alone on a desolate island. He calls ignoring his father's advice his “original sin”, so Defoe may want readers to see that a restless wish to go beyond safe limits can bring both hardship and survival.

**How to create it:** Decide what limit your character wants to cross, such as a border, a locked door or a rule. Show what makes them curious about what lies beyond it. Describe the new place through the character's eyes, so the reader notices what is strange. Let the character risk something they value at home. Ask a friend what your character wants to find; if they cannot say, state it in one line of the character's thoughts.

**Kinds of Explorer** — The figure who ventures beyond the known — told many ways, each a different frontier crossed.

- **Kinds of explorer** — The frontier crossed, and what the crossing costs
  - **The Physical Explorer** — Ventures into uncharted seas and unknown lands. _(e.g. “I went out too far” — the fisherman admits he sailed past the waters he knew — The Old Man and the Sea)_
  - **The Explorer of Knowledge** — Presses past the limits of what may safely be known. _(e.g. “I seemed to have lost all soul or sensation but for this one pursuit” — the search swallows everything human in the man doing the searching — Frankenstein)_
  - **The Inner Explorer** — The frontier is the self and its own conscience. _(e.g. “I’m not sure if I’m remembering it right” — her journey is into her own memory, and she keeps testing whether it can be trusted — Never Let Me Go)_
  - **The Escapist Explorer** — Flees the ordinary world for a stranger one. _(e.g. “He had invented a two-year-old son called Ned” — a man escapes his own empty life by making up a stranger one to live in — About a Boy)_
  - **The Doomed Explorer** — The crossing destroys the one who dares it. _(e.g. “wholly toward the worse” — the doctor’s own experiment moves him one way only, and there is no road back — Jekyll and Hyde)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Mentor `Mr`

A mentor is a character with more experience than the hero, who guides the hero with advice, teaching or example. The mentor may give the hero a lesson, a tool or a warning, but the hero still has to act. Some mentors leave the story, are taken away or step back, so that the hero must act alone; others stay to the end. A mentor can be wise, but can also be wrong, or be ignored.

**The concept:** A mentor gives the hero something to learn from, so the story can show how far the hero follows the advice or ignores it. Because the mentor knows more, the reader learns the lesson at the same time as the hero, and sees how well the hero uses it. In Romeo and Juliet, Friar Lawrence, a priest who advises Romeo, tells him “Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast”, but Romeo keeps hurrying, and his haste brings more danger. When you write about any mentor, say what the mentor knows, how the mentor guides the hero, and what the hero does with the guidance.

**Examples:** “I am here to-night to warn you, that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate” — Marley's Ghost, chained in death for the way he lived, tells Scrooge that he still has a chance to escape the same fate — A Christmas Carol; “lies is lies” — Joe Gargery, the blacksmith married to Pip's sister, tells Pip this after Pip admits that his story about Miss Havisham's house was made up, and tells him not to tell more lies — Great Expectations; “Have I, thy schoolmaster, made thee more profit” — Prospero, who has lived on an island with his daughter Miranda since she was a small child, reminds her that he has taught her more than other princesses learn — The Tempest

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the character who knows more than the hero, and at what the hero is told or shown. · Feel: We feel reassured when a wise guide is near, and uneasy when the hero ignores the advice or the guide goes. · Think: We ask what the hero has learned, and what the writer thinks makes advice worth following. · Act: We notice who guides us at school, in sport and in our family, and think about what they have taught us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any mentor, a character with more experience who guides the hero with advice, teaching or example. 1. What does the mentor know that the hero does not? 2. How does the mentor guide the hero: by telling, by teaching or by example? 3. What does the hero do with the guidance, and does the mentor stay, leave or step back? Try the questions on Jane Eyre. Helen Burns, an older girl at Lowood school, knows how to bear unfair treatment with patience, and she tells Jane that “Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs”. She guides Jane by speaking and by her own calm example. Jane does not fully agree: she says that when people are struck without a reason, they should “strike back again very hard”. Helen dies of consumption, an illness of the lungs, so she leaves the story while Jane is still a child.

**How to create it:** Decide one thing your mentor knows that the hero does not, such as a skill, a warning or a hard truth. Show the mentor passing it on in a short scene, through words or an action, not a long speech. Let the hero doubt, misunderstand or ignore part of it. Then put the hero in a situation where the lesson matters and the mentor is absent. Ask a friend what the mentor taught; if they cannot say, make the lesson clearer in one line.

**Kinds of Mentor** — The guide who shapes the hero — told many ways, each a different kind of wisdom offered.

- **Kinds of mentor** — The kind of guidance offered, and its motive
  - **The Sage** — Imparts wisdom and sets the hero on their path. _(e.g. “We don’t live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — the teaching is stated plainly, once, and the young are the ones who take it — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **The Protector** — Shields and trains the hero until they can stand alone. _(e.g. “climb into his skin and walk around in it” — the father hands his child a method she can still use after he has gone — To Kill a Mockingbird)_
  - **The Fallen Mentor** — Once wise, now compromised, and teaching harm. _(e.g. “Thou most lying slave, / Whom stripes may move, not kindness” — the man who taught him to speak now says only pain will work — The Tempest)_
  - **The False Mentor** — Guidance that serves the guide, not the hero. _(e.g. “Surely, comrades, you do not want Jones back?” — every lesson ends in the same threat, because the lesson is for the teacher’s benefit — Animal Farm)_
  - **The Sacrificial Mentor** — Dies so that the hero may go on. _(e.g. “My purse, my person, my extremest means / Lie all unlocked to your occasions” — he offers his body along with his money, and nearly pays with it — The Merchant of Venice)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Trickster `Tk`

A trickster is a character who fools, teases or breaks rules, often with wit, and so changes what other characters expected to happen. The trickster may fool the proud, expose hypocrisy (pretending to be better than you are), or simply enjoy the mischief. A trickster can be a hero, a helper or a trouble-maker, and can be funny, dangerous or both. Tricksters often change the people around them more than they change themselves.

**The concept:** A trickster often lets readers laugh at people who think they are important, by showing how easily they can be fooled. Readers often enjoy the trick, and then ask what it has shown about the person who was fooled, or about the trickster. In A Midsummer Night's Dream, Puck, a mischievous fairy, plays a trick on Bottom, a proud weaver, and tells Oberon “An ass's nole I fixed on his head”, meaning a donkey's head. When you write about any trickster, say who is fooled and how, what the trick shows about them, and what the writer wants us to understand.

**Examples:** “O, ay: stalk on. stalk on; the fowl sits.” — Claudio speaks like a hunter creeping up on a bird: Benedick, the "fowl", is hiding nearby and listening, because Claudio and Don Pedro are tricking him into believing that Beatrice loves him — Much Ado About Nothing; “I will throw you one which shall never come back at all” — the little tailor, much weaker than the giant, throws a live bird into the air instead of a stone, and the giant is impressed because it never comes back — The Valiant Little Tailor; “he now imitated the voice of Hook” — Peter Pan, hidden in the water, copies the voice of Captain Hook, the pirates' own captain, and orders the pirates to free their prisoner, Tiger Lily, and they obey — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the trick, and the proud or powerful person it is played on. · Feel: We feel amusement when the proud are fooled, and some unease when the trick turns out to have real consequences. · Think: We ask what the trick shows about the person fooled, and who really holds power in the story. · Act: We notice when people use jokes, disguises or clever words to challenge someone in charge, and ask what they are trying to show.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any trickster, a character who fools, teases or breaks rules, often with wit. 1. Who or what does the trickster fool or upset, and how? 2. What does the trick show about the person fooled, or about the plans and rules the trickster disturbs? 3. What does the writer want readers to understand through the trick? Try the questions on The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. The Wizard of Oz fools everyone by showing himself in different shapes: Dorothy sees a great Head, the Scarecrow a lovely Lady, the Tin Woodman a terrible Beast and the Lion a Ball of Fire. When Toto tips over a screen, the Wizard turns out to be a little old man who says “I am a humbug”, so the trick shows that the most powerful person in the Emerald City has no real magic. He then tells the Lion “You have plenty of courage, I am sure”, so Baum may want readers to see that people often have qualities they think they lack.

**How to create it:** Decide whom your trickster fools, and why that person deserves to be exposed, such as someone proud or someone who breaks their word. Plan one trick that uses cleverness, not force, and let the reader see how it works. Show the fooled person's face when they realise. Check that the trick shows something true about that person; if it is only a joke, change it so that it also shows what they are really like.

**Kinds of Trickster** — Writers use tricksters in different ways. Some tricksters play tricks for fun. Some act foolish so that they can say true things. Some use tricks to hurt people. Some have no power and use words as their only weapon, and some hide a loyal heart behind a rule-breaking life. When you write a trickster, decide what the tricks are for.

- **Kinds of trickster** — how the character uses cleverness, and what it is for
  - **A trickster who plays for fun** — The character enjoys mischief, jokes and breaking the rules. They stand up for pleasure and laughter against people who want to stop them. _(e.g. “Dost thou think because thou art virtuous there shall be no more cakes and ale?” — Sir Toby, who loves drinking and parties, says this to Malvolio, the steward who has told him to be quiet — Twelfth Night)_
  - **A fool who tells the truth** — The character acts foolish, but this is a mask. Behind it they say true things that other people are afraid to say. _(e.g. “I wear not motley in my brain” — Feste, the jester in Olivia's house, tells her that his fool's costume is the only foolish thing about him — Twelfth Night)_
  - **A trickster who means harm** — The character uses cleverness to hurt people. They hide what they want and make other people believe a lie. _(e.g. “I am not what I am” — Iago tells Roderigo that he is not what he seems, and later Othello and the others trust him and call him honest — Othello)_
  - **Someone with no power who fights with words** — The character has little power over events. Their quick wit is the only weapon they have. _(e.g. “I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick: nobody marks you.” — Beatrice mocks Benedick, who is talking, by saying that nobody listens to him, so her quick words are her weapon — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **A rule-breaker who is loyal underneath** — The character breaks rules and hides the truth, but is loyal to one person. The reader later learns how much they have done for that person. _(e.g. “I lived rough, that you should live smooth” — Magwitch, a convict, tells Pip that he lived a hard life so that Pip could live an easy one, and he has secretly paid for Pip's life as a gentleman — Great Expectations)_

**Related:** The Hero

### The Shadow `Sd`

The Shadow is a character type that stands for something the hero hides, denies or fears in themselves. It may be a person, a creature or a ghost, and it often stands for anger, guilt or a secret wish. A Shadow is often a villain, a rival or a double of the hero, and it may share the hero's strengths. The hero is the main character of the story. A hero who faces the Shadow must face something in themselves.

**The concept:** A Shadow shows that danger can come from a hero's own character. The psychologist Carl Jung used the word for the hidden parts of a person that they refuse to see. In Julius Caesar, Brutus helps to kill his friend Caesar, the ruler of Rome, and says he did it for the good of Rome. But later, Caesar's ghost appears to Brutus and calls itself “Thy evil spirit”, meaning Brutus's own evil spirit. When you write about any Shadow, say what the hero hides or denies, how the Shadow shows it, and what happens when the hero faces it.

**Examples:** “But you were always a good man of business, Jacob” — Scrooge says this to the ghost of his dead business partner, Jacob Marley, who regrets how he lived and wears a chain made of things such as cash-boxes and purses; as he speaks, Scrooge begins to apply Marley's regrets to himself — A Christmas Carol; “Thou canst not say I did it.” — Macbeth, at a feast, says this to the ghost of Banquo, the friend he has had killed, and the lords at the table only ask what he means, so the ghost shows the guilt he will not admit — Macbeth; “I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer.” — Victor Frankenstein knows that the creature he made has killed his young brother William, yet he does not tell his cousin Elizabeth when she talks of the murderer who is still free — Frankenstein

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the Shadow and then at the hero, and search for what the two share. · Feel: We feel dread, and then discomfort, as we begin to see that some of the danger belongs to the hero. · Think: We ask what part of the hero the Shadow stands for, and what the writer says about hiding our faults. · Act: We notice the faults in ourselves that we blame on other people, and ask whether we are hiding them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any Shadow, a character who stands for something the hero hides or denies in themselves. 1. What does the hero hide or deny, and what does the Shadow do that shows it? 2. Does the hero see the link between the Shadow and themselves, or deny it? 3. What does the writer want the reader to learn from the hero facing the Shadow, or avoiding it? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. Dr Jekyll, a respected doctor, hides a side of himself that he is ashamed of. He makes a drug that turns him into Mr Hyde, the evil side of his own nature. Hyde tramples a girl in the street and later kills a man. Jekyll sees the link: when he first sees himself as Hyde in a mirror, he writes, “This, too, was myself.” The author, Robert Louis Stevenson, may want readers to see that hiding a bad side does not make it go away. Hyde grows stronger, until Jekyll can no longer change back.

**How to create it:** Decide what your hero hides or fears in themselves, such as anger or a lie. Give the Shadow a form that shows it, such as a rival who shares your hero's strengths but uses them badly. Let the hero notice something familiar in the Shadow before they understand why. Decide what the hero does when they finally see it: face it or run. Check that your hero learns something about themselves from the Shadow; if not, link the Shadow more closely to what the hero hides.

**Kinds of Shadow** — A shadow is a character or force that stands against the hero and shows something dark. Writers use shadows in different ways. A shadow can be an enemy outside the hero, or a double of the hero, or a darkness inside the hero. It can also be a person who tempts the hero to do wrong, or an enemy the reader feels sorry for. When you write a shadow, decide what the darkness is and how it is linked to the hero.

- **Kinds of shadow** — the dark figure that stands against the hero, and how it is linked to the hero
  - **An enemy outside the hero** — The character is the hero's enemy, and the reader knows that they want to do harm. The hero must defeat them. _(e.g. “plain-dealing villain” — Don John, the Prince's bitter brother, calls himself a plain-dealing villain, so the audience knows from the start that he means harm — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **A double of the hero** — A second version of the hero looks like a separate person but is part of the hero. It shows the dark side that the hero hides. _(e.g. “He, I say—I cannot say, I.” — Dr Jekyll writes about Hyde, the double he becomes, and corrects himself from “he” to “I”, which shows that the double seems separate and is still part of Jekyll — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **A darkness inside the hero** — The dark side is inside the hero. There is no separate enemy to defeat. _(e.g. “Maybe there is a beast... maybe it’s only us” — Simon, a quiet boy, tells the other boys that the beast they fear may be something inside themselves — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **A person who tempts the hero to do wrong** — A character pushes the hero toward a wrong act. This character uses what the hero wants or fears. _(e.g. “When you durst do it, then you were a man” — Lady Macbeth tells her husband that he was a man only when he dared to kill the king, and she uses his pride to push him toward murder — Macbeth)_
  - **An enemy the reader feels sorry for** — The dark figure does harm, but the reader understands why. The reader feels sorry for the figure and still sees the harm. _(e.g. “I am malicious because I am miserable” — the creature tells Victor Frankenstein that he does harm because he is unhappy and alone — Frankenstein)_

**Related:** Plot Twist, Antihero, The Hero, The Fall, Duality

### The Hero `He`

The hero is the main character of a story: the person we follow and hope will succeed. A hero faces a danger or a test and has to act, often at a cost to themselves. Many heroes start with a weakness, and the story shows them change. A hero does not have to be perfect, strong or brave at the start. A related type, the Shadow, is a character who stands for something the hero hides in themselves.

**The concept:** A hero lets a writer show what courage and goodness mean, because we judge the hero by the choices they make. We follow the hero closely, so we feel what each choice costs. In the Bible story of David and Goliath, David, a young shepherd, faces Goliath, a giant warrior, and tells him: “I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts”. When you write about any hero, say what the hero wants, what it costs them, and what their choices show about courage.

**Examples:** “The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself” — Jane, who loves Rochester but has learned that he is already married, decides to leave him and accept a lonely life rather than lose her self-respect — Jane Eyre; “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.” — Scrooge, a man who begins the story caring only about money, promises to change his life — A Christmas Carol; “I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society” — Pip, who tells the story as a grown man, admits that as a boy he was ashamed of Joe, the kind blacksmith married to his sister — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the main character's choices, and notice what each one costs them. · Feel: We feel admiration and worry together, because the hero risks something that matters to them. · Think: We ask what we would do in the hero's place, and what the writer says about courage and goodness. · Act: We notice who shows courage in real life, even when it costs them, and ask whether we would do the same.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any hero. 1. What does the hero want, and what danger or test blocks them? 2. What does it cost the hero to act, and does the hero start with a weakness that the story tests? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand about courage or goodness through this hero? Try the questions on Treasure Island. Jim Hawkins, a boy whose father keeps an inn, wants to reach the buried treasure and to stay alive. The danger is Long John Silver, the ship's cook, who plans with other pirates to take the ship. Jim overhears this plan from inside an apple barrel, and he warns the captain and his friends. Jim admits that he is bold and foolish. He slips out of the stockade, the wooden fort where his friends shelter, without permission. Later he goes alone in a small boat to the pirates' ship and cuts its anchor rope. The author, Robert Louis Stevenson, shows that a boy can be brave and still make mistakes.

**How to create it:** Decide what your hero wants and what blocks the hero. Give the hero a weakness, such as pride or fear, that the story will test. Make the hero's choice cost something they care about, such as safety, a friend or their own good opinion of themselves. Show the cost in what the hero does, not only in what the hero says. Check that the hero could have chosen the easy way; if not, add a reason why the easy way tempts them.

**Kinds of Hero** — The central figure who acts and is tested — told many ways, each a different kind of heroism.

- **Kinds of hero** — The kind of heroism the figure embodies
  - **The Classical Hero** — Noble, brave and larger than ordinary life. _(e.g. “She loved me for the dangers I had passed, / And I loved her that she did pity them” — his deeds are so large that even his love grows out of them — Othello)_
  - **The Everyman Hero** — An ordinary person who rises to an extraordinary moment. _(e.g. “I need them. That’s all there is to it.” — a poor mother with no power says the one plain sentence that costs her everything — Blood Brothers)_
  - **The Anti-Hero** — Flawed or unheroic, yet the one we follow. _(e.g. “I hate and loathe it all” — the commander everyone admires admits in private that he is frightened — Journey’s End)_
  - **The Tragic Hero** — Greatness undone by a single error in action. _(e.g. “this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen” — the play’s last word on a soldier who began it as its bravest man — Macbeth)_
  - **The Byronic Hero** — Brooding, transgressive and magnetic. _(e.g. “Which is it to-day… morphine or cocaine?” — the brilliant man’s self-destruction is part of what draws us to him — The Sign of the Four)_

**Related:** The Mentor, Ally, The Shadow, The Trickster, Herald, Threshold Guardian, Shapeshifter, The Outsider, The Everyman, The Underdog, The Orphan, The Lost Soul, The Rebel, The Explorer, Antihero

### Hero’s Journey `Hj`

The Hero's Journey is a story pattern in which the hero leaves ordinary life, faces tests in an unfamiliar place, and comes back changed. Stories that use it often have a call to leave, a helper or teacher, a lowest point and a return. Many stories use only some of these stages, and in a different order. The Quest is a related pattern, built around a journey to one named goal.

**The concept:** The Hero's Journey makes a hero's change easy to see, because we can compare the hero who leaves with the one who returns. The American scholar Joseph Campbell described the pattern in 1949, after studying many myths. In the Bible story of the Prodigal Son, a younger son asks for his share of the family's wealth and wastes it far from home. He returns hungry and humble, telling his father that he is “no more worthy to be called thy son”. When you write about any Hero's Journey, say what the hero leaves, what the journey changes in them, and what the ending shows.

**Examples:** “I am not the man I was” — Scrooge, taken from his bedroom by three ghosts, says this to the last of them, and then wakes up in his own bed — A Christmas Carol; “Reader, I married him.” — Jane, who ran away from Rochester and found her own money and family, comes back to him and chooses him; the last chapter of the book opens with this line — Jane Eyre; “Oxen and wain-ropes would not bring me back again to that accursed island” — Jim Hawkins, home from the treasure hunt, says that nothing could take him back, and that he still has nightmares about the island — Treasure Island

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We follow the hero out of the ordinary world and into the tests, and watch for the lowest point. · Feel: We feel excitement and fear as the hero leaves safety, and relief and sadness when the journey ends. · Think: We compare the hero at the end with the hero at the start, and ask what the writer thinks change takes. · Act: We see our own hard times as journeys that can change us, and ask what we might bring back from them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any hero's journey, a story in which the hero leaves home, faces tests and comes back changed. 1. What does the hero leave behind, and what makes them go? 2. What tests does the hero face, and does anyone help them? 3. How is the hero different at the end, and what does the writer want us to understand from that change? Try the questions on Great Expectations. Pip, a blacksmith's apprentice, leaves his village when a London lawyer, Mr Jaggers, tells him that a secret person will make him rich. His tests include the return of the convict Magwitch, who is the secret person, and the end of his hopes of money and of marrying Estella. Pip also falls ill and is arrested for debt, and Joe, the blacksmith, nurses him and pays the debt. Pip once felt ashamed of his home and of Joe. At the end he returns to the village, thanks Joe and Joe's wife, Biddy, and promises to repay the money. Dickens seems to say that kindness and loyalty, which Joe shows, matter more than money.

**How to create it:** Decide the change you want, such as a coward who learns to act. Show the hero's ordinary world, then give them a reason they must leave it. Place the hardest test near the end, when the hero has lost help or hope. End with the hero coming back, seeing or doing something differently. Check that a reader can compare your opening and ending and see the change; if not, add one matching detail to each.

**Kinds of Hero's Journey** — One departure-and-return told through many callings — each a different shape the adventure takes and what the hero carries home.

- **Kinds of journey** — Why the hero leaves the known world, and what they bring back
  - **The Reluctant Hero** — The hero refuses the call, then rises to meet it. _(e.g. “live so easy” — he lists the free life he could have, and stays with the burden anyway — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **The Coming-of-Power** — An ordinary figure discovers a capacity they never suspected. _(e.g. “my voice is mine” — the daughter claims the one thing her mother’s world never offered her — Leave Taking)_
  - **The Inward Journey** — The road is psychological; the treasure is self-knowledge. _(e.g. “Till this moment, I never knew myself” — the journey turns out to have been about her own judgement, not his — Pride and Prejudice)_
  - **The Fallen Hero** — The quest curdles because the hero's own flaw poisons it. _(e.g. “one that loved not wisely, but too well” — he asks to be remembered by his own flaw, not by the man who tricked him — Othello)_
  - **The Return with Wisdom** — The hero comes home altered, to remake the world they left. _(e.g. “But this rough magic / I here abjure” — he gives up the power that made the journey possible before he goes home — The Tempest)_

**Related:** Coming of Age, Overcoming the Monster, Rags to Riches, Rebirth / Redemption, The Quest, Tragedy (plot), Voyage and Return

### Coming of Age `Cg`

A coming-of-age story follows a young person who grows from a child's view of the world to a more adult one. An event usually teaches them something hard about themselves or about other people. They often lose an illusion, which is a comforting belief that is not true, such as the belief that the world is fair. The Hero's Journey, a pattern of leaving home and coming back changed, is a related shape.

**The concept:** A coming-of-age story shows the moment when a young person sees themselves or the world in a new way and cannot go back. Readers recognise this because they are living through it, or remember it. The change often costs something, such as trust or comfort. In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice tells the Mock Turtle and the Gryphon, two creatures she meets in Wonderland: “it's no use going back to yesterday, because I was a different person then”. When you write about any coming-of-age story, say what the young person believes at the start, what experience changes it, and what the change costs or gives them.

**Examples:** “It is an honour that I dream not of.” — Juliet, who is not yet fourteen, says this when her mother asks about marriage; within days she marries Romeo in secret, without her parents knowing — Romeo and Juliet; “I am glad you are no relation of mine” — Jane, a young orphan, tells her aunt, Mrs Reed, who has treated her cruelly, that she will never call her aunt again — Jane Eyre; “She was one of the kind that likes to grow up.” — the narrator says this about Wendy, who comes home from Neverland, where Peter Pan never grows up, and chooses to grow up — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the young person's view of the world meet something harder, and see what changes. · Feel: We feel sympathy and a little sadness, because we remember our own growing up and what it cost us. · Think: We ask what the young person gains and loses by growing up, and what the writer thinks maturity is. · Act: We look back at moments when we saw the world differently, and think about how we have changed.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any coming-of-age story, a story about a young person growing towards adulthood. 1. What does the young person believe or want at the start? 2. What experience changes this, and what does it cost them? 3. How is the young person different at the end, and what does the writer want us to understand about growing up? Try the questions on Pride and Prejudice. Elizabeth Bennet believes that she is a good judge of people, and she trusts Wickham and dislikes Darcy. She reads a long letter from Darcy that shows Wickham has lied, and she realises that she was wrong. She cries that she has “prided myself on my discernment”, which means she was proud of judging people well, and it costs her that pride. By the end she has changed her view of Darcy and of herself, and she marries him. Jane Austen shows that growing up means seeing your own faults as well as other people's.

**How to create it:** Choose what your young character believes at the start, such as that adults are always right or that they are safe. Give them one clear experience that shows the belief is wrong. Show what they lose, as well as what they learn. Let them act differently near the end, so the change shows in what they do. Check that your last scene could not have happened in your first; if it could, the character has not changed.

**Archetypal Journeys** — The coming-of-age story is one arc told through many transformations — each a shift from one inner state to its opposite.

- **Archetypal journeys** — The before-and-after transformation the protagonist undergoes
  - **Innocence to Experience** — The protagonist loses a childhood certainty and meets the world’s complexity for the first time. _(e.g. “felt right sorry for her” — the children watch ordinary pity be turned into a crime, and stop trusting the court — To Kill a Mockingbird)_
  - **Ignorance to Knowledge** — The protagonist awakens to a truth — social, moral or personal — they were previously blind to. _(e.g. “I am not the man I was” — he can only say it after he has been shown what he actually looked like — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Selfishness to Responsibility** — The protagonist stops acting only for themselves and accepts a duty to others. _(e.g. “We did her in all right” — the young man puts himself inside the word we, and keeps himself there — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Illusion to Disillusionment** — The protagonist’s idealised expectations meet reality, and false values fall away. _(e.g. “the repugnance with which I shrank from him” — the moment his fortune arrives in person, the dream of being a gentleman collapses — Great Expectations)_
  - **Dependence to Independence** — The protagonist moves from relying on others to self-possession and moral autonomy. _(e.g. “I am independent, sir, as well as rich: I am my own mistress” — she returns on her own terms, and says so before anything else — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Conformity to Self-identity** — The protagonist breaks from what is expected of them to claim their own values. _(e.g. Holden resisting the "phoniness" he sees in the adult world as he searches for who he is — The Catcher in the Rye)_

**Related:** Hero’s Journey, Overcoming the Monster, Rags to Riches, Rebirth / Redemption, The Quest, Tragedy (plot), Voyage and Return

### Overcoming the Monster `Om`

Overcoming the Monster is a story shape in which a hero must defeat a powerful enemy that threatens other people. The enemy may be a creature, a tyrant (a cruel ruler) or a force such as a flood or a plague, and it usually seems stronger than the hero. The hero often wins by courage or cleverness, and the ending usually brings safety to the people who were threatened. The Hero's Journey, a pattern of leaving home and coming back changed, is a related shape.

**The concept:** Overcoming the Monster lets a writer turn a fear into a character who can be faced and beaten. Because the monster looks too strong, we fear for the hero, so the victory brings relief. In Macbeth, Macbeth has become a tyrant and has had the family of Macduff, a Scottish lord, killed. In the last battle Macduff finds him and calls out “Turn, hell-hound, turn!”, naming him a savage dog from hell. When you write about any story of this shape, say what the monster stands for, what lets the hero face it, and what the victory shows.

**Examples:** “So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone” — David, a young shepherd, defeats Goliath, the giant warrior whom the whole army of Israel has fled from in fear — The Bible (1 Samuel); “my name is Noman” — Odysseus tells this to Polyphemus, a one-eyed giant who has trapped him and his men in a cave, and the trick later makes the giant's neighbours ignore his cries for help — The Odyssey; “Hook or me this time” — Peter Pan swears this oath before he goes to find Captain Hook, the pirate who has taken the Darling children prisoner — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the threat grow, and look for what the hero has that the monster lacks. · Feel: We feel fear while the monster seems too strong, and then relief and pride when the hero wins. · Think: We ask what the monster stands for, and whether ordinary people can defeat a danger that seems too big. · Act: We face our own fears with a little more courage, and notice when people stand up to a bully or an unfair power.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any story in which a hero faces a monster. 1. What is the monster, and who does it threaten? 2. Why does the monster seem stronger than the hero, and how does the hero win? 3. What does the monster stand for, and what does the writer want the reader to feel about facing it? Try the questions on Dracula. Count Dracula, a vampire from Transylvania, comes to England and attacks Lucy, who dies, and later Mina. He seems stronger because he has more than human strength and cannot easily be killed. A group of friends, led by Professor Van Helsing, an expert from Amsterdam, hunt him together. They follow him back to Transylvania, where Jonathan Harker and Quincey Morris attack him with knives and his body crumbles into dust. The monster stands for fear of an outside force that invades a country and its families, and Bram Stoker shows ordinary people beating it together.

**How to create it:** Choose what your monster stands for, such as a fear or a cruel power. Make the monster look stronger than your hero, and show what it has already done to other people. Let your hero win by one quality that the monster lacks, such as cleverness or loyalty. Show the people who were threatened once the monster is gone. Check that the monster harms people, not only frightens them; if not, add something it takes from them.

**Kinds of Monster** — One confrontation told through many monsters — each the shape a threat takes when it must be faced.

- **Kinds of monster** — The form the threat takes, and how the protagonist must meet it
  - **The External Beast** — A literal predator embodying primal danger, to be hunted or fled. _(e.g. “I beheld the wretch — the miserable monster whom I had created” — Victor calls the creature a monster the moment he sees it, then runs from the thing he made — Frankenstein)_
  - **The Human Tyrant** — A person whose cruelty and power must be broken to restore order. _(e.g. “this dead butcher and his fiend-like queen” — Malcolm strips the tyrant of every title and leaves only the killing — Macbeth)_
  - **The Inner Demon** — The monster is within: appetite, ambition or a divided self. _(e.g. “man is not truly one, but truly two” — Jekyll admits the monster was never outside him — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **The Societal Monster** — An unjust system or comfortable complacency the protagonist confronts. _(e.g. “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — the Inspector names the real monster as a whole way of living, not one guilty person — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **The Monster We Become** — The protagonist turns into the very thing they first feared or fought. _(e.g. “Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood!” — the boys chant it while hunting a beast, and kill a boy — Lord of the Flies)_

**Related:** Hero’s Journey, Coming of Age, Rags to Riches, Rebirth / Redemption, The Quest, Tragedy (plot), Voyage and Return

### Rags to Riches `Rr`

Rags to Riches is a story shape in which a poor, powerless or despised character rises to wealth, high rank or respect. The rise may come from the character's qualities, such as patience or kindness, or from luck or help. Some stories show the rise going wrong, because the character gains money or power but loses something that matters more. The Hero's Journey, a pattern of leaving home and coming back changed, is a related shape.

**The concept:** Rags to Riches lets a writer ask what a person is worth and what they deserve. We hope for the humble character because most of us can imagine being overlooked. The French writer Charles Perrault published the fairy tale Cinderella in 1697. In his version the girl, after her housework, sits “among cinders and ashes”, and the prince marries her a few days after the glass slipper fits her foot. When you write about any rags-to-riches story, say what the character starts with, what causes the rise, and whether the writer shows the reward as deserved, empty or dangerous.

**Examples:** “Nothing of course to speak of—twenty thousand pounds, I think they say” — St John Rivers tells Jane, a poor village schoolmistress, that she has inherited twenty thousand pounds from her uncle — Jane Eyre; “he will come into a handsome property” — Mr Jaggers, a London lawyer, tells Pip, a blacksmith's apprentice, that a person he will not name wants to make Pip rich; later the money brings Pip unhappiness — Great Expectations; “The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again” — the pigs, who began as farm animals ruled by Mr Jones, now play cards with human farmers, and the animals watching cannot tell the pigs from the men — Animal Farm

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the character's climb, and notice how other people treat them before and after. · Feel: We feel hope for a character who is overlooked, and unease if the rise leaves something important behind. · Think: We ask what a person is worth, and whether the writer thinks the reward is deserved. · Act: We notice how people are treated when they have little and when they have more, and ask whether that is fair.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any rags-to-riches story, a story in which a character who starts poor or powerless rises to wealth, rank or respect. 1. What does the character start with, and how do other people treat them? 2. What causes the rise: the character's qualities, luck or help from others? 3. Does the character keep the reward, and what does the writer want the reader to think about what people deserve? Try the questions on Aladdin. Aladdin is the son of a poor tailor, and he is a careless, idle boy. His rise comes from luck and help, not from his own good qualities: a magician sends him into a cave for a magic lamp. With the help of the genie, a spirit in the lamp, he gets a palace and marries the Sultan's daughter, the Princess. He loses everything when the magician tricks the Princess into giving up the lamp, and the Sultan orders the executioner to cut off his head. Aladdin gets the palace and the Princess back, so he keeps the reward. The story seems to say that luck can lift a careless boy, but he must act to keep his good fortune.

**How to create it:** Choose where your character starts, and show what that costs them each day. Decide what causes the rise, such as hard work, kindness or a lucky meeting. Show the rise in small steps, not one jump. Show how the character uses the reward, so the reader can judge whether it fits them. Check what the reader should think at the end; if you want them to doubt the reward, show one thing the character has lost to get it.

**Kinds of Rise** — One ascent told many ways — each a different climb, and a different verdict on what the rise costs.

- **Kinds of rise** — How the fortune is won, and what the winning reveals
  - **The Earned Rise** — Integrity and merit rewarded with a fortune the protagonist deserves. _(e.g. “I am my own mistress” — Jane only rises when she owes nothing to anybody — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The Hollow Rise** — Wealth arrives but proves an empty measure of worth. _(e.g. “coarse and common” — Pip climbs, then hears Estella's insult coming out of his own mouth about Joe — Great Expectations)_
  - **The Corrupting Rise** — The climb is built on illusion or crime and rots what it touches. _(e.g. “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” — the pigs rewrite the rule that put them on top — Animal Farm)_
  - **The Dream Deferred** — The rise is longed for but stays forever out of reach. _(e.g. “live off the fatta the lan'” — Lennie asks for the farm again and again, and it never arrives — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **The Rise and Fall** — Fortune is seized and then lost, undone by the means that won it. _(e.g. “My way of life / Is fall'n into the sere, the yellow leaf” — Macbeth counts what the crown has cost him — Macbeth)_

**Related:** Hero’s Journey, Coming of Age, Overcoming the Monster, Rebirth / Redemption, The Quest, Tragedy (plot), Voyage and Return, The Fall

### Rebirth / Redemption `Rd`

Rebirth, or redemption, is a story shape in which a cold, cruel or selfish character is given a chance to change, and does. Something makes them see the harm they have done, such as a warning, a loss or a kindness. The character then chooses to act differently, and often tries to repair the harm they have done. Not every story shows a full change, and some characters change too late to avoid ruin. The Hero's Journey, a pattern of leaving home and coming back changed, is a related shape.

**The concept:** Rebirth, or redemption, lets a writer argue that people can change, and that a second chance is worth taking. We are often moved most when the change costs the character something. In A Christmas Carol, three ghosts show Scrooge, a miser, his past, his present and a lonely death. On Christmas morning he cries out: “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel”. When you write about any story of rebirth, say what is wrong with the character at the start, what makes them change, and what the change shows about second chances.

**Examples:** “I began to see and acknowledge the hand of God in my doom. I began to experience remorse, repentance” — Rochester, blinded and badly hurt in the fire at Thornfield Hall, tells Jane that only lately has he felt sorry for his past and begun to pray — Jane Eyre; “It is a far, far better thing that I do, than I have ever done” — Sydney Carton, a lawyer who has drifted through life, takes the place of Charles Darnay, who is to be killed, so that Darnay can go free to his family — A Tale of Two Cities; “I will never stir from your side” — Pip, who was horrified when the convict Magwitch came back into his life, promises the injured man, in the boat just after his capture, that he will stay with him — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the moment the character sees the harm they have done, and how they answer it. · Feel: We feel hope and relief as a hard character softens, and sadness for the time already lost. · Think: We ask whether anyone is past saving, and what the writer believes about guilt and forgiveness. · Act: We may think about who in our own lives deserves a second chance, and whether we need one ourselves.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any rebirth or redemption story, a story in which a cold or selfish character is given a chance to change. 1. What is wrong with the character at the start, and who is harmed? 2. What makes them see it, and do they choose to change? 3. What does the change cost them, and what does the writer want the reader to believe about second chances? Try the questions on The Selfish Giant. The Giant builds a high wall round his garden and puts up a notice to keep the children out, and spring never comes to his garden. He sees a little boy who is too small to climb a tree, and he says: “How selfish I have been!” He understands why the Spring would not come to his garden.
