How heavy is it and how long does it last: a light shower, a steady downpour or a storm? 2. Whose feelings does it seem to match? 3. When does it change or stop, and what happens at that moment? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the rain? Try the questions on The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald. The rain is heavy: “The day agreed upon was pouring rain.” That is the day Gatsby is to see Daisy again after nearly five years, and later the rain eases to a damp mist. It matches Gatsby's tense, nervous waiting before the meeting. Later, after Gatsby and Daisy have talked alone, Gatsby tells Nick “It's stopped raining”, and, smiling, repeats the news to Daisy, so the weather clears as the tension eases. Fitzgerald may want the reader to feel Gatsby's nerves, and then his happiness, through the weather before anyone says so.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character feels and when that feeling changes during the scene. Choose rain that fits the feeling, such as a light drizzle for quiet sadness or a heavy downpour for despair. Describe the rain through what your character sees, hears and feels on their skin. Make the rain change or stop at the moment the feeling changes. Check that the two changes happen together; if not, move one of them.

**Kinds of Rain** — Rain is sorted by what the writer does with it. Some rain is simply falling when a scene opens, and its job is to hand the whole scene a mood before anyone speaks. Other rain earns its place by doing something — stopping, giving, or turning into a weapon. The second kind is harder and better. If rain in your own writing only makes a sad scene sadder, push it: make it break, or make it arrive at the moment nobody wants it.

- **Rain that SETS THE MOOD — the sky colours the scene before a word is spoken** — the rain is already falling when the scene opens
  - **Rain that opens the scene** — Rain in the first line, so the reader is given the feeling before the story explains anything. The most efficient version of this kind sounds like small talk and is actually a warning. _(e.g. “The rain set early in to-night” — the calm, chatty opening of a poem that ends in a murder, the weather already disturbed before the speaker is — Porphyria's Lover)_
  - **The sky asked to feel it** — Instead of the weather matching the character, the character demands that it should. The gap between the grief and a sky that stays blank is the point, so this kind exposes how alone somebody is. _(e.g. “Is there no pity sitting in the clouds / That sees into the bottom of my grief?” — Juliet asking the weather to care, and getting no answer — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Rain as ordeal** — Not a mood at all but a physical punishment, piled up alongside mud, cold and cuts. Here rain measures how long somebody has been outside the shelter everybody else has. _(e.g. “soaked in water, and smothered in mud” — the escaped convict introduced as a list of what the weather has done to him — Great Expectations)_
  - **Rain as the smell of a life starting again** — Rain coming in through an open window as something the character wants, not something they endure. It is the one kind that arrives with relief in it, and writers use it at the moment a person realises they are free. _(e.g. “the delicious breath of rain was in the air” — a woman just told her husband is dead breathes in the wet air and finds, to her own shock, that she is glad — The Story of an Hour)_
- **Rain that DOES SOMETHING — the rain acts, and the action is the meaning** — the meaning is in what the rain gives, changes or becomes
  - **The break in the rain** — The most precise instrument of the four kinds here: the rain stops, and the stopping is the turn. Grief spent, an argument ended, a chance to speak — all carried by weather clearing rather than by anybody saying so. _(e.g. “The clouds had given their all” — two days of rain finish, and in the clear afterwards a couple who were not speaking find their hands together again — Winter Swans)_
  - **Rain as gift** — Rain falling on everyone equally, whether they deserve it or not — so it becomes the model for mercy, grace or generosity. This kind argues; it does not just decorate. _(e.g. “It droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven” — mercy explained by the one thing that falls on the guilty and the innocent alike — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **Rain that fills what violence emptied** — Rainwater standing in a hole that something terrible made. The water turns the wound into a mirror, so beauty and atrocity are held in the same image and neither cancels the other. _(e.g. “in those two rain-full shell-holes the boy sees / fragments of the splintered Pleiades” — craters left by a shell, filled with rain, reflecting stars — The Bright Lights of Sarajevo)_
  - **Rain turned into a weapon** — The shape of rain — falling, everywhere, unstoppable — borrowed for something that is not water. The familiar comfort of the word is what makes the violence land so hard. _(e.g. “it was raining exclamation marks” — a street full of flying metal described as weather, so the reader feels it coming down on them — Belfast Confetti)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### The Storm / Thunder `Sj`

A storm is violent weather, such as thunder, lightning or high wind. In stories and poems it can be symbolism, the use of an object or event to stand for an idea such as danger, anger or disorder. It can match a character's feelings, warn of trouble, or seem to judge what a character has done. Which of these it does depends on the text, and some storms are only part of the setting.

**The concept:** A storm can show a character's trouble, or a wrong act, in the sky, so that readers feel the disorder before anyone explains it. In King Lear, Lear, an old king whose daughters have refused to shelter him, stands out on a heath in a storm and shouts “Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! blow!”, and the storm seems to match his rage. When you write about any storm, say what it seems to match, warn of or judge, and what the writer wants us to see.

**Examples:** “The night has been unruly” — Lennox, a Scottish lord, tells Macbeth that the night was wild, with chimneys blown down, just before Macduff finds that King Duncan has been killed — Macbeth; “the great horse-chestnut at the bottom of the orchard had been struck by lightning in the night, and half of it split away” — the morning after Mr Rochester asks Jane to marry him under that tree, Adèle, the girl Jane teaches, tells her that lightning has split it — Jane Eyre; “A flash of lightning illuminated the object, and discovered its shape plainly to me” — Victor, walking in a thunderstorm after hearing that his young brother William has been killed, sees the creature he made — Frankenstein

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are pulled into the noise and danger of the storm, and look for whose trouble it seems to match. · Feel: We feel dread as the weather grows more violent, because the danger seems close and out of anyone's control. · Think: We ask whether the storm matches a feeling, warns of something or judges a wrong act, and what the writer wants us to see. · Act: We notice how news reports and films use storms to make events feel more dramatic or threatening.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any storm, violent weather such as thunder, lightning and high wind that seems to react to events in a story. 1. What is the storm like, and who is out in it or watching it? 2. Does it seem to mirror a character's feelings, warn of something, or judge someone? Which? 3. What happens in the story soon after the storm? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the storm? Try the questions on Julius Caesar by Shakespeare. Thunder and lightning fill Rome on more than one night before Caesar, the ruler, is killed. One night Casca, a Roman, is out in the storm with his sword drawn and says he has never gone through “a tempest dropping fire”. On the night before the murder the storm seems to be a warning: Calpurnia, Caesar's wife, begs him to stay at home and says “The heavens themselves blaze forth the death of princes.” Later that day Caesar goes to the Senate and is stabbed to death by a group of senators. Shakespeare may want readers to feel that killing a ruler upsets the natural order, so the sky seems to warn of it before it happens.

**How to create it:** Decide what has gone wrong in your story, such as a broken promise, a crime or a death. Choose the storm: thunder, a gale or lightning. Put your character out in it or watching it, and describe it through their senses. Let someone in your story read the storm as a sign. Check that the storm comes just before or during the wrong act; if it is only noisy, link it to what is going wrong.

**Kinds of Storm** — Storms are sorted by whose side they are on. One kind is a verdict: the sky registers what a person has done, and somebody in the story reads the weather as judgement. The other kind has intent — it is aimed at somebody, and you can hear that in the verbs, because attacking storms dive, knife, batter and strafe. Before you write a storm, decide which it is. A storm that only makes noise is scenery; a storm that judges or attacks is doing the work of a whole paragraph.

- **Storms that JUDGE — the sky passes a verdict on what people have done** — somebody in the story reads the weather as a message about themselves
  - **The struck tree** — The storm leaves one object damaged, and that object stands in for a person for the rest of the story. Better than lightning striking a character directly, because the damage waits, visible, until it is understood. _(e.g. “I am no better than the old lightning-struck chestnut-tree in Thornfield orchard” — Rochester finally reading the split tree as a description of himself — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The conjured storm** — A storm somebody MADE. Once a character can order the weather, every wreck and every rescue in the story becomes a moral question about that character rather than about nature. _(e.g. “Hast thou, spirit, / Performed to point the tempest that I bade thee?” — Prospero checking that the shipwreck he commissioned went to plan — The Tempest)_
  - **The storm shut out** — Somebody closes a door on the weather and lights a fire. The warmth is real, and so is the fact that the storm is still there — which is why this kind so often marks a safety that will not hold. _(e.g. “She shut the cold out and the storm” — a woman making a room warm inside a poem whose violence is already on its way — Porphyria's Lover)_
  - **The sky that mocks** — Not judgement and not sympathy, but indifference that feels personal. The character believes the weather is laughing at them, and the reader can see nobody is there — which is a lonelier effect than either. _(e.g. “stars and clouds and winds, ye are all about to mock me” — a ruined man accusing the sky of taunting him — Frankenstein)_
- **Storms that ATTACK — weather with intent, aimed at somebody** — the wind is doing something TO a person, and the verbs give it away
  - **The invisible bombardment** — War words used for weather: the storm becomes an enemy you cannot see or shoot back at. Frightening precisely because there is nothing to fight, only something to sit through. _(e.g. “We just sit tight while wind dives / And strafes invisibly” — an island community under fire from air that is not there — Storm on the Island)_
  - **The weather as the real enemy** — The storm replaces the human enemy entirely. Soldiers waiting to be shot are killed by cold instead, so the writer can say the war is pointless without ever saying it. _(e.g. “the merciless iced east winds that knive us” — the wind, not the Germans, doing the stabbing — Exposure)_
  - **The house under siege** — The storm tests a building, and the building stands in for the people inside. A house described as a ship is a house that could sink, which is the fear the writer actually wants. _(e.g. “The house felt like a ship at sea, battered by the gale that came roaring across the open marsh” — solid ground turned into open water by the wind alone — Whistle and I'll Come to You)_
  - **The storm inside a person** — Storm language used for human violence, so a beating reads as a natural disaster. It makes the attacker seem beyond control or blame, which can be the most disturbing thing about them. _(e.g. “hailing down a storm of blows” — a murder described as weather, so nothing about it looks like a decision — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **The wind that throws things** — No thunder and no lightning, just wind picking things up and putting them somewhere else. This kind works by scale: if the air can throw a bird, the reader knows what it could do to a person. _(e.g. “The wind flung a magpie away” — a whole living creature tossed aside in half a line, casually — Wind)_

### Fire / Heat `Fi`

Fire is flames or heat, and in stories and poems it can be symbolism, the use of an object to stand for an idea. A fire can suggest warmth, comfort and home, or it can suggest danger, anger, passion and destruction. The same fire can suggest both, and its meaning depends on the text. The size of a fire, such as a tiny flame or a blaze, can show how much comfort or danger there is.

**The concept:** Fire can show that the same thing may comfort a character and hurt them. Because readers know that fire warms and burns, they feel comfort and danger together. In Frankenstein, the creature that Victor Frankenstein made finds a fire left by wandering beggars, enjoys its warmth, then burns his hand in the embers and says “How strange, I thought, that the same cause should produce such opposite effects!”. When you write about any fire, say whether it warms, burns or does both, who controls it, and what the writer wants us to understand.

**Examples:** “glimpsing the sunk fires” — soldiers freezing in the open at night imagine going home and glimpsing fires burned low, and then say that “on us the doors are closed” — Exposure; “These violent delights have violent ends, / And in their triumph die; like fire and powder, / Which as they kiss consume.” — Friar Lawrence, who is about to marry Romeo and Juliet, warns that wild passion destroys itself, like fire and gunpowder that burn up when they meet — Romeo and Juliet; “a Ball of Fire, so fierce and glowing he could scarcely bear to gaze upon it” — the Cowardly Lion meets the Wizard, who appears as a ball of fire so hot that it singes the Lion's whiskers — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the size and state of the fire, and who controls it. · Feel: We feel comfort and unease together, because the same flame can warm a character and also burn them. · Think: We ask whether the fire warms or harms, and what that shows about what the character wants or fears. · Act: We notice how stories, films and adverts use flames to suggest comfort or danger, and ask what they want us to feel.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any fire, flames or heat in a story that can warm a person, comfort them, or harm them. 1. What kind of fire is it, and who controls it? 2. Does it warm, burn or do both? 3. What does the fire's size or state show about a character or place? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the fire? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens. In the first scene, the fires are coal fires in the office of Scrooge, a rich, mean old man. His own fire is “very small”, and he alone controls the coal because he keeps the coal-box in his own room. The fire warms, but only a little: his clerk, Bob Cratchit, has a fire “so very much smaller that it looked like one coal”, and he cannot add more. The tiny fire shows how mean Scrooge is, because he will not spare coal even for the man who works for him. At the end Scrooge tells Bob “Make up the fires”, so Dickens may want readers to see warmth as something people can choose to share or to hold back.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character craves and whether it could also harm them. Choose the form of fire: a hearth, a candle or a blaze. Show its warmth through one small action, such as holding out cold hands. Show its danger through one detail, such as a spark, a smell of smoke or a crackle. Check that the fire tells the reader something about your character; if it does not, change its size or who controls it.

**Kinds of Fire** — Fires differ by whether somebody is holding them. A fire in a grate is tended, so its size, its brightness and whether it has gone out all read the people who keep it — their meanness, their comfort, their hope of rescue. A fire that gets loose reads nobody: it takes whatever it touches, which is why writers reach for it when they mean passion, rage or judgement. Decide which kind you are lighting before you write it, because a tended fire tells us about a character and a loose one tells us what is coming.

- **Fires someone TENDS — a flame in a grate, and what its size says** — a person keeps this fire alive, so the state of it reads the people around it
  - **The hearth as a measure of meanness** — Two fires in one building, one much smaller than the other. The size of a fire a person is allowed says exactly what the man paying for it thinks they are worth. _(e.g. “Scrooge had a very small fire, but the clerk's fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal” — a single lump of coal measures what an employer thinks a man's comfort is worth — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **The hearth as safety** — A lit grate with tea laid out is a room saying nothing bad happens here. Writers build that safety deliberately so they have something to break. _(e.g. “the fire burning in the grate, the things laid out for tea” — a room arranged to look completely safe, in the chapter where the door is forced open — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **The fire as unending work** — Somebody on their knees blowing on it before dawn. This fire is not comfort but the first job of the day, and it measures a life spent keeping other people warm. _(e.g. “I rise in the dawn, and I kneel and blow / Till the seed of the fire flicker and glow” — the day starts on the floor at the grate, and the poem never lets her stop — Song of the Old Mother)_
  - **The fire that means rescue** — A fire kept alight as a signal to be seen from far off. Letting it go out is not carelessness, it is the only hope of getting home going out. _(e.g. “You let the fire out” — four words of accusation, because the signal fire was the boys' one way off the island — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **The hearth as rank** — Where a person is allowed to sit in relation to the fire tells you their place. The nearer the warmth, the more important they are held to be. _(e.g. “more important customers, who drank spirits and sat nearest the fire” — the seating round one fire maps the whole village's pecking order — Silas Marner)_
- **Fires that get LOOSE — heat nobody is holding** — nobody controls this flame, and it takes whatever it touches
  - **Fire as passion that burns itself out** — Fire joined to something explosive, so the moment of contact is also the moment of destruction. This is the kind for love that moves too fast to survive. _(e.g. “Like fire and powder, / Which, as they kiss, consume” — the word kiss makes the explosion sound romantic, which is how the warning gets missed — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Fire as the judgement coming** — Fire that has not happened yet, promised as what people will suffer if they refuse to change. This fire is a threat about the future, not a flame burning on the page. _(e.g. “they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish” — a warning delivered to a family who have just decided to learn nothing — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Fire as the revenge of someone shut away** — A locked-up character sets a fire on purpose. Arson becomes the only voice left to a person who has been denied every other way of speaking. _(e.g. “She set fire to the hangings of the room next her own” — the woman kept in the attic answers the house that holds her — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Fire as a lesson learned by pain** — A character meets fire with nobody to explain it, and finds out what it does by being burned. Fire here is knowledge bought the hard way. _(e.g. “thrust my hand into the live embers” — the creature teaches himself what warmth costs, because nobody has been left to teach him — Frankenstein)_
  - **Heat inside the head** — No actual flame at all — the heat is in a mind that has stopped working properly. Fire words describe a fever of thought, and the reader feels the temperature climb. _(e.g. “a dagger of the mind, a false creation / Proceeding from the heat-oppressed brain” — he knows the dagger is not there and follows it anyway — Macbeth)_

### The Desert / Wasteland `Dt`

A wasteland is an empty, barren place, such as a desert or a frozen plain, that gives people little or nothing to live on. Writers often use it to show what a person is like when comfort and company are taken away. It can also stand for a feeling, such as loneliness or loss, or for what is left when something great has ended. It is a kind of symbolism, where a place stands for an idea, and its meaning depends on who is there and what happens to them.

**The concept:** A wasteland lets a writer show a character, or a whole society, with nothing to rely on. Because the place offers no food, shelter or help, the reader sees what the character does alone. In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, a ship is becalmed (stuck with no wind) on the sea, and the poem says “Water, water, every where, / Nor any drop to drink”, because sea water cannot be drunk. When you write about any wasteland, say what it takes away, what the character does without it, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “the lone and level sands stretch far away” — the desert that stretches around the broken statue of a king, so the sand has outlasted the ruler's power — Ozymandias; “the merciless iced east winds that knive us” — soldiers keeping watch at night in winter, where the freezing wind cuts like a knife and nothing else happens — Exposure; “vast and irregular plains of ice, which seemed to have no end” — Captain Walton's crew, sailing north, see ice in every direction; soon after, they see a sledge driven by a giant, the creature Victor Frankenstein made — Frankenstein

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at a place that gives a character nothing, and watch what the character does without help. · Feel: We feel the loneliness of an empty place, because the writer wants us to see what a person has once comfort is gone. · Think: We ask what the emptiness stands for, such as loss, endurance or the end of a great power. · Act: We notice when news reports show empty, ruined places, and ask what they want us to feel about the people who left.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any wasteland, an empty, barren place, such as a desert or a frozen waste, that gives a character nothing back. 1. What does the place lack: water, food, shelter, warmth or company? 2. What does the character do when the place gives them nothing? 3. What does that show about the character? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the place? Try the questions on To Build a Fire by Jack London. The Yukon, a very cold region of Canada and Alaska, lacks warmth above all: “It was seventy-five below zero.” A man, new to the country, walks on with only a dog. After he breaks through the ice and wets himself half-way to the knees, he tries to build a fire, but snow falls from a spruce tree and puts it out. The way he acts shows that he is “without imagination”: he sees the cold only as uncomfortable, and he had been told that after fifty below zero a man should travel with a partner, yet he travelled alone. London may want readers to see that nature does not care how confident a person is.

**How to create it:** Choose the one thing your place will not give your character, such as water, warmth or company. Describe the place in plain, bare details, with very few signs of life. Show what your character does as each comfort runs out. Reveal one thing about them that a comfortable place would hide. Check that the character has no easy way out; if they have, take it away.

**Kinds of Wasteland** — Writers use wastelands in two ways. In the first way, the place itself is empty or harsh, such as a desert, a field of ice, a frozen trench or a strange country. In the second way, the empty place is inside a person, a love or a future, where nothing can grow. Writers often describe this second way with words for empty land, such as barren or frozen. Decide first whether the emptiness is in the place or in the person.

- **Wastelands OUTSIDE — an empty or harsh place** — the place itself is empty or harsh, or it feels strange to the person in it
  - **The desert that lasts longer than the king** — The desert does not attack anyone. It is simply still there after a king's power has gone. The empty sand shows that his power did not last. _(e.g. “Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare” — a traveller describes the broken statue of a king in the desert; the king's proud words on its base can still be read, but nothing else is left except empty sand — Ozymandias)_
  - **The icy waste** — A land of ice is as empty as a desert, but ice can move and crack. So the place is dangerous as well as empty. Choose this kind when you want the empty place itself to be a danger. _(e.g. “the ice began to move, and roarings like thunder were heard at a distance” — Walton, the captain of a ship stuck in Arctic ice, writes in a letter that the ice starts to move and split, and the ship is in great danger — Frankenstein)_
  - **The waste where nothing happens** — Soldiers wait in a bleak place, and the danger is the cold and the waiting, not an attack. They grow weaker as the hours pass. In Exposure, a line saying that nothing happens is repeated, so the reader feels the long wait too. _(e.g. “We cringe in holes, back on forgotten dreams, and stare, snow-dazed” — soldiers wait in the snow for a battle that does not come; they crouch in holes in the ground and stare, dazed by the snow — Exposure)_
  - **The wilderness of living far from home** — The character lives far from home, in a strange country. They feel as if they are in a wilderness, because nothing and nobody in the new place feels familiar. _(e.g. “Like Rama I have felt the Wilderness” — the speaker compares herself to Rama, the hero of an old Indian story, who was sent away to live in the wilderness; in England, English speakers find her name hard to say — Name Journeys)_
- **Wastelands INSIDE — the emptiness is in a person, a love or a future** — the emptiness comes from a person, a love or a future that cannot grow, not from the land
  - **The frozen heart** — One person makes another person's heart cold on purpose, so that it cannot love. Here the frozen, empty place is a heart, not a piece of land. _(e.g. “I stole her heart away and put ice in its place” — Miss Havisham, who brought Estella up, admits to Pip that she taught the girl not to love, and she is now sorry for it — Great Expectations)_
  - **The barren future** — Here the emptiness is in the future, not in the place around the character. A ruler may have no child to rule after them, so their family line will end. Nothing has been lost yet, so the character feels fear, not grief. _(e.g. “Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown, / And put a barren sceptre in my gripe” — Macbeth, now king, says the witches gave him a crown with no son to inherit it, and he fears that Banquo's children will be kings instead — Macbeth)_
  - **The barren person** — A narrator calls a person barren, meaning that nothing good grows inside them. The person may look impressive but has no real thought or kindness. This is the narrator's opinion, so it also tells you about the narrator. _(e.g. “her mind was poor, her heart barren by nature” — Jane, the narrator, says that Blanche Ingram, a beautiful guest at Thornfield, has many talents, but no real thought or kindness inside her — Jane Eyre)_
  - **A landscape that looks dead because a love died** — The place is ordinary, such as a pond on a winter day. A love has ended, so the speaker describes everything there as grey, hungry or dying. The land looks empty because of how the speaker feels. _(e.g. “And a few leaves lay on the starving sod” — the speaker remembers standing by a pond on a winter day with someone they loved; the love has ended, and even the ground seems hungry and dead — Neutral Tones)_

### The Forest / Woods `Fs`

In a story, a forest is a place of trees where a character can easily lose the way. Writers often use it for the unknown: the character leaves a safe, ordered place and meets danger, confusion or a truth they had avoided. It can also be a refuge, a place to hide from a harsh world. It is a kind of symbolism, where a place stands for an idea, and its meaning is not fixed.

**The concept:** A forest lets a writer take a character away from what they know and show what they do when nothing is familiar. Because paths look alike and no one can see far, the character must choose without certainty. In A Midsummer Night’s Dream, Lysander tells Hermia, who may not marry him under Athenian law, to meet him “in the wood, a league without the town”: a league is about three miles, and without means outside. When you write about any forest, say what the character leaves behind, what they lose there, and what they learn.

**Examples:** “just as Little Red-Cap entered the wood, a wolf met her” — a girl takes cake to her grandmother through the wood, and as soon as she goes in she meets a wolf, who tricks her into leaving the path — Little Red Riding Hood; “Then poor Snowdrop wandered along through the wood in great fear; and the wild beasts roared about her, but none did her any harm” — Snow White, sent by the queen into the wide wood so she will not be seen again, walks through it afraid, and the wild animals do not hurt her — Snow White; “And stole into the covert of the wood” — Benvolio tells Romeo's parents that he saw Romeo walking alone at dawn; when Romeo saw him coming, he slipped into the thick trees to avoid him — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at where the path ends and the trees close in, and at what the character leaves behind. · Feel: We feel unease and a little excitement, because the writer wants us to see that facing the unknown can change a person. · Think: We ask what the woods stand for, such as danger, confusion or a truth the character has avoided. · Act: We notice when films, news and adverts show someone leaving what is safe, and ask what they want us to think of the unknown.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any forest or woods in a story. 1. Who goes into the forest, and what ordered place do they leave behind? 2. What do they lose there, or become unable to see or know, such as the way, their safety or what will happen? 3. What do they meet or learn among the trees? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about the unknown? Try the questions on Hansel and Gretel. Hansel and Gretel, the children of a poor wood-cutter, go into the forest. They leave the home where they live with their father and stepmother. They lose their way, because the birds eat the bread crumbs Hansel dropped to mark the path. They meet a witch who lives in a house built of bread, cakes and sugar. The Brothers Grimm, who collected the tale, seem to show that the unknown is dangerous but can be beaten. Gretel tricks the witch, and the children bring jewels home.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character relies on at the start, such as a map, a rule or a plan. Send them into a forest where that thing stops working. Show them lost, with paths that look alike and nothing to tell them where they are. Let them meet or learn something among the trees that they could not face in the open. Check that your character loses something in the forest; if not, take away one more thing they rely on.

**Kinds of Forest** — Writers use forests in two ways. In the first way, the wood matters because of how a character feels in it or about it: afraid, safe or longing to be there. In the second way, the wood itself does or shows something. It moves, belongs to a ruler, has a full life without people, or is a picture of a crowd. Decide which way your forest works before you describe the trees.

- **Woods for the CHARACTER — a place the character is in, hides in or longs for** — the wood matters because of how the character feels in it or about it: afraid, safe or longing
  - **The dark wood of the unknown** — This forest is dark and hard to see into, so it stands for the unknown. Characters fear what may be hiding in it. They can lose their way there, and lose their certainty too. _(e.g. “darkness of the forest” — boys stranded on an island hold their meetings and make their rules on the sunlit beach, but the forest in the middle of the island is dark, and the youngest boys fear a beast hiding in it — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **The wood you hide in** — The trees hide the character from the world, so no one can see them or reach them. But a person hidden this deeply is also kept apart from other people. _(e.g. “Ferndean Manor... deep buried in a wood” — Rochester, who has lost his sight, a hand and his home, now lives in an old house hidden deep in a wood, away from the world — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The wood you dream of escaping to** — The character is not in the wood. They imagine it from a worse place and long to be there. The wood exists only in their mind, so the writing is about the longing. _(e.g. “And live alone in the bee-loud glade” — a speaker standing on grey city pavements imagines a glade, an open space in a wood, loud with bees, as a place to live alone — The Lake Isle of Innisfree)_
- **Woods that DO or SHOW something — the wood itself matters** — the wood moves, belongs to a ruler, has a full life without people, or is a picture of a crowd
  - **The wood that seems to march towards you** — The wood seems to move towards a character, like an attacking army. In many forest stories the character goes into the wood. Here the wood comes to the character. _(e.g. “Great Birnam Wood to high Dunsinane Hill / Shall come against him” — a vision tells Macbeth that he will not be beaten until Birnam Wood comes to Dunsinane Hill, which he thinks is impossible; later, soldiers carry branches cut from the wood, so it seems to move — Macbeth)_
  - **The wood ruled from the top** — A creature sits at the top of the wood, above everything else. The creature treats the wood as land that belongs to it. So the wood stops being wild: it becomes one ruler's property, and everything in it is under that ruler. _(e.g. “I sit in the top of the wood, my eyes closed” — a hawk sits at the top of the wood with its eyes closed, calm because it believes everything below belongs to it — Hawk Roosting)_
  - **The wood full of its own life** — The forest is full of its own life, such as old trees and loud birds. A person sitting in it feels outside that life. The feeling is envy, not fear. _(e.g. “The forest spat all the birds back, / and I was jealous” — a speaker who wears hearing aids sits in a forest; when he switches them back on, the birds' noise returns, and he is jealous of the strong, steady trees — With Birds You're Never Lonely)_
  - **The forest as a picture of a crowd** — The writer compares a great crowd, such as an army, to the leaves of a forest. The forest is only a comparison, so nobody walks in it. _(e.g. “Like the leaves of the forest when Autumn hath blown” — the poem compares a whole army to forest leaves: green at sunset, then lying dead and scattered the next morning, after the Angel of Death has breathed on them — The Destruction of Sennacherib)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### The Garden `Ga`

In a story, a garden is a place where plants are grown and looked after, often with a wall or fence around it. Writers often use it for safety, order, beauty or innocence. Because people make a garden, it can also show care, pride or neglect. It is a kind of symbolism, where a place stands for an idea, and a garden is not always safe: in some stories it holds danger or secrets.

**The concept:** A garden lets a writer show a protected place, and what happens to anyone who enters it or spoils it. Because it is shut in and cared for, a person who goes in is easy to notice. In The Tale of Peter Rabbit, Mrs Rabbit warns her children “don't go into Mr. McGregor's garden”, because their father “was put in a pie” there, so the garden is a place with strict rules and real danger. When you write about any garden, say who can enter it, what state it is in, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “The orchard walls are high and hard to climb” — Juliet tells Romeo that the walls of her family's orchard, a garden of fruit trees, are high, and that her kinsmen will kill him if they find him there — Romeo and Juliet; “No nook in the grounds more sheltered and more Eden-like” — Jane describes the orchard at Thornfield, full of flowers and shut off by a very high wall, where Mr Rochester soon joins her and proposes; Eden-like means like the Garden of Eden — Jane Eyre; “And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden” — the Bible's first garden, where God puts the first man; later he and the first woman are sent out of it after they eat the fruit God had forbidden — The Bible (Genesis)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the walls, the plants and the state of the garden, and at who is allowed in. · Feel: We feel the calm of a protected place and worry that it may be spoiled, because the writer shows innocence is easy to lose. · Think: We ask what the garden's condition shows about the people in it, such as their care, pride or neglect. · Act: We notice when news and adverts show a safe, protected place, such as a home or park, and ask who it is safe for.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any garden in a story. 1. Who can enter the garden, and is it open, walled or locked? 2. How does it look: cared for or neglected, in flower or bare? 3. Does anything threaten or spoil it, and if it does, what? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the garden? Try the questions on The Secret Garden. At first no one may enter: Mr Craven, Mary's uncle, locked the door and buried the key after his wife died. Mary, a lonely girl, finds the key and the hidden door, and later brings in her friend Dickon and her cousin Colin. At first the garden is overgrown and bare, and Mary wonders whether anything in it is alive. Then she finds pale green shoots, and in spring it flowers. It is spoiled by neglect, because no one has been in it for ten years. The author, Frances Hodgson Burnett, seems to show that caring for a living place can help people recover, as it helps Mary and her ill cousin Colin.

**How to create it:** Decide who owns the garden and why it is shut. Describe it as you want the reader to see it, such as bare, overgrown or in flower. Add one thing that threatens it, such as neglect, a death or a snake. Let your character change something in the garden and show what that does to them. Check that the garden's condition matches what is happening to your character; if it does not, change one detail.

**Kinds of Garden** — Writers use gardens in two ways. In the first way, a person looks after growing things, in real soil or in a comparison, and the story is about that care. In the second way, the garden is a paradise that nobody can walk into: it is promised, lies beyond death, or is carried in the mind. Here a paradise means any perfect place, not only a garden like Eden in the Bible. It can be fields or a beach as well as flowers. Decide first whether your character can reach the garden.

- **Gardens that are LOOKED AFTER — care for growing things** — a person cares for plants, in real soil or in a comparison, and the kind of care matters
  - **The everyday tended garden** — This is ordinary soil that someone digs and plants each year. The work follows the seasons, so the gardener notices each change in the year. A writer can set this garden beside an indoor life, to show what that indoor life is missing. _(e.g. “In February, digging his garden, planting potatoes” — a man in Yorkshire digs his garden, plants potatoes and sees the first lapwings return; the speaker, who receives his letters, works with words at a screen — Letters from Yorkshire)_
  - **The garden at home while someone dies far away** — On an ordinary day, someone at home works in a real garden. On that same day, someone they love is killed far away. The everyday garden work makes the loss feel sharper. _(e.g. “In our garden / We sowed our earliest seeds” — the speaker writes to a dead friend, the poet Edward Thomas, who was killed in battle on Easter Monday 1917, and remembers sowing the year's first seeds at home that same day — Easter Monday)_
  - **The poisoned garden** — A speaker looks after his anger as if it were a plant in a garden. The anger grows into a tree with a shining apple, and his enemy is found dead under it. Here the gardener's care grows something deadly. _(e.g. “And into my garden stole” — the speaker waters his anger like a plant until it bears an apple; his enemy steals into the garden at night and is found dead under the tree — A Poison Tree)_
  - **The wild rose outside the garden** — A character compares themselves to a plant. They would rather be a wild plant in a hedge, outside the garden, than a cared-for flower inside it. They refuse the care because it would come from someone they dislike. _(e.g. “I had rather be a canker in a hedge than a rose in his grace” — Don John says he would rather be a canker, a wild rose thought of as a weed, growing in a hedge, than a garden rose cared for by his brother's kindness — Much Ado About Nothing)_
- **Gardens that are OUT OF REACH — a paradise that is not here** — the garden is in the future, beyond death or only in the mind, so nobody can walk into it
  - **The paradise you carry** — A paradise is kept inside a person as a private picture of a loved place, so it can go everywhere with them. No one else can steal it. The person can turn to it when life is hard. _(e.g. “empty your paradise onto a desk: / your white sands, green hills and fresh fish” — a grandmother tells the speaker to carry a private paradise hidden on them, and in hard times to spread it out and look at it: white sands, green hills and fresh fish — A Portable Paradise)_
  - **The paradise past the end** — The paradise lies beyond death, so the character can only look towards it. It is not shown as a sad place, because the people the character loved are waiting there. _(e.g. “They are waiting for me somewhere beyond Eden Rock” — the speaker sees his dead parents, young again, having a picnic on the far bank of a stream, and they call him to cross — Eden Rock)_
  - **The promised garden** — A paradise is promised for the future. A leader can use the promise to win people over. The story is then often about the promise being broken. _(e.g. “the fruitful fields of England / Shall be trod by beasts alone” — Old Major, an old pig, sings a song promising that one day only animals will live on England's rich fields; later in the story, the pigs take the farm for themselves — Animal Farm)_
  - **A garden that appears in the mind** — In a moment of great danger, a peaceful garden appears in a character's mind. The garden shows that the danger has not destroyed what the character hopes for. _(e.g. “to an orchard in full bloom” — a schoolgirl is shot in the head and walks on; the poem says the bullet cuts a path in her mind to an orchard, a garden of fruit trees, and that the bullet has failed — A Century Later)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### The Mountain `Mu`

A mountain is a very high, steep piece of land that is hard to climb. In a story or poem, a writer can use it as symbolism, so that the mountain stands for an idea such as effort, danger or a goal that is hard to reach. A mountain can also stand for the power of nature. It is so huge that a person seems weak beside it, and it fills them with wonder and fear. Its meaning depends on what happens to the people who face it.

**The concept:** A mountain lets a writer show effort, danger or hope, or a power greater than any person. In both the Bible and the Qur'an, God speaks to Moses at a mountain: in Exodus, “Moses went up into the mount of God” to receive the law. In the Qur'an, Moses asks to see God and is told to look at the mountain instead; when God's glory appears to it, the mountain collapses and Moses falls down unconscious. Its collapse shows a power far greater than any mountain. When you write about any mountain, say whether it is climbed, towers over someone or is out of reach, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary power instinct” — a boy rowing at night in a boat he has taken without asking sees a mountain rise as if it were alive and stride after him; for days afterwards huge shapes trouble his dreams, so the mountain shows the power of nature, and perhaps his guilt — The Prelude; “reaching for the summit, / where gasping for breath I can only lie” — the speaker imagines climbing their grandfather's body as if it were a mountain; at the top, out of breath, they feel his warmth and his slow heartbeat, so the climb stands for getting to know him closely — Climbing My Grandfather; “Sugarcandy Mountain, that happy country where we poor animals shall rest for ever from our labours” — a mountain beyond the clouds that Moses the raven promises the tired animals, a reward never reached while they work harder than ever — Animal Farm

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the mountain's height, and at the people who climb it or stand beneath it. · Feel: We feel the strain of a climb, or wonder and fear when a mountain towers over a person. · Think: We ask what the mountain stands for, such as ambition, a test of character, an unreachable hope, or the power of nature. · Act: We notice when speeches and adverts compare success to climbing a mountain, and ask what that success really costs.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any mountain in a story or poem. 1. Who faces the mountain: someone who climbs it, looks up at it, or longs to reach it, and why? 2. What does the mountain demand of them, or do to them: does it test them, frighten them, or make them seem weak beside it? 3. What do they see, find or learn because of the mountain? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the mountain? Try the questions on Frankenstein. Victor Frankenstein, a scientist, climbs Montanvert, a mountain in the Alps above a glacier, because the mountain scenery had comforted him in his grief. The climb is steep. From the top he looks down on a “sea of ice”, then spends nearly two hours crossing it, and from the far side he sees Mont Blanc, a great peak, and feels something like joy. There he also meets the creature he made, who bounds towards him over the ice. Mary Shelley seems to show that the great size and beauty of nature can comfort a person, but cannot free Victor from what he has done.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character wants from the mountain, such as a goal, an escape or a test. Make the climb hard: show the cold, the steepness and their tiredness. Show what they can see from the top that they could not see below. Let the climb change what they want or believe. Check that the summit gives your character something they did not have at the bottom; if not, change what they see or decide there.

**Kinds of Mountain** — Writers use mountains in different ways. In some stories a character climbs the mountain, and the effort of climbing matters most. In others, a mountain towers over a person and shows the power of nature. In others again, nobody climbs it, and the mountain is used to show the size of something else. Decide which kind you are writing before you begin, because a mountain that can be climbed leads to a different ending from one that cannot.

- **Mountains that are CLIMBED — the climb is a test** — a character goes up, and what happens on the way up gives the scene its meaning
  - **A climb with no rope or safety** — The character chooses to climb without any safety, so the danger is their own decision. The climb shows how brave they are, or how much they trust someone, more than how strong they are. _(e.g. “I decide to do it free, without a rope or net” — the speaker imagines climbing their grandfather's body like a mountain, and choosing to climb without a rope shows how much they trust him — Climbing My Grandfather)_
  - **A climb towards something frightening** — At the top is something the climbers are afraid to meet. Going higher does not mean success here. Each step up leaves them with fewer places to hide. _(e.g. “the figure sat on the mountain-top and bowed and sank and bowed again” — the body of a dead parachutist, moving in the wind on the mountain-top, is mistaken by the boys for the beast they fear — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **A small climb at home** — An ordinary climb inside a home, such as up a ladder, stands for a big change in someone's life. The climb is small, but the change it shows is huge. _(e.g. “climb / the ladder to the loft, to breaking point” — in a new home, the speaker climbs into the loft while their mother holds the end of a tape measure two floors below; the climb stands for leaving her and starting an adult life — Mother, Any Distance)_
  - **A climb to reach someone you love** — The wall is not there to be beaten. It shows how much danger the character will face to reach someone they love. The real danger comes from who the character is, not from the climb. _(e.g. “The orchard walls are high and hard to climb, / And the place death, considering who thou art” — Juliet warns Romeo that the walls are hard to climb, and that her family will kill him if they find him, because he is a Montague — Romeo and Juliet)_
- **Mountains that TOWER over a person — the power of nature** — nobody conquers the mountain; it is so huge that it makes a person feel small, full of wonder and fear
  - **A mountain that seems to come after you** — The mountain is so huge that the character feels small and afraid. It seems almost alive, and it shows the power of nature, which no person can control. _(e.g. “a huge peak, black and huge” — a boy rowing at night in a boat he has taken without asking sees a mountain rise up as if it were alive and stride after him; for days afterwards huge, dark shapes trouble his dreams — The Prelude)_
  - **A mountain that cannot stand before God** — Even a mountain, the biggest and strongest thing a person can see, is shown to be weak beside a far greater power. The size of the mountain makes that power seem even greater. _(e.g. “He sent it crashing down. And Moses fell down senseless.” — Moses asks to see God and is told to look at the mountain instead; when God's glory appears to it, the mountain collapses and Moses faints — The Qur'an (Surah 7))_
- **Mountains that are NOT climbed — a way to show size** — nobody climbs; the mountain is used to show the size of something that is not a mountain
  - **Height used to measure a feeling** — Nobody climbs anything. The writer uses height to show how big a feeling is, because a feeling cannot be measured. _(e.g. “I love thee to the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach” — the speaker uses three measurements of space to show how great her love is — Sonnet 43)_
  - **Mountains that touch the sky** — The mountain is not something to get past. It is one half of a pair, joined to the sky. It shows that even the biggest things in nature belong with something else. _(e.g. “See the mountains kiss high heaven” — the speaker points to mountains touching the sky to argue that everything in nature has a partner, so the person he loves should kiss him too — Love's Philosophy)_
  - **Mountains that never end** — Nobody can ever arrive. Behind each mountain there is another one, so the mountains stand for something that never ends. _(e.g. “On the other side of mountains are mountains, more mountains and mountains again” — the word “mountains” is used again and again, so the sentence never seems to reach an end — Beyond the Sky and Earth)_
  - **Beautiful mountains behind a terrible event** — The mountains stay in the background, calm and beautiful, while something terrible happens in front of them. The calm, beautiful view makes the terrible event more shocking. _(e.g. “Five mountain ranges one behind the other / Under the sunset far into Vermont” — this beautiful view is described while a boy works at a saw that will soon cut his hand — Out, Out—)_
  - **A mountain to hide in** — The character goes up a mountain because nobody will follow. So the climb shows loneliness and being shut out by other people, not ambition. _(e.g. “desert mountains and dreary glaciers” — the Creature lives in the coldest, emptiest mountains, because only there is he left alone — Frankenstein)_

**Related:** Symbolism, The Fall

### Light vs Darkness `Lg`

Light and darkness are opposites that writers use to show contrasts, such as knowledge and ignorance, safety and danger, or good and evil. Light is often linked with truth, hope or life, and darkness with secrets, fear or death. The meaning comes from the contrast between them in the scene. Light set against darkness is a kind of duality, a pair of opposites, and a form of symbolism. These meanings can also be reversed: darkness can give rest or protection, and a harsh light can expose or hurt.

**The concept:** Light and darkness let a writer show what a character knows, hides or fears without saying it. Where light falls, things can be seen, so light can also stand for being found out. In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Past has a bright jet of light on its head, and when Scrooge presses a cap over it, “he could not hide the light”. The light seems to stand for the past he wants to forget. When you write about any light and darkness, say what each one shows, which characters go with each, and whether the balance changes.

**Examples:** “made the cheerless grate / Blaze up, and all the cottage warm” — Porphyria comes in out of the cold storm and makes the fire blaze, and later in the same bright, warm room the speaker strangles her, so the light and warmth make his dark act more shocking — Porphyria's Lover; “O, she doth teach the torches to burn bright!” — Romeo, seeing Juliet for the first time at a night-time party, says she makes the torches seem to burn more brightly — Romeo and Juliet; “And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness” — in the Bible's first story of creation, God separates light from darkness, so the two are opposites from the start — The Bible (Genesis)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at where the light comes from, where it does not reach, and who stands in each. · Feel: We feel safe in light and uneasy in shadow, because writers link brightness with truth and darkness with secrets. · Think: We ask what is being shown or hidden, and whether the character is moving towards the truth or away from it. · Act: We notice when films, news and adverts use bright or dark lighting to make us trust or fear someone, and ask why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any use of light and darkness in a story. 1. Where do light and darkness appear, and which characters or actions go with each? 2. What does each seem to stand for, such as goodness, knowledge and hope, or evil, ignorance and secrecy? 3. Does the balance between them change as the story goes on? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the contrast? Try the questions on Macbeth. In Act 1 Macbeth says “Stars, hide your fires; Let not light see my black and deep desires”. Darkness goes with his hidden plan to take the crown, and light with whatever could see it. Darkness seems to stand for secret evil, and light for being seen and found out. The balance changes: in Act 5 the Gentlewoman tells the doctor that Lady Macbeth, troubled by guilt, has a light by her continually. Shakespeare seems to show that evil hides in the dark but cannot escape the conscience.

**How to create it:** Decide what light and what darkness stand for in your story, such as hope and fear, or truth and secrecy. Set one scene in light and one in darkness, and say where the light comes from or why it is missing. Let a character move from one to the other when something changes. Check that each mention of light or dark links to something that matters in the scene; if one does not, cut it or change it.

**Kinds of Light and Dark** — Light and dark come as a pair, so the meaning never sits in the word — it sits in which one wins the moment, and who that suits. Ask two questions of any lit or unlit scene: what is being made visible, and who wanted it that way. That is why the same brightness can mean a loved face in one poem and a bomber's aim in another, and why a character calling for the dark is making a choice the reader can watch them make.

- **Kinds of LIGHT — what one particular brightness means** — something is lit, and the lighting carries the judgement
  - **Light as the face you love** — A person described as the source of the light rather than as something the light falls on. It tells you the speaker's whole world has reorganised itself around one face. _(e.g. “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun” — she is not standing in the light, she is where the light comes from — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Light as truth dragged into the open** — Light as the moment a hidden thing is finally seen. What gives this kind its sting is usually who does the dragging — often the least clever people in the play. _(e.g. “What your wisdoms could not discover, these shallow fools have brought to light” — the clever men miss the plot and the bumbling watchmen find it — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **A life as a lamp that can be put out** — A person's life described as a flame, so killing them becomes putting out a light. The comparison is how the killer makes the act sound small and tidy to himself. _(e.g. “Put out the light, and then put out the light” — the same three words used first for a candle and then for a woman — Othello)_
  - **Light as fragile hope** — Light seen through something thin — paper, skin, cloth. The point is not the brightness but that the thing letting it through tears easily, so the hope is real and barely held. _(e.g. “Paper that lets the light / shine through, this / is what could alter things” — the flimsiest material in the poem is the one that could change the world — Tissue)_
  - **Light as danger — being seen means being a target** — The reverse of everything above. Here the brightness helps the people trying to kill you, so light stops meaning safety and starts meaning exposure. _(e.g. “ideally bright and clear for bomber's eye” — a beautiful clear night described from the point of view of the man aiming at it — The Bright Lights of Sarajevo)_
- **Kinds of DARK — and who the missing light is helping** — the light is withheld, and who that suits is the meaning
  - **Dark called for on purpose** — A character asks the light to go away before acting. The request itself gives them away: they already know the deed could not bear being looked at. _(e.g. “Let not light see my black and deep desires” — he asks the stars to look away, which tells us he knows exactly what he is about to do — Macbeth)_
  - **Dark as cover for shame** — Not hiding a crime but hiding a face. Darkness lets a character be present without being looked at, and what they are ashamed of is the whole point of the line. _(e.g. “I am glad ’tis night, you do not look on me” — she is grateful the dark spares her being seen — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **Dark inside a person, not in the room** — Darkness with no lighting involved at all — it is a quality of people. This is the kind that ends a book, because it says the frightening thing was never the island or the night. _(e.g. “the darkness of man's heart” — the boys are rescued from the island and not from the thing that made it terrible — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Dark as meanness** — A man who simply will not pay for light. Nothing supernatural or moral is claimed — the dark is a household expense, and choosing it says everything about him. _(e.g. “darkness is cheap, and Scrooge liked it” — the reason he sits in the dark is that candles cost money — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Dark as mercy** — The rare kind — darkness that protects rather than threatens. Where people are killed for what they are, not being able to see which side somebody belongs to is what keeps them alive. _(e.g. “black shapes impossible to mark / as Muslim, Serb or Croat in such dark” — the dark hides exactly the difference people are being shot for — The Bright Lights of Sarajevo)_

**Related:** Duality, Symbolism

### The Seasons `Sv`

The seasons are the four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn and winter. Writers often link them to stages of a life or of a feeling: spring with birth or hope, summer with fullness, autumn with ageing, and winter with death or sadness. A change of season can show a change in a character without the writer stating it. When a time of year stands for an idea in this way, it is symbolism. The links are not fixed: a writer can make winter peaceful or spring cruel.

**The concept:** The seasons let a writer show what a character or a life is like by linking it to a time of year. Readers know what each season brings, so a writer can show a stage of life by naming its season. In Macbeth, near the end, Macbeth says “my way of life / Is fall’n into the sere, the yellow leaf”: a leaf that is dry and yellow is autumn, and he means he has grown old. He expects curses, not the love and friends old age should bring. When you write about any season, say what it stands for, whether it changes, and what that change shows.

**Examples:** “We stood by a pond that winter day” — the poem is set on a cold winter day, and the speaker and a lover stand together as their love is ending, so the cold day matches the end of the love — Neutral Tones; “It was a divine spring; and the season contributed greatly to my convalescence” — Victor Frankenstein, ill for months after bringing the creature to life, begins to recover as spring arrives — Frankenstein; “This bud of love, by summer’s ripening breath, / May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet” — Juliet says that, as summer comes, their love, a young bud, may be a flower when they next meet; in the play they die before their love can grow into a lasting marriage — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at which season is shown, and at whether it changes or stays the same. · Feel: We feel the sadness or hope that a season brings, because the writer is showing that a life passes through stages. · Think: We ask what stage of life the season stands for, and whether the writer is showing growth or loss. · Act: We notice when films, songs and adverts use a season, such as winter or spring, to make us feel hope or sadness about change.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any use of the seasons in a story or poem. 1. Which season is shown, and what do the weather, plants or light look like? 2. What does that season seem to stand for, such as birth, fullness, decline or death? 3. Does the season change, or does the writer stop it from changing? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the season? Try the questions on Shakespeare's Sonnet 18. The season is summer, shown through “Rough winds” that “shake the darling buds of May” and a sun that is sometimes too hot. Summer is the weaker comparison: the speaker says the person is “more lovely and more temperate”, and that summer’s “lease hath all too short a date”, so summer stands for beauty that ends. Only the person’s own “eternal summer shall not fade”. The poem is what keeps that summer from fading: “So long lives this, and this gives life to thee.” The speaker seems to want the reader to see that poetry can keep a person alive.

**How to create it:** Choose the season that matches the stage your character or subject has reached, such as spring for a beginning or winter for an ending. Show it through two or three details, such as light, weather or plants. Let it change, or refuse to change, at the moment something in the story turns. Ask a friend to read it; if they cannot say what stage your character has reached, add one more detail.

**Kinds of Season** — Seasons are sorted by whether the year agrees with the person. When they agree, the season quietly names the stage of a life — ripeness, fading, cold — and nothing has to be explained. When they disagree, the mismatch itself becomes the meaning: spring outside a death, a winter that never turns, a summer that arrives at exactly the wrong moment. The disagreeing kind is the sharper tool. Ask what season your own character is in, then ask whether the world around them is in the same one.

- **Seasons that AGREE — the year and the person move together** — the season names the stage of life the character has reached
  - **Ripeness before the end** — Autumn written as fullness rather than decay — everything at its heaviest and best, with the cold implied and not yet arrived. The tenderest way to write an ending, because nothing has ended yet. _(e.g. “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness” — a poem that spends its first lines loading autumn with abundance before letting the light start to go — To Autumn)_
  - **Summer fading on time** — The season turning exactly when it should, and that ordinariness is the cruelty. Nothing dramatic happens to these lives; the year simply moves on, and so does youth. _(e.g. “Summer is fading” — two words, in the present tense, deciding the whole poem about young mothers whose lives are quietly closing — Afternoons)_
  - **The season that slips away unnoticed** — Change so gradual that nobody catches the moment it happened. Useful for grief or for love ending, both of which are usually noticed long after they went. _(e.g. “As imperceptibly as Grief / The Summer lapsed away” — the summer compared to a feeling that also left without announcing it — As Imperceptibly as Grief)_
  - **The summer already over** — The season named only in the past tense, so the reader never sees it and feels its absence instead. Strongest when the speaker is remembering what they had rather than describing what they have. _(e.g. “summer sang in me / A little while, that in me sings no more” — a season of love reported entirely as something finished — What lips my lips have kissed)_
  - **Winter as work** — Not a mood but a set of jobs — ice to break, snow to shift. Winter measured in labour makes a life feel real and specific, and it quietly says this person is still going. _(e.g. “breaking ice on a waterbutt, / clearing a path through snow” — winter given as a list of things somebody actually does in it — Letters from Yorkshire)_
- **Seasons that ARGUE — the year and the person disagree** — the season is the wrong one for what is happening, and the mismatch is the point
  - **The untimely frost** — A death out of season — cold arriving on something that had not finished growing. The word untimely does the whole job: it says this was not the natural order, so somebody is to blame. _(e.g. “Death lies on her like an untimely frost / Upon the sweetest flower of all the field” — a young girl's death written as weather that came months too early — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **The winter that never turns** — The cruellest kind. The year is supposed to come round; here it does not, and a season becomes a permanent condition. Use it for injustice rather than for sadness, because a stuck winter accuses somebody. _(e.g. “It is eternal winter there” — poverty described as a country where spring is simply not allowed to arrive — Holy Thursday (Experience))_
  - **Spring outside a death** — New life put in the window of a room where somebody has just been told terrible news. The season refuses to match the grief, and the reader feels the world's indifference — or, more unsettlingly, the character's relief. _(e.g. “the tops of trees that were all aquiver with the new spring life” — what a newly widowed woman sees from her chair, and finds she is glad of — The Story of an Hour)_
  - **The summer that refuses to end** — The writer flatly overrules the cycle: this one season will not turn, because the poem says so. It only works if the poem admits first that every real summer does end. _(e.g. “But thy eternal summer shall not fade” — a poem promising to hold one season open for ever, having just listed everything that fades — Sonnet 18)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### Blood `Bl`

Blood is the red liquid in the body, and in stories it often stands for life, family or violence. Writers use it for family, as in a family line, or for guilt, when a stain cannot be washed away. Blood that is spilled shows that someone has been hurt or killed. It may also stand for courage or sacrifice. Blood is a kind of symbolism, where an object stands for an idea, and a text may use it for more than one meaning at once.

**The concept:** Blood lets a writer show that a deed has consequences that cannot be undone. Because blood leaves a mark, it can show guilt that a person cannot hide, or a bond of family that cannot be broken. In Macbeth, Macbeth has just killed King Duncan, and he asks “Will all great Neptune’s ocean wash this blood / Clean from my hand?”, which shows that his guilt feels too large to clean. When you find any blood in a text, say whose it is, what it links or marks, and whether anyone can clean it away.

**Examples:** “his bloody life in my bloody hands” — a soldier who shot a man says that man's life is now in his own hands, so the killing stays with him back at home — Remains; “Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean” — the Chorus, the speaker who opens the play, says that in Verona the fighting between two families spills blood and makes the citizens' hands unclean — Romeo and Juliet; “Runs in blood down palace walls” — the speaker hears a soldier's sigh and says it runs as blood down the walls of the royal palace, so the blood seems to mark the rulers who send soldiers to die — London

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at whose blood it is, where it is shown, and who has it on their hands. · Feel: We feel dread or sorrow, because the writer wants us to see that a violent act leaves a mark that stays. · Think: We ask what the blood stands for, such as guilt, family loyalty or the cost of violence. · Act: We notice how news reports and films show violence, and ask whether they show what it costs the people involved.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any use of blood in a story. 1. Whose blood is it, and is it spilled, shown or only spoken about? 2. Does it link people as family or loyalty, stand for life, or point to violence and guilt? 3. Can anyone undo or escape what the blood means? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through it? Try the questions on Blood Brothers, a play by Willy Russell. The blood is that of the twins Mickey and Eddie. As boys they swear to be blood brothers and cut their hands, so at first the blood is only a small cut and a promise. It links them as family and loyalty: they are twins separated at birth, so the oath is truer than they know. They cannot escape it: the class system pulls them apart, but they remain brothers, and the play tells us at the start that both die. Russell seems to show that class can divide people who are as close as family, at a terrible cost.

**How to create it:** Decide what the blood means in your story: a family tie, a life, or the guilt of an act. Show it once, as a drop, a stain or a promise, in a scene that matters. Let it come back later, so the reader sees that it has not gone away. Check that every mention of blood links to your meaning; if one does not, change it or cut it.

**Kinds of Blood** — Blood changes meaning the moment it leaves the body. Inside, it stands for family, temperament and what a person is made of — a bond, a nature, a life. Spilled, it becomes evidence: a mark that stays, proves what was done, and cannot be put back. Work out which one your scene needs, because blood inside the body ties people together and blood outside it accuses somebody.

- **Blood still INSIDE — kinship, nature, what a person is made of** — nothing has been spilled, and the blood names a bond or a temperament
  - **Blood as a bond you swear, not one you are born with** — Two people cut themselves and make a promise, inventing a family tie. It is the strongest bond in a story because it is chosen — and the cruellest when the two turn out to be real brothers who were never told. _(e.g. “Do you wanna be my blood brother, Eddie?” — two boys invent the very tie they already have, and nobody tells them — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Blood as the small print of a promise** — An agreement mentions flesh but not blood, so blood becomes a legal detail. This kind carries no feeling at all — it turns a bond into words on a page, and shows how a promise can be twisted. _(e.g. “This bond doth give thee here no jot of blood” — the whole trial turns on the one substance the agreement forgot to name — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **Blood as evidence written in the face** — A blush is blood rising, and a character reads it as proof of guilt. Blood here is not a wound but a supposed confession — and the accusation is false. _(e.g. “The story that is printed in her blood” — a father takes his daughter's blush as a written record of a crime she has not committed — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **Blood as the place feelings live** — A character asks for their own blood to be altered so that they will stop feeling. Blood stands for the softness they want removed, so the request is really a wish to become somebody else. _(e.g. “make thick my blood” — she asks for her own blood to be thickened so that pity cannot get through it — Macbeth)_
  - **Blood as ripeness, in a thing that is not a person** — Blood used for fruit, sap or summer — life at its fullest rather than any injury. It brings the shiver of the body into a harmless description, so pleasure starts to feel greedy. _(e.g. “summer's blood was in it” — a blackberry described as though it were alive, until picking it feels like killing — Blackberry-Picking)_
- **Blood SPILLED — the mark a deed leaves** — the blood is out of the body and cannot be put back
  - **Blood as proof a promise has been broken** — Blood appearing where it never used to be. Nothing has to be argued: the smell on its own proves the new rulers have turned into the old ones. _(e.g. “The air was heavy with the smell of blood, which had been unknown there since Jones had been expelled” — the farm the animals freed now smells exactly as it did under the farmer — Animal Farm)_
  - **Blood that used to look glamorous** — The same blood remembered twice — once as something a boy was proud of, once as the wound that ruined him. Showing both is how a writer makes the reader feel a lie about war. _(e.g. “One time he liked a blood-smear down his leg, / After the matches, carried shoulder-high” — a football injury he enjoyed, set against the legs he no longer has — Disabled)_
  - **Blood as a chant that makes killing easy** — Blood spoken as a rhythm by a group. Repeated together often enough, the words stop meaning a living animal and turn into a game — which is how a crowd talks itself into cruelty. _(e.g. “Kill the pig! Cut her throat! Spill her blood!” — a chant turns a hunt into a ritual, and every boy hides inside it — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Blood worn as defiance** — The rare kind — blood as endurance rather than guilt or horror. The speaker is injured and says so proudly, so the blood measures what has been survived instead of what has been done. _(e.g. “my head is bloody, but unbowed” — the wound is admitted, and the head still will not go down — Invictus)_
  - **Blood that dirties everybody's hands** — Blood belonging to a whole city rather than to one killer. It spreads the guilt outwards, so ordinary people who never struck a blow are marked by the feud as well. _(e.g. “civil blood makes civil hands unclean” — the citizens' own blood, staining the citizens' own hands — Romeo and Juliet)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### The Moon `Mb`

The moon is the bright body seen in the night sky, which shines with the sun's light and changes shape through the month. Writers often use it for night, secrets, change, madness or love, because its light is dim and it keeps changing. Moonlight can also reveal what darkness hid, and a night with no moon can make a scene more dangerous. The moon is a kind of symbolism, where an object stands for an idea, and it does not always mean the same thing.

**The concept:** The moon lets a writer link a scene to night, change and the things people hide in the dark. Because its shape changes and its light is weak, it can suggest that people or feelings are changing too. In Frankenstein, Victor wakes from a nightmare, and “by the dim and yellow light of the moon” he sees the creature he made standing by his bed, so the moonlight shows him what he has done. When you find any moon in a text, say what shape and light it has, what happens while it shines, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “swear not by the moon, th' inconstant moon, / That monthly changes in her circled orb” — Juliet will not let Romeo swear by a light that changes every month, in case his love changes the same way — Romeo and Juliet; “the lane, which the maid’s window overlooked, was brilliantly lit by the full moon” — on the night Mr Hyde kills Sir Danvers Carew, a maid sees it all from her window by the moonlight — Jekyll and Hyde; “The moon is down; I have not heard the clock” — Fleance, Banquo's son, notes that the moon has set on the night Macbeth murders King Duncan, so the dark hides the deed — Macbeth

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the shape and light of the moon, and at what happens in its light. · Feel: We feel uneasy or excited, because the writer uses night and moonlight to show that people may act differently when hidden. · Think: We ask what the moon stands for, such as secrets, change, danger or love, and what the writer wants us to see. · Act: We notice when films and news treat night as a time for hidden acts, and ask what they want us to fear.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any moon in a story. 1. What is said or shown about the moon: its shape, its light, or how close it is? 2. What is happening to the characters while it shines? 3. What does it seem to stand for, such as secrecy, change, madness or desire? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through it? Try the questions on Othello. In Act 5 the moon is not described, but Othello says “She comes more nearer earth than she was wont”. Othello has just killed his wife Desdemona. Her maid Emilia has come in to report a killing in the town. The moon stands for madness: “And makes men mad.” Shakespeare may want the audience to notice that Othello looks for a cause outside himself, when his own jealousy has driven him.
