**Examples:** “get thee to church a Thursday, / Or never after look me in the face.” — Capulet orders his daughter Juliet to marry Paris, a young nobleman, on Thursday, so she must find a way out of marrying Paris before that day — Romeo and Juliet; “Tomorrow, as he purposes.” — Macbeth tells Lady Macbeth that King Duncan, who is coming to stay at their castle tonight, plans to leave the next day, so they have one night if they mean to kill him — Macbeth; “If you repay me not on such a day” — Shylock, a moneylender, agrees to lend Antonio money for three months, but if it is not repaid on the day, Shylock may cut a pound of flesh from Antonio's body — The Merchant of Venice

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the time that is left and measure every action against it. · Feel: We feel anxious, because we know how little time is left and fear the characters will be too late. · Think: We ask what the deadline forces the characters to choose, and what that choice shows about them and the writer's message. · Act: We notice how adverts and news reports use countdowns to hurry us, and ask who gains when we rush.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any ticking clock, a deadline that makes the action hurry. 1. What deadline does the text set, and who or what fixes it? 2. What must be done before the deadline, and what is lost if it is missed? 3. How does the text remind the reader of the time, such as a clock, a date, or a character counting? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand as time runs out? Try the questions on Cinderella, in Charles Perrault's version of the fairy tale, as translated in The Blue Fairy Book. Cinderella's fairy godmother, who has turned a pumpkin into a coach and her rags into clothes of gold and silver, sets the deadline: she is “not to stay till after midnight”. Cinderella must leave the ball before then. If she stays longer, the coach becomes a pumpkin again and her clothes turn back into her old rags. The text reminds the reader with the clock: on the first night she hears it strike “eleven and three-quarters”. On the second night she forgets, counts the clock striking twelve, and runs, leaving a glass slipper behind. Perrault may want the reader to feel the thrill of an evening that she can only have until midnight, and the fear of losing it.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character needs to do, and fix one time limit for it. Tell the reader the limit early, in speech, a date or a clock. Mention the time again at two or three later points, each time with less left. Decide what is lost if the time runs out, and show it at the end. Check that the limit matters in every scene: if a scene would be the same without it, add a reminder or cut the scene.

**Related:** Tension, Suspense

### Flashback `Fb`

A flashback is a part of a story that jumps back in time to show something that happened earlier. After it, the story returns to the present. It may show a memory, a dream or a scene from the past. Writers use it to give the reader a fact from the past at the moment it matters most. A flashback is different from foreshadowing, which hints at what will happen later, because a flashback shows what has already happened.

**The concept:** A flashback shows that the past is still active in the present. The writer chooses the moment when an earlier event will affect the reader most, and past and present then explain each other. In Remains, a soldier home from war cannot stop seeing a man that he and other soldiers shot: “he's here in my head when I close my eyes”. The poem keeps jumping from the present to that day, so the past will not stay finished. When you find any flashback, say what brings it back, what earlier moment it shows, and how it changes the way you read the present.

**Examples:** “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.” — the Ghost of Christmas Past takes Scrooge, now a rich old man, back to his old school, where he sees himself as a lonely boy at Christmas — A Christmas Carol; “Yet who would have thought the old man to have had so much blood in him?” — Lady Macbeth, walking in her sleep, speaks of King Duncan's blood as if she were back in the night he was killed — Macbeth; “I am a Worcestershire man myself,—born near Pershore.” — Jonathan Small, caught by Holmes and the police, tells his story, and the last chapter goes back to his youth — The Sign of the Four

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We follow the story back in time and read the earlier moment as an explanation. · Feel: We feel the weight of the past, because we now know what an earlier moment led to. · Think: We read the present again in the light of the past, and ask what the writer is saying about memory, guilt or change. · Act: We notice when a smell or a song brings a memory back, and think about how the past shapes what we do now.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any flashback, a jump back in time to show an earlier moment. 1. What signals the move from the present into the past? 2. What earlier moment does it show? 3. Where does the story return to the present? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by showing that earlier moment at this point? Try the questions on The Great Gatsby by F. Scott Fitzgerald. In Chapter 8 the narrator, Nick Carraway, signals the move with “It was this night that he told me”, which begins Gatsby’s account of his youth. Gatsby tells Nick his past through the night. The earlier moment is Gatsby's first love for Daisy. He visits her house as a young army officer, and she marries Tom Buchanan while Gatsby is studying at Oxford, where the army sent him after the war. The story returns to the present at “It was nine o’clock when we finished breakfast”, with Gatsby still unwilling to leave until he knows what Daisy will do. Fitzgerald may want readers to see, as Gatsby's hope fades, how much of his life is built on that lost time with Daisy.

**How to create it:** Decide which earlier moment the reader needs, and where in the present it will matter most. End the present scene with a detail that triggers the memory, such as a smell, a sound or a name. Tell the memory as its own scene. Return to the present with a clear marker, such as a time or a place. Check that the memory changes how the reader sees the present; if it does not, cut it.

**Related:** In Medias Res, Foreshadowing

### Prologue `Pg`

A prologue is a short passage placed before the main story begins. It may give background, name the subject, set a mood, or tell the reader how the story will end. It is often spoken by a narrator, or by a chorus, a speaker or group outside the story who comments on it. An epic is a long poem about heroes, and many epics begin with a prologue that names their subject. A prologue does not have to give the ending: some only set the scene.

**The concept:** A prologue tells the audience what a story is about before it begins, and sometimes how it ends. This gives the reader something to watch for, not only what will happen but why it matters. In Blood Brothers, the Narrator opens by telling us how the twins Mickey and Edward die: a mother cries “My own dear sons lie slain.” We watch the whole play knowing that both boys will die, so each happy moment is sadder. When you write about any prologue, say who speaks it, what it tells the reader to expect, and how that changes the way you read the story.

**Examples:** “A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life” — the Chorus tells the audience that Romeo and Juliet will die; “star-cross'd” means ruined by fate — Romeo and Juliet; “Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans.” — before the story begins, the poet asks a goddess to sing of a quarrel and the harm it caused to the Greeks, so we know the subject at once — The Iliad; “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” — the Gospel opens with a prologue before the story of Jesus's life, saying that Jesus, called “the Word”, was with God from the beginning — The Bible (John)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are told what a story is about before it begins, and we read each scene with that in mind. · Feel: We feel expectation, and sometimes dread, because the prologue has told us what kind of story this will be. · Think: We ask how the ending will come, or why the story matters, and what the writer wants us to learn. · Act: We notice when trailers and headlines tell us what to expect before we see anything, and ask what they want us to feel.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any prologue, a short passage placed before the main story. 1. Who speaks the prologue, and who is spoken to? 2. What does it give the reader: background, a mood, a hint of the ending, or something else? 3. What does the writer want the reader to expect or understand before the story begins? Try the questions on the opening lines of the Odyssey, the Greek epic poem by Homer, in Samuel Butler’s English translation. The poet speaks. He asks the Muse, a goddess of poetry and inspiration, to tell the story: “Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero”. The prologue gives background: the hero travelled far and wide after the Greeks took the city of Troy, and suffered much at sea. It also gives a hint of the ending: he cannot save his men, who die through their own folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god, so the god stops them reaching home. The poet may want the audience to expect a long, hard journey home and the loss of his crew, and to wonder how the hero will fare.

**How to create it:** Decide what the reader needs before the story starts: background, a mood, or a hint of the ending. Choose who speaks it, such as a narrator or a character standing outside the story, and who they speak to. Write it as a short passage that stops before the action begins. Check that each line prepares something that happens later; if a line does not, cut it.

**Related:** Epic

### Deus Ex Machina `Dx`

A deus ex machina is a sudden rescue from outside the story's events. It may be a god, a coincidence, a stranger who arrives at the right moment, or an unexplained sign. The Latin means a god from a machine: in ancient Greek theatre, a crane lowered an actor playing a god onto the stage. It often comes in the denouement, the part of a story where the problems are settled. If the story prepared for the rescue earlier, it is not one.

**The concept:** A deus ex machina ends a problem without the characters solving it. When the rescue comes from outside the story, the characters are spared the choice that the story was building towards, so the ending can feel like a trick. In The War of the Worlds, the Martians who invaded England are killed by bacteria, tiny living things that cause disease, which their bodies could not resist. Wells says they were “slain, after all man's devices had failed, by the humblest things”. When you write about any deus ex machina, say what problem it solves, who or what solves it, and whether the story prepared for it.

**Examples:** “The huntsman was just passing the house” — a wolf has swallowed Little Red Riding Hood, and a hunter who has not appeared earlier in the tale happens to pass by and save her — Little Red Riding Hood; “Jane! Jane! Jane!” — Jane is being pressed by St John, a clergyman, to marry him and go to India, when she hears Rochester's voice calling her from far away, and she leaves to find him — Jane Eyre; “clap your hands; don't let Tink die” — Tinker Bell, a fairy, is dying, and Peter Pan asks children outside the story to clap, and the clapping saves her — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch for the moment a solution arrives from outside the story, and ask where it came from. · Feel: We feel relief at the rescue, mixed with a sense that the ending is a trick. · Think: We ask whether the characters solved their problem or it was simply stopped, and what the writer's message is about luck, fate or power. · Act: We notice when films and news stories end with a lucky rescue, and ask whether the problem was really solved.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any deus ex machina, a sudden rescue from outside the story that solves a problem the characters could not solve. 1. What problem do the characters seem unable to solve? 2. What ends the problem, and where does it come from: a character's own choice, nature, chance, or magic or a god? 3. Is the rescue set up in advance, or does it arrive suddenly? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand about the ending? Try the questions on Cinderella, in Charles Perrault's version. The problem: Cinderella, who works as a servant in her stepmother's house, cannot go to the ball given by the king's son. She has no dress, coach or horses, and her stepsisters have left without her. The rescue is her godmother, a fairy, who turns a pumpkin into a coach and dresses her for the ball. It comes from magic: a fairy, much like a god, who steps in from outside. It is not set up: the godmother is first mentioned at the moment Cinderella is crying, and Cinderella does nothing to bring her. Perrault may want a wish granted to a good girl, so the story feels like a gift rather than a problem she solves herself.

**How to create it:** Choose a problem your characters cannot solve with what they have. Bring the rescue from outside their control, such as a ruler arriving, a storm or a message. Do not prepare the reader for it: nothing earlier should point to it. Keep the rescue scene short. Check that nothing earlier in your story points to the rescue; if something does, the story has prepared for it, and it is no longer a deus ex machina.

**Related:** Denouement

### Juxtaposition `Jx`

Juxtaposition is placing two very different things next to each other: two images, ideas, scenes or people. Each one then stands out more clearly because of the other. Juxtaposition is not quite the same as contrast. Contrast is any difference; juxtaposition is the choice to put the two different things side by side, often in one line or one moment. Writers use juxtaposition to expose hypocrisy, to create irony, or to make a gap hard to ignore, such as the gap between rich and poor.

**The concept:** With juxtaposition, a writer makes a point by placing two things side by side instead of stating it. The word comes from the Latin “juxta”, meaning “next to”, and the method works in a single line or between two scenes. Because the reader makes the comparison, the conclusion can feel like the reader's own. In An Inspector Calls, the Inspector rings the doorbell just as Birling says “a man has to mind his own business”, so the play challenges his selfish belief as he states it. When you find any juxtaposition, say what conclusion the writer wants you to reach, and why the writer leaves you to reach it.

**Examples:** “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.” — the Ghost of Christmas Present, a jolly spirit surrounded by food and plenty, reveals two starving children hidden in his robe, named Ignorance and Want (an old word for poverty), so plenty and poverty stand side by side — A Christmas Carol; “Two approaching donkey-carts in front of a cloud of fumes and dust created by some fifty vehicles roaring up in their wake” — two small donkey-carts lead a huge, roaring crowd of fifty vehicles, and that mismatch is the joke — A Game of Polo with a Headless Goat; “Did he who made the Lamb make thee?” — the gentle lamb and the fierce tiger (“thee”) share one line, which makes the reader ask how one maker could create both — The Tyger

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: Our eye is pulled between the two things placed together. · Feel: The sudden clash can shock us, or make us angry when one thing shows the other to be false. · Think: We read the meaning their nearness creates, which neither carries alone. · Act: We notice when two things are placed side by side in news, adverts or speeches, and ask what conclusion we are being led to.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any juxtaposition. 1. Which two things are placed side by side, and how close together: in one line, or in two scenes? 2. Exactly how are they different? 3. What does putting them together show that neither shows on its own? 4. What conclusion does the writer want the reader to reach without saying it? Try the questions on Ozymandias. “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” stands right beside “Nothing beside remains”. The king's boast and the empty desert, placed together, show that his power has gone. The reader concludes that no ruler's power lasts for ever.

**How to create it:** To use juxtaposition, choose two things from the same scene or subject that clash, such as a rich family's dinner and a hungry worker outside. Put them next to each other, in one sentence or in two moments one after the other. Do not explain the difference: let the reader see it and draw the conclusion.

**Related:** Contrast, Antithesis

### Red Herring `Rk`

A red herring is a false clue that leads the reader to suspect the wrong thing. It is common in mystery stories, where the writer plants it so that the real answer comes as a surprise. The name comes from a strong-smelling smoked fish, which was said to be dragged across a trail to put hunting dogs off the scent. A red herring differs from foreshadowing, which is a true hint of what will happen later. A fair red herring says nothing false, but it points the wrong way.

**The concept:** A red herring keeps a mystery alive by making a wrong answer look right. A fair one tells no lies, so when the truth arrives the reader can look back and see how they were led astray. In Great Expectations, Pip, a poor boy, is told a secret person will make him a gentleman, and he decides it is Miss Havisham, a rich old woman: “Miss Havisham was going to make my fortune on a grand scale.” He is wrong, and the truth stays hidden for many chapters. When you write about any red herring, say what it makes the reader suspect, and what the truth is.

**Examples:** “perhaps Grace Poole” — Jane hears a strange laugh in Thornfield Hall, and Mrs Fairfax, the housekeeper, names Grace Poole, a servant, but the laugh really comes from Rochester's wife, who is hidden in the attic — Jane Eyre; “the late Mr. Darcy bequeathed me the next presentation of the best living in his gift” — Wickham tells Elizabeth that Darcy cheated him of a church post, which makes Darcy look cruel until Darcy's letter shows that Wickham lied — Pride and Prejudice; “I arrest you in the Queen's name as being concerned in the death of your brother.” — the detective Athelney Jones arrests Thaddeus Sholto for the murder, which points the case at the wrong man, and Holmes says he can clear him — The Sign of the Four

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We follow the false clue and fix our attention on the wrong person or thing. · Feel: We feel sure of ourselves, then surprised and a little foolish when the clue fails. · Think: We look back to see how the writer led us wrong, and ask what the mistake shows about how easily appearances mislead. · Act: We notice when a news story, rumour or advert points us towards the wrong cause, and check the evidence before we agree.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any red herring, a false clue that leads the reader to suspect the wrong thing. 1. What false clue does the text plant, and what does it make the reader suspect? 2. How does the writer make the clue seem important? 3. When and how is the clue shown to be false, or to lead somewhere else? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand when the clue fails? Try the questions on The Hound of the Baskervilles by Arthur Conan Doyle. Dr Watson, the friend of the detective Sherlock Holmes, sees Barrymore, the butler of Baskerville Hall, creeping at night with a candle to a window. The reader may suspect that Barrymore is plotting against Sir Henry Baskerville, the hall's new owner. Watson describes the butler's appearance as “indescribably guilty and furtive”, and he and Sir Henry sit up two nights to catch him. Barrymore's wife then explains that the candle is a signal to her brother Selden, an escaped convict hiding on the moor, who needs food. The secret is real, but it is not a plot against Sir Henry; the real villain is a neighbour, Stapleton. Conan Doyle may want the reader to look first at the household, so that the real danger comes as a surprise.

**How to create it:** Decide who or what is really behind the mystery, and keep it hidden. Choose a different suspect, and give that person a secret that looks guilty. Show the secret early, with a detail that points to the wrong answer. Later, show what the secret really is. Check that every line you wrote is true, even if it misleads; if a line states something false, change it.

**Related:** Foreshadowing, Mystery

### Parallel Narrative `Xc`

A parallel narrative is a story told in two storylines of equal importance, which the writer switches between. The two storylines may be about different people, places or times, and they often move towards a meeting. It is different from a subplot, a smaller story that supports the main one, because neither storyline is the smaller one. It is also different from a framed narrative, a story told inside another story. A parallel narrative does not always bring its storylines together.

**The concept:** A parallel narrative makes the reader compare. When two storylines run side by side, each is read against the other, so a difference between them becomes a point about the world. Blood Brothers begins with twin boys born to one mother, and the Narrator says that “one was kept and one given away”. Mickey grows up poor and Edward grows up rich, and the play moves between their lives. When you write about any parallel narrative, say what the two storylines share, how they differ, and what the writer wants us to learn by setting them side by side.

**Examples:** “There were a king with a large jaw and a queen with a plain face, on the throne of England; there were a king with a large jaw and a queen with a fair face, on the throne of France.” — Dickens describes England and France in matching sentences, and the novel then moves between London and Paris — A Tale of Two Cities; “a boy was born to a poor family of the name of Canty, who did not want him. On the same day another English child was born to a rich family of the name of Tudor, who did want him.” — two boys are born on one day, one poor and one rich, and the novel then follows both — The Prince and the Pauper; “In the meantime I will go to Ithaca, to put heart into Ulysses' son Telemachus” — the goddess Minerva says this while the gods plan to send Ulysses home, so the poem starts two storylines, the father's journey and the son's search, which meet in Ithaca — The Odyssey

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We switch between two storylines and look for what they have in common. · Feel: We feel suspense as the storylines move closer, because we can see a meeting coming. · Think: We compare one storyline with the other and ask what the difference teaches us about the world the writer shows. · Act: We put two people or places side by side in real life, and ask what the contrast shows.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any parallel narrative, two storylines of equal weight told side by side. 1. Which two storylines does the text run side by side? 2. What do the two storylines have in common? 3. Do the two storylines meet, and if they do, where? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by setting the storylines side by side? Try the questions on The Merchant of Venice by William Shakespeare. One storyline is in Venice, where Antonio, a merchant, agrees a bond with the moneylender Shylock to borrow money for his friend Bassanio. The other is in Belmont, where Bassanio courts Portia, a rich heiress. Both depend on a risky choice made for love or friendship: Bassanio chooses among three caskets, and Antonio risks a pound of his own flesh. They meet in Belmont, in Act 3 Scene 2, when Bassanio reads a letter saying that Antonio's “ships have all miscarried” and that he cannot repay Shylock. They meet again in Venice when Portia, dressed as a doctor of laws, comes to Antonio's trial. Shakespeare may want the reader to compare the two risks, one that leads towards love and one that leads towards danger.

**How to create it:** Choose two storylines with a clear link, such as two people who will meet or two choices that affect each other. Give each storyline its own place or characters, and decide where they will meet. Cut between them, ending each section on a question or a worry. Repeat an object, a phrase or a kind of event in both storylines. Check that the meeting changes both storylines; if one of them stays the same, rewrite the meeting.

**Related:** Subplot, Framed Narrative

### Withholding Information `Wh`

Withholding information means that the writer keeps an important fact from the reader and reveals it later. The reader knows less than the writer, and sometimes less than a character, so questions stay open and suspense grows. Suspense is the anxious feeling of waiting to find out what happens. Withholding is the opposite of dramatic irony, where the reader knows more than a character does. Often the fact comes out in the end, but a writer may leave part of it unsaid.

**The concept:** Withholding makes the reader's ignorance part of the story. While we do not know a fact, we ask questions, guess and feel suspense, and when the fact arrives it changes how we read what came before. In Never Let Me Go, the narrator says in her first lines, “I've been a carer now for over eleven years”, but does not explain what her job involves. Only gradually do we learn what it is and who the people she cares for are. When you find any withholding of information, say what is held back, how the writer hides it, and what the reveal changes.

**Examples:** “I've made a gentleman on you!” — Magwitch, a convict whom Pip helped as a boy, tells Pip that he, not Miss Havisham, has paid for Pip's life as a gentleman — Great Expectations; “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together.” — the Duke tells a visitor how his late wife's smiles ended, but never says what the commands were, so the reader must work out what he did — My Last Duchess; “Any particular reason why I shouldn't see this girl's photograph, inspector?” — Gerald, Sheila's fiancé, asks this after the Inspector, a police officer, shows a photograph of a dead girl to Mr Birling alone, so the audience does not know what it shows or who else knew her — An Inspector Calls

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the gap where a fact should be, and keep looking for clues to fill it. · Feel: We feel unease and curiosity, because we sense that something important is being kept from us. · Think: We build a picture from what we are given, then ask what the secret says about the people and society in the story. · Act: We ask what is missing when a story, advert or news report seems to be telling us everything.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any withholding of information, where the writer keeps an important fact from the reader until a chosen moment. 1. What fact does the text keep from the reader, and who already knows it? 2. How does the text hide it: what does it show or suggest instead? 3. When and how is it revealed? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand when the truth comes out? Try the questions on The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson. The hidden fact is that Dr Jekyll, a respected doctor, and Mr Hyde, a cruel man, are the same person. Jekyll knows it from the start, but Utterson, Jekyll's lawyer, does not, and neither does the reader. The text shows only strange links. Jekyll's will leaves everything to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde”, and Utterson's relative Mr Enfield guesses that Hyde is blackmailing a respectable man: “Blackmail, I suppose”. The truth comes in the last two chapters, first in a letter from Dr Lanyon, who sees a visitor drink a potion and turn into Jekyll: “there stood Henry Jekyll!”. Then Jekyll's own written account follows. Stevenson may want readers to look back and see that Jekyll's respectable life and Hyde's crimes belong to one man.

**How to create it:** Decide the one fact you will hold back, and the moment you will release it. Write the early scenes so that every sentence is true but that fact is left out. Give the reader a clue or two that point in a different direction. Release the fact in one clear scene. Check that the early scenes still make sense when you reread them knowing the secret; if one does not, rewrite it.

**Related:** Suspense, Unreliable Narrator

### Match Cut `Mq`

A match cut joins two parts of a work by ending one on an image and starting the next with a similar image. The term comes from film, where a shape or movement continues across a cut between shots. In writing, the image can be an object, an action or a phrase that ends one scene, stanza or chapter and begins the next. A motif is an image that returns many times in a text, but a match cut joins only two neighbouring parts.

**The concept:** A match cut makes two parts of a work feel connected. The echo tells the reader that the two moments belong together, and the difference between the two images shows what has changed. In Macbeth, Act 2 Scene 2 ends with Macbeth's cry, “Wake Duncan with thy knocking!”, and Scene 3 opens with the Porter, a drunken servant, saying “Here's a knocking indeed!” The knocking that frightens Macbeth is a joke to the Porter. When you find any match cut, say what is repeated, what has changed, and what the writer wants us to connect.

**Examples:** “YES! and the bedpost was his own.” — Stave Four ends with the Phantom of the Future shrinking into a bedpost, and Stave Five opens on that bedpost, so Scrooge's terror turns to joy at being back in his own bed — A Christmas Carol; “Three nights later old Major died peacefully in his sleep.” — Chapter One ends with the whole farm asleep after Major's speech, and Chapter Two opens by saying that Major died in his sleep — Animal Farm; “But the privations, or rather the hardships, of Lowood lessened.” — Chapter Eight ends with Jane saying she would not swap Lowood, her school, with all its privations for her old home, and Chapter Nine opens by repeating the word “privations” — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We carry an image from the end of one part into the start of the next. · Feel: We feel the pleasure of a clever link, and sometimes a shock when the same image means something new. · Think: We notice what the repeated image shows, and ask what idea in the story the link supports. · Act: We notice how films, adverts and speeches join two ideas with one repeated image, and ask what the link wants us to believe.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any match cut, where one scene or stanza ends on an image that the next one picks up. 1. What image, object or movement ends the first part? 2. What picks it up at the start of the next part, and what has changed? 3. What does the writer or filmmaker want the reader or viewer to understand by joining the two parts? Try the questions on the opening sequence of the Pixar film Up. Carl's wife Ellie has died. After her funeral Carl sits on some steps, holding a balloon, and then climbs the steps. Those steps become the steps up to his own house, so the first part ends on the funeral steps and the next picks them up at his home. What has changed is the place: he has gone from the funeral to the house he shared with Ellie, and he goes in alone, pulling the balloon in after him. The filmmakers may want the viewer to feel that his grief comes home with him, and that the house keeps their memories.

**How to create it:** Choose two parts of your piece that you want to join, such as two scenes or two stanzas. End the first part on one clear image, object or phrase. Begin the second part by returning to that image, object or phrase, in a new place, time or voice. Check that the image has changed in size, meaning or feeling between the two parts; if it has not, choose a different image.

**Related:** Cyclical Structure, Motif

### Omniscient Narrator `Oi`

An omniscient narrator is a storyteller outside the story who can know everything about it. This narrator can describe any character's thoughts, move between places and times, and say what will happen later. Omniscient means all-knowing. It is a kind of third-person narrator, who says he or she, but a limited third-person narrator knows only one character's thoughts. An omniscient narrator may say “I” to speak to the reader, but unlike a first-person narrator, it is not a character in the story.

**The concept:** An omniscient narrator gives the story a voice that can see and judge everything. Because the narrator knows more than any character, the writer can show a whole society and guide what we think of each person. Jane Austen opens Pride and Prejudice by stating a belief as if everyone shares it: “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” The narrator jokes about a belief the nearby families share. When you write about any omniscient narrator, say what it knows that no character knows, whom it judges, and how that guides the reader.

**Examples:** “Mollie, the foolish, pretty white mare who drew Mr. Jones's trap” — the narrator, standing outside the animals, calls Mollie “foolish” before she has said or done anything, and so tells us what to think of her — Animal Farm; “All children, except one, grow up.” — the narrator opens with a fact about every child, and about the one who never grows up, before we have met any of them — Peter Pan; “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times” — the narrator describes a whole age and two countries in one breath, which no single character could do — A Tale of Two Cities

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are guided by a voice that sees everything, including inside people's minds. · Feel: We feel guided and sure, because someone who knows everything is telling us what matters. · Think: We weigh the narrator's judgements of people and society against what the characters say about themselves. · Act: We ask who is telling us the story when we read a news report or a history, and what they chose to leave out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any omniscient narrator, a storyteller outside the story who can know every character's thoughts. 1. Whose thoughts and feelings does the narrator tell us directly? 2. Where does the narrator know something no single character could, or speak straight to the reader? 3. Does the narrator judge anyone, and how can you tell? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through this wide view? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens. The narrator tells us Scrooge's hidden fear of Marley's ghost: he jokes “as a means of distracting his own attention, and keeping down his terror”. It also tells us the Cratchit family's thoughts: “nobody said or thought it was at all a small pudding”. It knows that “no man or woman ever once in all his life inquired the way” of Scrooge. It also speaks as “I”, saying “I don't mean to say that I know”. It judges Scrooge harshly, calling him “a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner”. Dickens may want readers to compare Scrooge, whom even dogs avoid, with the poor but loving Cratchits.

**How to create it:** Decide how much your narrator can know: the thoughts of several characters, and events they cannot see. Show one character's hidden feeling in a sentence, such as a person who looks calm but is afraid. Show what a whole group thinks. Add one comment in the narrator's own voice, to the reader or about a character. Check that the comments make the reader see something the characters cannot; if they just repeat the action, cut them.

**Related:** Third-Person

### Second-Person Narration `Yo`

Second-person narration speaks to “you” as if the reader or listener is the person the text is about. The writer uses “you” and words such as “your”, and often the present tense. “You” may be the reader, or one person whom the speaker addresses, such as a child or a friend. It differs from first-person narration, which says I, and from third-person narration, which says he, she or they. A text may use “you” throughout, as a whole poem or book does, or only for a few lines.

**The concept:** Second person puts the reader inside the text. When a writer says “you”, the reader feels spoken to and may imagine being that person. In If, Rudyard Kipling speaks to “you”, a son, and tells him how to behave: “If you can keep your head when all about you are losing theirs and blaming it on you”. The advice fits any reader, so we imagine ourselves in the place of “you”. When you write about any second-person text, say who “you” is, what “you” is asked to feel or do, and why the writer chose “you”.

**Examples:** “you might have got a hearse up that staircase” — the narrator speaks to “you”, the reader, and asks us to picture Scrooge's wide staircase, so we imagine standing on it — A Christmas Carol; “If in some smothering dreams you too could pace Behind the wagon that we flung him in” — after describing a gas attack as “we”, Owen turns to “you” and asks the reader to imagine walking behind the cart that carries a soldier hurt by gas — Dulce et Decorum Est; “You might think that the sea is company” — in a poem told by “we”, the people of an island, Heaney speaks to “you”, so the reader is asked to imagine living there — Storm on the Island

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the word “you” and ask who it points to, and whether it points to us. · Feel: We feel addressed and involved, and sometimes uncomfortable, because we cannot simply watch from outside. · Think: We ask whether “you” is really us, and what the writer wants us to understand about the subject by putting us in that place. · Act: We notice when adverts, instructions and speeches say “you”, and ask what they want us to do or think.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any second-person narration, a story told as “you”. 1. Who is “you”: the reader, or a particular character the reader is asked to become? 2. Does “you” choose anything, or is “you” carried along by events? 3. How does the text make the reader feel: comfortable, uneasy or excited? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel by using “you” instead of “I”, “he” or “she”? Try the questions on Choose Your Own Adventure books. “You” is the reader, who takes the role of a character such as a detective or an explorer. “You” chooses at set points by turning to a numbered page, and each choice decides what happens next. The text tells you where you are and what you see, then asks what you do, so it feels more like a game than a story. The feeling is mostly excitement, with some unease when a choice leads to a bad ending. The writer wants the reader to feel responsible for the outcome, because every choice leads to a result the reader has to live with.

**How to create it:** Decide who “you” is: a named character, or a role such as a detective or a runner. Write one page in the second person, with “you” doing and feeling things in the present tense. Give “you” a choice that the reader may not want to make. Check that the narration still treats “you” as the one acting and has not slipped into “I” or “he”. Then ask a friend whether they felt inside the scene; if not, add one thing that “you” can see, hear or touch.

**Related:** Third-Person, First-Person, Direct Address

### Scene vs Summary `Vs`

Scene and summary are two ways of telling an event. A scene shows the event moment by moment, with speech and action, so the reader watches it happen. A summary reports the event in a few words, so a long time passes quickly. Writers mix the two to control pacing, which means how fast or slow the story feels. A writer can also leave an event out completely, which is called an ellipsis.

**The concept:** A writer often shows the moments that matter in full and reports the rest in a few words. A scene slows time, so the reader looks closely. A summary speeds time up, so the reader moves quickly to what comes next. In chapter 6 of Animal Farm, “All that year the animals worked like slaves” reports a whole year of work in one sentence. When you write about any scene or summary, say which moments are shown in full, which are only reported, and what that choice tells readers about what matters.

**Examples:** “brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name)” — a wounded soldier tells King Duncan about a battle that the audience never sees, so the whole battle reaches us as a report — Macbeth; “Winter, spring, and summer passed away during my labours” — Victor Frankenstein reports months of work in one sentence, and the next chapter opens on a single night — Frankenstein; “He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew” — after showing Christmas morning in full, the last chapter reports the rest of Scrooge's life in a few sentences — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look closely at the moments shown in full, and pass quickly over the moments that are only reported. · Feel: We feel a moment more strongly when time slows into a scene, and feel the story hurry on when a summary skips ahead. · Think: We ask why the writer shows one event in full and only reports another, and what the writer wants us to care about. · Act: We notice when news reports, films and adverts show some events in full and skip others, and ask what they want us to remember.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any use of scene and summary. A scene shows an event moment by moment, with speech and action; a summary reports it quickly. 1. Which event does the writer show as a scene, and which does the writer report as a summary? 2. How much time does each cover, and how much space does each take on the page? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand about which moments matter, from what is shown in full and what is only reported? Try the questions on Jane Eyre by Charlotte Brontë. In chapter 1, Jane’s fight with her cousin John Reed is a scene: he hurls a book at her, and she answers “Wicked and cruel boy!” In chapter 10, her eight years at Lowood School are a summary: she writes “I now pass a space of eight years almost in silence”. The fight lasts a few minutes and takes a page or more of speech and action, while eight years take a few paragraphs, where Jane says “my life was uniform”. Brontë wants the reader to see that moments of conflict and change shape Jane, and that years of routine do not need to be watched.

**How to create it:** List the moments of your story, then mark the one or two that matter most to your reader. Write those as scenes, with speech, action and detail, moment by moment. Cover the rest in a sentence or two of summary, saying how much time has passed. Then check each summary: if it holds a moment the reader would want to watch, turn it into a scene. If a scene has no reason to be slow, shorten it to a summary.

**Related:** Pacing, Narrative Ellipsis

### Cause-and-Effect Plotting `Ce`

Cause-and-effect plotting means building a story so that each important event is caused by an earlier one. In an episodic story, events simply follow one another, and one could often be removed without changing the rest. A reader can test a plot by joining its events with the word therefore, which shows a cause, or with the words and then, which show none. Foreshadowing, a hint planted early about what will happen later, often helps this kind of plot.

**The concept:** Cause-and-effect plotting makes the ending of a story feel like the result of everything before it. Each event happens because of an earlier one, so the reader can trace the ending back step by step. In Frankenstein, the creature tells Victor Frankenstein, the scientist who made him, “I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.” He says that the misery he suffered turned him from a good creature into a cruel one. When you write about any cause-and-effect plot, say what causes each event, and what the writer wants us to learn from where the chain leads.

**Examples:** “each of you helped to kill her” — the Inspector tells the Birlings and Gerald Croft that each of them played a part in Eva Smith's death, after showing how each person's action added to her troubles — An Inspector Calls; “blood will have blood” — Macbeth says this after the ghost of Banquo, whom he had ordered killed, has appeared: he killed Duncan, then ordered Banquo's death, and now says that one killing brings another — Macbeth; “I made it link by link, and yard by yard” — the ghost of Marley, Scrooge's dead business partner, says he made his own chain while he was alive, so what he did then causes what he suffers now — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We trace each event back to the event that caused it, and stop expecting things to happen by chance. · Feel: We feel dread as each cause leads to its result, because the ending seems to come closer with every step. · Think: We ask who or what is responsible for each result, and what the writer wants us to learn about blame and consequences. · Act: We notice when news reports and adverts claim that one thing caused another, and ask whether the link is real.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any cause-and-effect plot, a plot where each event directly causes the next. 1. What is the first event in the chain, and what does it directly cause? 2. What does each later event cause, until the end? Join each pair with “therefore”, not “and then”. 3. Does any link depend on chance or a mistake, and if it does, what does that do to the chain? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from the way the events are linked? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. Tybalt kills Mercutio, and that makes Romeo kill Tybalt. Therefore the Prince banishes Romeo from Verona, and therefore Juliet weeps; Capulet, her father, thinking she is grieving for Tybalt, hurries her marriage to Paris. Therefore Juliet asks Friar Lawrence for help, and he plans for her to fake her death. Therefore he must send word of the plan to Romeo in Mantua. The message is stopped, so Romeo hears only that Juliet is dead. Therefore he buys poison and dies at her tomb, so when Juliet wakes from the drink and finds him dead, she kills herself. Yes: the message is stopped by chance, because plague inspectors shut Friar John, the messenger, inside a house, so the deaths follow from bad luck as well as from the feud. Shakespeare may want the audience to see that the feud turns small events into deadly ones, and that the lovers pay for a quarrel they did not start.

**How to create it:** Write your main events in order, one per line. Between each pair of events, write “therefore” and check that the second event is caused by the first. If a pair only works with “and then”, change the second event or add an event that connects them. Show the first cause early, so the reader can see the first link. Last, cover one event in the middle of your list; if the events on either side of it still join with “therefore”, the covered event is not needed.

**Related:** Foreshadowing

### Late Point of Attack `La`

A late point of attack means starting a scene as late as possible, when the action or conversation is already under way. The events that led up to the scene are left out, or mentioned only briefly. Writers who start a scene late often end it early too, soon after its most important moment. In medias res, a Latin phrase meaning in the middle of things, is a similar choice, but it usually describes where a whole story begins.

**The concept:** A late point of attack lets a writer cut what leads up to a scene, and spend the scene on what matters most. The reader often works out what came before from what the characters say. In Romeo and Juliet, Act 4 Scene 1 opens with Friar Lawrence answering Paris, who wants to marry Juliet: “On Thursday, sir? The time is very short.” The audience never hears what Paris said, but the reply shows Paris has said his wedding to Juliet is on Thursday. When you write about any late point of attack, say where the scene starts, what it leaves out, and why the writer cut it.

**Examples:** “I beheld the accomplishment of my toils” — a new chapter begins on the night Victor Frankenstein's long work is finished, and a few lines later the creature he has made opens its eyes — Frankenstein; “Come, Friar Francis, be brief: only to the plain form of marriage” — the wedding scene opens with Leonato, the bride's father, asking the friar to keep the service short, and soon after, Claudio refuses to marry the bride, Hero — Much Ado About Nothing; “Three thousand ducats, well.” — the scene opens partway through a talk: Shylock, a moneylender, is repeating the sum that Bassanio has asked to borrow, and the request itself is never shown — The Merchant of Venice

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We meet the characters close to the scene's key moment, when events are already under way. · Feel: We feel a sense of urgency and some uncertainty, because events are already under way and we have to catch up. · Think: We work out what happened before the scene, and ask what the writer wants us to notice by leaving it out. · Act: We notice when films, videos and news reports start at the most dramatic moment, and ask what they have left out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any late point of attack, a scene that starts at the last possible moment before its key action. 1. At what moment does the scene begin, and what is already happening when the reader arrives? 2. What does the scene not explain, so that the reader must work it out or wait? 3. At what moment does the scene end, and what is left unresolved? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand from arriving late and leaving early? Try the questions on Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 1. The scene begins with a doctor and a gentlewoman who serves Lady Macbeth already keeping watch for her. The doctor's first words are “I have two nights watched with you”. Lady Macbeth enters soon after, walking in her sleep. The scene does not show the two earlier nights. The gentlewoman will not repeat what Lady Macbeth said in her sleep, so the audience must wait to hear it from Lady Macbeth herself. The scene ends a few lines after Lady Macbeth goes back to bed. The doctor says, “I think, but dare not speak”, so what he thinks is left unsaid. Shakespeare may want the audience to feel shock, because Lady Macbeth's guilt is shown at once, in her own words, after only a short warning.

**How to create it:** Choose a scene and write down its key moment, such as an arrival, an argument or a decision. Start the scene as close to that moment as you can, with the characters already in the middle of what is happening. End the scene just after the key moment has happened. Cut any opening lines that explain how the characters got there. Then ask a friend to read from the new first line; if they cannot follow, add back one line of explanation.

**Related:** In Medias Res

### Zoom-In / Zoom-Out Ending `Zi`

A zoom-in or zoom-out ending is a way of closing a story by choosing how far away the reader stands at the end. A zoom-in ending finishes on one close detail, such as a single person, a hand or an object. A zoom-out ending pulls back to a wide view, such as a whole town, a crowd or a stretch of time. Either kind can end happily, sadly or without an answer. A cyclical ending, which returns to where the story began, is a different choice.

**The concept:** The distance at which a story ends can change what the reader is left thinking about. A close ending leaves the reader with one person or one detail, and a wide ending leaves the reader with a whole place, group or period of time. The last lines of Animal Farm stay close: the animals look through a farmhouse window at the pigs and the men, and the book says that “already it was impossible to say which was which”. When you write about any ending, say how close or how far away the last lines are from what they show, and what that distance leaves the reader thinking about.

**Examples:** “He was soon borne away by the waves and lost in darkness and distance.” — the creature leaves a ship's cabin and drifts out over the sea until he is out of sight, so the book ends on a wide, empty view — Frankenstein; “Some shall be pardon'd, and some punished” — the Prince's last speech looks past the two dead lovers to the people of the whole city, so the ending is a wide view — Romeo and Juliet; “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end” — the book closes inside one man's own letter, as Henry Jekyll finishes writing the account of his life, so the ending is a close one — Jekyll and Hyde

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice how near or how far away the last lines stand from what they show. · Feel: A close ending can feel personal and painful, and a wide one can feel calm or lonely, because one life looks small. · Think: We ask what the writer wants us to take away: the importance of one life, or how small it looks against the world. · Act: We notice how films, news reports and photographs end on a close face or a wide view, and how that changes our feelings.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any zoom-in or zoom-out ending, which closes on one close detail or pulls back to a wide view. 1. How close is the reader to the action in the last lines: close on one person, object or moment, or pulled back to a whole place, group or time? 2. How does that distance compare with the lines before it? 3. What feeling does the last image or line leave with the reader? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from ending at this distance? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol. The last lines pull back to everyone: “May that be truly said of us, and all of us!” Before this, the story stays mostly with Scrooge, who “knew how to keep Christmas well”, so the final sentences widen from one man to “us, and all of us”, which includes the readers. The last words are a blessing, “God bless Us, Every One!”, which leaves a warm, hopeful feeling. Dickens wants the reader to see that Scrooge’s change is something anyone can share in, so he ends by including the reader.

**How to create it:** Decide what feeling your last lines should leave, such as comfort, loss or hope. Choose a distance: close on one person, hand or object, or pulled back to a whole place or group. Write the last paragraph at that distance. Then ask a friend whether the ending feels close or far; if they say the opposite of your choice, change one detail.

**Related:** Cyclical Structure

### Callback `Ka`

A callback is a line said early in a story that comes back later, repeated or turned into its opposite. A different speaker can say it. The second moment makes the reader remember the first, and see what has changed in between. A callback is different from a motif, which is an image that returns many times, and from a refrain, which is a line repeated in a poem or song. A callback usually returns once, and the gap between the two moments carries the meaning.

**The concept:** A callback lets a writer show change without describing it: the reader hears the same words in a new situation and sees the difference. Because the reader makes the link, the second moment can feel sharper. In Macbeth, the three witches say “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” in the first scene. When Macbeth first appears, he says “So foul and fair a day I have not seen”, using their words, which he has not heard them say. When you find any callback, say where the line first appears, how it returns, and what has changed between the two moments.

**Examples:** “Are there no prisons?” — Scrooge says this to men collecting money for the poor in the first chapter, and in the third chapter the Spirit of Christmas Present says it back to him — A Christmas Carol; “Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast” — Friar Lawrence says this to Romeo in act two, and in act five, going to the tomb, he says “how oft tonight have my old feet stumbled at graves”, using the word “stumbled” again — Romeo and Juliet; “He said that Christmas was a humbug, as I live!” — Scrooge's nephew Fred says this at his party in the third chapter, repeating the word “humbug” that Scrooge used about Christmas in the first chapter — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look back to where the line was first heard, and compare the two moments. · Feel: We feel satisfaction or unease when words return, because we notice what has changed since we first heard them. · Think: We measure how far the speaker or the situation has changed, and what the writer is saying about that change. · Act: We notice when someone's old words are quoted back at them in the news or in an argument, and ask what has changed since.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any callback, a line planted early and echoed or reversed later. 1. Which line comes back, and where do we first hear it? 2. Is it repeated exactly, reversed or changed, and how? 3. What has changed between the two moments: the speaker, the situation or who has power? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from the gap between the two moments? Try the questions on Animal Farm. “All animals are equal” is first said by Old Major, an old pig, in chapter 1, and in chapter 2 it is painted on the barn wall as the Seventh Commandment. It returns in chapter 10, changed by the addition of “but some animals are more equal than others”. At first the line promises that no animal will rule the others; by chapter 10 the pigs rule the farm, and the new line gives them more rights than the rest. George Orwell wants the reader to see that rulers can change their own rules, and that a promise of equality can be turned into the opposite.

**How to create it:** Choose a line that a character says early, one that fits what that character believes at that moment. Plant it where the reader will hear it clearly. Later, bring the line back with one change, such as a different speaker, a reversed word or a new situation. Check that the situation has changed between the two moments; if it has not, add an event first, so the returning line shows how far things have moved.

**Related:** Motif, Foreshadowing

### Theme Stated `Tz`

Theme stated is a technique in which a minor character says the story's main idea aloud, in plain words, early on. The idea is usually about how people should live or what the world is like. The main character often ignores the line. Later events then test the idea, and the ending shows whether it was true. Most themes are not said aloud, and the reader works them out from what happens in the story.

**The concept:** A stated theme gives the story's main idea to a character to say aloud. The line comes early and sounds like ordinary talk, so the reader may not notice it, but the ending later answers it and proves the idea or breaks it. In Pride and Prejudice, Mary, one of Elizabeth's sisters, says in chapter 5, “Vanity and pride are different things”. Near the end, Darcy admits that he was given good principles but “left to follow them in pride and conceit”. When you find any stated theme, say who says it and when, what idea it states, and how the ending answers it.

**Examples:** “a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” — Scrooge's nephew Fred, not Scrooge, says this about Christmas in the first chapter, and by the end Scrooge has learned it is true — A Christmas Carol; “These violent delights have violent ends” — Friar Lawrence warns Romeo, just before his secret wedding, that intense joys can end in destruction, and the play ends with both lovers dead — Romeo and Juliet; “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” — the three witches say this in the first scene, before Macbeth has appeared, and Macbeth later says “So foul and fair a day I have not seen” — Macbeth

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice a line that sounds like ordinary talk but states an idea, and keep it in mind as the story goes on. · Feel: We feel a quiet unease, because an idea has been said aloud that we expect the story to test. · Think: We hold the stated idea against the events that follow, and ask what the writer wants us to learn from it. · Act: We notice when advice we ignored turns out to describe what happened later, and ask what it was telling us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any stated theme, a line in which a minor character says the story's main idea aloud, early on. 1. Which line states the idea, and who says it early in the story? 2. What does the line claim about life or people? 3. How do the story's events and ending treat the line: do they prove it, break it, or prove it at a cost? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from the way the story answers the line? Try the questions on Animal Farm. Old Major, an old prize boar, says it in chapter 1, before the animals rebel: “no animal must ever tyrannise over his own kind”. It claims that no animal should rule over others, because all animals are brothers. The story breaks the claim: Napoleon, a pig, takes charge and uses his dogs to frighten the other animals, and in the last chapter the pigs walk on two legs. George Orwell may want the reader to see that a promise of equality can be broken by the people who make it.

**How to create it:** Choose the idea your story will test, and write it as one plain sentence. Give it to a minor character near the start, and make it sound like that character's own opinion, spoken in passing. Let your main character ignore or misunderstand it. Make the ending answer the line by proving it, breaking it, or proving it at a cost. Check the line: if you can delete it and nothing in the story changes, rewrite the ending so that it answers the line.

**Ways to State the Theme** — A stated theme is a line of ordinary dialogue doing extraordinary work. These are the recurring ways writers plant one so it never sounds like a lesson — and the same moves are the ones to use in your own writing. The test for all of them: if you could delete the line and nothing later changes, it was decoration, not a stated theme.

- **WHO says it, and WHEN** — the line lands early, and never from the protagonist
  - **Given to a secondary character** — The protagonist has not earned the idea yet, so someone beside them says it — a nephew, a friend, a mentor. It also keeps the line free of the hero's self-justification. _(e.g. Fred calls Christmas “a kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” while Scrooge is still refusing to hear it — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Placed before we can understand it** — Stated so early that it registers as strange rather than as meaning; the reader only cashes it in at the end. _(e.g. “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” is spoken by the witches in the opening scene, before Macbeth has even appeared — Macbeth)_
  - **Aimed at someone not ready to hear it** — The listener's inability to take it in is the point — it dramatises the gap the story will close. _(e.g. “These violent delights have violent ends” — Friar Laurence warns a Romeo far too much in love to take the warning — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Restated at the close, so the story answers it** — The same argument returns once the events have tested it, and now it lands with everything behind it. _(e.g. “We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — the Inspector states the play's thesis only after every character has proved it — An Inspector Calls)_
- **HOW it stays disguised, so it never preaches** — it has to sound like the speaker's own words, not the writer's
  - **Said as a complaint, not a lesson** — Wrapped in the speaker's own grievance, so it reads as character rather than moral. _(e.g. “A guy needs somebody — to be near him” — Crooks is talking about his own loneliness, and states the novel's argument by accident — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **Said as a confession** — The speaker explains the theme about THEMSELVES, which makes it evidence rather than instruction. _(e.g. “man is not truly one, but truly two” — Jekyll's written confession states the book's whole argument about divided nature — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Given to the character nobody listens to** — The truth is spoken by the one voice the group dismisses, so the reader hears it while the characters do not. _(e.g. “What I mean is… maybe it's only us” — Simon names the real beast and is laughed down — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Said as a warning drawn from the speaker's own ruin** — Earned authority: the speaker has already paid for the knowledge, so the line carries cost rather than opinion. _(e.g. “Learn from me… how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge” — Victor states the novel's warning out of his own wreckage — Frankenstein)_

**Related:** Theme

### Enjambment `En`

Enjambment is when a sentence or phrase carries on past the end of a line of poetry into the next line, with no pause. The reader's eye reaches the end of the line, but the meaning is not finished, so the reader has to read on to complete it. A line that ends with a pause, usually a punctuation mark, is called end-stopped.

**The concept:** Enjambment lets a poet run a sentence past the end of its line, so the sentence can sound hurried, breathless or unstoppable. The reader gets no rest at the line-end, and the next line can add to the meaning or change it. In My Last Duchess, the Duke says, “I call / That piece a wonder”, as his sentence runs on while he shows a visitor the portrait of his last wife. When you write about any enjambment, say which words come before the line break, what the next line adds, and what the run-on shows about the speaker or the subject.

**Examples:** “If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well / It were done quickly” — Macbeth, alone, thinks about killing King Duncan, and the first line has no punctuation at its end, so the reader has to read on to the next line to finish the thought — Macbeth; “Such a waggoner / As Phaeton would whip you to the west” — Juliet, waiting for night so that Romeo can come to her, speaks to the horses that pull the sun, and her sentence runs over the line-break — Romeo and Juliet; “until the swans came and stopped us / with a show of tipping in unison” — the first line ends on “stopped us”, and the next line says how the swans stopped the walkers, so the reader has to read on — Winter Swans

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are carried over the end of the line, because the sentence has not finished. · Feel: We feel hurried or breathless, as if the speaker's feeling is too strong to stay inside each line. · Think: We ask why the poet lets the sentence run on at this point, and what that shows about the speaker's state of mind. · Act: We notice when speakers in speeches or interviews run on without pausing, and ask whether they are excited, nervous or hiding something.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any enjambment, a sentence that runs on past the end of a line. 1. Which words end a line before the sentence is finished, and which words finish it on the next line? 2. What does the reader expect at the line-end, and what does the next line add or change? 3. Does the run-on hurry the reader, hold the reader back, or surprise the reader? 4. What does the poet want the reader to understand about the speaker or the subject? Try the questions on Storm on the Island by Seamus Heaney, a poem about people preparing for a storm. The line “Which might prove company when it blows full” ends before the sentence is finished, and “Blast” on the next line completes it. The reader expects “full” to lead on to something, and the next line adds the force of the wind. The phrase “full blast” is split across two lines, so the wind seems to arrive with a jolt. The speaker begins with “We are prepared”, and the run-on may show that the storm's force is harder to control than the islanders say.

**How to create it:** Choose a sentence in your poem that carries a feeling of hurry, fear or longing. Break the line in the middle of that sentence, so the reader has to read on to finish it. Put the word you most want noticed at the end or the start of a line. Check each run-on by reading it aloud: if the line break does not change how the line sounds or what it means, move the break.

### Caesura `Ca`

A caesura is a pause in the middle of a line of poetry, usually made by punctuation. A full stop, comma, dash or semicolon can make one. It breaks the rhythm of the line, which is its pattern of beats. A line can have one caesura or several. The reader stops, so the words on each side of the pause stand out.

**The concept:** A caesura makes the reader stop in the middle of a line, so a line can show hesitation, shock or a change of thought. The words on each side of the pause feel separate, and the pause gives them weight. When Romeo sees Juliet at her window, he says, “It is the east, and Juliet is the sun”. The comma makes the reader pause between the place where the sun rises and the claim that Juliet is the sun. When you write about any caesura, say where the pause falls, which words come before and after it, and what the pause shows about the speaker or the subject.

**Examples:** “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” — the words on the statue's base; the commas split the line into three parts: the order to look, the people it speaks to, and the order to despair — Ozymandias; “This grew; I gave commands;” — the Duke describes his wife's smiling at everyone, and the semicolons cut his account into short steps without saying what the commands were — My Last Duchess; “I have thee not, and yet I see thee still” — Macbeth, alone, sees a dagger in the air and cannot grasp it, and the comma splits his line into two facts that disagree — Macbeth

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We stop in the middle of a line, and notice the words on each side of the stop. · Feel: A sudden stop can feel like hesitation, shock or held breath, because the flow of the line is broken. · Think: We ask why the poet stops the line at this point, and what the speaker is hesitating over or holding back. · Act: We notice the pauses in people's speech, such as in interviews or apologies, and ask what they are holding back.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any caesura, a pause in the middle of a line of poetry. 1. Where in the line does the pause fall, and which punctuation mark makes it? 2. Which words come before the pause, and which come after it? 3. What does the pause do to the rhythm: does it hesitate, shock, separate or slow? 4. What does the poet want the reader to understand about the speaker or the subject from the pause? Try the questions on Remains by Simon Armitage, a poem spoken by a soldier. The line ends with the words “probably armed, possibly not”, and in them the pause falls after “armed”, made by a comma. “Probably armed” comes before the pause, and “possibly not” comes after it. The comma splits two guesses, and the second guess weakens the first, so the line sounds uncertain. Armitage may want the reader to see that the soldiers fired without knowing whether the man was a threat.

**How to create it:** Choose a moment in your poem where the speaker hesitates, is shocked or changes their mind. Place a full stop, comma, dash or semicolon in the middle of that line, so that the line breaks into two parts. Put the word you want to stand out just before or just after the pause. Check the pause by reading the line aloud: if you can read straight through without stopping, move the punctuation or choose a stronger mark.

### Foreshadowing `Fo`

Foreshadowing is a hint, planted early in a story, about something that will happen later. The hint can be a line of speech, an object, a dream or a piece of weather. On a first reading it may seem unimportant, and when the event arrives the reader sees what it pointed to. A red herring is a false hint that makes the reader expect something that does not happen.

**The concept:** Foreshadowing makes a later event feel as though it was coming all along, even when it surprises the reader. The early hint gives a feeling of unease, and looking back, the reader can find it. In chapter 1 of Animal Farm, the old pig Old Major tells Boxer, a strong cart-horse, “Jones will sell you to the knacker”, which means a person who buys horses that are too old to work. In chapter 9, a van marked “Horse Slaughterer” takes Boxer away. When you find any foreshadowing, say what the hint is, what event it points to, and what the writer wants the reader to see in that link.

**Examples:** “my mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars” — Romeo says this on his way to a feast at the Capulets' house, where he will meet Juliet, and the play ends with both lovers dead — Romeo and Juliet; “the instruments of darkness tell us truths” — Banquo warns Macbeth that evil can tell small truths to lead people to harm, and Macbeth is then led to murder King Duncan — Macbeth; “disappearance or unexplained absence” — Dr Jekyll's will says that Edward Hyde gets his property if Jekyll disappears, and near the end of the book Jekyll cannot be found — Jekyll and Hyde

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice a small early detail, and cannot yet tell why it matters. · Feel: We feel a quiet unease, because we sense that something is waiting, though we do not know what. · Think: We ask what the hint says about where the story is going, and whether the writer thinks the outcome could have been avoided. · Act: We watch for early warning signs in a friend's mood or in the news, and think about what they might lead to.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any foreshadowing, a hint planted early about something that will happen later. 1. Which early detail points forward to a later event, and where does the story first show it? 2. Which later event does the detail point to? 3. How is the reader likely to feel on meeting the detail, before knowing what it means? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from the link between the early detail and the later event? Try the questions on Frankenstein. In chapter 5, soon after the creature comes to life, Victor Frankenstein dreams that he kisses Elizabeth, the girl he will marry, and that she turns into the dead body of his mother. The dream points to Elizabeth's death: in chapter 23 the creature kills her on her wedding night. A reader is likely to feel horror and unease, because a kiss turns into death for no reason that the story gives. Mary Shelley may want the reader to see that Victor's choice to make life leads to the loss of the people he loves.

**How to create it:** Choose the event you want to prepare readers for, such as a loss, a betrayal or a death. Plant a small hint near the start of your story, such as an object, a line of speech or a dream. Place it among other details, so that it does not stand out on a first reading. When the event arrives, bring the hint back, so the reader can link the two. Check by asking a friend to find the hint after reading the ending: if they cannot, make it clearer.

**Kinds of Foreshadowing** — One way of seeding what is to come, told many ways — each a different kind of hint the writer plants along the path of the story.

- **Kinds of foreshadowing** — How the writer signals what is to come
  - **Prophecy** — A foretelling spoken within the story that the plot then works to fulfil, often with a bitter twist. _(e.g. the witches hail Macbeth as one who "shalt be king hereafter" — Macbeth)_
  - **Direct Foreshadowing** — The narrator states the ending openly at the outset, so we read on to see how it comes about, not whether. _(e.g. the Prologue reveals the "star-cross'd lovers take their life" — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Character Premonition** — A character voices a private dread that the story later proves well-founded. _(e.g. “My mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars” — Romeo says he fears this night will begin something fatal, and it does — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Symbolic Image** — An object or image quietly carries the meaning of what is to come. _(e.g. “the rectangle of sunshine in the doorway was cut off” — she is only standing there, and every time she does the light goes out of the room — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **Ominous Atmosphere** — Weather and setting breed a dread of misfortune felt in the moment — foreboding. _(e.g. the creature stirs "on a dreary night of November" — Frankenstein)_
  - **Structural Mirror** — An earlier event rehearses a later one, so the first quietly predicts the second. _(e.g. “trampled calmly over the child's body” — Hyde's first act of violence rehearses the murder he commits much later — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Chekhov's Gun** — A detail deliberately placed early must "go off" later; nothing is left idle. _(e.g. "in case of the decease of Henry Jekyll" his possessions pass to Hyde — a will planted in chapter two that becomes the key to the whole mystery — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Flash-Forward (Prolepsis)** — The story depicts a future moment outright, rather than merely hinting at it. _(e.g. “You are about to show me shadows of the things that have not happened, but will happen in the time before us” — the story shows the future outright instead of hinting at it — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Dragon's Teeth** — A planted seed — a detail, a line, a place name — that sits between foreshadowing and foreboding and sprouts into significance later (Roy Peter Clark). _(e.g. "the devil's got your number" — the Narrator plants the line early and it returns to collect at the end — Blood Brothers)_

**Related:** Setup & Payoff, Red Herring, Flashback, Cause-and-Effect Plotting, Callback

### Rhyme Scheme `Rs`

A rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhyming sounds at the ends of the lines in a poem. Poets and students show it with letters: in ABAB, the first and third lines rhyme with each other, and the second and fourth lines rhyme with each other. Some poems keep one pattern all the way through, some change it, and some do not rhyme at all. A half-rhyme, where two sounds are similar but not the same, can also be part of a rhyme scheme.

**The concept:** A rhyme scheme can make a poem sound ordered, like a song or a spell. A break in the pattern can sound like unease or a loss of control. The reader hears the pattern before thinking about it, so a change stands out. In Macbeth, the three witches chant “Double, double, toil and trouble; / Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble” in rhyming pairs, which makes their words sound like a spell. When you write about any rhyme scheme, say what pattern the poem keeps, where it changes or stops, and what the order or the break shows.

**Examples:** “That's my last Duchess painted on the wall, / Looking as if she were alive. I call” — the Duke's lines rhyme in pairs, such as “wall” and “call”, but his sentences run over the line-breaks, so the rhyme is easy to miss — My Last Duchess; “Nothing beside remains.
