What a character avoids saying can tell us as much as what they say. In My Last Duchess, a duke, showing a portrait of his dead wife, says only, “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together.” He never says what the commands were, but the reader may suspect he had her killed. When you find any subtext, say what the character says, what they may really mean, and what stops them saying it.

**Examples:** “Yet if my name were liable to fear, / I do not know the man I should avoid / So soon as that spare Cassius.” — Caesar tells his friend Antony that he does not fear Cassius, then names Cassius as the first man he would avoid; the fear is under the words — Julius Caesar; “Nothing, my lord.” — Cordelia answers her father, King Lear, when he asks her to say how much she loves him; her private words, “Love, and be silent”, show that she loves him but will not praise him in showy words — King Lear; “I beg that you will spare me any allusion to one whom I regard as dead.” — Dr Lanyon tells Mr Utterson, a lawyer, that he wants no more contact with Dr Jekyll but does not say why; later the reader learns that Lanyon had seen something that shocked him badly — Jekyll and Hyde

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen for what a character avoids, what they leave out, and what they say instead of what they feel. · Feel: We feel the tension of an unspoken truth, because we sense a strong feeling that the character is holding back. · Think: We work out what the character really means, and ask what stops them saying it, such as fear, shame or politeness. · Act: We notice what people leave unsaid in real conversations, such as a short answer or a changed subject, and ask what they may mean.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any subtext, the meaning beneath the words that a character does not say. 1. What does the character say on the surface, and what is the situation? 2. What might the character really mean or feel, and which words, pauses or changes of subject point to it? 3. What stops the character saying it plainly, such as fear, shame, politeness or a plan to hide? 4. What does the writer want the reader to realise by leaving it unsaid? Try the questions on Macbeth, Act 3 Scene 1, when Macbeth talks to Banquo. Macbeth, now king, speaks politely to Banquo, his friend and fellow general, asking “Ride you this afternoon?”, how far he is riding, and whether his son Fleance goes with him. He seems to be checking when Banquo will be away and who will be with him, because he fears Banquo, as he admits when alone: “Our fears in Banquo”. He is king and wants to seem a friendly host, and saying his plan aloud would warn Banquo. Shakespeare lets the audience hear the plan inside the friendly words, so we see how a king can hide cruelty behind politeness.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character really wants to say but cannot. Choose a topic they can talk about instead, such as the weather, a meal or a journey. Write their speech about that topic, and let one detail show what they really mean, such as a pause, a question or a changed subject. Then show the lines to a friend and ask what the character is really thinking; if they cannot say, make the clue clearer.

**Related:** On-the-Nose, Show, Don't Tell, Blocking

### Subplot `Sl`

A subplot is a second, shorter story told alongside the main plot, usually about different characters with a problem of their own. Usually the subplot matches or contrasts with the main plot, and sometimes it changes what happens in the main plot. In a parallel narrative, by contrast, two stories of equal importance are told side by side.

**The concept:** A subplot lets a writer make the same point twice, or show its opposite, through a different story. Because readers compare the two stories, each one can make the other's meaning clearer. In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge is rich and lives alone, while his clerk, Bob Cratchit, earns fifteen shillings a week and has a loving family. When the Ghost of Christmas Present says that Bob's sick son, Tiny Tim, may die, and repeats Scrooge's own harsh words about the poor, Scrooge is ashamed. When you write about any subplot, say how it matches or contrasts with the main plot, and what the two stories show together.

**Examples:** “I ask only a comfortable home” — Charlotte Lucas, Elizabeth Bennet's friend, explains why she has agreed to marry Mr Collins, a clergyman whom Elizabeth refused because he could not make her happy, so Charlotte's story contrasts with Elizabeth's — Pride and Prejudice; “Will there still be sugar after the Rebellion?” — Mollie, a foolish, pretty white mare, asks Snowball this question; later she leaves the farm for a man who feeds her sugar, while the other animals stay and work, so her small story contrasts with theirs — Animal Farm; “Monster, I will kill this man: his daughter and I will be king and queen” — Stephano, a drunken butler, plans with Caliban to kill Prospero, who rules the island; this comic plot echoes the main one, in which Prospero's brother took his place as Duke of Milan — The Tempest

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch a second story beside the main one, and look for what the two stories have in common. · Feel: We feel the second story's own mood, such as amusement or worry, and it can change how we feel about the main one. · Think: We compare the two stories and ask what each one says about the theme, such as pride, duty or poverty. · Act: We notice when a news report or a film turns to a second person's story, and ask what it is meant to add.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any subplot, a second story running alongside the main plot. 1. What is the main plot, and what second story runs beside it? 2. How does the second story echo, contrast with or change the main one? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand from setting the two stories side by side? Try the questions on The Merchant of Venice by Shakespeare. The main plot is about a loan. Antonio, a merchant, borrows money from Shylock, a moneylender. If Antonio cannot repay it on time, Shylock may take a pound of his flesh. The second story is about Shylock's daughter, Jessica, who runs away from her father's house with Lorenzo, one of Antonio's friends, taking her father's money and jewels. The second story changes the main one. Antonio's friends mock Shylock about his daughter's escape. Straight afterwards, he calls his deal with Antonio “another bad match”, meaning another bad bargain, and warns three times, “let him look to his bond”. Shakespeare may want us to see how losing his daughter, and being mocked for it, makes Shylock want revenge even more.

**How to create it:** Decide the main problem of your story and the idea it tests. Choose a second character whose problem connects to it. Write the second story so that it matches or contrasts with the first. Check that a reader would notice the link; if they would not, make it clearer.

**Related:** Parallel Narrative

### Framed Narrative `Fn`

A framed narrative is a story told inside another story. A narrator may recall the past, read a found letter, or retell a tale that someone passed on. In a multiple-viewpoint story, several voices tell the tale side by side; in a frame, one voice sits inside another, so one account can shape or judge another. An epistolary narrative is a frame made of letters and other documents. A frame can be as short as one opening line.

**The concept:** A framed narrative reminds readers that every story has a teller, who chooses what to say. Because the reader sees the teller, we ask who is speaking, to whom, and why. In the Arabian Nights, a traditional collection of tales, Scheherazade tells the king a new story each night so that he will not put her to death. The outer story explains why the inner stories exist. When you write about any framed narrative, say who tells each layer, what each teller wants, and what the layers show together.

**Examples:** “1801—I have just returned from a visit to my landlord—the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with.” — Lockwood, a tenant, opens the novel in his diary, and his housekeeper, Nelly Dean, later tells him the long story of two families — Wuthering Heights; “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise” — Walton, a ship's captain, writes to his sister, and his letters hold Victor Frankenstein's story, which holds the creature's own account — Frankenstein; “He holds him with his glittering eye— / The Wedding-Guest stood still” — the Ancient Mariner stops a wedding guest and tells him his story, and the guest has to listen — The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice who tells each layer of the story, as well as what happens in it. · Feel: We feel some distance from events because someone else describes them, and we may trust or doubt that person. · Think: We ask why this teller tells this story, and what the teller's choices show about the story's subject. · Act: We ask who is telling us a story in the news, in adverts and in gossip, and what they leave out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any framed narrative, a story told inside another story. 1. Who tells the main story, and which other tellers, letters or documents sit inside it? 2. Who is each teller speaking to, and how much do they know? 3. What does each teller leave out or shape? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through these layers? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde by Robert Louis Stevenson. Most of the book follows Mr Utterson, a lawyer, as he investigates the strange behaviour of his friend Dr Jekyll. Near the end come two documents: “Dr Lanyon's Narrative” and “Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case”. Utterson reads both, so the reader sees them through him. Both documents are written for Utterson: Lanyon left his for “G. J. Utterson ALONE”, and Jekyll’s letter to go with his statement begins “My dear Utterson”. Dr Lanyon, a doctor and old friend of Jekyll, knows only what he saw on one night, while Jekyll knows the whole secret. Lanyon cannot say why it happened, and Jekyll tells the story in his own favour. Stevenson keeps the truth hidden until these last chapters, so the reader pieces it together as Utterson does.

**How to create it:** Decide the story you want to tell and the person who will tell it. Choose who that teller is speaking to and why they are telling it now. Let the teller shape the story by leaving something out or making themselves look better. Add a second teller or a document if you want another view. Then rewrite one paragraph as if a different person told it; if it reads the same, make your first teller's voice more distinct.

**Related:** Parallel Narrative, Epistolary Narrative, Multiple Viewpoint

### Ambiguous Ending `Ab`

An ambiguous ending is an ending that does not settle what happens, or what it means. The writer stops with the question still open, so a reader can reasonably reach two or more different answers. The story still reaches its last page; only the answer is missing. An ending is ambiguous only if the text supports more than one reading.

**The concept:** An ambiguous ending hands the last decision to the reader. The word "ambiguous" comes from a Latin word meaning doubtful. Because the writer gives no answer, the reader keeps thinking about the story's main question after the last page. In The Giver by Lois Lowry, Jonas, a boy who has left his community with a baby, sees lights and hears music at the end, but the book does not say plainly whether they are saved. When you write about any ambiguous ending, say what it leaves open, what each possible reading is, and what the earlier story says for each.

**Examples:** “a police inspector is on his way here – to ask some – questions” — Mr Birling repeats a telephone message that a girl has died and an inspector is coming, then the curtain falls before we learn what happens next — An Inspector Calls; “I saw no shadow of another parting from her.” — Pip, meeting Estella in the ruins of Miss Havisham's garden, sees no sign that they will part again, but the book does not say plainly whether they stay together — Great Expectations; “Was it a vision, or a waking dream? / Fled is that music:—Do I wake or sleep?” — the last lines ask whether the song was a vision or a waking dream, say that the music has gone, then ask whether the poet is awake or asleep, and give no answer — Ode to a Nightingale

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We stay with the question the ending leaves open, and look back for clues that point each way. · Feel: We feel unsettled and curious because the story stops before it answers its question, and we are left to decide. · Think: We weigh each possible ending against earlier events, and ask what question about the theme the writer wants us to keep asking. · Act: We notice when films, news stories or adverts stop before the answer, and ask what we are being left to decide.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any ambiguous ending, an ending that does not settle what happens. 1. What does the ending leave unsettled? 2. What different readings does it allow of what happens next? 3. What evidence earlier in the text supports each reading? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or take away by refusing a clear answer? Try the questions on Frankenstein by Mary Shelley. The ending leaves unsettled whether the Creature, the being Victor Frankenstein made, really kills himself. Either he burns his body on a funeral fire and dies, as he promises, or he drifts away alive. He says “I shall die” and speaks of his “funeral pile”. But the last sentence says only that he was “lost in darkness and distance”, and Walton, the ship's captain who tells the story, does not see him die. Shelley may want readers to keep thinking about whether the Creature, rejected by Victor, can ever escape the harm done to him.

**How to create it:** Decide the question you want your reader to keep thinking about. Plan two possible answers and give clues for both. Show your characters facing the choice, but stop before the result is clear. Leave the reader one clear image or line to think about. Then ask a friend what they think happened; if they see only one possible answer, add a clue for the other.

### Resolved Ending `Rn`

A resolved ending settles the story's main question or conflict. The reader finds out what happens to the main characters, and the main threads of the story are brought to a close. A resolved ending can be happy or sad: what matters is that the question is answered. Many resolved endings still leave one small thread open.

**The concept:** A resolved ending shows the result of a character's choices, so the reader leaves knowing what those choices cost or won. It works best when it follows from earlier events, because then the outcome seems fair and not accidental. In the best-known versions of Cinderella, the slipper fits, the prince finds the girl he has searched for, and they marry. That answers the question the story has asked all along: whether her kindness will be rewarded. When you write about any resolved ending, say what question it answers, which earlier events make that answer possible, and what it shows about the theme.

**Examples:** “Reader, I married him.” — Jane, who tells the story, says in the last chapter that she has married Rochester, after she left him and refused St John Rivers, so the question of whether they will be together is answered — Jane Eyre; “it was always said of him, that he knew how to keep Christmas well” — Dickens tells us near the end that Scrooge's change lasted, which answers whether he would stay kind — A Christmas Carol; “For never was a story of more woe / Than this of Juliet and her Romeo.” — after the lovers are dead and the two families have made peace, the Prince speaks these as the last lines of the play — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch each thread of the story come to its end, and check that none is left. · Feel: We feel relief or sadness at the outcome, and it feels fair when earlier events caused it. · Think: We ask whether the ending follows from what came before, and what it proves about the story's theme. · Act: We notice when news stories and adverts promise a neat solution, and ask what has been left out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any resolved ending, an ending that settles the story’s main conflict. 1. What conflict or question runs through the story, and how does the ending settle it? 2. Which questions or problems raised earlier does the ending answer, and does it leave any unanswered? 3. Does the outcome follow from what came before? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from what the ending gains and what it costs? Try the questions on Macbeth. The conflict is Macbeth’s seizing the crown by murder, and whether he will be punished. It ends when Macduff comes in with Macbeth’s head, says “the time is free”, and Malcolm is hailed “King of Scotland”. Malcolm promises to make his thanes earls and to call exiled friends home, and he says it is thought that Lady Macbeth killed herself. The witches’ promise that Banquo’s descendants will be kings is not settled, and Banquo’s son Fleance does not return on stage after he escapes in Act 3. Yes, it follows. The witches’ apparition told Macbeth that no man born of woman could harm him, and Macduff answers that he was “Untimely ripp’d” from his mother’s womb. The gain is a Scotland freed from a tyrant and ruled by a rightful king. The cost includes Macduff’s wife and children, killed earlier, and Siward’s son, killed in the battle. Shakespeare may want the reader to see that seizing power by murder destroys the ruler and many others, and that order returns under a rightful king.

**How to create it:** Choose the question your story asks at the start, such as whether a character will win something or lose it. Decide what the main character wins and what it costs. Write an ending in which the character’s own action answers the question. Answer each question or problem you raised in the middle. Check that you can name an earlier event that makes the ending possible; if you cannot, add one to your middle.

### IUMVCC `Iu`

IUMVCC is a plan for writing a persuasive piece, such as a speech, in six stages. The stages are Introduction (the opening), Urgency (why the problem matters now), Methodology (the steps to take), Vision (the better future), Counter-argument (an answer to people who disagree) and Conclusion (the ending). The name comes from the first letter of each stage. Writers using the plan write the stages in this order. In a piece written without this plan, you may find these stages in another order, joined together, or missing.

**The concept:** IUMVCC helps a writer to put all six stages into a persuasive piece, so that none is forgotten. Each stage has its own job, such as getting the audience's attention, giving steps to follow, or answering people who disagree. At Caesar's funeral in Julius Caesar, Mark Antony makes a Counter-argument to Brutus's claim that Caesar was ambitious: “When that the poor have cried, Caesar hath wept”. Antony argues that an ambitious man would not weep for poor people. When you write about any persuasive piece, say which stages it uses, in what order, what each one makes the audience feel or think, and which it leaves out.

**Examples:** “Let us face it: our lives are miserable, laborious, and short.” — this is Urgency: Old Major, a prize boar, shows the farm animals that the problem is happening now, in their own hard, short lives, before he calls for a rebellion against the humans — Animal Farm; “From this day to the ending of the world, / But we in it shall be remembered” — this is Vision: before the Battle of Agincourt, King Henry tells his outnumbered soldiers that they will be remembered every year on the day of the battle, Saint Crispin's day, until the end of the world — Henry V; “that government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth” — this is the Conclusion: Abraham Lincoln ends his speech at a cemetery for soldiers killed in the American Civil War by asking his listeners to decide, with him, that government by the people will not end — The Gettysburg Address

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice which stage we are reading or hearing, such as the problem, the plan or the better future. · Feel: We feel concern about the problem, hope for the better future, and trust when our doubts are answered fairly. · Think: We ask what the writer wants us to do, and whether the argument is fair to people who disagree. · Act: We notice when speeches, adverts and campaigns use some of these stages, and decide for ourselves before we agree.

**How to analyse it:** Ask five questions of any persuasive piece, using the six IUMVCC stages: Introduction, Urgency, Methodology, Vision, Counter-argument and Conclusion. 1. How does the opening get the audience's attention, and what does it make them see or feel? 2. Where does it make the problem feel urgent now? 3. What action does it ask the audience to take, and what better future does it show if they take it? 4. Does it answer an objection, and if it does, how fairly? 5. How does it end, and what does the writer want the audience to do or feel? Try the questions on Elizabeth I's speech to her soldiers at Tilbury in 1588, when England feared an invasion from Spain. The speech opens with a warm greeting, “My loving people”, so the soldiers can feel close to their queen from the first words. The urgency comes where she says she has come “at this time” to live and die among them, and names the danger: Spain might “invade the borders of my realm”. She asks for “obedience to my general”, agreement in the camp and bravery in battle, and she promises that these will bring “a famous victory”. Straight after the greeting, before the urgency, the speech answers an objection: people who cared for her safety had warned her to be careful among “armed multitudes”, or armed crowds. She answers them fairly, without blaming them: she will not distrust her “faithful and loving people”. Her three requests, the victory and the ending all come in the last sentence, which ends with “those enemies of my God, of my kingdom, and of my people”. Elizabeth wants her soldiers to obey their general, fight bravely and feel sure that they will win.

**How to create it:** Choose the change you want your reader to make. Open in a way that gets the reader's attention, then show the problem happening now, with one fact or scene. Give clear steps and show the life that follows them, then answer the strongest objection fairly. End by saying what you want the reader to do or feel. Check that your piece has all six stages in order: opening, urgency, steps, better future, objection and ending; if one is missing, add it.

**The IUMVCC Persuasive Toolkit** — Techniques for each stage of a persuasive or transactional piece

- **Introduction**
  - **Counterintuitive Fact** — Open with a statistic that contradicts common assumption, to disrupt the reader’s mental model. _(e.g. “A high percentage of the prison population are dyslexic, and a high percentage of the architect population.” — one fact pointing two opposite ways, so the reader’s assumption breaks in the opening line — Young and Dyslexic? You've Got It Going On)_
  - **Personal-Consequence Question** — A direct question that makes the reader picture themselves inside the scenario. _(e.g. “Does my sassiness upset you?” — the question is aimed straight at the reader, who has to answer it about themselves — Still I Rise)_
  - **Sensory Snapshot** — A vivid, specific opening image that activates the senses and bypasses rational filtering. _(e.g. “all my characters were white and blue-eyed, they played in the snow, they ate apples” — snow and apples are things you can see and taste, so the idea arrives as a picture before it arrives as an argument — The Danger of a Single Story)_
- **Urgency**
  - **The Deadline** — Specify an exact timeframe for why now matters more than later. _(e.g. “If it were done when 'tis done, then 'twere well / It were done quickly” — the whole case rests on timing rather than on the act itself: waiting is what will cost him — Macbeth)_
  - **Cumulative Consequence** — Show the compounding cost of inaction over time to reveal the scale of harm. _(e.g. “show a people as one thing, as only one thing, over and over again, and that is what they become” — the harm is not in one telling but in the repetition adding up — The Danger of a Single Story)_
  - **Opportunity Window** — Highlight what becomes possible — or impossible — depending on action taken now. _(e.g. “I am here to-night to warn you, that you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate” — names the chance and the fact that it will close, in the same breath — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Methodology / Authority**
  - **Transparent Acknowledgement** — Admit what you don’t know, to paradoxically increase credibility. _(e.g. “I too am just as guilty in the question of the single story” — admitting her own fault is what earns her the right to ask it of us — The Danger of a Single Story)_
  - **Lived Experience** — Use a personal example anchored in data to illustrate a broader pattern. _(e.g. “I'm of the generation where teachers didn't know what dyslexia was.” — one life placed inside a whole generation, so the personal becomes evidence — Young and Dyslexic? You've Got It Going On)_
  - **Source Transparency** — Reference where claims come from gracefully, without academic footnoting. _(e.g. “The Ministry of Defence said the taxpayer would pick up the bill” — the claim carries the name of whoever said it, so the reader can weigh it — Explorers or boys messing about?)_
- **Vision**
  - **Vivid Before/After** — Compare the current failure with a possible future — both specific and sensory. _(e.g. “Out of the huts of history's shame / I rise” — the huts are the past and the rising is the future, and one line holds both — Still I Rise)_
  - **Momentum Narrative** — Show how similar change happened before, to imply it can happen again. _(e.g. “He became as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man, as the good old city knew” — a change that has already happened is the strongest argument that it can happen again — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Domino Effect** — Trace how one individual action cascades into systemic change. _(e.g. “Each of you helped to kill her” — five small separate acts added up into one death, so no single act looks harmless again — An Inspector Calls)_
- **Counter-argument**
  - **Legitimate-Concern Acknowledgement** — Validate the opposing view before explaining why it is incomplete. _(e.g. “Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize” — the objection is granted in full first, which is what makes the answer land — The Danger of a Single Story)_
  - **Evidence Counter** — Present data that directly answers the objection. _(e.g. “The rescue involved the Royal Navy, the RAF and British coastguards” — three named forces answer the excuse that it was only a bit of fun — Explorers or boys messing about?)_
  - **Respectful Refusal** — Acknowledge the objection while refusing to accept its framing. _(e.g. “If someone oppresses me because of my race I don't sit down and think, 'How can I become white?' It's not my problem, it's theirs.” — he takes the objection seriously and still refuses the way it was framed — Young and Dyslexic? You've Got It Going On)_
- **Conclusion / Call to Action**
  - **Escalating Commitment** — Offer tiers of engagement so everyone can act at their own level.
  - **Concrete Outcome** — Show exactly what happens when people act, using specifics not abstraction. _(e.g. “He was a second father to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die” — the result is one named child alive, not a general improvement — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Permission to Imperfection** — State plainly that imperfect action beats perfect inaction. _(e.g. “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year” — the word try admits he may fail, and promises to begin anyway — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Stylistic Craft**
  - **Mind Style** — Reveal a consciousness through the grammar and syntax of its sentences. _(e.g. “there are an infinite number of things which didn't happen” — the sentence counts what is absent, and counting is how this narrator’s mind works — The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time)_
  - **Foregrounding** — Deliberate deviation from the expected pattern, to make something demand attention. _(e.g. “And they, since they / Were not the one dead, turned to their affairs” — a boy has just died and the words go flat and ordinary, and that wrongness is what makes you stop — Out, Out—)_
  - **Paradigmatic Deviation** — Choose an unexpected word in a slot, forcing a new connection (“a grief ago”). _(e.g. “The multitudinous seas incarnadine, / Making the green one red” — incarnadine sits where redden was expected, so the reader has to slow down and feel the word — Macbeth)_
  - **Syntagmatic Deviation** — Break the expected sequence — repetition, odd parallels — so form itself makes meaning. _(e.g. “no possibility of Africans being similar to her in any way, no possibility of feelings more complex than pity, no possibility of a connection as human equals” — the same phrase three times closes three doors, so the shape of the sentence is the argument — The Danger of a Single Story)_
  - **Register Shift** — A deliberate change of formality or tone to create effect or reveal perspective. _(e.g. “Bloody non-dyslexics... who do they think they are?” — a serious article drops into playground language for one line, and the joke carries the anger — Young and Dyslexic? You've Got It Going On)_

### Psychic Distance `Zm`

**Also known as:** Narrative Distance

Psychic distance is how close the narration stands to a character's mind. It can be far, describing a character only from outside, as a stranger might see them. It can be close, giving the character's own thoughts and feelings. It does not depend on person: a first-person narrator can stay far away, and a third-person narrator can sit inside a character's head.

**The concept:** Psychic distance controls how much a reader judges a character and how much the reader feels with them. A writer can start far away, to show a person from outside, and move closer when the character's feelings matter most. In Animal Farm, the narrator describes Mr Jones from outside: he “was too drunk to remember to shut the pop-holes”, the small doors that the hens use. We judge him as the narrator does. When you write about any narration, say where it stands, whether it moves, and how that changes whether we judge or feel with the character.

**Examples:** “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” — the opening sentence speaks for a whole society, so the narration stands very far from any one character — Pride and Prejudice; “secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster” — the narrator describes Scrooge from outside, as a stranger might see him, and gives none of his thoughts in this line — A Christmas Carol; “I resisted all the way: a new thing for me” — Jane Eyre, a girl telling her own story, is carried upstairs to be locked in the red-room, and we are given her own feelings — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice how near or far the narration stands from a character's thoughts. · Feel: We feel more sympathy when the narration shares a character's feelings, and more coolness when it stands far away. · Think: We ask why the writer chose to stand there, and what we are meant to understand about the character and the story's subject. · Act: We notice when news reports, adverts and videos show a person from close up or from far away, and ask why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any psychic distance, the gap between the narrating voice and a character’s mind. 1. Where does the narration stand at the start: far from the character, close to their thoughts, or between? 2. Does the distance change as the text goes on, and what moment prompts the change? 3. How does the distance affect whether you judge the character or feel with them? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by standing there? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. At the start of the book the narration stands outside Mr Utterson, a London lawyer. It describes his face, “never lighted by a smile”, and his habits, with only a glimpse of what he feels. Yes, it moves closer. Utterson hears Enfield's story of Mr Hyde, a cruel man who hurt a child. Then, in the next chapter, he takes out Dr Jekyll's will, which leaves everything to Hyde, and we are told he feels a strong curiosity to see Hyde's face. His own thought is quoted: “I shall be Mr. Seek.” From outside, we judge him as the narrator does: “dreary and yet somehow lovable”. Closer in, we share his curiosity. Stevenson may stay outside Utterson at first, so we meet him as others see him, then move close as he searches, so we feel the mystery through him.

**How to create it:** Decide, for each moment, whether the reader should judge your character or feel with them. Open from a distance: describe what a stranger watching could see. Move closer as the moment matters more: add one thought, then one feeling. Pull back when you want the reader to judge. Check by marking each sentence far or close; if every mark is the same, change one sentence.

**Related:** Deep POV, Filter Words, Free Indirect Discourse, Third-Person, Camera-Eye Narration

### Camera-Eye Narration `Oe`

**Also known as:** Objective Narration

Camera-eye narration tells only what a camera and a microphone could record: actions, appearances and speech. It gives no thoughts or feelings, so the reader must work out what a character feels from what the character does. It sits at the far end of psychic distance, the scale of how close narration stands to a character's mind, and it is the opposite of narration that sits inside a character's head. A writer may use it for one passage only.

**The concept:** Camera-eye narration treats behaviour as evidence. Because the narrator gives no thoughts, every gesture and word becomes a clue, and the reader must do the thinking. This can make a scene feel colder and more tense, and it suits characters who hide their feelings. In Jekyll and Hyde, Enfield tells the lawyer Utterson what he saw one night: “the man trampled calmly over the child's body and left her screaming on the ground”, and Enfield gives no reason for the man's act. When you write about any camera-eye passage, say what the narrator shows, what it leaves unsaid, and what the reader must decide.

**Examples:** “who limped, and shivered, and glared, and growled; and whose teeth chattered in his head as he seized me by the chin” — in these words Pip, telling his own story, reports what the convict he meets in the graveyard does, and gives none of the man's thoughts — Great Expectations; “Scrooge had a very small fire, but the clerk's fire was so very much smaller that it looked like one coal.” — the narrator reports only what can be seen in the office, and the reader must judge Scrooge from the facts — A Christmas Carol; “The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again” — at the end, the animals outside watch the pigs and the men, and we are told what they see, not what any one of them thinks — Animal Farm

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at what people do and say, because nothing tells us what they think. · Feel: We feel unease and suspense because we cannot be sure what anyone feels or wants. · Think: We work out motives from actions, as we must in real life, and ask what the writer wants us to see in those actions. · Act: We watch what people do as well as what they say, because actions can show more than words.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any camera-eye narration, narration that records only what a camera and a microphone could capture. 1. Does the narration ever reach inside a mind, and if it does, where? 2. What do the gestures, objects and speech show, and what is left unsaid? 3. What must the reader work out alone? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from being given only the outside? Try the questions on the second sentence of Animal Farm, where Mr Jones, a farmer, goes to bed: “he lurched across the yard, kicked off his boots at the back door”. The sentence never reaches inside his mind. It records only what a camera and a microphone could catch: the lantern light dancing, his lurching, his boots, a last glass of beer and Mrs Jones snoring. Together these show a man who has drunk a lot and is going to bed. What is left unsaid is how he feels, or why he drinks. The first sentence of the book is different: it tells us that Jones was “too drunk to remember to shut the pop-holes”, the small doors the hens use. The second sentence shows the same drunkenness through what he does, so it is camera-eye even though the sentence before it is not. Orwell lets us judge Jones by his actions here, so we see a careless owner without being asked for sympathy.

**How to create it:** Choose a scene where a character hides what they feel. Write only what a camera and a microphone could record: what people do, wear, touch and say. Show the feeling through one gesture or object, and leave it unnamed. Leave out every thought. Check each sentence: if it states a thought or feeling, rewrite it as something a reader could see or hear.

**Related:** Third-Person, Observer-Narrator, Psychic Distance

### Naïve Narrator `Nv`

**Also known as:** Innocent Narrator

A naïve narrator tells a story honestly but understands less than the reader does. This is often because the narrator is a child, or is new to the world they describe. A naïve narrator is not lying: an unreliable narrator may deceive the reader, but a naïve one simply cannot see what the events mean. A narrator is rarely naïve about everything.

**The concept:** A naïve narrator lets the reader see more than the narrator can. Because the narrator reports without understanding, the reader fills in the meaning, and events can feel more shocking than if an adult had explained them. In Flowers for Algernon, Charlie Gordon, a man who finds reading and writing hard, writes his own progress reports and does not see that some of the people around him are laughing at him. When you write about any naïve narrator, say what the narrator reports, what the reader understands that the narrator does not, and what the writer wants us to learn from that gap.

**Examples:** “They won them in a war.” — Harri, a boy of eleven, says that the Dell Farm Crew, a gang, own the steps outside the school cafeteria, and he reports it as an ordinary rule — Pigeon English; “The shape of the letters on my father's, gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man” — Pip, remembering himself as a small child, reports the idea he formed from the letters on his father's gravestone, and the reader can see it has no basis — Great Expectations; “while my noble and beloved country was so injuriously treated” — Gulliver, the traveller who tells the story, has just described England to the king of Brobdingnag, a land of giants; he reports the king's harsh judgement of the English and complains only that his country was treated unfairly — Gulliver's Travels

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the gap between what the narrator reports and what the events really mean. · Feel: We feel worry and sympathy because we can see a danger or an unfairness that the narrator cannot. · Think: We supply the meaning the narrator cannot, and ask what the writer wants us to understand about the world described. · Act: We look past what a person says to what is really happening, and ask what a child or newcomer may not yet see.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any naïve narrator, a narrator who reports honestly but understands less than the reader. 1. Who is telling the story, and what does that person know and understand about what they describe? 2. What does the narrator report without understanding it? 3. What does the reader understand that the narrator does not? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through that gap? Try the questions on Adventures of Huckleberry Finn by Mark Twain. Huck, a boy, tells his own story in his own words. He understands what happens, but he believes what he was taught: that helping Jim, a man escaping slavery, is a sin. When Jim is held prisoner, Huck writes a letter telling Jim’s owner where he is. Then he remembers Jim’s kindness and tears the letter up, saying “All right, then, I’ll go to hell”. Huck reports this without seeing that it shows he is choosing to do right. The reader understands that helping Jim is good, and that what Huck was taught is wrong. Mark Twain may want us to see that a society can teach a good person to call kindness a sin, and so to question what we are taught.

**How to create it:** Choose a narrator who does not understand something the reader can, such as a young child or a newcomer. Decide what the reader should understand. Write the narrator reporting events plainly, with no explanation from the writer. Let the narrator give a simple or wrong explanation of their own. Check that the reader understands more than the narrator does; if the narrator explains it correctly, cut that explanation.

**Related:** Unreliable Narrator, Dramatic Irony, First-Person

### Epistolary Narrative `Es`

**Also known as:** Letters & Documents

An epistolary narrative is a story told through documents such as letters, diaries, reports and telegrams. The word epistolary comes from a Greek word for letter. Each document has a writer, a reader it is written for, and a moment when it was written. A book may be made entirely of documents, or may place a few documents inside an ordinary story.

**The concept:** Epistolary narrative asks the reader to act as a reader of evidence. Each writer knows only what they know when writing, and writes for a particular reader, so we see one version of events at a time. Differences between documents can show who is hiding something. In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth has heard Wickham say that Darcy treated him badly, and Darcy then writes her a letter that gives another account, so she must decide whom to believe. When you write about any epistolary narrative, say who writes each document, who it is for, and what each writer leaves out.

**Examples:** “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise” — Walton, a ship's captain, opens Frankenstein with a letter to his sister, written before he knows how his voyage will end — Frankenstein; “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll” — Utterson, a lawyer, finds these words on a sealed envelope inside a packet left by Dr Lanyon, and he reads the book's final truth in documents — Jekyll and Hyde; “1801—I have just returned from a visit to my landlord—the solitary neighbour that I shall be troubled with.” — the novel opens with a date and the words of Lockwood, a tenant, written like a diary entry, so we first see the strange household only through what he writes — Wuthering Heights

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice who wrote each document, who it was for, and when it was written. · Feel: We feel suspense because each writer does not know what comes next, and we may suspect more than they do. · Think: We compare the documents, weigh each writer's reasons, and ask what the writer wants us to see about the story's subject. · Act: We read letters, messages and reports as one person's version, and ask who wrote them and why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any epistolary narrative, a story told through letters, diaries and other documents. 1. What kinds of document make up the story, and who writes each? 2. Who is each document for, and what does its writer know at that moment? 3. What might each writer leave out or shape for the person reading? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from being given the story in this form? Try the questions on Dracula. It is made of journals, letters, telegrams and Dr Seward’s diary, which he speaks into a phonograph, a machine that records the voice. Jonathan Harker’s journal begins on 3 May as a travel record he keeps in shorthand, before he knows the danger he is in. Mina Murray writes to her friend Lucy on 9 May with ordinary news. Harker knows the Count may read what he writes, so he decides he “should be careful what I wrote”. He writes to Mina in shorthand but explains his situation “without the horrors”. Because every writer knows only part, the reader must put the documents together like evidence. Stoker may want the story to feel like a set of real records.

**How to create it:** Choose two or three characters who would write things down, and a form for each, such as a letter, a diary or a report. Decide who each document is for and what its writer does not yet know. Write each one before its writer knows the ending. Let each writer leave out something that suits their reader. Check that a fact one writer hides appears in another document; if it does not, add it.

**Related:** Framed Narrative, Observer-Narrator, Multiple Viewpoint

### Filter Words `Fu`

**Also known as:** Filtering

Filter words are verbs such as saw, heard, felt and noticed that tell us a character perceived something. They put the character's seeing or hearing between the reader and the thing itself. A writer can cut them, so that a sentence about someone hearing a door slam becomes one where the door simply slams. Filter words make the narration feel further from the character's mind, while deep point of view, which stays inside the character's head, uses few of them.

**The concept:** Filter words add a layer between reader and event: “I saw” tells us that someone saw, while leaving it out shows the thing itself. Cutting a filter word often makes writing feel closer, but a writer may keep one when the seeing is the point. In Jekyll and Hyde, Poole, Jekyll's butler, tells the lawyer Utterson “It was but for one minute that I saw him”. The filter stays because Poole is a witness who is not sure who he saw. When you find any filter word, say what the character perceives, what the sentence loses without it, and why the writer kept it.

**Examples:** “I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open” — Victor has just brought the creature to life, and the words “I saw” keep us watching through his eyes — Frankenstein; “Is this a dagger which I see before me” — Macbeth, alone before he goes to kill King Duncan, says “I see” because he cannot tell whether the dagger is real — Macbeth; “Oh! I saw a light, and I thought a ghost would come.” — Jane, a girl locked in the red-room, tells the servant Bessie what she saw and what she thought, so the line reports her fear — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice whether a sentence shows the thing itself or tells us that someone saw it. · Feel: We feel close to a scene when nothing stands between us and it, and warier when someone's report does. · Think: We ask why a writer lets us see through one character's eyes, and what that character may be missing or hiding. · Act: We notice whether news reports and stories give us the event itself or only someone's report of it, and ask why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any filter words, the verbs such as saw, heard and felt that put a character’s perceiving between the reader and what is perceived. 1. Which words in the passage show a character seeing, hearing or feeling something? 2. Rewrite one sentence without its filter word. What changes, and what stays the same? 3. If any filter word earns its place, why? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand from how the sensations are given? Try the questions on the arrival of Marley’s ghost in A Christmas Carol. The filter words are “then he heard the noise much louder”, “saw it standing before him” and “felt the chilling influence of its death-cold eyes”. Without the filter, “and then the noise came much louder” puts the sound first, but we no longer feel Scrooge listening in fear. Yes: the filters matter because Scrooge’s senses tell him the ghost is real while he refuses to believe it, since the text says “he was still incredulous, and fought against his senses”. Dickens keeps us with Scrooge’s senses, so we watch him refuse what they tell him.

**How to create it:** Take a passage of description you have written. Circle every saw, heard, felt, noticed, watched and realised. For each one, write the thing itself: “She heard the door slam” becomes “The door slammed”. Keep a filter word only where the character’s act of noticing is the point. Check that each sentence starts with the thing itself; if one starts with the character perceiving it, ask whether the perceiving is the point.

**Related:** Psychic Distance, Deep POV

### Deep POV `Dp`

**Also known as:** Deep Third-Person

Deep point of view (deep POV) tells a story in the third person ('he' or 'she') as if we were inside one character's head. The narration uses that character's own words, thoughts and feelings, and avoids labels such as 'he thought' or 'she felt'. The opposite is camera-eye narration, which describes only what a camera could see and hear, with no thoughts. A story can move closer to a character and then further away again.

**The concept:** Deep POV shows who a character is through the words the story uses: what they notice and how they would say it. It also hides whatever that character cannot see, which can build suspense. In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge, the mean old businessman, wakes on Christmas morning and opens his window, and the narration gives what he sees in his own excited words: “No fog, no mist; clear, bright, jovial, stirring, cold”. When you write about any deep POV, say whose mind it is, which words sound like that person's own, and what we cannot see from inside it.

**Examples:** “Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon began talking again.” — Alice is falling down a very deep hole, and the narration gives her own reasoning, that there is nothing else to do, with no label such as ‘she thought’ — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; “this sleek, sinuous, full-bodied animal, chasing and chuckling” — Mole has never seen a river before, so the narration describes it as a playful animal, in his own wondering words — The Wind in the Willows; “Anne was not dressed like the other girls!” — Matthew Cuthbert, the quiet man who has taken Anne in, has spent two hours smoking his pipe and thinking, and the narration gives his answer in his own surprised words — Anne of Green Gables

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We see only what one character notices, and we read it in the words that character would choose. · Feel: We feel close to the character, as if their joy, fear or anger were our own, though no one says 'I'. · Think: We read the character's own words as clues to who they are, and ask what the writer wants us to understand about them. · Act: We notice when a news story or an advert is told through one person's feelings, and we ask what it leaves out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any deep POV, close third-person narration written in a character’s own thoughts and words. 1. Whose mind is the narration in, and does it give their thoughts directly or label them with “he thought”? 2. Whose words and attitudes does it use: the character’s, or a narrator standing outside? 3. What does the reader notice only through this character, and what stays hidden because of that? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel by staying in this mind? Try the questions on Dorothy's meeting with the little old woman, the Witch of the North, in The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum. The narration is mostly in Dorothy's mind. It gives her question directly, with no label: “What could the little woman possibly mean by calling her a sorceress, and saying she had killed the Wicked Witch of the East?” The words are hers: “possibly” is how a puzzled girl would think. The next sentence, “Dorothy was an innocent, harmless little girl”, describes her from outside, so the narration steps back there. The first sentence, “Dorothy listened to this speech with wonder”, also describes her from outside. We share her puzzle, because the narration gives only her question and not the Witch's reasons. Baum may want us to feel Dorothy's innocent surprise, so that we see she did not expect to be called a sorceress.

**How to create it:** Choose one character and one moment. List what that character would notice first, and what they would ignore. Write each sentence in words that character would use, including their slang and their judgements. Give the thought itself, without “he thought” or “she felt”. Check each sentence by asking whether this character would say it this way; rewrite any that sounds like an outside narrator.

**Related:** Psychic Distance, Filter Words, Free Indirect Discourse, Third-Person, Head-Hopping

### Multiple Viewpoint `Vp`

**Also known as:** Shifting Viewpoint

Multiple viewpoint tells one story through the eyes of two or more characters, one after another. The change from one character to the next is clear, such as a new chapter, a new scene or a new narrator. Each character may tell their own part as 'I', or a narrator may follow each of them as 'he' or 'she'. It differs from head-hopping, where the telling slips into another character's mind in the middle of a scene, without a break.

**The concept:** Multiple viewpoint shows that no single character knows the whole story. Each viewpoint adds facts and feelings that the others lack. The note at the start of Dracula calls its records “given from the standpoints and within the range of knowledge of those who made them”: journals and diaries kept by Jonathan Harker, Mina Murray, Dr Seward and others. When you write about any multiple viewpoint, say whose mind each part gives us, what each one knows that the others do not, and what the writer wants us to understand from seeing more than one side.

**Examples:** “It is with considerable difficulty that I remember the original era of my being” — Victor Frankenstein has been telling the story, and here the creature he made takes over and tells his own life in his own voice — Frankenstein; “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end” — most of the book follows the lawyer Utterson, but these are the last words of Jekyll's own written statement, so the secret is explained from inside — Jekyll and Hyde; “waiting no farther invitation to her story” — Lockwood, the new tenant, has told the story so far, and here Nelly Dean, the housekeeper, begins to tell him the history of the two families — Wuthering Heights

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch one story from more than one position, and notice what each character knows and what each one misses. · Feel: We feel sympathy for characters on opposite sides, because each one's reasons make sense when we hear them from inside. · Think: We put together a whole picture that no single character can see, and ask what the writer wants us to learn. · Act: We remember that people who disagree each hold a view we have not yet heard, and we ask for it.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any multiple viewpoint, a story that passes between the minds of different characters. 1. Whose viewpoints does the story use, and in what pattern does it move from one to another? 2. Who is each viewpoint character, and what separates them from the others? 3. What does hearing from more than one mind show the reader that one viewpoint could not? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by showing more than one side? Try the questions on Noughts & Crosses by Malorie Blackman. The story uses two viewpoints, Sephy’s and Callum’s, and the chapters take turns: Sephy’s are the odd-numbered chapters and Callum’s the even-numbered ones. Sephy is a Cross, the daughter of a powerful politician, and Callum is a Nought, whose mother once worked as a nanny for Sephy’s family. They are secret friends, because their society keeps Noughts and Crosses apart. Hearing both lets the reader see the friendship from each side of the divide between them. Blackman may want readers to understand how the same unfair society looks different from each side.

**How to create it:** Choose two characters who live through the same event but see it differently. Decide what each one wants and what each one knows. Write each part in one character’s voice, and show the change with a heading or a name. End each part at a moment of uncertainty. Check that you tell the reader something only one character knows. If that fact does not change how the reader feels when the other character acts, add a fact that does.

**Related:** Conflicting Accounts, Head-Hopping, Framed Narrative, Epistolary Narrative

### Conflicting Accounts `Cc`

**Also known as:** Rival Testimony

Conflicting accounts are two or more versions of the same event, told by different people, that cannot all be true. The reader has to decide which version to believe, or whether any of them is complete. It differs from multiple viewpoint, where each teller shows their own side without contradicting the others. A teller may lie, may be mistaken, or may remember the event in the way that suits them.

**The concept:** With conflicting accounts, we must decide which version to believe. Because the versions cannot all be true, we ask not only what happened but who is telling it, and what they gain or risk. In Animal Farm, Boxer says of Snowball, who was wounded in a battle, “We all saw him running with blood”. Squealer, who speaks for the leader Napoleon, answers “That was part of the arrangement!”, which supports Napoleon's claim that Snowball was a traitor. When you write about any conflicting accounts, say who tells each version, where they disagree, and what each teller gains, risks or may have got wrong.

**Examples:** “I thrice presented him a kingly crown, / Which he did thrice refuse” — at Caesar's funeral, Antony answers Brutus's claim that Caesar was ambitious with a different account of the same man, in which Caesar refused a crown three times — Julius Caesar; “I have deceived even your very eyes” — Claudio and Don Pedro believe they saw Hero talking with a man at her window, but Borachio now says it was he, speaking to Margaret, Hero's servant, who was wearing Hero's clothes — Much Ado About Nothing; “He resigned all claim to assistance in the church” — Darcy's letter says Wickham gave up his claim to a church job and took three thousand pounds instead, but Wickham had told Elizabeth that the job was given to someone else — Pride and Prejudice

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at where the versions disagree, and at who is telling each one, as well as at the event itself. · Feel: We feel unsure and uncomfortable, because we cannot accept one account without rejecting another. · Think: We test each version against what its teller gains or risks, and ask what the writer wants us to learn about truth. · Act: We ask who is telling a story in the news, in a dispute or online, and what that person gains from it.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any conflicting accounts, the same event told differently by rival witnesses. 1. Who tells each version of the event, and what does each say happened? 2. Exactly where do the versions disagree? 3. What might each teller gain or lose if their version is believed? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand from the clash? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet, Act 3 Scene 1, after Tybalt is killed. Benvolio, who was at the fight, tells the Prince that Tybalt killed Mercutio and that Romeo killed Tybalt only after Tybalt came back. Lady Capulet, Tybalt’s aunt, was not at the fight, but she says Benvolio is lying. They disagree about whether Benvolio can be believed and about who is to blame: he blames Tybalt for the quarrel, while she says “Romeo slew Tybalt, Romeo must not live.” She also says “Some twenty of them fought”, which Benvolio does not. She says Benvolio “speaks not true” because he is “a kinsman to the Montague”, and she is grieving for Tybalt. Benvolio swears “This is the truth, or let Benvolio die”, and he may want to protect Romeo. Shakespeare shows each family hearing only its own side, so loyalty can weigh more than evidence.

**How to create it:** Choose one event, such as a fight, and decide what really happened. Write two tellers who describe it differently. Give each teller a reason to want their version believed, such as loyalty, fear or shame. Make the two versions disagree on at least one clear detail. Check that a reader could say why each teller needs their version; if not, make one reason clearer.

**Related:** Multiple Viewpoint, Unreliable Narrator, Dramatic Irony

### Head-Hopping `Hh`

**Also known as:** Unsignalled POV Slip

Head-hopping is when the telling moves from one character's mind into another's in the middle of a scene, without a clear break. It differs from multiple viewpoint, where each change of mind comes at a clear break such as a new chapter. Many modern editors treat head-hopping as a fault, because readers can lose track of whose scene it is. In older books, an all-knowing narrator who sees into every mind may do it on purpose.

**The concept:** A reader's sympathy follows the mind that a scene is told through, so moving into other minds can leave us unsure whose scene it is. It can also show how a whole group feels at once. In Pride and Prejudice, Mrs Bennet embarrasses her daughter Elizabeth in front of Mr Bingley and Mr Darcy. The scene is Elizabeth's, but the narrator says “Nothing but concern for Elizabeth could enable Bingley to keep his countenance”, which means to keep a straight face. When you write about any head-hopping, say whose minds we enter, whether anything marks each move, and what we gain or lose.

**Examples:** “These sounds made the little girl's heart beat fast, for she did not know what made them; but Toto knew” — in one sentence the narration moves from Dorothy's mind, where she does not know what the sounds are, to her dog Toto's, where he does — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz; “But the Mole was very full of lunch, and self-satisfaction, and pride” — the sentence before shows the Rat's dreamy mood, and the word ‘But’ takes us straight into the Mole's feelings in the same scene — The Wind in the Willows; “nobody said or thought it was at all a small pudding for a large family” — the narrator tells us what every member of the Cratchit family thinks at once, as Scrooge watches their Christmas dinner — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice that the telling has moved into a different mind, and we ask whose scene this is. · Feel: We feel our sympathy spread across several people, or lose its centre, when the telling does not stay with one mind. · Think: We work out whose feelings matter most in the scene, and what the writer gains or loses by showing everyone's mind. · Act: We notice when a news report or a retelling moves between several people's feelings, and we ask whose side it favours.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any passage that head-hops, which means it slips from one character's mind into another's without warning. 1. Whose mind do we enter first, and who has most at stake in the scene? 2. Where does the narration enter a second character's mind, and does anything signal the move, such as a new paragraph? 3. After the move, do you still know whose scene it is? 4. What does the move cost the reader? Try the questions on Peter Pan by J. M. Barrie, in the lagoon scene where Wendy and Peter watch Captain Hook, the pirate captain, swim to his men's boat. We enter Wendy's mind first: she sees Hook's “evil swarthy face” and “she would have liked to swim away”. Wendy has most at stake, because she is frightened of Hook. Soon after, “He was tingling with life and also top-heavy with conceit” describes how Peter feels inside, and nothing signals the move, because it is the same paragraph. The paragraph then returns to Wendy with “though she thought so also”, so it is no longer clear whether the scene belongs to Wendy's fear or to Peter's pride. The cost is that her fear is interrupted by a joke about his conceit. Barrie's narrator openly knows everything, so many readers accept this, but a writer without that voice would lose the scene's centre.

**How to create it:** Decide whose scene it is: choose the character with most at stake in this moment. Write every sentence of the scene from inside that character's mind. Show the other characters through what your chosen character sees, hears and guesses. If you want a second character's thoughts, start a new scene or chapter for them. Check each paragraph: if it states a thought your chosen character could not know, rewrite it as something they see or guess.

**Related:** Multiple Viewpoint, Deep POV

### Free Indirect Discourse `Fe`

Free indirect discourse is narration that slips into a character's thoughts and words without saying 'she thought'. It stays in the third person ('he' or 'she'), but a question, an exclamation or a word the character would use shows whose mind we are in. It differs from deep POV, which tells a whole passage entirely in the character's own voice; here the narrator's voice and the character's mix. Sometimes it is hard to say whose view a sentence gives.

**The concept:** Free indirect discourse lets a reader share a character's thoughts and also judge them, because the narrator's voice is still present. A writer can show feelings the character would not state, and can make us doubt them. In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge is shown the Cratchits' home and hears a Bible verse read aloud, and the narration asks “Where had Scrooge heard those words?” as Scrooge would ask himself, with no ‘he wondered’. When you write about any free indirect discourse, say whose thoughts are blended in, which words sound like the character, and whether the narrator seems to agree.

**Examples:** “How improperly had she been acting by Harriet!” — Emma Woodhouse has just realised that she loves Mr Knightley, and the narration gives her own shocked exclamation about how she has treated her friend Harriet — Emma; “How it sang in his ears as he went down, down, down!” — the boat has tipped over and Mole is under the water, and the narration gives his own frightened exclamation, not a report of it — The Wind in the Willows; “What could the little woman possibly mean by calling her a sorceress, and saying she had killed the Wicked Witch of the East?” — the Good Witch of the North has just called Dorothy a sorceress, and the narration asks Dorothy's own puzzled question — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen for words that sound like the character's own, such as a question or an exclamation, inside the narrator's report. · Feel: We feel close to the character's thoughts, while also sensing that the narrator may see more than the character does. · Think: We decide whether the narrator agrees with the character, and what the writer wants us to understand about how this person sees things. · Act: We notice when a news story or a retelling takes on one person's voice, and we ask whether we are being invited to agree.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any free indirect discourse, which is narration that slips into a character's own thoughts and words without saying “she thought”. 1. Which words sound like the character's own thoughts rather than the narrator's, such as a question, an exclamation or a word the character would use? 2. Does anything announce them as thought? 3. Does the narrator seem to agree with the character's view, or to stand apart from it? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by blending narrator and character? Try the questions on Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen, where Elizabeth Bennet's aunt suggests visiting Pemberley, the home of Mr Darcy. The words “It would be dreadful!” are Elizabeth's own exclamation about meeting him, not the narrator's calm report. Nothing announces them: there is no “she thought”, and the paragraph runs from the narrator's report straight into her feeling. The narrator does not say whether meeting Darcy would really be dreadful, but reports that “She blushed at the very idea”, so we feel her alarm and also see it from outside. Austen may want us to feel Elizabeth's dread from inside her, and to see that she now cares what Darcy thinks of her.

**How to create it:** Choose a character and a moment when they feel strongly, such as fear, pride or embarrassment. Write the narration in the third person, but use the character's own rhythm and words, such as a short exclamation or a question. Leave out tags such as “she thought”. Add one plain outside detail, such as a blush, so the reader can also see the character from outside. Check that a reader can still tell it is the character's voice; if not, add a word the character would use.

**Related:** Psychic Distance, Deep POV

### Refrain `Rf`

A refrain is a line, or part of a line, that returns several times in a poem, song or speech. In a poem it often ends each stanza, which is a group of lines, but it can also open stanzas or return less regularly. Its words stay the same or change a little. A refrain is one kind of repetition, which means using the same word or phrase more than once. A villanelle is a nineteen-line poem built on two refrains.

**The concept:** A refrain can make a line mean more each time it returns, because the lines between its appearances change how we hear it. In Julius Caesar, Antony says “Brutus is an honourable man” several times at Caesar’s funeral. The first time it sounds polite, but each later time comes after a reason to doubt Brutus, so the words start to sound like mockery. Soon a citizen in the crowd shouts “They were traitors: honourable men!”, using Antony's own words as an insult. When you write about any refrain, say what the line is, where it returns, and whether its meaning changes or stays the same.

**Examples:** “Double, double, toil and trouble; Fire, burn; and cauldron, bubble.” — the three witches chant these words three times as they add things to their cauldron, a large pot, so the chant returns after each new item or list — Macbeth; “Nevermore.” — in this poem a raven answers each question from the grieving speaker with this one word, and it ends stanza after stanza, so the speaker's hope is refused again and again — The Raven; “Dem tell me” — in the speaker's own way of speaking this means ‘they tell me’, and the words open the poem and many later lines, often before something he was told about, such as 1066 or Lord Nelson — Checking Out Me History

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the line that comes back, and watch how its meaning changes or grows each time it returns. · Feel: We feel an insistence that grows with each return, and it can feel like grief, anger or defiance, depending on what comes between. · Think: We ask why the speaker cannot leave this line behind, and what idea or feeling the whole work keeps returning to. · Act: We notice repeated lines in songs, speeches and adverts, and ask what each one wants us to remember or do.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any refrain, a line or part of a line that returns in a poem, song or speech. 1. What is the repeated line or phrase, and where does it return? 2. Does the wording stay the same each time, and does what comes before it change what it means? 3. What feeling does the repetition build, such as insistence, boredom or grief? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand by repeating it? Try the questions on Exposure by Wilfred Owen, a poem about soldiers waiting through a freezing night in the trenches. The repeated line is “But nothing happens.” It ends four of the poem's eight stanzas: the first, third, fourth and last. The wording stays the same, but the meaning grows. The first time it follows sentries whispering, “Worried by silence”, so it means that the threat has not come yet. The last time it follows the burying party pausing over “half-known faces”, so it now includes the dead. The repetition builds a numb, helpless feeling, like waiting that never ends. Owen seems to want the reader to understand that for these soldiers the war is mostly cold, waiting and death, not battle.

**How to create it:** Choose one short line that carries the main feeling or idea of your poem. Decide where it will return, such as at the end of each stanza. Write the lines between the returns so the same words mean something new each time. Keep the wording the same, or change one word at a moment you choose. Check by reading each refrain together with the lines just before it: those lines should show how the feeling grows or changes. If they do not, change the lines between them.

**Related:** Repetition

### Epilogue `Ei`

An epilogue is a short closing part that comes after the main story has ended. It may show the characters years later, sum up what happened, or, in a play, speak to the audience. It is the opposite of a prologue, a short opening part before the story begins. An epilogue usually adds no new plot events, and many stories have none.

**The concept:** An epilogue can change how the whole story is remembered, because it is the last thing a reader meets. It can settle the meaning of the ending, or open it up again. At the end of A Midsummer Night's Dream, Puck, a fairy, asks the audience to think “That you have but slumber'd here / While these visions did appear”, meaning they have only slept and dreamed the play. When you write about any epilogue, say how much time has passed, what has changed, and what the writer wants us to remember about the whole story.

**Examples:** “Let your indulgence set me free” — Prospero, the magician who has given up his magic, asks the audience, with their kindness, to set him free, so the play ends with an actor asking the audience for something — The Tempest; “Seven years ago we all went through the flames” — the closing note, written seven years after the story's main events, tells how the survivors' lives went on, including the birth of Jonathan and Mina's son — Dracula; “Happy for all her maternal feelings was the day on which Mrs. Bennet got rid of her two most deserving daughters.” — the last chapter, after the weddings, tells how the lives of Mrs Bennet, Lydia and the others went on — Pride and Prejudice

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look past the climax to what is left once the main events are over. · Feel: We feel a settled calm, or a quiet unease if the closing glimpse is less complete than we hoped. · Think: We reconsider the whole story in the light of what came after, and ask what the writer wants us to remember about it. · Act: We ask what happened afterwards to people in the news, whose stories are dropped once the main event is over.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any epilogue, a final section set after the climax that shows the aftermath. 1. How long after the climax is it set, and who or what does it show? 2. What has changed since the climax, and what has stayed the same? 3. Does it close the story completely, or leave something open? 4. What does the writer want the reader to take away from seeing this? Try the questions on Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows by J. K. Rowling. Its epilogue is set nineteen years later, and shows Harry and his friends seeing their children off to Hogwarts. Voldemort, the villain, is gone, and Harry and Ginny are now married with three children, while Ron and Hermione have two. What stays the same is that the friends are still together and Hogwarts is still the school the next generation attends. It closes the story: the danger is over, and the characters we followed have grown up and have families. Rowling may want readers to feel that the long fight was worth it, because the next generation is going to the school where it began.

**How to create it:** Decide how long after your climax to jump: a day, a year or a lifetime. Choose two or three details that show what has changed, such as a new home or a job. Decide whether to close the story completely or to leave one question open. Write the epilogue shorter than your last chapter. Check that it shows the aftermath through those details and does not repeat your ending; if it does, cut the repeated lines.

### Setup & Payoff `Ck`

Setup and payoff is when a writer shows a detail early and then uses it later in a way that matters. The detail may be an object, a skill, a promise or a threat. The early showing is the setup, and the later use is the payoff. It is different from foreshadowing, which only hints that something will happen. A setup may be given extra attention, or placed quietly so that readers hardly notice it until it returns.

**The concept:** Setup and payoff makes a story feel planned, because a detail that returns links two moments. It also lets a writer change what a detail means between the two moments. In Macbeth, Lady Macbeth says after Duncan's murder “A little water clears us of this deed”. Later, walking in her sleep and rubbing her hands, she asks “What, will these hands ne'er be clean?”, so her early confidence returns as guilt. When you find any setup and payoff, say what is set up, how the payoff uses or changes it, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS” — early on, seven rules are painted on the barn wall, the last being ‘All animals are equal’, and at the end only this one remains, with new words added that contradict it — Animal Farm; “to Tiny Tim, who did NOT die, he was a second father” — in the third stave the Ghost says Tiny Tim, a sick child, will die if nothing changes, and in the last stave Scrooge helps the family and the child lives — A Christmas Carol; “I shall be with you on your wedding-night” — the creature says this to Victor Frankenstein as a threat when Victor refuses to make a female companion for him, and on Victor's wedding night his wife Elizabeth is killed — Frankenstein

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We keep hold of a detail shown early, because we expect it to matter later. · Feel: We feel quiet expectation while we wait, and satisfaction or shock when the detail returns. · Think: We see the ending as shaped by what came before, and ask what the writer wants us to understand about choices and their results. · Act: We remember warnings and promises made early in real life, and check later whether they came true.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any setup and payoff, where a detail shown early comes back later and matters. 1. What detail, such as an object, a warning, a skill or a promise, is shown early with extra attention? 2. Where does it return, and how much later? 3. What does it change when it returns? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand when the early detail is used? Try the questions on Cinderella, in Charles Perrault's version.
