  - **The double** — Two figures who are one — the respectable self and the appetite it disowns. _(e.g. “man is not truly one, but truly two” — he names the split as something in everyone, not only in himself — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **The creature made, not born** — Something assembled or summoned by human ambition, which then will not obey. _(e.g. “the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart” — the maker’s pride turns to horror the moment the thing lives — Frankenstein)_
  - **The past that will not stay buried** — A guilt, a crime or a death that returns in bodily form. _(e.g. “I wear the chain I forged in life... I made it link by link, and yard by yard” — old guilt comes back as a weight the dead man has to carry — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Transformation** — A body or a self that changes against its will, so identity itself stops being safe. _(e.g. “lean, corded, knuckly, of a dusky pallor and thickly shaded with a swart growth of hair” — he wakes and does not recognise his own hand — Jekyll and Hyde)_
- **The reader's dread** — why it unsettles rather than merely frightens
  - **The uncanny** — The familiar made subtly wrong — recognisable, but not right. _(e.g. “You should be women, / And yet your beards forbid me to interpret” — they look almost familiar, and the almost is what unsettles him — Macbeth)_
  - **The sublime** — Vastness that overwhelms — awe and terror at once, the self made small. _(e.g. “boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away” — the empty desert dwarfs a king who thought himself enormous — Ozymandias)_
  - **Recognition** — The turn where the horror proves to be ours: we are what we feared. _(e.g. “Ralph wept for the end of innocence, the darkness of man’s heart” — the danger was never the beast; it was the boys — Lord of the Flies)_

### Romance `Ro`

Romance is a genre of stories, poems and films about love, in which two characters are drawn together but something keeps them apart. This obstacle may be a feud, pride, class, a secret or a difference of belief. A romance often ends with the couple united, but it may also end in loss or death. It often opens with a meet-cute, the scene in which the two first meet.

**The concept:** Romance shows that love can make people take risks and change. We hope that the pair will unite and fear what keeps them apart, and the obstacle often shows what is wrong with their world. In Jane Eyre, Jane leaves Rochester when she learns that he is already married. They are free to marry only after a long separation, and Jane tells her reader, “Reader, I married him”. When you write about any romance, say what draws the pair together, what keeps them apart, and what the ending says about love.

**Examples:** “You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.” — Darcy proposes to Elizabeth Bennet, but in the same speech he says that her family's lower rank made him struggle against his love, and she refuses him — Pride and Prejudice; “She lov'd me for the dangers I had pass'd, / And I lov'd her that she did pity them.” — Othello, a general, tells the leaders of Venice why he and Desdemona fell in love, after her father has complained about their marriage — Othello; “Whatever our souls are made of, his and mine are the same” — Catherine says this to Nelly, the family's servant, while explaining that she cannot marry Heathcliff because he has been brought so low — Wuthering Heights

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch two people drawn together, and notice each thing that keeps them apart. · Feel: We feel hope that the pair will unite and fear that they will not, because we have come to care about their bond. · Think: We ask what the obstacle shows about the world around the lovers, such as its rules about class, family or pride. · Act: We think about what we would risk for someone we love, and about the rules of family or class that we may never question.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any romance, a story about love in which something keeps two people apart. 1. Who are the two people, and what draws them together? 2. What keeps them apart: pride, class, a feud, a secret or something else? 3. Do they overcome the obstacle, and how does the story end: with union, loss or something in between? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about love through this story? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. Romeo and Juliet are drawn together at a Capulet feast, and Juliet says “My only love sprung from my only hate!” Their families, the Montagues and the Capulets, are enemies. They marry in secret, but Romeo is banished for killing Tybalt, Juliet's cousin, and a message to him goes wrong. They do not overcome the obstacle: both die, and only then does Juliet's father, Capulet, offer his hand to Montague. Shakespeare may want the audience to see how hatred between families can destroy the young.

**How to create it:** Choose two characters and decide what draws them together. Give them one obstacle that matters in the world they live in, such as a feud, a class difference or a family rule. Show a moment when each of them risks something to be with the other. Decide whether they unite, lose each other or end somewhere between, and make the ending show whether the obstacle is overcome. Ask a friend what keeps your two characters apart; if they cannot say, show the obstacle in the first scene.

**Conventions of Romance** — Romance is the genre of connection, and its mechanism is the obstacle. The barrier is never incidental: it externalises whatever in the protagonist, or their world, resists love. Choose the obstacle first — the feeling follows from it.

- **The obstacle** — the force that keeps them apart
  - **An inherited feud** — A division neither chose and neither can simply step out of. _(e.g. “From ancient grudge break to new mutiny, / Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean” — the quarrel is older than either lover and belongs to neither — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Pride or misjudgement** — The barrier is inside one of them: a first impression that has to be dismantled. _(e.g. “I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine” — Elizabeth lets slip that part of the barrier is her own — Pride and Prejudice)_
  - **Class or circumstance** — Money, rank or duty stand where feeling wants to go. _(e.g. “Do you think, because I am poor, obscure, plain, and little, I am soulless and heartless?” — Jane names the rank standing between them — Jane Eyre)_
  - **A rival** — A third figure whose claim forces the choice into the open. _(e.g. “I claim you — not for my pleasure, but for my Sovereign’s service” — St John’s offer forces Jane to say out loud what she wants — Jane Eyre)_
- **The arc** — how the bond is tested
  - **The charged first meeting** — An encounter staged so the reader files the pair together long before they admit it. _(e.g. “palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss” — they meet and build a single sonnet between them, a line each — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **The moment of choosing** — One of them gives up something real, proving the bond is not merely wanted but chosen. _(e.g. “Kill Claudio.” — Beatrice asks Benedick to give up his closest friend for her — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **Union — or the loss of it** — The genre pays out in one of two directions, and the obstacle decides which. _(e.g. “Reader, I married him” — Jane reports the ending herself, in four plain words — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Love as self-knowledge** — To win connection the protagonist must overcome the very flaw the obstacle embodied. _(e.g. “Till this moment I never knew myself” — Elizabeth discovers the obstacle was her own judgement — Pride and Prejudice)_

**Related:** Meet-Cute

### Dystopia `Dy`

A dystopia is a story set in an imagined society that has gone badly wrong. The cause is often a harsh government or a harmful use of technology, and the people are controlled through fear, spying, lies or machines. The story often follows one person who sees the problem and resists. A dystopia is a warning, because it takes a problem from the writer's own world to an extreme. Its opposite is a utopia, an imagined perfect society.

**The concept:** Dystopia lets a writer show where a problem in their own society could lead if nobody stopped it. In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller visits the future and finds two groups: the Eloi, who live above ground, and the Morlocks, who live below it. He first thinks the cause is the widening gap between “the Capitalist and the Labourer”, a business owner and a worker, in his own time. The future grows from the present, so readers recognise their own world in it. When you write about any dystopia, say what real problem it takes to an extreme, how its society controls people, and what warning the writer gives.

**Examples:** “ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS” — on the farm's barn wall the pigs, who now rule, have changed the one rule that said all animals were equal — Animal Farm; “a small room, hexagonal in shape, like the cell of a bee” — the story begins in the windowless room of a woman who lives alone, where a machine makes the music and moves her chair — The Machine Stops; “illness of any sort was considered in Erewhon to be highly criminal and immoral” — a traveller finds that in the imagined land of Erewhon a person can be put in prison for catching a cold — Erewhon

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the rules, machines and slogans that control the people of the imagined society. · Feel: We feel unease and anger, because the controlled world looks like a possible future that grows out of our own. · Think: We ask which real problem the writer has taken to an extreme, and who gains from the control. · Act: We question the rules, machines and slogans in our own world that watch us or limit what we may say, and ask who benefits.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dystopia, a story set in an imagined society that has gone badly wrong. 1. How does the society control its people: through fear, spying, lies, machines or something else? 2. Which real problem in the writer's own world has the story taken to an extreme? 3. Does anyone resist, and if so, what happens to them? 4. What warning does the writer want the reader to take from it? Try the questions on Nineteen Eighty-Four. The Party watches people with telescreens, screens in the flats and workplaces of Party members that send and receive at the same time, and the Thought Police punish forbidden thoughts. The Party also controls the past: Winston Smith's job is to change old newspaper articles to fit what it now says. Orwell may be taking to an extreme the way a government can use spying, fear and false news to control what people believe. Winston resists by writing a private diary and loving Julia, but he is arrested, and in Room 101 he begs the Party to punish Julia instead of him. The last words are “He loved Big Brother.” Orwell may want readers to guard against giving any government the power to watch them and decide what is true.

**How to create it:** Choose one real problem in your world, such as constant watching or companies that control information, and imagine it taken to an extreme. Decide how the rulers use it to control people, and show it in daily life through a rule, a poster or a machine. Give your main character one small act of resistance and show what it costs. Ask a friend what real problem your story is about; if they cannot say, make the link clearer.

**Conventions of Dystopia** — The typical elements of a dystopian world. Each is a present tendency carried to its logical end, so every choice is an argument about our own society. Pick the pressures your world applies, then show a person living under them.

- **How the regime holds power** — the system as antagonist
  - **Surveillance** — Being watched, or never knowing when — so people police themselves. _(e.g. “BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU” — the caption sits on a poster in an ordinary hallway, so being watched becomes part of the furniture, and a person who might be watched starts policing themselves — Nineteen Eighty-Four)_
  - **Controlled language** — Words are removed, renamed or simplified until the thought becomes hard to have. _(e.g. “Don’t you see that the whole aim of Newspeak is to narrow the range of thought?” — the state shrinks the dictionary, because an objection nobody has the words for cannot be made — Nineteen Eighty-Four)_
  - **Rewritten history** — The record of the past is edited, so there is nothing to measure the present against. _(e.g. “Dem tell me / Wha dem want to tell me” — the lessons chose what happened, so the past arrives already edited — Checking Out Me History)_
  - **Ritual and spectacle** — Ceremonies and enemies-of-the-week bind the crowd and drown out doubt. _(e.g. “Out came Napoleon himself, majestically upright, casting haughty glances from side to side, and with his dogs gambolling round him. He carried a whip in his trotter.” — a parade of power answers questions by not allowing them — Animal Farm)_
  - **A comfort that costs freedom** — Safety, plenty or order offered in exchange for something people do not notice giving up. _(e.g. “Surely, comrades, you do not want Jones back?” — safety is offered as the only other option, so nobody asks for more — Animal Farm)_
- **The individual under it** — the struggle to stay a person
  - **The one who notices** — A protagonist who sees the gap between what is said and what is true — and cannot unsee it. _(e.g. “Benjamin could read as well as any pig, but never exercised his faculty.” — he can see the lie and says nothing, which is its own defeat — Animal Farm)_
  - **The forbidden connection** — A friendship, love or private thought the system cannot permit, because it is not shared with it. _(e.g. “I thought we were... were blood brothers” — a friendship across class that the world around them will not allow — Blood Brothers)_
  - **The small act of resistance** — A diary, a hidden object, a remembered song — resistance long before rebellion. _(e.g. “But now I checking out me own history” — one person quietly deciding to learn what he was never taught — Checking Out Me History)_
  - **The breaking** — The regime does not merely defeat the protagonist; it makes them agree. _(e.g. “He loved Big Brother.” — the novel’s last line: the regime has not merely beaten him, it has won his affection, and that is the only defeat that never wears off — Nineteen Eighty-Four)_

### Bildungsroman `Bd`

A bildungsroman is a coming-of-age story that follows a young person as they grow up and learn about themselves and the world. The word is German, from Bildung, meaning education, and Roman, meaning novel. The hero often begins with an innocent or mistaken view of life and meets experiences that test it. By the end, the hero often understands something about themselves, other people and the society that raised them.

**The concept:** A bildungsroman shows that people are shaped by what they live through and by the society around them. The hero often has to give up a mistaken belief, and that loss can feel sad. In Great Expectations, Pip, a village boy who has just met the rich girl Estella, says “I wanted to make Joe less ignorant and common, that he might be worthier of my society”. Pip is now ashamed of Joe, the kind blacksmith who is his sister's husband. When you write about any bildungsroman, say what the hero believes at the start, what experiences change that belief, and what the hero understands at the end.

**Examples:** “Whether I shall turn out to be the hero of my own life, or whether that station will be held by anybody else, these pages must show.” — David, the narrator, begins the story of his life by saying that these pages will show whether he is the hero of it — David Copperfield; “She was one of the kind that likes to grow up.” — after her adventure in Neverland, Wendy grows up while Peter stays a boy, and the book says she did it of her own free will — Peter Pan; “Oxen and wain-ropes would not bring me back again to that accursed island” — Jim Hawkins, who went to sea as a boy to find buried treasure, writes as an adult that nothing would take him back, and that the island still gives him bad dreams — Treasure Island

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We follow one young person over time, and notice how their beliefs and actions change from the start to the end. · Feel: We feel tenderness and a little sadness as the hero learns hard truths, because learning them costs the hero some innocence. · Think: We ask what the hero was taught to believe, and what the hero's growth says about the society that taught it. · Act: We think about how we ourselves have changed, and ask which of our own beliefs we should now question.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any bildungsroman, a story that follows a young person as they grow up. 1. What does the hero believe or want at the start? 2. Which experiences test those beliefs? 3. What does the hero understand about themselves or the world by the end? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about the society that shaped the hero? Try the questions on Jane Eyre. Jane begins as an orphan living with her aunt, Mrs Reed, who treats her unkindly, and she wants to be treated fairly. At Lowood school she is shamed in front of everyone by Mr Brocklehurst, and her friend Helen Burns dies. At Thornfield she falls in love with Mr Rochester, but learns on her wedding day that he is already married. By the end she has inherited money from her uncle and returns to Rochester as an equal. She told him earlier: “I am no bird; and no net ensnares me”. Brontë may want readers to see that a society that treats a poor orphan girl as unimportant is unjust, and that Jane grows by refusing to accept it.

**How to create it:** Choose a young hero and decide one wrong belief they hold at the start, such as thinking that money or rank makes a person worth more. Give them three experiences that test that belief, one after another, and show how each one changes what the hero does. Near the end, let the hero say or do something that shows what they now understand. Ask a friend what the hero has learned; if they cannot say, make the last choice clearer.

**Conventions of the Bildungsroman** — The coming-of-age form traces a moral education, not merely ageing. Its real subject is the unlearning of what a society taught before the protagonist could question it. Pick the stages your story needs — the ache is in what the growth costs.

- **The passage** — innocence to understanding
  - **The inherited view** — The assumptions the protagonist starts with, absorbed before they could judge them. _(e.g. “I want to be a gentleman” — Pip has absorbed the idea that rank is what makes a person worth something — Great Expectations)_
  - **The wider world opens** — A move, an inheritance, a school or a city exposes the protagonist to a life they had not imagined. _(e.g. “I desired liberty; for liberty I gasped; for liberty I uttered a prayer” — Jane’s world is about to widen because she can no longer bear its size — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The mentor, true or false** — A guide who shapes them — sometimes wisely, sometimes by teaching the wrong lesson well. _(e.g. “Break their hearts, my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!” — Miss Havisham teaches Estella cruelty, and teaches it thoroughly — Great Expectations)_
  - **The humiliation** — The fall that cannot be argued away and forces the protagonist to see themselves plainly. _(e.g. “And what coarse hands he has! And what thick boots!” — Estella names what Pip cannot argue with, and he never forgets it — Great Expectations)_
  - **The unlearning** — Dismantling the inherited view — the hardest and most important movement in the form. _(e.g. “God bless this gentle Christian man!” — Pip finally values the plain, kind man he had been ashamed of — Great Expectations)_
- **What it means** — why the form turns outward
  - **Clear sight, bought not given** — Understanding arrives, but never restores the certainty it replaced. _(e.g. “I don’t know whether I trust you. Maybe. But it will take time” — Christopher accepts his father without pretending nothing happened — The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time)_
  - **The society revealed** — As the protagonist learns to see, the world that raised them is exposed too — one child maturing becomes a society revealing itself. _(e.g. “a white baby. And you’re not” — one child’s question exposes what every adult around him has been assuming — My Name Is Leon)_

### Pastoral `Pa`

Pastoral is writing about country life, often about shepherds, that shows the countryside as peaceful, simple and good. It is often set against the noise and pressure of the city or a king's court, or against war. The word comes from the Latin pastor, meaning shepherd. The countryside may be a place of comfort, escape or a lost home. Sometimes the peace is broken by danger or grief.

**The concept:** Pastoral shows what people long for: peace, rest and a simple life close to nature. In Psalm 23, in the Bible, the speaker describes God as a shepherd who looks after him like a sheep: “He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters.” The same psalm mentions “the valley of the shadow of death”, so the peace sits beside danger. When you write about any pastoral, say what place is shown as peaceful, what it is set against, and whether the peace lasts.

**Examples:** “There will we sit upon the rocks / And see the shepherds feed their flocks” — a shepherd invites the woman he loves to leave everything else and live with him in the hills and fields — The Passionate Shepherd to His Love; “half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats” — the Water Rat tells the Mole, who has never been in a boat, that nothing is as worth doing as being on the river — The Wind in the Willows; “Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home” — a soldier who imagines his own death abroad describes the English rivers and sunshine that made him, so a corner of a foreign field will be English — The Soldier

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We linger on fields, rivers and animals, and notice what the countryside is set against. · Feel: We feel calm and longing together, because the peaceful place may be one that the speaker has lost or can only remember. · Think: We ask what the countryside stands for, such as innocence or home, and whether its peace is real or only imagined. · Act: We look for calm places in our own lives, and think about what we need from them and what we are escaping.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any pastoral, writing that shows the countryside as peaceful and simple. 1. What place is described, and which words make it seem peaceful, simple or beautiful? 2. Is the place set against something else, such as a city, a war or the speaker's own trouble, and if so, what? 3. What does the place give the speaker or characters, such as comfort or escape, and does the peace last or break? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel about the countryside? Try the questions on Daffodils by William Wordsworth. The poem describes a crowd of golden flowers beside a lake and beneath trees, “Fluttering and dancing in the breeze”. The place is set against the speaker's own mood, because he walks “lonely as a cloud” and later lies on his couch “in vacant or in pensive mood”. The memory of the flowers gives him comfort: it flashes on his “inward eye”, and his heart “with pleasure fills”. So the peace lasts, because he carries it with him. Wordsworth may want readers to feel that nature can bring lasting happiness, even to a lonely person.

**How to create it:** Choose a place in nature, such as a field, a river bank or a hill, and decide what it gives your character, such as rest, safety or a sense of home. Describe it through sounds, light and slow movement. Set it against something harder, such as a noisy city, a war or a worry. Decide whether the peace lasts or breaks, and let your last image show which. Ask a friend what the place gives the character; if they cannot say, add one detail that shows it.

**Conventions of the Pastoral** — Pastoral is the genre of refuge: the countryside held against the city as innocence against strain. Its deepest meaning usually arrives when the refuge proves false.

- **The green world** — the refuge as it is promised
  - **Idealised countryside** — Rural life as simplicity, innocence and consolation. _(e.g. “To bend with apples the moss’d cottage-trees” — the countryside pictured as generous, and generous without effort — To Autumn)_
  - **Set against the city** — The urban world as corruption, ambition and noise — the thing being escaped. _(e.g. “I wander thro’ each charter’d street, / Near where the charter’d Thames does flow” — even the river is owned, and the city with it — London)_
  - **Retreat** — The protagonist withdraws into the green world seeking what the city cannot give. _(e.g. “A host, of golden daffodils” — the speaker walks out alone and finds what no street could give him — I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud)_
  - **The remembered place** — A landscape already lost, held in memory rather than reachable. _(e.g. “a body of England’s, breathing English air, / Washed by the rivers, blest by suns of home” — a home held in the mind by a soldier who may never reach it — The Soldier)_
- **The turn** — when the refuge fails
  - **Threat invades the green world** — Violence, grief or time enters the place that promised safety. _(e.g. “a huge peak, black and huge, / As if with voluntary purpose” — the quiet lake turns on the boy, and he rows back frightened — The Prelude)_
  - **Consolation denied** — The landscape withholds the peace it seemed to offer, and the loss is sharper for it. _(e.g. “A sunny day with leaves just turning” — a beautiful afternoon that gives the watching father no comfort at all — Walking Away)_
  - **A wholeness we may have invented** — The quiet question of whether the peace was ever there, or only needed. _(e.g. “Each year I hoped they’d keep, knew they would not” — the perfect summer was never going to hold, and he always knew — Blackberry-Picking)_

### Realism `Rl`

Realism is a way of writing that shows ordinary people and everyday life as they really are, without magic or adventure. It often shows how money, class, work and family limit what people can do. Realist writers choose small, exact details, such as food, clothes and rooms. A realist story may end without a neat solution, so that readers recognise real life in it.

**The concept:** Realism shows that forces such as hunger, money and class shape ordinary lives. Small, exact details make readers believe the story and feel that it could happen to them. In Oliver Twist, boys in a workhouse, a place where poor people got food and a bed in return for work, are given only a basin of thin porridge, called gruel. Oliver, an orphan, asks “Please, sir, I want some more”, and the master turns pale. When you write about any realist text, say which ordinary details are chosen, what pressure shapes the characters, and what the writer wants us to notice.

**Examples:** “it was a sufficient dinner for the whole family” — this scene in a ghost story is realistic: one small goose with apple sauce and mashed potatoes feeds the poor Cratchit family, and Mrs Cratchit is delighted that they have not even eaten it all — A Christmas Carol; “Off-hand like—just as I— / Was out of work—had sold his traps—” — a soldier imagines that the man he killed in war joined the army for an ordinary reason, as he did himself: he was out of work and had sold his belongings — The Man He Killed; “Worried by silence, sentries whisper, curious, nervous, / But nothing happens.” — Owen describes soldiers keeping watch in the cold, where nothing happens and the snowy air is more deadly than the bullets — Exposure

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at small, ordinary details, such as food, clothes and rooms, because they show how people really live. · Feel: We feel recognition and sympathy, because the characters face problems such as hunger or poverty that real people face. · Think: We ask what pressures, such as money or class, shape the characters' lives, and which of them the characters cannot see. · Act: We notice how money, class and work shape the lives of people around us, and ask what could be changed.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any realist text, a text that shows ordinary people and everyday life as they really are. 1. Which ordinary details of daily life, such as food, clothes, work or rooms, does the writer choose? 2. What pressure, such as money, class, work or family, shapes what the characters can do? 3. Does the text end with a neat solution, or does it leave a problem unsolved? 4. What does the writer want the reader to notice about real life? Try the questions on Great Expectations. Early in the book, Pip says that his sister has brought him up “by hand”, and he knows she has “a hard and heavy hand”: daily life in his home is plain and strict. Money and class shape his choices, because he is a poor blacksmith's boy who begins to want to be a gentleman after he meets Estella. The book does not end neatly: its last sentence says only that Pip saw “no shadow of another parting from her”, so the reader decides what happens next. Dickens may want readers to see that wanting to rise in society can make a person ashamed of those who love them.

**How to create it:** Choose an ordinary person and an ordinary place, such as a kitchen, a school or a workplace. Pick four exact details that show how the person lives, such as food, clothes and objects. Decide one pressure, such as money, class or family, that limits what the person can do, and show it in one daily event. End without a neat solution, so that the reader decides what happens next. Ask a friend what pressure the character faces; if they cannot say, add one more detail.

**Conventions of Realism** — Realism offers a mirror rather than an escape. Its drama comes from the pressure of ordinary life, not spectacle, and its key emotion is recognition. Choose the constraint your character cannot see.

- **Ordinary pressure** — where the drama actually comes from
  - **Money and class** — Constraints the protagonist is shaped by and often cannot name. _(e.g. “the same answer everywhere, nothin’, nothin’ down for y’” — unemployment closes around Mickey without a single dramatic event — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Work and routine** — The job, the hours, the repetition — plot generated by circumstance rather than event. _(e.g. “I iron the clothes, I cook the food, I clean the house. What more they want from me?” — Enid’s repeated days are the plot — Leave Taking)_
  - **Domestic detail** — Rooms, meals and objects carrying the weight that spectacle carries elsewhere. _(e.g. “my bride / she put a half price sign on di veg” — a shop sign carries a whole marriage — Singh Song!)_
  - **The unspoken** — What a family or a community has agreed not to say aloud. _(e.g. “he’s dark brown and I’m light brown” — Leon names the difference no adult in the family will explain — My Name Is Leon)_
- **Form** — how realism shapes a story
  - **Compressed time** — A short span examined closely, rather than years surveyed. _(e.g. “one line of inquiry at a time” — one evening and one family, examined slowly — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **The epiphany** — A sudden surfacing of a truth that was there all along. _(e.g. “I could have been him!” — Mickey suddenly sees the shape of his whole life, and it was there all along — Blood Brothers)_
  - **The ironic or open ending** — Comfort refused, because life rarely grants full understanding or a clean close. _(e.g. “There are no fences between the gardens” — the book closes on an opening rather than an answer — My Name Is Leon)_

### Satire `Sa`

Satire is writing that makes fun of foolish or harmful behaviour or ideas in order to criticise them. Its tools include exaggeration, which makes a fault bigger than it is, and irony, which says or shows the opposite of what is meant. The target may be a person, a group, a government or a way of life. Satire can be funny, but its purpose is serious: it often hopes to change how readers think or act.

**The concept:** Satire lets a writer criticise something serious through laughter, so readers see a fault that they usually accept. It often works by exaggeration: the fault is made so large that it looks ridiculous. In Gulliver's Travels, a Lilliputian tells Gulliver about two groups in Lilliput, a land of tiny people, who quarrel over which end of an egg should be broken. Eleven thousand people, he says, “have at several times suffered death, rather than submit to break their eggs at the smaller end”. When you write about any satire, say what the target is, how the writer makes it look foolish or harmful, and what change the writer wants.

**Examples:** “a fair, cheap and easy method of making these children sound and useful members of the commonwealth” — the narrator speaks like a calm planner who wants to help Ireland's poor children, but the plan he reaches is shocking, and Swift does not mean it seriously — A Modest Proposal; “But the Emperor has nothing at all on!” — everyone praises the Emperor's new clothes, which they cannot see, until a little child says what is true — The Emperor's New Clothes; “they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population” — Scrooge, a mean businessman, says this about poor people who would rather die than go to the workhouse, and the Ghost of Christmas Present later repeats his words back to him — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at one foolish or harmful habit that the writer makes bigger and plainer than it really is. · Feel: We feel amusement mixed with discomfort, because we are laughing at a fault that we or our society usually accept. · Think: We ask what the writer is attacking and what better behaviour the laughter asks for, and whether we are part of the target. · Act: We challenge foolish rules and empty promises when we meet them, in the news, in adverts or at school.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any satire, writing that makes fun of foolish or harmful behaviour or ideas in order to criticise them. 1. What is the target: a person, a group, an idea or a system? 2. How does the writer make it look foolish or harmful, for example by exaggeration, which makes it bigger than it is, or irony, which shows the opposite of what is meant? 3. What change or better behaviour does the writer want? Try the questions on Animal Farm. The target is leaders who take power by promising equality and then rule for themselves: the pigs take over the farm after the animals drive out the farmer, Mr Jones. The pigs change the Seven Commandments to suit themselves, and the last rule reads “ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS”. That rule is irony, because it contradicts itself. In the last scene the other animals look from pig to man and cannot say which is which. Orwell may want readers to ask whether the rules apply to everyone, and to watch for leaders who use big promises to keep power.

**How to create it:** Choose one foolish or harmful habit, such as boasting, cruelty or empty promises, and decide what you want readers to change. Make a character or a place that shows the habit in an exaggerated way. Let a calm narrator describe it as if it were reasonable, so that readers see the problem for themselves. Include one moment when the truth shows. Ask a friend what you are making fun of; if they cannot say, make the habit clearer.

**Conventions of Satire** — Satire makes fun of foolish or harmful behaviour in order to change how readers think. Writers use tools such as exaggeration, irony and contrast. They aim these tools at a target, such as a person, a habit or an unfair practice. Choose the fault you want to expose, then choose the tool that shows it most clearly.

- **The tools** — how the writer makes the fault look foolish
  - **Exaggeration** — A real attitude is pushed to an extreme until it looks absurd. The reader sees how foolish it is. _(e.g. “a young healthy child well nursed is at a year old a most delicious, nourishing, and wholesome food” — Swift's narrator calmly suggests that poor families should sell their babies as food for the rich. The idea is extreme, so the reader sees how the poor were being treated. — A Modest Proposal)_
  - **Irony** — The writer shows a gap between what is said and what is true. Often the writer says the opposite of what is meant, and the reader works out the real judgement. _(e.g. “I profess in the sincerity of my heart that I have not the least personal interest” — The narrator sounds calm, reasonable and kind while he suggests selling children as food. The reader must supply the horror that his voice never shows. — A Modest Proposal)_
  - **The mirrored scene** — Two speeches or scenes are set against each other. The reader compares them and decides which is right. _(e.g. “a man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own” — Mr Birling tells his son and Gerald that a man must look after himself and his own family. At the end the Inspector argues the opposite. — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **The foil** — A sensible or kind character stands beside the foolish one. The difference shows how foolish the other is. _(e.g. “kind, forgiving, charitable, pleasant time” — Fred, Scrooge's nephew, calls Christmas a kind and forgiving time. His warmth shows how cold Scrooge is. — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Reducing an idea to a slogan** — A complicated idea is cut down to a short slogan. People can repeat it without thinking. _(e.g. “Four legs good, two legs bad” — Snowball cuts the seven commandments down to this one saying, so that every animal can learn it. — Animal Farm)_
- **The target** — what the writer wants the reader to see as wrong
  - **A person who thinks too highly of themselves** — A character is very sure of their own importance, and the text shows that they are wrong. _(e.g. “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable” — Mr Birling boasts that the Titanic cannot sink, and the audience knows that the ship sank. — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **An injustice that people call normal** — A cruel practice is shown in a way that makes it look strange. The reader can no longer accept it as ordinary. _(e.g. “Are there no prisons? Are there no workhouses?” — Two men ask Scrooge for money for the poor. He answers by asking if there are no prisons and no workhouses, as if these were a good answer to poverty. — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **A belief the story shows to be false** — A statement about how society works is set beside what happens. The gap shows that the belief is false, and the reader is left uncomfortable. _(e.g. “in this country our courts are the great levellers” — Atticus tells the jury that courts treat everyone equally. Then the jury finds Tom Robinson guilty, so the story shows that the claim was not true in that court — To Kill a Mockingbird)_

### Allegory `Ag`

An allegory is a story in which characters, places and events stand for ideas or real events. The story has a surface meaning, which is what happens, and a hidden meaning, which is what it stands for. Allegory is related to symbolism, in which one object or person stands for an idea; in an allegory, most parts of the story do this together. The hidden meaning is often about politics, religion or right and wrong.

**The concept:** Allegory lets a writer teach an idea through a story that readers can picture and remember. Many parts are chosen to stand for something, so readers enjoy working out the match. In the Bible, Jesus tells of a farmer who scatters seed on different kinds of ground, and then explains: “The sower soweth the word”, meaning God's message. The seed on stony ground stands for people who hear the message with joy but “have no root in themselves”, so they give up when trouble comes. When you write about any allegory, say what the surface story is, what each main part stands for, and what idea the writer teaches.

**Examples:** “Napoleon is always right” — Boxer, the strong cart-horse, adopts this as his second motto, and readers often take him to stand for workers who trust their leader without question — Animal Farm; “The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom” — after a story about good seed and weeds growing in a field, Jesus tells his followers what each part of it stands for — The Bible (Matthew); “come with me to my garden, which is Paradise” — a child with nail marks on his hands and feet, whom the Giant once helped, invites the Giant to his garden, and the nail marks and the word Paradise suggest that the child stands for Christ — The Selfish Giant

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We treat each person, place and event as a sign, and look for what it stands for. · Feel: We feel curiosity, then a wary recognition, because the invented story turns out to describe something real that matters. · Think: We match each part of the story to its hidden meaning, and ask why the writer chose this disguise to teach the idea. · Act: We look for the real idea behind the stories, slogans and cartoons we meet, and ask what they want us to believe.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any allegory, a story whose characters, places and events stand for ideas or real events. 1. What is the surface story, and which parts of it seem chosen to stand for something else? 2. What does each main part stand for? 3. What idea or warning does the writer want the reader to take from the hidden meaning? Try the questions on The Pilgrim's Progress. The surface story is a journey: a man in rags, with a book in his hand and a great burden on his back, walks from the City of Destruction towards the Celestial City. On the way he sinks into a bog called the Slough of Despond and later passes through a town fair called Vanity Fair. The burden stands for his sin, because he calls himself “a poor burdened sinner”. The bog stands for the fears and doubts that come when a person sees their own sin, and Vanity Fair stands for things that have no lasting value, because the book says that all that is sold there “is vanity”. Bunyan may want readers to see life as a hard journey in which they must pass despair and temptation.

**How to create it:** Choose one idea you want to teach, such as greed, courage or an unfair rule. Invent a simple story, such as a journey or a farm, in which the main characters and places stand for parts of that idea. Keep the surface story clear enough to enjoy without the hidden meaning. Give each important part a name or a detail that points to what it stands for. Ask a friend what the story is really about; if they cannot say, make one clue clearer.

**Conventions of Allegory** — Allegory builds a surface that stands, point for point, for a real one. Nothing in it is accidental. Decide what your invented world is FOR, then make every element earn its parallel.

- **How it is built** — the design rules
  - **One-to-one correspondence** — Each figure or place maps onto a real counterpart, and the map holds throughout. _(e.g. “Beasts of England” — the animals’ anthem stands in for the real revolutionary song, and the pattern holds all the way through — Animal Farm)_
  - **Names that signal** — Naming does interpretive work — a name tells you what the figure stands for. _(e.g. “Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler” — the name painted on the van tells the reader Boxer’s fate before the animals can read it — Animal Farm)_
  - **The fable's distance** — The disguise lets a writer say what could not be said directly. _(e.g. “I should have thought that a pack of British boys… would have put up a better show” — an invented island lets Golding say this about all of us — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Every element deliberate** — Because the surface is invented, nothing in it can be incidental — each choice is a comment. _(e.g. “the conch exploded into a thousand white fragments and ceased to exist” — a shell breaks, and with it every rule the boys had agreed — Lord of the Flies)_
- **How it is read** — what the reader does with it
  - **Decoding the parallel** — The reader runs the real argument underneath the story as they read. _(e.g. “Snowball was in league with Jones from the very start” — a lie told about a pig, which readers recognise as a real show trial — Animal Farm)_
  - **The second meaning of the fall** — The protagonist's downfall carries a political or moral meaning beyond the literal one. _(e.g. “The lone and level sands stretch far away” — one king’s ruin becomes the future of every empire — Ozymandias)_
  - **A truth we would resist head-on** — Seen at one remove, the argument becomes impossible to look away from. _(e.g. “Man is not truly one, but truly two” — a monster story gets us to accept what we would deny about ourselves — Jekyll and Hyde)_

**Related:** Symbolism

### Wonder (Fantasy & Sci-Fi) `Wo`

**Also known as:** Wonder and Awe

Wonder is the name for fantasy and science fiction, stories in which something impossible or not yet real exists or happens in the story's world. Fantasy uses magic, myth and creatures. Science fiction uses science and machines, real or imagined. Both aim to give readers a feeling of amazement, and they often use the strange world to say something about our own.

**The concept:** Wonder lets a writer show a real hope or fear in an imagined form that readers can look at safely. A monster or an alien can stand for something people dread. In Frankenstein, Victor, a student of science, brings a creature to life and sees “the dull yellow eye of the creature open”. He then rushes out of the room in horror, so the story asks what a scientist owes to what he creates. When you write about any fantasy or science fiction, say what is impossible or new, what real hope or fear it stands for, and what the writer wants us to think.

**Examples:** “this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man's” — the narrator opens by saying that creatures cleverer than humans were watching the Earth from across space — The War of the Worlds; “Curiouser and curiouser!” — Alice, who has just eaten a cake in a strange hall, finds that she is growing taller and taller, and is so surprised that she forgets how to speak good English — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; “Second to the right, and straight on till morning.” — Peter tells Wendy the way to the Neverland, a place beyond the real world, as if it were an ordinary address — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the impossible or unfamiliar thing, and learn the rules of the world that it belongs to. · Feel: We feel amazement at something beyond ordinary life, and sometimes fear, because the strange thing may stand for a real danger. · Think: We ask what real hope or fear the strange thing stands for, and what it shows about our own world. · Act: We question what we took to be fixed, such as who has power or what is possible, and imagine how our world could change.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any fantasy or science fiction story, a story in which something impossible or not yet real exists in the story's world. 1. What is impossible or new in this world, and how does it work? 2. How do the characters react to it: with amazement, fear or acceptance? 3. What real hope or fear in our own world might it stand for? 4. What does the writer want the reader to think about our own world? Try the questions on The Wonderful Wizard of Oz. A cyclone lifts Dorothy's farmhouse from Kansas and drops it in Oz, a land with talking animals and a living Scarecrow. Dorothy is amazed, but what she wants most is to go home. The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Cowardly Lion each hope for brains, a heart and courage. The Wizard turns out to be a plain man from Omaha who says “I am a humbug”, and he tells the Scarecrow, “You are learning something every day.” Baum may want readers to see that people already have much of what they long for.

**How to create it:** Choose one impossible or new thing, such as a flying island, a talking machine or a visitor from another planet. Decide its rules and keep to them. Show your character seeing it for the first time, with details of sight and sound. Decide which real hope or fear it stands for, such as loneliness or power, and let that shape the story. Ask a friend what the strange thing stands for; if they cannot say, make one rule or one detail clearer.

**Conventions of Fantasy & Science Fiction** — The genre of amazement and possibility — and a mirror. Every element of the invented world is a choice, and every choice comments on ours. Build the rules first; the meaning rides on them.

- **Building the world** — the invented made coherent
  - **Rules that hold** — Magic or technology with limits and costs — power without rules carries no tension. _(e.g. “I’ll break my staff, / Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, / And deeper than did ever plummet sound / I’ll drown my book.” — the magic has a price, and paying it is what gives it weight — The Tempest)_
  - **The marked or chosen figure** — A protagonist singled out, whose burden is the story's engine. _(e.g. “All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter!” — one sentence marks him out, and the rest of the play is its weight — Macbeth)_
  - **Civilisational stakes** — What is threatened is a world or a people, not only a life. _(e.g. “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” — it is no longer one man in danger; it is a whole country — Macbeth)_
  - **The threshold crossing** — The move from the known world into the other one, which changes the rules of both. _(e.g. “This is our island. It’s a good island.” — they claim the new world, and its rules begin replacing the old ones — Lord of the Flies)_
- **The mirror** — why the impossible is about us
  - **The creature stands for something human** — Monsters and marvels embody real qualities, fears and social forces. _(e.g. “I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel” — the monster names himself as the thing his maker refused to love — Frankenstein)_
  - **A present fear at epic scale** — The invented distance lets a real dread be looked at directly. _(e.g. “The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.” — talking animals let a real political fear be looked at head-on — Animal Farm)_
  - **The inner doubt** — The protagonist must master something in themselves before facing the force outside. _(e.g. “vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself” — he names his own weakness before any enemy lays a hand on him — Macbeth)_

### Mystery `My`

A mystery is a story built around a puzzle, often a crime, that the reader and a main character try to solve by following clues. The writer holds back information, and may use a red herring, a clue that points the wrong way, to make the answer harder to guess. Most mysteries end by revealing the answer and showing how the clues fit together. The main character is often a detective, but may be an ordinary person who is drawn into the puzzle.

**The concept:** Mystery makes readers look closely, because the clues to the answer are often in the story from the start. A missing event can be a clue as well as a present one. In Silver Blaze, Holmes points to “the curious incident of the dog in the night-time”: the police inspector says “The dog did nothing in the night-time”, and Holmes answers “That was the curious incident”. Holmes later explains that a watchdog which stays quiet must have known the visitor. When you write about any mystery, say what puzzle is set, which clues are given, and how the clues lead to the answer.

**Examples:** “You see, but you do not observe.” — Holmes tells Watson this when Watson cannot say how many steps lead up to their room, although he has climbed them hundreds of times — A Scandal in Bohemia; “Mr. Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!” — Dr Mortimer tells Holmes that, near the body of his friend Sir Charles Baskerville, he saw these prints, and the puzzle begins — The Hound of the Baskervilles; “It's me wot has done it!” — Pip has long believed that the rich Miss Havisham is paying for his new life, but Magwitch, the convict Pip helped as a boy, says this when he comes to Pip's room — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look closely at small details and gaps, such as a missing sound, a strange object or a changed story. · Feel: We feel curiosity and suspense, because something is hidden and we are kept partly in the dark until the answer. · Think: We piece clues together, test each idea against the next fact, and ask what the answer shows about the people involved. · Act: We look more carefully at details in news stories, adverts and daily life, and ask what has been left out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any mystery, a story built around a puzzle, often a crime, that the reader tries to solve by following clues. 1. What is the puzzle, and who is trying to solve it? 2. Which clues are given, and does any clue point the wrong way? 3. How does the writer hold back the answer, and when is it revealed? 4. What does the answer show about the people or the society in the story? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. The puzzle is why Mr Hyde, a violent and hated man, has power over Dr Jekyll, a respected doctor. Mr Utterson, Jekyll's lawyer, tries to find out. The clues include Jekyll's will, which leaves everything to his “friend and benefactor Edward Hyde”. Mr Enfield, a relative of Utterson's, guesses that the strange story of the door and the cheque is blackmail. That guess is a red herring. The answer comes only near the end, in Dr Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's own full statement. Stevenson may want readers to see that a respectable person can hide a darker side.

**How to create it:** Choose a puzzle, such as a missing object or a strange event, and decide the true answer before you write. List three clues that point to it, and one red herring that points the wrong way. Show each clue in a plain scene, so that it does not stand out. Hold back the answer until the end, and explain how the clues fit together. Ask a friend to guess the answer from your story; if they cannot, add one clue that is easier to see.

**Conventions of Mystery** — Mystery runs on the controlled release of knowledge: suspense from what is withheld, surprise from what is reversed. Decide what your reader is allowed to know, and when.

- **The puzzle** — managing what the reader knows
  - **The withheld fact** — The one piece of information the whole story is arranged around not giving you yet. _(e.g. “I’ve made a gentleman on you!” — the answer the whole novel has kept back lands in one sentence — Great Expectations)_
  - **The clue in plain sight** — Evidence shown early and passed over, so the reveal feels earned rather than sprung. _(e.g. “A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life” — the ending is announced before the play starts, and we still hope — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **The red herring** — A false trail that is fair — it explains the facts, just not all of them. _(e.g. “none of woman born shall harm Macbeth” — a true promise that he reads in the wrong way — Macbeth)_
  - **The untrustworthy surface** — Ordinary appearances the story exists to prove unreliable. _(e.g. “I gave commands; Then all smiles stopped together” — polite talk lets a murder slip out — My Last Duchess)_
- **Who sees** — point of view as the instrument
  - **The claustrophobic viewpoint** — We know only what one character knows, and are blind to what stands beside them. _(e.g. “I don’t know how it was where you were” — she assumes her narrow world is everyone’s, so we see only what she sees — Never Let Me Go)_
  - **The investigator** — A detective, or an ordinary person thrust into danger, who must read the evidence to survive. _(e.g. “Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.” — his rule is to read the evidence, not his feelings — The Sign of the Four)_
  - **The re-read** — A resolution that makes the reader want to go back — everything meant something else. _(e.g. “A police inspector is on his way here — to ask some — questions —” — the last line sends you back to the first — An Inspector Calls)_

**Related:** Red Herring

### Horror `Ho`

Horror is a genre of stories, poems and films that aim to frighten the audience and make them feel dread, fear or disgust. The threat may be a monster, a ghost or a person who has lost control of themselves, and it is hard to stop or to explain. Horror is related to the Gothic, a genre of fear and suspense in dark, lonely places. Horror often focuses more directly on the frightening threat itself than the Gothic does.

**The concept:** Horror lets a writer show what people fear most, such as losing control, by making the reader feel it in the body. In The Tell-Tale Heart, the narrator has killed an old man and hidden his body under the floor. When the police sit in the room, he thinks he hears the dead man's heart, and he cries out “I admit the deed!”. The threat seems to come from inside him, and he cannot control it. When you write about any horror, say what threatens the character, how the writer builds dread, and what the character loses control of.

**Examples:** “Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me.” — at a feast, Macbeth sees the ghost of Banquo, whom he has had killed, in his seat, and the guests see nothing, so Macbeth seems to lose control in front of everyone — Macbeth; “I saw what I saw, I heard what I heard, and my soul sickened at it” — Dr Lanyon writes this after watching Mr Hyde change into his friend Dr Jekyll, and says he cannot write down what Jekyll then told him — Jekyll and Hyde; “The knocking ceased suddenly, although the echoes of it were still in the house.” — after Mr White makes his last wish on the monkey's paw, the knocking at his door stops, and his wife opens it to a deserted road — The Monkey's Paw

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen and look for sounds, shadows and small signs at the edge of what we can see, and wait for the shock. · Feel: We feel dread in our bodies, because the threat is close and the character cannot stop it or fully understand it. · Think: We sense how little control people have over fear, and ask what real danger or guilt the threat stands for. · Act: We notice how films, news stories and rumours use fear to hold our attention, and we ask what they want from us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any horror, a story that aims to frighten the audience with dread, fear or disgust. 1. What threatens the character, and why is it hard to stop? 2. How does the writer build dread: by hiding the threat, by sound or silence, or by turning something familiar into something dangerous? 3. What does the character lose control of: the situation, other people, or their own mind or body? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about the fear that the threat stands for? Try the questions on Dracula. Count Dracula threatens Jonathan Harker, an English solicitor's clerk who visits his castle to arrange the sale of a London house. The Count is hard to stop because he is not an ordinary man: Harker sees him crawl down the castle wall “face down with his cloak spreading out around him like great wings”. Stoker builds dread with small signs, such as the Count's “sharp, canine teeth” and the locked doors. Harker loses control of his situation: “The castle is a veritable prison, and I am a prisoner!” Stoker may want readers to feel that a dangerous stranger can arrive in an ordinary English town and home, because the Count plans to move to London.

**How to create it:** Choose one threat, such as a presence in the house or a voice on the phone, and decide what your character cannot control. Show small signs of it first, such as a sound, a cold room or an open door. Hold back the full sight of the threat until late, and use short sentences when the danger is close. Ask a friend to read your first page; if they do not feel uneasy, add one more small sign.

**Conventions of Horror** — Horror makes the threat personal and present — where the Gothic broods, horror closes in. These are the elements that strip a character's control away. Choose the ones that fit your threat, then withhold.

- **The threat** — what cannot be reasoned with
  - **A malicious force** — Something that wants harm and cannot be bargained with, only survived or fled. _(e.g. “I shall be with you on your wedding night” — a calm promise of harm that no bargain can undo — Frankenstein)_
  - **The familiar turned monstrous** — A friend's face, a home, a body — safe ground giving way. _(e.g. “That fierce face... the lips were swelled and dark; the brow furrowed” — a face that is not hers appears in her own bedroom at night — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The half-seen** — Suggestion beats display: a shape, a sound, a shadow the reader completes. _(e.g. “A thing, a dark thing, a beast.” — three vague words, and the reader’s mind supplies the rest — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **The body betrayed** — Illness, injury or change that makes the protagonist's own body the site of terror. _(e.g. “all the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand” — her own hand keeps the guilt her mind cannot wash off — Macbeth)_
- **Loss of control** — how the ground is taken away
  - **Isolation** — Help removed — no signal, no neighbours, no one who believes them. _(e.g. “I was a discord in Gateshead Hall; I was like nobody there” — a child in a full house with nobody on her side — Jane Eyre)_
  - **The silence before** — Stillness stretched until the reader begs for the shock, which is the point. _(e.g. “It thrilled him with a vague uncertain horror” — the spirit says nothing at all, and the silence is what frightens him — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Rehearsing mortality** — The genre lets us practise our own death at a safe distance, which is why we consent to it. _(e.g. “Am I that man who lay upon the bed?” — he is made to look at his own death while there is still time to change — A Christmas Carol)_

## Other

### Inciting Incident `Ii`

An inciting incident is the event that first disturbs a character's ordinary life and gives them something to want. It might be a message, a death, an arrival or a discovery. The want is often general at first, such as to escape, to take revenge or to get home. The inciting incident usually comes early in a story. This event starts the rising action, the part of a story in which the problems grow until the climax.

**The concept:** An inciting incident starts the main story: it gives a character a new want, and readers read on to see what the character will do. When a character could ignore the event, their choice to act on it shows who they are. In Macbeth, three witches greet Macbeth, a Scottish lord, and the third calls him the man “that shalt be king hereafter”. Macbeth begins to want the crown, and the rest of the play follows what he does to get it and keep it. When you find any inciting incident, say what it makes the character want, and what they do about it.

**Examples:** “I shall be Mr. Seek.” — after his relative Mr Enfield tells him about a cruel man called Hyde, Mr Utterson, a lawyer, wants to find Hyde, and jokes to himself about the children's game hide-and-seek — Jekyll and Hyde; “It happened that the King's son gave a ball” — Cinderella, made by her stepmother to do the lowest work in the house, wishes she could go to the ball, and her fairy godmother helps her to go — Cinderella; “The house whirled around two or three times and rose slowly through the air.” — a cyclone carries Dorothy's house from Kansas to the Land of Oz, and from then on she wants to get home — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the event that disturbs a character's ordinary life, and watch how they respond to it. · Feel: We feel curious and a little anxious, because the character's ordinary life has changed and we do not know what will happen. · Think: We ask what the character now wants, and what that want shows about the story's main idea, such as ambition or justice. · Act: We notice when a message or a loss makes someone change their plans in real life, and ask what they want now.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any inciting incident. 1. Which event first interrupts the ordinary life of the main character or group, and roughly where in the story does it fall? 2. What does the character or group want straight afterwards that they did not want before, such as to escape, to take revenge or to get home? 3. Could they ignore the event? If not, what makes that impossible? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about the characters or the story through this event? Try the questions on Animal Farm. The event is old Major's speech to the animals in chapter one, where he says that “Man is the only creature that consumes without producing”. Afterwards the animals want to drive out the humans who take what they make. They could have ignored an old boar's dream, but two things make that hard: his speech tells them that their work is being stolen, and he dies three nights later, so his words stay with them. George Orwell wants readers to see that a story of change begins when ordinary people are shown that their situation is unfair.

**How to create it:** Choose one event that disturbs your main character's ordinary life. Place it early, before the story spends long on ordinary life. Make the event give your character a clear want, such as to escape, to take revenge or to get home. Show why they choose to act on it: something is lost, something is owed, or something is offered. Check that most of what follows comes from this event; if the main story would happen without it, change the event or the story.

**Kinds of Inciting Incident** — The recurring shapes the opening disturbance takes. Browse them, pick the one that fits your story, then write it as a specific moment — not the label.

- **Someone or something ARRIVES** — a new force enters the ordinary world
  - **The summons** — A call, an invitation, an offer or a mission that asks the protagonist to leave the life they know. _(e.g. “You will be haunted by Three Spirits” — Marley’s warning turns one ordinary night into a journey Scrooge cannot refuse — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **An arrival** — A stranger comes to town, or an outsider enters a closed world and unsettles it. _(e.g. “Please, sir, an inspector’s called” — five words let an outsider into a closed family party, and nothing after them is the same — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **A fateful meeting** — An encounter with the one person who will change everything — the meet-cute, the rival, the accomplice. _(e.g. “My only love sprung from my only hate!” — one meeting decides who Juliet will love and what that love will cost her — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **A rescue** — Someone needs saving, and answering that need pulls the protagonist out of their ordinary life. _(e.g. “Wake! wake!” — Jane drags Rochester out of a burning bed, and answering that need ties her to a house full of secrets — Jane Eyre)_
- **Something is LOST or TAKEN** — the ordinary world is removed rather than invaded
  - **A death** — A parent, mentor, friend or stranger dies, and the protagonist's world reorganises around the absence. _(e.g. “Marley was dead: to begin with.” — the book opens on an absence, and every event afterwards grows out of it — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **A departure** — The protagonist leaves, is sent away, or is forced out — school, home, country, family. _(e.g. “Romeo is banished” — two words push him out of the city, and the desperate plan that kills them both starts here — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **A loss of home, job or status** — Eviction, dismissal, ruin or disgrace strips away the position the protagonist was standing on. _(e.g. “she’d had a lot to say — far too much — so she had to go” — Eva is dismissed for speaking up, and losing the job begins her fall — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **A rejection** — A refusal — of love, of entry, of belonging — that redirects the protagonist's whole course. _(e.g. “Cursed, cursed creator! Why did I live?” — being refused by his own maker is the wound the Creature spends the novel answering — Frankenstein)_
  - **An escape** — A break for freedom out of confinement, captivity or an intolerable situation. _(e.g. “chased her, flying like a hare / Before our lanterns” — the bride breaks out of a marriage she never chose, and the chase shows us her whole life — The Farmer's Bride)_
- **Something is REVEALED** — the world was not what the protagonist believed
  - **A discovery** — A letter, a body, a secret, an object or a truth is found, and cannot be unfound. _(e.g. “a clothed hyena” — the woman locked upstairs is finally seen, and Jane’s wedding day ends in that room — Jane Eyre)_
  - **A betrayal** — A trusted person is exposed as false, and the protagonist's map of who is safe is redrawn. _(e.g. “nine enormous dogs wearing brass-studded collars came bounding into the barn” — the comrade who shared the revolution turns on his partner — Animal Farm)_
  - **A prophecy or prediction** — A foretelling that plants an idea, a fear or an ambition the protagonist then acts on. _(e.g. “All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter!” — one sentence plants an ambition, and Macbeth begins acting on it — Macbeth)_
  - **A crime committed or witnessed** — The protagonist does something they cannot undo, or sees something they cannot unsee. _(e.g. “with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim under foot” — a murder seen from a window pulls every character into the search — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **A diagnosis or illness** — News about a body — their own or someone else's — that puts a limit on the time available. _(e.g. “I see a vacant seat... and a crutch without an owner” — the Spirit shows Scrooge a child’s death, and suddenly there is a limit on the time — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Something is DEMANDED or IMPOSED** — pressure is applied from outside
  - **An offer that cannot be refused** — A deal, a wager or a bargain whose terms trap the protagonist whichever way they answer. _(e.g. “an equal pound / Of your fair flesh” — the bond sounds like a joke and traps Antonio whichever way he answers — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **A threat or ultimatum** — A deadline or a danger is imposed, and inaction becomes its own choice. _(e.g. “You won’t tell anyone about this, Mrs Johnstone, because if you do, you will kill them” — a threat that makes staying silent a choice too — Blood Brothers)_
  - **An accusation or arrest** — The protagonist is blamed, charged or suspected — often falsely — and must answer for it. _(e.g. “Give not this rotten orange to your friend.” — Hero is accused at the altar and must answer a charge that is not true — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **A disaster** — A storm, a crash, an outbreak or a war breaks in and rewrites what is possible. _(e.g. “Suddenly he awoke and was running — raw” — the war breaks in mid-sentence, and everything the soldier believed is gone — Bayonet Charge)_
  - **A forbidden act** — A rule, law or taboo is broken, and the consequence sets the story running. _(e.g. “I saw the dull yellow eye of the creature open” — Victor breaks the one rule that cannot be unbroken — Frankenstein)_
- **Something is GAINED** — the disturbance arrives disguised as good fortune
  - **An inheritance or windfall** — Money, property, a title or an opportunity lands — and brings obligations the protagonist did not choose. _(e.g. “I’ve made a gentleman on you!” — the money that lifted Pip came with an owner he never chose — Great Expectations)_

**Related:** Rising Action, Climax, Protagonist, Dramatic Situations, Stunning Surprise, Stakes

### Dark Night `Dk`

The dark night is the lowest point near the end of a story, when the main character seems to have lost all hope. It need not happen at night: the name means a time of deep despair. It comes just before the climax, the final struggle that settles the story. In a story with a happy ending, things then get better; in a tragedy, the low point can lead to the character's death.

**The concept:** A dark night shows a character at their lowest point, just before the end of the story. Because readers share the character's despair, they feel the ending more strongly, whether it is happy or sad. In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows Scrooge, a mean old businessman, a neglected grave with his own name on it. Scrooge cries, “Why show me this, if I am past all hope!”, and the next morning he wakes and begins to live differently. When you find any dark night, say what the character has lost or fears losing, what they now believe about their chances, and what happens next.

**Examples:** “full of sound and fury” — just before the final battle, Seyton, an officer who serves him, tells Macbeth that his wife is dead, and Macbeth says that life is a tale full of noise that means nothing — Macbeth; “she could have been happy with him; when it was no longer likely they should meet” — Elizabeth Bennet, who refused Mr Darcy's first proposal, now believes he will never marry into her family, because her sister Lydia is to marry Wickham, a man Darcy scorns — Pride and Prejudice; “and they will kill me, because I am so ugly” — after a hard winter, the ugly duckling swims towards some beautiful swans, expecting them to kill him; instead he sees in the water that he has become a swan, and the swans welcome him — The Ugly Duckling

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at a character at their lowest point, when the thing they want seems lost. · Feel: We feel pity, and sometimes fear, for a character with no hope left, because we have watched them lose what they wanted. · Think: We ask whether anything can be saved, and what the writer shows about how people act when hope is gone. · Act: We notice when people in the news seem to lose everything, and ask what helps them carry on.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dark night, the low point just before the climax, when the hero seems to have lost everything. 1. What has been taken from the character just before the climax: allies, hope or the goal itself? 2. Does the character believe the goal is lost? What do their words or actions show? 3. What does the character decide or do next because of this low point, if the story gives them a next step? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand from this low point? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. In Act 5, Scene 1, Romeo, banished from Verona, is living in Mantua. His servant Balthasar tells him that Juliet is dead, so his goal, to be with Juliet, is taken from him. Yes, he believes his goal is lost. He cries “Then I defy you, stars!”, which shows that he believes he has lost her and will fight his fate. He decides to buy poison and go back to Verona. The audience knows that Juliet is only drugged, so Shakespeare makes us feel pity and see how a mistaken belief destroys him.

**How to create it:** Take the thing your character wants most and remove it, just before the end of your story. Show the loss in what they do or say, not by naming the feeling. Let them reach their lowest point with no help and no easy way back. Make their next choice come from this low point. Check that the ending depends on that choice; if luck or a rescue could replace it, rewrite it.

**Related:** Climax

### Turning Point `Tu`

A turning point is a moment after which a character cannot go back to their old life. It is usually an act the character chooses, not an accident. It can come early, in the middle or late in a story. The climax, by contrast, is the final struggle that settles the story, and it comes near the end. In a tragedy, the turning point often leads the character towards ruin.

**The concept:** A turning point shows that some moments cannot be undone, especially a character's own choices. Because the character cannot go back, much of what follows is a result of that one moment. In Frankenstein, Victor, a young scientist, works for nearly two years to bring a body to life, then sees “the dull yellow eye of the creature open”. From that moment Victor cannot undo what he has made, and the rest of the novel follows what happens between him and the creature. When you write about any turning point, say what happens, what the character can no longer go back to, and what changes afterwards.

**Examples:** “I have done the deed.” — Macbeth tells his wife, Lady Macbeth, that he has killed King Duncan; he can never again be the loyal soldier he was at the start of the play — Macbeth; “Please, sir, I want some more.” — Oliver, a hungry boy in a workhouse, asks the master for a second helping; next morning a notice offers five pounds to anyone who will take him, and soon he is sent away to work for an undertaker — Oliver Twist; “she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat” — Eve, the first woman, eats the fruit God had forbidden and gives some to Adam, her husband; God then sends them out of the Garden of Eden, and they never live there again — The Bible (Genesis)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the exact moment when something happens that a character cannot undo. · Feel: We feel dread, and sometimes relief, because the character can no longer go back to the old life. · Think: We ask what the character has lost, and what the writer shows about actions and their results. · Act: We think harder before making real choices that cannot be undone, such as breaking a promise or telling a lie.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any turning point, the moment after which a character cannot go back to their old life. 1. What happens that cannot be undone? 2. What can the character no longer go back to because of it? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel through this moment? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. In Act 3, Scene 1, Romeo kills Tybalt, Juliet's cousin, in a street fight, after Tybalt has killed Romeo's friend Mercutio. Romeo can no longer live in Verona, where Juliet lives: the Prince of Verona banishes him, and says that if he is found there, “that hour is his last”. Shakespeare wants the audience to feel pity, and to see that one moment of anger, in a feud between two families, cannot be taken back.

**How to create it:** Choose an act that your main character decides to do, not an accident. Make it impossible to undo, for example a secret told to the wrong person or something broken that cannot be repaired. Show at once what the character can no longer go back to. Check whether the character could return to their old life and lose nothing; if they could, make the act cost them more.

**Related:** Climax, Stunning Surprise

### MacGuffin `Mk`

A MacGuffin is an object or goal that the characters chase, and the chase sets the plot moving. It matters a great deal to the characters, but what exactly it is matters little to the reader: another prize could start the same story.
