What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand through the waiting? Try the questions on Frankenstein by Mary Shelley. Victor Frankenstein has destroyed the female creature he was making, and the creature he made warns him: “I shall be with you on your wedding-night.” The reader fears what will happen on that night, and knows only what Victor knows: the creature has promised to come. The threat is made, and then the story moves on to other events, including the death of Victor's friend Henry Clerval, before the wedding night comes, so the answer is delayed. Shelley may want the reader to feel dread, and to see that Victor cannot protect the people he loves from the creature he made.

**How to create it:** Choose one question you want the reader to wait for, such as whether a character will be caught or hurt. Tell the reader about the question early, with a threat, a promise or a clue. Delay the answer with another scene or a small problem. Give the answer later than the reader expects. Check by asking a friend what they think will happen next; if they cannot say, make the question clearer.

**How Suspense Is Generated** — Suspense is dread stretched across time — a gap between what is known and what is coming, held open until it finally closes. Browse the levers that open the gap and the ones that keep it open. (For pressure inside a single present moment, browse Tension.)

- **We know MORE than they do** — open the gap downward — hand the reader a truth the character has not reached
  - **Let us in on it** — Give the audience a fact the character lacks, so every confident line they speak gathers a second meaning and we wait, helpless, for them to learn it. _(e.g. "the Titanic… unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable" — Birling's certainty collapses for an audience who knows the ship sank — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Words built to mislead** — Have the character receive a promise that is literally true and fatally misread — false certainty handed over exactly when they most crave reassurance. _(e.g. "none of woman born / Shall harm Macbeth" — a truth shaped to deceive, and he walks on believing it — Macbeth)_
  - **Tell them the ending first** — Announce the outcome before the story starts, so the reader watches every scene knowing where it lands. _(e.g. the prologue reveals the twins' deaths, so the childhood gunplay — "I got y'. I shot y' dead" — is watched as rehearsal — Blood Brothers)_
  - **A narrator who sees further** — Use a narrating voice that can look where the characters cannot, and let it show us the danger being assembled off to one side. _(e.g. Napoleon "put them in a loft so secluded that the rest of the farm soon forgot their existence" — the reader senses the puppies' purpose while the animals forget them — Animal Farm)_
  - **Two viewpoints, one blind spot** — Alternate between characters so the reader assembles a whole picture that neither of them holds. _(e.g. “So did y' hear the story of the Johnstone twins? / As like each other as two new pins... / How one was kept and one given away” — we follow both brothers holding a fact that neither of them ever has — Blood Brothers)_
  - **The confession only we hear** — Let the character speak their real intention alone on stage, so we carry their secret into every scene that follows. _(e.g. “It is engendered. Hell and night / Must bring this monstrous birth to the world's light” — Iago gives us his plan while alone on stage, so we carry it into every scene that follows — Othello)_
  - **The aside the others miss** — A line turned outward, heard by the audience and not by the people on stage — a gap opened in a single breath. _(e.g. “Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires” — Macbeth turns to us for one line, and the men standing beside him hear none of it — Macbeth)_
- **We know LESS — and cannot trust what we know** — open the gap upward — keep a fact from the reader, or make the fact unreliable
  - **Hold the fact back** — Show the reader the effect and refuse the cause, releasing the explanation only at a moment you choose. _(e.g. "I not unfrequently heard Grace Poole's laugh: the same peal, the same low, slow ha! ha!" — a laugh from the third storey Brontë will not explain for hundreds of pages — Jane Eyre)_
  - **A witness who may be wrong** — Filter the story through someone who lies, omits, or sincerely believes an untruth, so the reader must read past the telling. _(e.g. "I never saw a man I so disliked, and yet I scarce know why" — Enfield feels the threat and cannot name it, so neither can we — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **The false trail** — Plant a clue that points confidently in the wrong direction — fair misdirection, never a cheat. _(e.g. “the whole story's just a lot of moonshine” — the audience is handed a comfortable explanation, and almost accepts it, moments before the telephone rings — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Accounts that will not agree** — Give the same event twice from two sources that contradict, so the reader cannot settle which version to fear. _(e.g. “I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel” — the creature tells the same events a different way, so we cannot settle which version to fear — Frankenstein)_
  - **Tell it at a remove** — Nest the story inside another telling, so we always know we are being handed a version — and wonder what the teller left out. _(e.g. Victor's confession reaches us only through Walton's letters home — "I have no friend, Margaret" opening the frame that holds it — Frankenstein)_
  - **Open on the unexplained** — Begin with an image or event that demands an explanation and withhold it, so the question itself pulls the reader forward. _(e.g. "The door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and distained" — the novel opens on a door it refuses to explain — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Cut out the middle** — Skip the stretch of time in which the crucial thing happened, and let the reader dread what the white space contains.
- **Plant a promise the story must pay** — engineer the dread in advance, so the reader is waiting long before the moment arrives
  - **Seed the hint early** — Place a detail whose full meaning only lands later, so when the event comes the reader feels it was always coming. _(e.g. "I got y'. I shot y' dead" — the children's gunplay is charming in isolation and unbearable in retrospect — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Make it a debt, not a hint** — Set up an object, a skill or a threat that the story then owes the reader; the promise is explicit and must be paid. _(e.g. “If I see any thing to-night why I should not marry her to-morrow, in the congregation, where I should wed, there will I shame her.” — he announces the scene the play now owes us, and names the place it will happen — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **Let them feel it coming** — Give the character a premonition they cannot act on, so the reader watches them proceed anyway. _(e.g. "My mind misgives / Some consequence yet hanging in the stars" — Romeo perceives the danger and walks into the feast regardless — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **The prophecy** — State the outcome as a foretelling. The reader now watches for the mechanism rather than the result — and for the clause that was misread. _(e.g. "All hail, Macbeth, that shalt be king hereafter!" — the prophecy plants an ambition the play then spends five acts fulfilling — Macbeth)_
  - **The image that keeps returning** — Repeat one object, phrase or picture at intervals, each return altered, so the reader learns to read its next appearance as a warning. _(e.g. "Four legs good, two legs bad" becomes "Four legs good, two legs better!" — the slogan's drift measures the betrayal — Animal Farm)_
  - **Name the theme early** — Have someone state the story's central idea near the start; the reader then waits to see the story test it. _(e.g. “Mankind was my business. The common welfare was my business” — Marley states the book's central idea in the first stave, and we wait to see whether Scrooge will be tested by it — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Promise the scene we are owed** — Signal the confrontation the whole story is building toward, then make us wait for it — the power is in the length of the wait. _(e.g. "the lady Hero hath been falsely accused, the prince and Claudio mightily abused" — the confession we have waited for arrives only after the damage is done — Much Ado About Nothing)_
- **Hold the gap OPEN** — everything that stops the answer arriving — suspense dies the moment the gap closes
  - **Break off at the worst moment** — End the chapter or scene on the question, not the answer, so the reader must carry the gap across the break. _(e.g. “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek” — the chapter ends on the hunt, not the finding, so the reader carries the unanswered question across the break — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Cut to the other storyline** — Leave one thread mid-crisis and pick up the other, so both gaps stay open and the threads edge toward each other.
  - **Slow down instead of summarising** — Where a summary would cover the wait in a sentence, write it as a scene — the reader's time is spent at the same rate as the character's. _(e.g. “Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds” — Juliet's wait is written as a whole speech, so we wait at her speed instead of being told that she waited — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Step back into the past** — Interrupt the approaching moment with the scene that explains why it matters — the delay itself raises the cost of the return. _(e.g. “a solitary child, neglected by his friends” — the story stops and returns to Scrooge's boyhood, and the delay makes what comes next matter more — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **The silence that will not answer** — Give the threatening presence no voice at all. A figure that refuses to explain itself cannot be argued with, and the reader fills the vacuum. _(e.g. the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come is "shrouded in a deep black garment", never speaks, and only points — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **End where you began** — Return to the opening situation so the reader realises the danger was never resolved, only postponed. _(e.g. "a police inspector is on his way here — to ask some — questions —" — the play closes on the call it opened with — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Refuse to close it** — Leave the outcome genuinely undecided at the end, so the reader must sit with the gap rather than be released from it. _(e.g. “The creatures outside looked from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which.” — the last line settles nothing, and the reader is left holding the gap — Animal Farm)_

**Related:** Dramatic Irony, Tension, Withholding Information, Ticking Clock

### Surprise `Tw`

Surprise is a shock when something happens, or is revealed, that the reader did not expect. It comes with little or no warning, so the reader does not spend time waiting for it. This makes it different from suspense, which is waiting to find out, and from tension, which is strain in a moment that is happening now. A surprise may be small or large, and it works best when earlier details make it believable afterwards.

**The concept:** Surprise breaks what the reader expects, so the reader looks again at what came before. The sudden change can make earlier pages mean something new, which is part of the pleasure. In Animal Farm, the pigs, who walked on four legs like the other animals, come out of the farmhouse “all walking on their hind legs”. The animals had learned that “Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy”, so the sight suggests the pigs have become like humans. When you write about any surprise, say what the reader expected, what happened instead, and what the writer wants the reader to understand.

**Examples:** “there stood Henry Jekyll!” — Dr Lanyon, a doctor, watches the violent Hyde drink a potion and change into his old friend Dr Jekyll, a fact the reader has not been told — Jekyll and Hyde; “Thou canst not say I did it” — at the feast, Macbeth, the new king, speaks to the ghost of Banquo, a friend he has had killed, which appears suddenly and which the other guests cannot see — Macbeth; “Yes, Pip, dear boy, I've made a gentleman on you!” — Pip, who believed his secret money came from Miss Havisham, a rich woman, learns that the man who paid for him is Magwitch, the convict he helped as a child — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the exact moment when what we expected stops being true. · Feel: We feel a jolt of shock or delight, because something happens that we did not see coming. · Think: We look back for clues we missed, and ask what the reveal shows about the characters and the writer's idea. · Act: We notice how news stories, adverts and trailers use a sudden reveal to catch our attention, and ask what they want next.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any surprise, a revelation the reader did not see coming. 1. What fact is revealed? 2. How does it arrive: who reveals it, and what moment does it interrupt? 3. What does it change about what happened before it, or about what happens next? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand? Try the questions on Jane Eyre by Charlotte Brontë. The fact revealed is that Mr Rochester already has a wife, Bertha Mason, whom he married fifteen years before. A stranger in the church interrupts Jane and Rochester's wedding, just before the vows, saying: “The marriage cannot go on: I declare the existence of an impediment.” The wedding stops, and Jane has to decide whether she can stay with a man who hid this from her. Brontë may want the reader to share Jane's shock and to doubt whether Rochester can be trusted.

**How to create it:** Choose one fact your reader does not expect and your character does not know. Decide the moment it will land, ideally when your character feels safe. Reveal it in one short, plain sentence, spoken by someone with a reason to say it. Show your character's first reaction straight away. Check that the reveal changes how your reader sees something that happened earlier; if it only adds a new fact, rewrite it so it changes how the reader understands an earlier event.

**Related:** Plot Twist, Subverted Expectation, Stunning Surprise

### Fresh News `Nw`

Fresh news is new information that changes what a character wants or must do next. Writers often place it at the end of a scene or chapter, so that the character starts the next one with a new aim or problem. The news can be large, such as a death, or small, such as a person's name.

**The concept:** Fresh news links one scene to the next, because it gives a character a new aim or problem to deal with. The reader often learns the news at the same moment as the character, and wants to see what the character will do about it. In Macbeth, King Duncan gives his son Malcolm the title “The Prince of Cumberland”, which means that Malcolm will be the next king. Macbeth hopes to be king himself, so he now faces a new obstacle: Malcolm. When you write about any fresh news, say what the character wanted before the news, what the news is, and what the character must now do or decide.

**Examples:** “My only love sprung from my only hate!” — at the end of the feast, Juliet learns that Romeo, the boy she has just kissed, is a Montague, her family's enemy, and in her next scene she wishes that one of them could give up their family name — Romeo and Juliet; “brought up as a gentleman” — Jaggers, a London lawyer, tells Pip, a blacksmith's apprentice, that a secret helper wants him to leave home and be brought up as a gentleman, and in the next chapter Pip orders new clothes and leaves home for London — Great Expectations; “Expect the first to-morrow, when the bell tolls One.” — before it leaves, Marley's ghost, the spirit of Scrooge's dead partner, gives Scrooge a new problem: three spirits will visit him, and the first will come when the bell tolls one — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice a new fact that a character learns, and what it changes for that character. · Feel: We feel eager or anxious to read on, because the news raises a new question about whether the character will get what they want. · Think: We ask what the character will do with the news, and what that choice shows about the story's ideas, such as love or ambition. · Act: We notice when episodes and chapters end on a new fact that makes us want to return, and ask why the writers chose it.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any fresh news, new information that gives a character a new goal, often at the end of a scene. 1. What does the character want when the scene begins? 2. What new information does the character or the reader have when it ends? 3. What new goal does that information give the character? 4. What does the writer want the reader to wonder or feel as the scene ends? Try the questions on Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 1. Horatio, a friend of Hamlet, doubts the guards' story of a ghost, so he wants to see for himself. When the ghost first appears, looking like the dead king, Horatio says “It harrows me with fear and wonder.” (“Harrows” means torments.) By the end of the scene the ghost has appeared twice, and the new goal is to tell Prince Hamlet: “Let us impart what we have seen tonight”. Shakespeare may want the audience to wonder what the ghost will say, since Horatio expects that “This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him.”

**How to create it:** Decide what your character wants in this scene. Let them get it, miss it or find something they did not expect. Choose one new fact that the scene ends on, which the reader did not have at the start. Make that fact give the character a new goal for the next scene. Check by imagining that you remove this scene: if the next scene still makes sense without it, add a new fact to this scene that the next scene needs.

### Pacing `Pc`

Pacing is how fast or slow a story moves. A writer speeds it up with short sentences, quick events and summary, which skips over time. A writer slows it down with scene, which stays inside one moment, and with detail and long sentences. Pacing often shows how much each part matters, because writers tend to spend more words on what matters most.

**The concept:** Pacing controls how long the reader spends on each moment, so it can show what matters most. The word “pace” comes from a Latin word meaning “step”. In Romeo and Juliet, Friar Lawrence, a priest, warns Romeo: “Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.” Romeo and Juliet then marry the day after they meet, and the story rushes towards their deaths a few days later. When you write about any pacing, say where the story speeds up or slows down, what the speed shows about that moment, and what the writer wants the reader to feel.

**Examples:** “And strangled her. No pain felt she” — after many slow lines in which Porphyria arrives and settles beside the speaker, the killing is told in a few short words — Porphyria's Lover; “Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow” — Macbeth, hearing that Lady Macbeth is dead, says that time creeps from one day to the next, and the repeated word makes the line move slowly — Macbeth; “I now pass a space of eight years almost in silence” — Jane, who is telling the story of her own life, skips eight years in one sentence — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice where a story speeds up or slows down, and which moments get the most words. · Feel: We feel rushed when sentences are short and events come quickly, and we feel the weight of a moment when the story slows. · Think: We ask why the writer gives one moment many words and skips another, and what idea that choice makes important. · Act: We notice how speeches, films and adverts speed up or slow down to steer our feelings, and ask why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any pacing, how fast or slow a story moves. 1. Where does the story move quickly, and where does it slow down? 2. At each point, does it use summary, which skips over time, or scene, which stays inside one moment? 3. What does the speed show about how much each part matters? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel as the pace changes? Try the questions on Frankenstein by Mary Shelley. It moves quickly over the months Victor spends building his creature, and slows down for one night. The months are summary: “Winter, spring, and summer passed away during my labours” covers many months in one sentence. The night is scene: Chapter 5 gives the hour, one in the morning, the rain and the candle, then the moment the creature opens its eye. The speed shows that the one night matters more than the months of work, because it is when Victor's dream turns to “breathless horror and disgust”. Shelley may want the reader to feel that night's horror and shock.

**How to create it:** Decide which moment in your story matters most. Cover the time before it in one or two quick sentences. Slow down for that moment: give the hour, one sound and one thing the character sees. Use short sentences where the scene should race and longer ones where it should settle. Check that your most important moment takes more words than the time you skipped; if not, add detail to it.

**Related:** Scene vs Summary

### Dialogue `Dg`

Dialogue is the words that characters say to each other in a text. Good dialogue does more than pass on facts: it shows what each speaker wants, how each one speaks, and what they leave unsaid. A speaker may mean more than they say, and this hidden meaning is called subtext. Speakers often want different things, so a conversation can work like a contest.

**The concept:** Dialogue lets readers hear characters, so they learn about people from what they say and how they say it. Readers overhear instead of being told, so they can work out the hidden meaning themselves. In Macbeth, Macbeth asks his wife about their plan to kill King Duncan: “If we should fail?” Lady Macbeth repeats his words, “We fail?”, and then tells him they will not fail. Her reply shows what she wants, and how little room she leaves for his doubt. When you write about any dialogue, say what each speaker wants, what is left unsaid, and what the conversation shows about them.

**Examples:** “What! my dear Lady Disdain, are you yet living?” — Benedick greets Beatrice with a joke name, “Lady Disdain”, after she has insulted him, so the two trade sharp words in every line — Much Ado About Nothing; “O, beware, my lord, of jealousy” — Iago, Othello's officer, pretends to warn him against jealousy, and the warning also makes Othello wonder whether he has a reason to be jealous — Othello; “What right have you to be dismal? What reason have you to be morose?” — Scrooge's nephew Fred repeats his uncle's question with the words turned round, and the two argue about Christmas, Scrooge in short, sharp words and Fred cheerfully — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen to what each speaker says, how they say it, and what they leave unsaid. · Feel: We feel curious, and sometimes uneasy, when the words say one thing and the speaker seems to mean another. · Think: We read between the lines to work out what each speaker wants, and what the conversation shows about them. · Act: We listen for what people leave unsaid in interviews and everyday talk, and ask what they really want.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dialogue. 1. What does each speaker want from the conversation? 2. Does anyone say one thing and mean another, and if so, what do they mean? 3. How does each voice sound: what do their word choice, sentence length and tone show about the speaker? 4. What does the conversation show about the speakers or their relationship that the writer wants the reader to see? Try the questions on the opening conversation of Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen. Mrs Bennet wants her husband to visit Mr Bingley, a rich new neighbour, so that Bingley may meet their daughters. Mr Bennet seems to want to tease her: he pretends not to care about the news she is eager to tell. She says she is thinking of Bingley marrying one of their daughters. He asks, “Is that his design in settling here?” This treats the plan as Bingley's, when it is hers. Mrs Bennet is impatient and gives orders (“you must visit him as soon as he comes”), while Mr Bennet gives short, calm replies (“I see no occasion for that”). Austen may want the reader to see, from the first page, an anxious wife and a husband who is amused and unmoved.

**How to create it:** Decide what each speaker wants from the conversation, and make those wants different. Let each speaker say less than they mean, so the reader works out the rest. Give each speaker their own way of talking, such as long breathless sentences or short dry ones. Make any line that passes on information also show what the speaker wants. Check by covering the names: could a reader tell who speaks from the words alone? If not, change one speaker's wording.

**Kinds of Dialogue** — Speech that does real work, told many ways. Each kind is a different job dialogue can do on the page — open a card, name the kind, and look for what the words reveal beneath what they say.

- **Voice & characterisation** — How a character's diction, rhythm and vocabulary expose who they are — class, age, education, self-image
  - **Pride and Prejudice** — Mrs Birling's clipped, superior phrasing turns a whole class into an object of contempt — the diction itself is the snobbery. _(e.g. “In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed.” — the strain in the syntax says what the speaker will not: that loving her is something he has been fighting — Pride and Prejudice)_
  - **Great Expectations** — Magwitch's rough, imperative speech marks his low status and menace before we know anything else about him. _(e.g. "Hold your noise!" — Great Expectations)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — Scrooge's curt, dismissive exclamation is his whole miserly character compressed into two syllables. _(e.g. "Bah! Humbug!" — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Subtext — the unsaid** — When a line means the opposite of, or far more than, its surface — the real meaning sits underneath the words
  - **Macbeth** — Lady Macbeth names the very method of subtext: present an innocent surface while the true intent hides beneath it. _(e.g. "look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't" — Macbeth)_
  - **Jekyll and Hyde** — Utterson's grim pun hides real dread beneath a play on words — the light tone is the mask over his fear. _(e.g. "If he be Mr Hyde... I shall be Mr Seek" — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — Scrooge's cool economic phrasing hides a monstrous indifference to human life beneath the language of book-keeping. _(e.g. "decrease the surplus population" — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Conflict — dialogue as combat** — Speech as a power struggle: each line tries to win, wound or dominate the other speaker
  - **Pride and Prejudice** — The Inspector seizes control of the exchange, cutting Birling down and reversing the play's social hierarchy through speech alone. _(e.g. “I have never desired your good opinion, and you have certainly bestowed it most unwillingly.” — she refuses him in the politest words available, and every one of them lands — Pride and Prejudice)_
  - **Romeo and Juliet** — Tybalt's provocation is pure verbal aggression, a challenge thrown down that forces the fight the scene has been building towards. _(e.g. "thou art a villain" — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Lord of the Flies** — The hunters' chant turns speech into a weapon of the mob, the chanted imperatives driving the boys towards violence. _(e.g. "Kill the pig! Cut her throat!" — Lord of the Flies)_
- **Exposition through speech** — Dialogue that delivers background or context — best when it also does a second job (character, irony, tension)
  - **An Inspector Calls** — Birling's dinner-table lecture feeds us the setting while his certainty, undercut by dramatic irony, exposes his folly. _(e.g. the Titanic is "absolutely unsinkable" — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — The charity gentlemen's request draws Scrooge's worldview out of him in his own words, delivering his character as exposition. _(e.g. "Are there no prisons?" — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Jekyll and Hyde** — Enfield's retold account delivers the novel's founding mystery through speech, the calm verb making the horror land harder. _(e.g. "trampled calmly over the child's body" — Jekyll and Hyde)_
- **Interruption, overlap & pace** — Broken turn-taking — cutting in, clipped exchanges, shared lines — that speeds the scene and shows who holds power
  - **Macbeth** — After the murder the lines fracture into short, frightened half-exchanges, the broken rhythm enacting the couple's panic. _(e.g. "Did not you speak?" / "When?" — Macbeth)_
  - **Romeo and Juliet** — The lovers finish each other's lines, their shared sonnet rhythm making two voices sound like one. _(e.g. "Then move not while my prayer's effect I take" — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **An Inspector Calls** — Priestley's stage direction has the Inspector break across the others, the interruption itself dramatising his authority. _(e.g. "(cutting through, massively)" — An Inspector Calls)_
- **Dialect & idiolect** — Regional or class-marked speech, or a character's unique verbal signature, used to place and distinguish them
  - **Blood Brothers** — Mrs Johnstone's colloquial Liverpool register sets her working-class world against Mrs Lyons's careful, formal speech. _(e.g. "By the time I was twenty-five I looked like forty-two" — Mrs Johnstone's plain, everyday Liverpool speech, set beside Mrs Lyons's careful formality — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Great Expectations** — Joe's warm, ungrammatical idiolect and his repeated endearment mark his class and his gentleness at once. _(e.g. "old chap" — Great Expectations)_
  - **Romeo and Juliet** — The Nurse's rambling, circling idiolect — repetition and digression — makes her comic, earthy voice unmistakable. _(e.g. "Even or odd, of all days in the year" — Romeo and Juliet)_
- **The stinger — the loaded line** — A short line placed to land with maximum weight, threat or finality — often at the end of a speech or scene
  - **An Inspector Calls** — The Inspector's parting warning lands as a threat to the whole society, its plosive triad ringing after he leaves. _(e.g. "fire and blood and anguish" — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Macbeth** — Lady Macbeth's brisk, loaded line dismisses the murder as trivial — a stinger whose confidence the play will later shatter. _(e.g. "A little water clears us of this deed" — Macbeth)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — Marley's anguished correction lands the book's whole moral in four words, redefining what a life is for. _(e.g. "Mankind was my business" — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Silence & understatement** — What a character will not say, or says too mildly — the gap or the restraint carries the feeling
  - **Romeo and Juliet** — Mercutio's dying understatement makes light of a fatal wound, the mildness sharpening the horror of his death. _(e.g. "'tis enough" — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Macbeth** — Macbeth greets his wife's death with a chillingly flat line, the understatement measuring how numb he has become. _(e.g. "She should have died hereafter" — Macbeth)_
  - **Twelfth Night** — Sheila's quiet, ironic understatement exposes her family's pretence that nothing has changed. _(e.g. “She never told her love, / But let concealment, like a worm i'th' bud, / Feed on her damask cheek” — she is describing herself, and the silence she is praising is the one she is keeping — Twelfth Night)_

### Action Hook `Ac`

An action hook is an opening that puts the reader in the middle of events that are already happening, before anything is explained. Usually someone is in danger or under pressure, in a fight, a chase, a storm or a tense argument. What the person does shows us who they are. It is close to in medias res, the Latin phrase for starting a story partway through its events.

**The concept:** An action opening shows character through what a person does, not through description. We judge the person by their choices, because they are already under pressure. In Hamlet, the first words are a challenge in the dark: Barnardo, a guard, calls “Who's there?” and Francisco, the guard already on duty, answers “Nay, answer me. Stand and unfold yourself.” Both men are on edge, and we learn that from what they say. When you write about any action hook, say what danger or pressure the person faces, what they do, and what that shows about them.

**Examples:** “Half a league, half a league, / Half a league onward, / All in the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred.” — the poem starts with six hundred riders already moving into the valley of Death, so we are inside the charge before anything is explained — The Charge of the Light Brigade; “Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, / Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge,” — the speaker and the men with him are already bent double, coughing and cursing their way through mud, so we meet them under strain before we are told why — Dulce et Decorum Est; “I sprang to the stirrup, and Joris, and he; / I galloped, Dirck galloped, we galloped all three;” — the speaker and two other riders set off at a gallop at once, so we race with them before we know why — How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch what a person does under pressure, before we are told who they are or why they are there. · Feel: Arriving in the middle of danger feels like alarm, because we are given the threat and none of the explanation. · Think: We work out what the writer is saying about courage, duty or fear from how people act in danger. · Act: We judge people in the news and in daily life by what they do under pressure, not only by what they say.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any action hook, an opening that drops the reader into events already happening. 1. What is happening, and what has the reader not been told yet? 2. Who is under pressure, and what do they do? 3. What does that reaction show about the person? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel by starting here? Try the questions on the opening of The Tempest. A ship is caught in a storm and may run aground, and the Boatswain, the sailor in charge of the crew, is giving orders. We are not told why there is a storm; the next scene shows it was made by magic. The Boatswain is under pressure: he orders the crew to work and tells the king's party to go below, saying “To cabin: silence! trouble us not.” That shows he is brave and practical, and cares more about saving the ship than about rank. Shakespeare may want us to feel the danger at once, and to see that a storm treats a king like anyone else.

**How to create it:** Choose a character and a danger that is near them. Begin in the middle of that danger, with the character already moving or speaking. Show how they react, because the reaction shows who they are. Hold back who they are and how the danger began. Check that a stranger could say what kind of person your character is from your first paragraph; if not, add one more action.

**Related:** Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook, In Medias Res

### Dialogue Hook `Dh`

A dialogue hook is an opening that begins with characters already speaking, so the reader joins the conversation partway through. The first lines often carry tension, such as a threat, a secret or one speaker having more power than the other. A dialogue opening can also be quiet or comic, as long as the words mean more than they say. It is a quieter relative of the action hook, which begins with events instead of speech.

**The concept:** A dialogue opening shows a relationship before it explains it. The reader overhears people talking and must work out what each wants, so the words often mean more than they say. In The Merchant of Venice, the play begins with Antonio, a merchant, speaking to his friends Salarino and Solanio: “I know not why I am so sad”. His friends guess that he is worried about his ships, and then that he is in love, and he says no to both, so the cause stays hidden. When you write about any dialogue hook, say who is speaking to whom, what each person wants, and what the words leave unsaid.

**Examples:** “Gregory, on my word, we'll not carry coals.” — Sampson, a servant of the Capulet family, tells his friend Gregory that they will not put up with insults, and the joking talk soon leads to a fight — Romeo and Juliet; “Tush, never tell me, I take it much unkindly / That thou, Iago, who hast had my purse,” — Roderigo angrily tells Iago that Iago, who has had his money, knew about something and said nothing, so we begin in the middle of a quarrel — Othello; “Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour / Draws on apace;” — Theseus, Duke of Athens, tells Hippolyta, the woman he is to marry, that their wedding hour is coming fast, so the play starts in the middle of a conversation between the two of them — A Midsummer Night's Dream

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen to voices before we can see the room, and try to place who is speaking to whom. · Feel: Overhearing a tense exchange makes us curious and uneasy, because the speakers know things that we do not. · Think: We work out what each speaker wants from the other, and what that shows about the story's themes of power, trust or loyalty. · Act: We notice, in real arguments and interviews, how much more is meant than is said.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dialogue hook, an opening that starts in the middle of a conversation. 1. Who is speaking to whom, and does one speaker have more power than the other? 2. What is the tone, and what does each speaker want? 3. What is left unsaid that the reader has to work out? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel by starting here? Try the questions on Julius Caesar. Two Roman officials, Flavius and Marullus, stop a crowd of workers in the street, and the officials have the power: they give orders, such as “Hence! home, you idle creatures, get you home”. The tone is angry and scornful. Flavius wants the workers back at work, and asks, “Is this a holiday?” The workers say they are out “to rejoice in his triumph”, meaning Caesar's, and Marullus asks, “What conquest brings he home?” He then scolds them for strewing flowers for Caesar, who “comes in triumph over Pompey's blood”. Until the crowd has gone, no one says outright that the officials fear Caesar is growing too powerful; the reader works that out from how angrily they stop the celebration. Shakespeare may want us to see at once a city divided over Caesar.

**How to create it:** Choose two characters who want different things, and decide which one has more power. Write the first two lines as speech, one from each character, that show who has more power, such as an order, an accusation or a warning. Leave out greetings and explanation. Hold back why they are arguing. Check that a stranger could tell who has more power from the first two lines; if not, make that character's words more commanding.

**Related:** Action Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Monologue Hook `Mo`

A monologue hook is an opening that begins inside one person's thoughts or voice, so the reader hears a single mind first. The speaker may be a narrator telling a story or a character talking aloud. We see events only through that person, so we may share their views, fears and mistakes. It is related to the dialogue hook, which gives us two voices already speaking; this hook gives us one.

**The concept:** A monologue opening shows how one person thinks, and asks us to trust that person. Because we hear one voice first, we often share its view, and the writer can later show that the view was wrong. In Poe's story The Cask of Amontillado, the narrator Montresor begins: “The thousand injuries of Fortunato I had borne as I best could; but when he ventured upon insult, I vowed revenge.” We hear only Montresor's side, so we cannot check what he says he suffered. When you write about any monologue hook, say whose mind we are in, what that person wants us to believe, and what might make us doubt them.

**Examples:** “I was born in the year 18— to a large fortune, endowed besides with excellent parts, inclined by nature to industry,” — Dr Jekyll begins his own written statement by praising his own character and prospects, so we hear his version of himself first — Jekyll and Hyde; “I was sick—sick unto death with that long agony; and when they at length unbound me, and I was permitted to sit, I felt that my senses were leaving me.” — the narrator speaks only of his own suffering and his failing senses, so we hear one mind before we are told where he is — The Pit and the Pendulum; “My father's family name being Pirrip, and my Christian name Philip, my infant tongue could make of both names nothing longer or more explicit than Pip.” — Pip begins by telling us in his own voice how he came by his name, so we meet the story through him alone — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are inside one person's voice before we have seen anything that the voice describes. · Feel: Hearing someone's private thoughts feels like closeness, so we side with the speaker before we have a reason to. · Think: We ask whether this voice can be trusted, and what the writer wants us to see about pride, guilt or self-deception. · Act: We ask who is telling us a story, and what they might leave out, when we read a confession, a diary or an interview.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any monologue hook, an opening that begins inside one person's private thoughts. 1. Whose mind are we inside, and what does that person want us to think of them? 2. What does the voice sound like: calm, anxious, proud or defensive? 3. Is there anything that makes you doubt the narrator, or trust them? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel by starting here? Try the questions on The Tell-Tale Heart by Edgar Allan Poe. We are inside the mind of an unnamed narrator, who wants us to think he is sane: “but why will you say that I am mad?” His voice sounds excited and defensive, with dashes and repeats such as “very, very dreadfully nervous”. He says “The disease had sharpened my senses”, but the harder he insists he is well, the more we doubt him. Poe may want us to feel how close we are to this mind, and to notice that insisting on calm can show the opposite.

**How to create it:** Choose a narrator and one belief about themselves that a careful reader could doubt. Open with a line in their own voice, speaking to the reader, that states that belief. Use short phrases, repeats or interruptions to show how they feel. Ask a friend to read your first paragraph and say whether they trust the narrator; if they trust fully, add one detail that sounds slightly wrong.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Mystery Hook `Mx`

A mystery hook is an opening that leaves one important thing unexplained. It may be a strange object, a missing person, or a fact that does not add up. The reader wants the answer, so they keep reading to find it. A mystery can be small, and it need not be a crime. It is different from the premonition hook, which builds dread of something bad that has not happened yet.

**The concept:** A mystery opening makes the reader want an answer. The writer gives one clear piece of information and holds back another, and the gap pulls us forward. It also makes a promise, because the answer must be worth the waiting. In Treasure Island, the narrator, Jim Hawkins, says he will write the whole story “keeping nothing back but the bearings of the island”, meaning its position, so we are told at once that one fact is secret. When you write about any mystery hook, say what is left unexplained, what the writer reveals about it, and why we keep reading.

**Examples:** “I cannot, for my soul, remember how, when, or even precisely where, I first became acquainted with the lady Ligeia.” — the narrator says he cannot remember how or where he met the lady Ligeia, so the story begins with a question about their past — Ligeia; “When shall we three meet again? / In thunder, lightning, or in rain?” — three witches arrange a meeting, but these first lines do not say who they are or why they will meet — Macbeth; “For the most wild, yet most homely narrative which I am about to pen, I neither expect nor solicit belief.” — the narrator warns that his story is wild and that he does not expect to be believed, so we ask what he is about to tell — The Black Cat

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We fix on the one thing the writer has left unexplained, and read everything else for clues about it. · Feel: An unanswered question feels like an itch, so the opening creates a need to know that pulls us on. · Think: We guess what the gap hides, and ask what truth about the characters or their world the writer is keeping back. · Act: We notice when headlines, adverts and trailers leave a question open to make us click, watch or buy.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any mystery hook, an opening that leaves one thing unexplained. 1. What is unexplained, or does not add up? 2. What does the writer tell you about it, and what do they hold back? 3. What does it make the main character, or the reader, want to do? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand by leaving it unexplained? Try the questions on Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll. A White Rabbit says to itself “Oh dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!”, then takes a watch out of its waistcoat-pocket, looks at it and hurries on, and a rabbit with a watch does not add up. We are told that Alice “had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a watch to take out of it”, but not why it is late or where it is going. It leaves Alice “burning with curiosity”, so she runs after it. Carroll may want the odd detail to send Alice, and us, into the story.

**How to create it:** Choose one fact in your story that you will not explain yet, such as an object, a missing person or a sound that does not fit. Describe it in your first lines in plain words. Let your main character notice it and react. Do not explain it yet. Ask a friend what question your opening raises; if they cannot name one, make the odd detail clearer.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Premonition Hook `Pm`

A premonition hook is an opening that makes the reader feel that something bad is coming. The feeling may come from a character's fear, a warning, a strange sign, or a narrator who knows the future. Often there is no proof, only dread. Sometimes the opening says plainly that a disaster will happen, and the dread lies in waiting for it. It differs from the mystery hook, which leaves something unexplained instead of building fear of what is to come.

**The concept:** A premonition opening makes the reader expect something bad before it happens. Each ordinary detail afterwards then reads like a sign, and dread often comes from waiting rather than from seeing. In Poe's story The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator comes within view of a gloomy old house and says: “with the first glimpse of the building, a sense of insufferable gloom pervaded my spirit.” He cannot say why, so the feeling is all the evidence we have. When you write about any premonition hook, say what feeling is created, what the writer lets us expect, and why we are made to wait.

**Examples:** “You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.” — Robert Walton, an explorer, tells his sister that his enterprise has begun without disaster, though she feared one, so the book opens with disaster in our minds — Frankenstein; “The ‘Red Death’ had long devastated the country. No pestilence had ever been so fatal, or so hideous.” — Poe opens by telling us that a deadly disease has been killing people across the country, so we expect it to matter before any character appears — The Masque of the Red Death; “Now the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and cry against it; for their wickedness is come up before me.” — the book opens with God telling Jonah to warn the city of Nineveh because of its wickedness, so we expect trouble to follow — The Bible (Jonah)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look ahead to the thing the writer has promised is coming, and read each present detail as a sign of it. · Feel: Waiting for a bad event we cannot yet see feels like dread, because ordinary moments now seem fragile. · Think: We ask what the characters cannot yet see, and what the writer is saying about fate, pride or warnings that are ignored. · Act: We notice how films, news reports and adverts build dread of what might happen next, and ask what they want from us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any premonition hook, an opening that makes the reader feel something bad is coming. 1. Who feels the dread, and what do they say about it? 2. Is there any proof of danger, or is the feeling all there is? 3. What do the time and place add to the feeling? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand by starting here? Try the questions on the opening of Hamlet. Francisco, a guard at the end of his watch, says “I am sick at heart”, but does not say why. There is no proof of danger: asked whether his watch was quiet, he answers, “Not a mouse stirring.” The time and place add to the feeling, because Bernardo says “’Tis now struck twelve”, and Francisco says it is bitter cold. Shakespeare may want us to feel that something is wrong before anything is shown.

**How to create it:** Choose a character and a fear they cannot prove. Open with a quiet, ordinary moment, such as a meal, a walk or a night watch. Let the character say or do one small thing that shows the fear, without saying why. Add one ordinary detail, such as the cold or the hour, that adds to the unease. Ask a friend whether they feel something is wrong; if they do not, add a second small sign.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Profound Statement Hook `Ps`

**Also known as:** Bold Statement with Imagery

A profound statement hook is an opening that makes one bold claim about life, people or the world. The claim sounds like wisdom, and the reader wants to know whether it is true. Often it states the theme of the whole piece in one line, which the rest of the piece proves, tests or overturns. In persuasive writing it states the thesis, the main argument the writer will defend. It is related to the intriguing quote hook, which borrows someone else's striking words.

**The concept:** A profound statement argues before the story begins. A bold claim about life can make the reader take a side, so the rest of the piece is read as evidence for or against it. In Hard Times, the character Mr Gradgrind, speaking in a schoolroom, says: “Facts alone are wanted in life.” The novel then follows people brought up on this belief and tests whether he is right. When you write about any profound statement hook, say what is claimed, whose voice makes it, and whether the rest of the piece proves it or challenges it.

**Examples:** “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.” — the narrator states a claim about money and marriage as if everyone agreed, and the first conversation in the novel is a mother hoping that a rich man will marry one of her daughters — Pride and Prejudice; “It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness,” — the narrator says that one period was both the best and the worst, a claim that makes us ask how this can be true — A Tale of Two Cities; “Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher, vanity of vanities; all is vanity.” — the Preacher, the speaker of the book, opens by claiming that all is vanity, a word the Bible uses here for something empty or passing, and the rest of the book explores that claim — The Bible (Ecclesiastes)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are held on one large idea before there is any character or place to look at. · Feel: A sweeping claim gives us a small push of agreement or doubt, and either feeling keeps us reading. · Think: We ask whether the claim is true, and treat the rest of the piece as evidence about the theme it names. · Act: We question confident sayings in speeches, adverts and everyday talk, and ask what evidence supports them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any profound statement hook, an opening that makes one bold claim about life. 1. What claim is made, and who or what is it about? 2. Does the claim feel true, doubtful or surprising, and which words make it feel that way? 3. What might the rest of the piece do with the claim: prove it, test it or overturn it? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel? Try the questions on Peter Pan by J. M. Barrie, which opens “All children, except one, grow up.” The claim is that every child grows up except one. It feels true at first, then surprising, because the words “except one” make us ask who that child is. The story tests the claim: the one is Peter Pan, who never grows up, and the last chapter shows Wendy grown up. Barrie may want us to feel that growing up is certain and a little sad, like Wendy's mother exclaiming, “Oh, why can't you remain like this for ever!”

**How to create it:** Decide the one claim about life that your story or argument will test. Write it as one short sentence with no names in it. Make it bold enough that a reader could disagree. Put it first, then follow it with a person or an event that tests it. Ask a friend whether they agree; if they have no opinion, make the claim sharper.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Setting Hook `Sg`

A setting hook is an opening that shows the place, time or weather of the story before the action starts. The writer picks a few details that set a mood, such as cold, darkness or heat, and that hint at what the place will do to the people in it. The details work best when we see them through a character's eyes, not in a list. It differs from the action hook, which begins with an event instead of a place.

**The concept:** A setting opening shows that a place can shape the people in it. The writer picks a few details that set a mood, and the reader expects what might happen there. In Wuthering Heights, Mr Lockwood, a new tenant, calls the lonely countryside where he lives “A perfect misanthropist's Heaven”, a place for someone who dislikes other people. He adds that he and his landlord, Mr Heathcliff, will share the loneliness, so the place and a character are linked at once. When you write about any setting hook, say what the place is like, what mood it creates, and what it suggests about the people in it.

**Examples:** “London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting in Lincoln's Inn Hall. Implacable November weather.” — the novel opens with the name of a city, the law courts in session and harsh November weather, before anyone speaks — Bleak House; “It was seven o'clock of a very warm evening in the Seeonee hills when Father Wolf woke up from his day's rest,” — the first sentence gives the hour, the warm weather and the hills, and only then a wolf waking up — The Jungle Book; “I leant upon a coppice gate / When Frost was spectre-gray,” — the speaker stands at a gate beside a small wood in winter frost, and the ghostly grey sets a cold, lifeless mood — The Darkling Thrush

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at a place, its weather and its small details, and read them for clues about what will happen there. · Feel: A place described through the senses sets a mood in us, such as cold, calm or dread, before anyone acts. · Think: We ask how the place might shape the people in it, and what it suggests about themes such as loneliness or power. · Act: We notice how places in films, adverts and news stories are lit and described to make us feel safe or uneasy.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any setting hook, an opening that shows the place where the story happens before the action starts. 1. What place is described, and which details does the writer choose? 2. Whose eyes do we see it through, if anyone's? 3. What mood do the details create? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel about this place? Try the questions on The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum. The place is a flat Kansas farm: “Not a tree nor a house broke the broad sweep of flat country”, and even the grass is not green. We see it through Dorothy's eyes, as she looks from the doorway and sees “nothing but the great gray prairie on every side”. The mood is bleak and empty. Baum may want us to feel how harsh her home is, so that the strange country she reaches feels very different.

**How to create it:** Choose the place where your story starts and one mood you want. Pick three details that a character can see, hear or feel there, and that match the mood. Describe them through that character's eyes, in short clear sentences. Leave out details that do not match the mood. Ask a friend what mood the place has; if their answer is not yours, change one detail.

### Question Hook `Qh`

**Also known as:** Provocative Question

A question hook is an opening that asks the reader a question. The reader answers it in their head, so they take part from the first line. The writer may answer it later or leave it open. A good question leads towards the main idea of the piece, while a question that only grabs attention is quickly forgotten. It is related to the mystery hook: both open a gap in what the reader knows, but a question hook asks the reader to fill it.

**The concept:** A question opening gets the reader to take part before the writer has argued anything. We answer a question automatically, and the writer can then agree with that answer, surprise us, or leave the question open. In Blake's poem The Lamb, the speaker asks a lamb: “Little lamb, who made thee?” Most readers start to answer at once, perhaps with God or nature, so the poem has begun an idea in our minds before it states it. When you write about any question hook, say what question is asked, what answer the reader gives, and what the writer does with that answer.

**Examples:** “Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?” — the speaker asks whether he should compare the person he is addressing to summer, so the reader begins by weighing that comparison — Sonnet 18; “Why William, on that old grey stone, / Thus for the length of half a day, / Why William, sit you thus alone, / And dream your time away?” — one speaker asks William why he sits alone on a stone, dreaming for half a day, and we start to guess the reason — Expostulation and Reply; “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” — the psalm opens with a cry to God that is also a question, and we wait to see what answer, if any, will come — The Bible (Psalms)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We turn inward to answer the question, so our own thinking becomes the first thing on the page. · Feel: Being asked directly feels as if the question is meant for us alone, and a question we can answer feels like a small success. · Think: We notice what our answer commits us to, and watch the writer use it to build the idea behind the piece. · Act: We notice how adverts, interviews and speeches use questions to make us agree before they have argued.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any question hook, an opening that asks the reader a question. 1. What is asked, and what answer does the reader give in their head? 2. What does that answer make the reader believe or agree with? 3. Does the writer answer the question, or leave it open? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel? Try the questions on The Tyger by William Blake. It asks, “What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?”, meaning what god-like maker could create so frightening and perfectly balanced a creature. The reader answers that it must be some great creator. So the reader has already agreed that a powerful being made the tiger. The poem does not answer: it asks more questions, such as “Did He who made the lamb make thee?”, and ends by repeating the first question with “Dare” in place of “Could”. Blake may want us to wonder at the power that made both gentle and fierce things, and to feel some fear of it.

**How to create it:** Choose the claim you want the reader to accept. Write a question that has one honest answer, and let that answer be the start of your argument. Put it first, in plain words. Then answer it yourself and go on to explain why. Ask a friend to answer it aloud; if their answer is not the one you wanted, rewrite the question.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Statistic / Fact Hook `Sf`

**Also known as:** Shocking statistic, Surprising Historical Fact

A statistic or fact hook is an opening that begins with a fact or a number that can be checked. It makes the reader accept something as true before the main argument starts. A bare number means little until the reader can picture its size, so writers often add a comparison. It differs from the profound statement hook, which opens with an opinion. In persuasive writing it is the Facts technique from MAD FATHERS CROPS, the memory aid for persuasive devices that this course teaches.

**The concept:** A fact opening makes the reader feel sure, because a fact sounds settled and the reader accepts it at once. The fact must also matter to what follows, or it is only decoration. In A Study in Scarlet, the narrator, Dr Watson, begins with a date and his qualifications: “In the year 1878 I took my degree of Doctor of Medicine of the University of London”. Details like these make him sound like a careful witness. When you write about any statistic or fact hook, say what fact is given, why it feels reliable, and what the reader must accept because of it.

**Examples:** “Four score and seven years ago our fathers brought forth” — Lincoln opens with a length of time: a score is twenty, so four score and seven is eighty-seven years, counted back to the start of the nation — The Gettysburg Address; “And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus that all the world should be taxed.” — the story of the birth of Jesus begins with a named ruler and an order he gave, so it starts from something that can be dated — The Bible (Luke); “Mr. Phileas Fogg lived, in 1872, at No. 7, Saville Row, Burlington Gardens, the house in which Sheridan died in 1814.” — the novel opens with a year, a street address and the year a man died in that house, so we treat the world of the story as real and checkable — Around the World in Eighty Days

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We stop on one plain fact, such as a date, a name or a number, and take it as the starting point. · Feel: A plain fact at the start makes us feel sure, so we trust the speaker and accept the world of the story as real. · Think: We ask whether the fact is true and where it comes from, and what the writer wants us to accept because of it. · Act: We check numbers and claims in news, adverts and speeches, and ask who gathered them and why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any statistic or fact hook, an opening that begins with a fact or figure. 1. What fact or figure is given, and what proof, if any, is offered? 2. How does the writer make it feel solid? 3. What does the reader have to accept before the story or argument can go on? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol. The fact is that Marley is dead: “Marley was dead: to begin with.” The proof is that “The register of his burial was signed by the clergyman, the clerk, the undertaker, and the chief mourner.” The writer makes it feel solid by listing who signed the register of his burial, and by saying “There is no doubt whatever about that.” The reader has to accept that Marley is really dead. Dickens may want us certain of this, so that Marley appearing later as a ghost is astonishing.

**How to create it:** Choose one fact or figure that your reader can check and that supports your main point. Find its source. If it is a number, write it exactly, and add one detail that helps the reader picture its size. Put it in your first sentence. Follow it with one sentence that links the fact to your argument. Check the fact in a second source; if you cannot confirm it, choose another.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Anecdote Hook `Ah`

An anecdote hook is an opening that tells a short story about one person or one moment. The story is chosen to make a larger point, so the wider idea grows out of it. It may be a real memory, an imagined scene or a story told by someone else. It is related to the action hook, which also begins inside a moment, but an anecdote is told to support an argument.

**The concept:** An anecdote opening makes an idea personal before it makes it general. A reader who has pictured one small moment understands the point more easily. In the Bible, Jesus compares people to two builders, and begins with “a wise man, which built his house upon a rock”. The story is told to support one point: a person who hears Jesus's words and acts on them stands firm in a storm, and one who does not falls. When you write about any anecdote hook, say what moment is told, what point it supports, and how the writer moves from the moment to the wider point.

**Examples:** “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves,” — Jesus answers a question about who our neighbour is with a short story about one traveller who is attacked by thieves — The Bible (Luke); “Hearken; Behold, there went out a sower to sow:” — Jesus begins a story about a farmer scattering seed, an everyday scene that he uses to explain how people receive his teaching — The Bible (Mark); “There were two men in one city; the one rich, and the other poor.” — the prophet Nathan tells King David a story about a rich man and a poor man, so that David will judge the rich man and then see that the story is about himself — The Bible (2 Samuel)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are inside one small moment, and the larger idea is hidden inside it. · Feel: A single human scene makes a big issue feel close and personal, so we care before we are asked to. · Think: We ask what this moment stands for, and notice that we have begun to accept the writer's wider point. · Act: We notice when adverts, charity appeals and speeches open with one person's story, and ask what point it is meant to prove.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any anecdote hook, an opening that tells a short story from one person's experience. 1. What moment or story is told, and who is in it? 2. Which details make it vivid? 3. What larger issue does this one moment stand for? 4. What does the writer want the reader to conclude from it? Try the questions on Shooting an Elephant by George Orwell, which opens “In Moulmein, in Lower Burma, I was hated by large numbers of people”. The story is the writer's own: a young British police officer in Burma, who later shoots an elephant that has killed a man. Concrete details make it vivid: he names the town, gives his job, and says people would spit betel juice over a European woman's dress. The moment stands for British rule in Burma. Orwell may want us to conclude that a ruler who forces his rule on others loses his own freedom.

**How to create it:** Choose one real or believable moment that shows your issue. Start in the middle of it, with a person doing something. Give two or three details a reader can see or hear. Stop once the problem is clear. Write one sentence that links the moment to the wider issue. Check that a stranger who reads only the scene can say what the issue is; if not, choose a clearer moment.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Direct Address Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Direct Address Hook `Du`

A direct address hook is an opening that speaks straight to someone, using the word you or a command such as listen or remember. The reader cannot stay a bystander, because the writer seems to be talking to them. The person addressed may be the reader, a crowd, or someone who is not the reader, such as a lost friend. It is related to the question hook: both involve the reader at once, but direct address names the listener instead of asking.

**The concept:** Direct address makes the reader or audience part of the piece. A person who is spoken to cannot easily watch from outside, so the writer can ask them to listen, agree or act. In Julius Caesar, Mark Antony begins his speech at Caesar's funeral by speaking to the crowd: “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears;”. He calls them friends and asks for their attention, and he then turns them against the men who killed Caesar. When you write about any direct address hook, say who is spoken to, what the speaker asks of them, and how being spoken to affects the reader.

**Examples:** “Remember me when I am gone away, / Gone far away into the silent land;” — the speaker begins by telling someone to remember them after death, so the poem opens with a command and a listener — Remember; “You are old, Father William,” — a young man speaks straight to an old man, so the poem begins as one person talking to another — You Are Old, Father William; “Hear the voice of the Bard, / Who present, past, and future, sees;” — the first line is an order to the reader to listen to the Bard, a poet who sees past, present and future — Introduction to Songs of Experience

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We are looked at directly, so the subject of the piece becomes us. · Feel: Being spoken to by name or by command feels as if the words are meant for us alone, which can be flattering or uncomfortable. · Think: We ask what the speaker wants from us, and who the writer imagines the listener to be. · Act: We notice when speeches, posters and adverts say you to make us feel that the message is meant for us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any direct address hook, an opening that speaks straight to the reader as “you”. 1. Who is “you”, and who else might it include? 2. What does the writer ask or demand of “you”? 3. How does being addressed make the reader feel? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or do? Try the questions on If— by Rudyard Kipling. “You” is the person the poem is spoken to; the last line, “you'll be a Man, my son”, shows the speaker is talking to a son, but any reader can place themselves in it. It asks a list of hard things, beginning “If you can keep your head when all about you / Are losing theirs and blaming it on you”. Each “If you can” sets a test, so the reader feels challenged and a little pressed to answer. Kipling may want the reader to see steady self-control as the way to become a grown-up.

**How to create it:** Choose one reader and one thing you want them to do or face. Write “you” into your first sentence, so the issue is about them. Tell them something they do or feel in their own day, such as “You walk past it every morning”. Keep the tone steady, not shouting. Check that the opening could not be about anyone else; if it could, add a detail specific to that reader's day.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Intriguing Quote Hook

### Intriguing Quote Hook `Iq`

**Also known as:** Intriguing Quote, Quotation Hook

An intriguing quote hook is an opening that borrows someone else's striking words, so the reader wants them explained. The words may come from the text being studied, from its author, from a critic or from a famous source. In an essay, the writer then explains what the quotation means and how it leads to the argument. In a book, a quotation placed before the first chapter is called an epigraph. It is related to the profound statement hook, which opens with the writer's own claim.

**The concept:** An intriguing quotation hook opens with words that belong to someone else. The borrowed words hold a clash or a surprise, so the reader wants them explained. In Macbeth, the three witches say “Fair is foul, and foul is fair” at the end of the first scene. An essay about appearance and truth could open with this line, then explain how good and bad are mixed up in the play. When you write about any intriguing quote hook, say whose words are borrowed, what clash or idea they hold, and what the writer does next with them.

**Examples:** “Did I request thee, Maker, from my clay / To mould me man? Did I solicit thee / From darkness to promote me?” — Mary Shelley puts these lines from Milton's poem Paradise Lost on the title page of her novel, so the reader meets a creature's complaint against its maker before the story begins — Frankenstein; “What song the Syrens sang, or what name Achilles assumed when he hid himself among women, although puzzling questions, are not beyond all conjecture.” — Poe opens the story with words by Sir Thomas Browne saying that even puzzling questions can be guessed at, so we expect a puzzle to be solved — The Murders in the Rue Morgue; “And the will therein lieth, which dieth not.” — Poe opens the story with words that he attributes to Joseph Glanvill, saying that the will does not die, so the reader begins with an idea about whether anything in a person can survive death — Ligeia

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We start on words that belong to someone else, and wait to hear what the writer will make of them. · Feel: A borrowed line that clashes with itself feels like a puzzle set for us, and we want it solved. · Think: We ask what the quotation claims about the theme, and whether the writer will prove it or challenge it. · Act: We notice when speeches and articles open with a famous saying, and ask whether it really supports the writer's point.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any intriguing quote hook, an opening that borrows a striking line from someone else, usually the text you are writing about. 1. Who says the line, and where does it come from? 2. What big idea does the line hold, and is there a clash or surprise in it? 3. What topic or argument could an essay open with this line? 4. What does the writer of the text want the reader to understand? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. The line is “man is not truly one, but truly two”, written by Henry Jekyll, a doctor, in his last statement near the end of the book. The idea is that each person is made of two natures, and the clash is between “one” and “two”. An essay on duality, or on hidden selves, could open with it. Stevenson may want readers to see that respectable people can have a hidden side.

**How to create it:** Choose the one line of your text that holds your main argument. Check the exact words in your book and copy them, with quotation marks. Open your essay with that line, then write one sentence saying what it means. Link that sentence to the question you are answering. Check that your sentence about the line would not fit any other quotation; if it would, rewrite it to say what is special about this line.

**Related:** Action Hook, Dialogue Hook, Monologue Hook, Mystery Hook, Premonition Hook, Profound Statement Hook, Setting Hook, Question Hook, Statistic / Fact Hook, Anecdote Hook, Direct Address Hook

### Focus `Fc`

Focus is the first of the four effects of a text on a reader: it is what the writer makes us look at. The writer picks one detail, such as an object, a place, a name or even a missing fact, and puts it where we cannot miss it. The detail is chosen because it carries the writer's theme or purpose. The other three effects are feeling, thinking and acting.

**The concept:** Focus lets a writer decide what the reader looks at first, and so what seems important. A detail that is repeated, described at length or set against a plain background pulls the eye. In Macbeth, Macbeth, alone on stage, sees a dagger: “Is this a dagger which I see before me”. He speaks to it, so our eyes stay on the weapon, which points to the murder he is about to commit. When you find any moment of focus, say what the reader is made to look at, how the writer draws the eye, and what theme or purpose the detail serves.

**Examples:** “Marley was dead: to begin with.” — Dickens opens by fixing our attention on one fact, that Marley is dead, and at once adds that there is no doubt about it, so we dwell on it before his ghost appears — A Christmas Carol; “my first fancies regarding what they were like were unreasonably derived from their tombstones” — Pip, the narrator, never saw his dead parents, so he imagined them from the letters on their gravestones, and the detail makes us look at how alone he is — Great Expectations; “that spot / Of joy into the Duchess' cheek” — the Duke, showing a visitor the portrait of his late wife, complains that it was not only her husband's presence that brought a blush of joy to her cheek, so we look at what he resents — My Last Duchess

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look where the writing points, and notice less of whatever it leaves out of view. · Feel: A detail held up for us feels important, and not yet knowing why it matters makes us uneasy and curious. · Think: We assume the writer chose the detail on purpose, so we ask what theme or idea it carries. · Act: We notice when adverts, headlines and speeches hold our attention on one detail, and ask what they want us to overlook.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any moment of focus, where the writer makes the reader look closely at one detail. 1. Which one detail is the reader made to look at? 2. How does the writer draw the eye to it: by repeating it, describing it at length, or contrasting it with what is around it? 3.
