What does the writer want the reader to understand or suspect because of that detail? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. A London street shows “general cleanliness and gaiety”, but one building stands out: a door with “neither bell nor knocker”. The writer, Robert Louis Stevenson, draws the eye by contrast: the street is bright, while the door is “blistered and distained”, meaning blistered and stained, and the building is called “sinister”. He wants the reader to suspect that something hidden and unpleasant lies behind that door.

**How to create it:** Choose the one detail you want your reader to remember, such as an object, a name or a missing thing. Describe the ordinary details around it quickly. Describe the chosen detail slowly, with one or two exact words. Keep every other detail short so the eye stays on it. Ask a friend which detail they remember most; if it is not your chosen one, shorten the rest or add one exact word to it.

### Emotions (Feel) `Em`

Emotion is the second of the four effects: what the writer makes us feel. Writers build it by making us care about a character, through what that person wants, loves, fears or loses. Two main forms are empathy, which is feeling with a character as if from inside, and sympathy, which is feeling sorry for a character from outside. Name the exact feeling, such as dread, grief or hope, and not just a vague feeling.

**The concept:** Emotion lets a writer make a reader care, and a reader who cares pays attention and thinks about the ideas. In Romeo and Juliet, Capulet, Juliet's father, finds his daughter apparently dead on her wedding morning: “Death lies on her like an untimely frost / Upon the sweetest flower of all the field.” The image of a flower killed by an early frost makes us feel grief for a young life cut short. When you find any moment of emotion, say which exact feeling it creates, which words or details create it, and what the writer wants readers to understand by feeling it.

**Examples:** “All my pretty ones? Did you say all?” — Macduff, a Scottish lord, is told that his wife and children have been killed, and his broken questions make us feel his grief — Macbeth; “They're taking you to your death!” — Clover, a mare, cries out to Boxer, the horse who always said “I will work harder”, as a van carries him away, and we feel pity and anger — Animal Farm; “God bless us every one!” — Tiny Tim, Bob Cratchit's sick young son, says this at the family's small Christmas dinner, and his kindness makes us feel warmth and worry for him — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the person who is suffering or hoping, and care less about everything else in the scene. · Feel: We care about someone who is not real, and that feeling makes the writer's ideas about loss or injustice hard to ignore. · Think: We accept an idea more easily when we have felt it first, and then ask why the writer made us feel it. · Act: We may give to a charity, forgive a person or speak up for someone after a story has made us care about them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any moment of emotion, where the writer makes the reader feel something strongly. 1. Which feeling does the moment create? Name it in a word or two. 2. Which words, actions or details create that feeling? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand through feeling it? Try the questions on Julius Caesar. Antony, a friend of the Roman leader Julius Caesar, speaks at Caesar's funeral after Caesar has been killed. The moment creates grief. Antony stops mid-speech: “My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar,” and says he must pause until it comes back to him. The pause makes his sorrow seem too heavy to speak through. Shakespeare shows how a speaker's grief can move a crowd: the citizens who hear it soon turn against the men who killed Caesar.

**How to create it:** Choose one precise feeling you want your reader to have, such as dread, grief or hope. Give a character something they care about, and show it clearly early on. Put that thing at risk, or take it away. Show the feeling through what the character does or notices, not by naming it. Ask a friend to name the feeling after reading; if their word differs from yours, change the details.

**Making Readers & Audiences Feel** — The wider palette of emotions a writer can craft, beyond empathy itself (Iglesias)

_Other Key Emotions_

- **Interest & Fascination**
  - **Clear cause and effect** — Each event triggers the next, so the reader is pulled along. _(e.g. “I wear the chain I forged in life… I made it link by link, and yard by yard” — every selfish act became one more link, so the reader sees each choice producing the next — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Unique, complex characters** — People we have not quite met before. _(e.g. “that man is not truly one, but truly two” — one sentence tells us a second person lives inside this man, so we can never predict him — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Conflict that matters** — Meaningful struggle with something real at stake. _(e.g. “Which is better — to have rules and agree, or to hunt and kill?” — the struggle is put as a plain choice, and the boys' lives depend on the answer — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Change through discovery and decision** — Keep the situation moving, never static. _(e.g. “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year” — a decision spoken out loud, so we watch the man leave behind who he was — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Freshness of vision** — An original angle, not the expected one. _(e.g. “Not a red rose or a satin heart” — the poem refuses the expected love gift in its first line, so we read on to see what replaces it — Valentine)_
  - **Subtext** — Meaning beneath the words, for the reader to read into. _(e.g. “I wonder that you will still be talking, Signior Benedick: nobody marks you.” — the words are an insult; underneath them we hear attraction — Much Ado About Nothing)_
- **Curiosity & Intrigue**
  - **Pose a central story question** — One big unanswered question driving the whole piece. _(e.g. “If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek” — the whole novel is set up as one hunt, and we read on to see it finished — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Layer smaller questions** — One for each chapter, scene, even paragraph. _(e.g. “one line of inquiry at a time” — the Inspector opens a fresh question about each person, so a new small mystery starts as the last one closes — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Withhold information** — Leave a deliberate gap the reader aches to fill. _(e.g. “distinct, formal, mirthless” — we hear a laugh through a wall and are told nothing about who is laughing — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Secrets and cover-ups** — Characters hiding the very thing we want to know. _(e.g. “I am not what I am” — he tells us he is hiding something and still will not say what it is — Othello)_
  - **Mystery** — An image or event left, for now, unexplained. _(e.g. “a certain sinister block of building thrust forward its gable on the street” — a door is described closely and never explained, so it stays in the reader's mind — Jekyll and Hyde)_
- **Anticipation, Hope & Dread**
  - **Set a clear goal early** — So we want to see whether it is reached. _(e.g. “A new species would bless me as its creator and source” — the goal is stated plainly, so every later page is measured against it — Frankenstein)_
  - **Deadlines and appointments** — A fixed point we count down towards. _(e.g. “get thee to church o' Thursday, / Or never after look me in the face” — a named day is fixed, and the reader starts counting towards it — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Foreshadowing and warnings** — Hint at what lies ahead. _(e.g. “These violent delights have violent ends” — a warning is placed early, so the reader carries dread through the happy scenes — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Plans and daydreams** — Share what a character hopes for; secret plans hook hardest. _(e.g. “Hearken to my joyful tidings / Of the golden future time” — we are shown the future the animals want, so we start wanting it with them — Animal Farm)_
  - **Premonitions** — A sense that something is coming. _(e.g. “The devil's got your number, y' know he's gonna find y'” — the Narrator promises a bad ending before it arrives, so every later scene feels watched — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Dramatic irony** — Let the reader know more than the character, and dread for them. _(e.g. “the Titanic… unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable” — the audience knows the ship sank, so every confident word he says sounds foolish — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **An object of pursuit** — A prize everyone chases — a 'MacGuffin'. _(e.g. “The treasure is lost” — the prize everyone has chased is gone, and the chase was what kept us reading — The Sign of the Four)_
- **Suspense & Tension**
  - **Remind us of the stakes** — And raise them as the story goes on. _(e.g. “Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood!” — the chant tells us exactly what waits if the boys lose control — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **A ticking clock** — Time pressure — the outcome is due now. _(e.g. “I shall be with you on your wedding-night” — the threat is fixed to one coming night, so the waiting itself becomes the tension — Frankenstein)_
  - **The crucible** — Trap the characters in a place with no easy exit. _(e.g. “Why can't I escape?” — the speaker knows every street around him and still cannot get out of them — Belfast Confetti)_
  - **Obstacles and complications** — Block the goal, again and again. _(e.g. “Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?” — a powerful woman is placed directly across the path of the marriage we want — Pride and Prejudice)_
  - **Cross-cut parallel action** — Cut away at the worst possible moment. _(e.g. “Of one womb born, on the self same day, / How one was kept and one given away?” — two lives are set running side by side, and the play cuts between them — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Delay the outcome** — Prolong the wait to stretch the tension. _(e.g. “Tarry a little, there is something else.” — the knife is already raised; five words stop it and stretch the wait — The Merchant of Venice)_
  - **Force a dilemma** — A choice between two bad options. _(e.g. “I care for myself. The more solitary, the more friendless, the more unsustained I am, the more I will respect myself” — she must choose between love and self-respect, and either choice costs her — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Make a character face a fear** — Set them against the thing they dread. _(e.g. “Hold your noise!” — the frightening thing speaks first, and the boy has to stand in front of it — Great Expectations)_
  - **Release, then tighten** — A beat of humour or relief, then back to the pressure. _(e.g. “Knock, knock, knock! Who's there, i' th' name of Beelzebub?” — a joke arrives seconds after a murder, and the laugh makes the next scene harder to bear — Macbeth)_
- **Surprise & Shock**
  - **Reversals** — Turn the situation to its opposite. _(e.g. “from pig to man, and from man to pig, and from pig to man again; but already it was impossible to say which was which” — the rulers have become the thing they overthrew — Animal Farm)_
  - **Revelations** — Drop information that recasts everything before it. _(e.g. “I've made a gentleman on you!” — one sentence rewrites everything the reader believed about where the money came from — Great Expectations)_
  - **Reveal a secret** — Of the story, the scene, or a character. _(e.g. “Bertha Mason is mad; and she came of a mad family” — the secret is said out loud at the worst possible moment, and the wedding stops — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Plant and pay off** — Set up a detail early, cash it in later. _(e.g. “Macduff was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped” — the promise made to him in Act 1 is kept here, and the trap closes — Macbeth)_
  - **Red herrings** — Honest misdirection that still plays fair. _(e.g. “Snowball was in league with Jones from the very start.” — a false explanation is given confidently, and it points away from the real culprit — Animal Farm)_
  - **Keep the logic** — A twist must make sense looking back, never a cheat. _(e.g. “I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end” — the last chapter explains the whole mystery, so the twist makes sense when you look back — Jekyll and Hyde)_
- **Thrill, Joy & Sorrow**
  - **Spectacle** — A set-piece, a wow moment. _(e.g. “the ice began to move, and roarings like thunder were heard at a distance” — a huge event fills the page, and the reader stops to watch it — Frankenstein)_
  - **Escape** — From danger, or from confinement. _(e.g. “Don't you want to be rescued?” — the question names the way out that the boys are slowly losing — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Separate and reunite** — Part characters we love, then bring them back. _(e.g. “Reader, I married him” — after a long separation, four words give us the reunion we have waited for — Jane Eyre)_
  - **Victories and losses** — Alternate wins and setbacks across the arc. _(e.g. “Into the valley of Death / Rode the six hundred” — the charge is brave and doomed at the same moment, so pride and grief arrive together — The Charge of the Light Brigade)_
  - **Poetic justice** — The villain punished, the innocent vindicated. _(e.g. “Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare” — the boastful king is answered by empty sand — Ozymandias)_
  - **Earn the emotional beat** — Release through humour or tears once it is deserved. _(e.g. “I could have been him” — the tears come only because the whole play has built towards this one comparison — Blood Brothers)_

### Thoughts (Think) `Tt`

Thought is the third of the four effects: what the writer leads us to work out for ourselves. The writer does not state a judgement but gives details that point towards it, often through irony, contrast or symbols. Irony is saying one thing while meaning another, or showing what a character does not know. A symbol is an object or image that stands for an idea. We often trust a conclusion we reached ourselves more than one we were told.

**The concept:** Thought lets a writer argue without stating it, through irony, contrast and symbols that leave a gap between what is said and what is meant. In A Christmas Carol, two men ask Scrooge, a rich businessman, for money to help the poor. He answers “Are there no prisons?”, so we work out that he would rather see the poor locked away than spend his own money. We reach Dickens's criticism of rich people who ignore the poor without being told it. When you find any moment of thought, say what the surface says, what the reader works out beneath it, and what conclusion the writer wants.

**Examples:** “All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others” — the pigs add these words to the farm's last rule, “All animals are equal”, and we work out that the pigs now think they deserve more than the others — Animal Farm; “For Brutus is an honourable man” — Antony says this about Brutus, one of the men who killed Caesar, and repeats it as he describes the killing, so we work out that he means the opposite — Julius Caesar; “If you prick us, do we not bleed?” — Shylock, a Jewish moneylender whom Christians insult, asks whether Jews do not share the same bodies and feelings as everyone else, so we judge how unfairly he is treated — The Merchant of Venice

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at the gap between what is said and what is meant, not only at what happens next. · Feel: Working out an idea that nobody states can feel like a discovery, and an unfair situation can make us uneasy or angry. · Think: We reach the writer's judgement of a character or a society ourselves, so it feels like our own conclusion. · Act: We question what politicians, adverts and friends say, and ask what they leave unsaid or mean differently.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any moment of thought, where the writer leads the reader to a judgement without stating it. 1. What does the text say on the surface? 2. What does the reader see beneath that, and which details or events lead there? 3. What does the writer want the reader to conclude? Try the questions on Macbeth. Duncan, the king of Scotland, speaks about the Thane of Cawdor, a lord who has just been executed as a traitor. On the surface he says there is “no art” to read a mind from a face, and that he trusted Cawdor completely. Just after this, Macbeth enters and Duncan welcomes him warmly; the reader has already heard Macbeth think about becoming king, so sees Duncan make the same mistake again. Shakespeare wants the reader to conclude that Duncan trusts too easily and is in danger. Duncan is later killed.

**How to create it:** Choose the judgement you want your reader to reach, such as that a character cannot be trusted. Do not write that judgement yourself. Instead, show two details that point towards it, such as what a character says and what they do. Place them close together so the gap between them is clear. Ask a friend what they think of the character; if they do not reach your judgement, make the second detail clearer.

### Actions (Act) `Ao`

Action is the fourth of the four effects of a text on a reader, after focus, feeling and thinking. It is what a reader might do, or decide to do, in their own life because of the text, such as helping someone or speaking out. Some texts tell the reader directly what to do, often with a command. Many stories and poems never ask for an action, but they may change what a reader thinks about a problem, and that reader may then decide to do something about it.

**The concept:** Action lets a writer try to change what readers do, not only what they think. It comes last of the four effects, because what a reader does usually follows from what they have noticed, felt and thought. In An Inspector Calls, the Inspector tells the Birling family in his last speech that people are “responsible for each other”. The audience hears the same words, and an audience member may then decide to do more to help other people. When you find any text that may lead readers to act, say what they might do, whether the text asks for it directly, and which words or details encourage it.

**Examples:** “Go, and do thou likewise.” — after the story of the Good Samaritan, a traveller who stopped to care for a man robbed and left half dead, Jesus tells the man who had questioned him to act as the Samaritan did; a reader can follow this command too, by helping a person in need — The Bible (Luke); “My friend, you would not tell with such high zest” — Wilfred Owen describes a soldier dying in a gas attack, then says that no one who had seen this death would eagerly tell children that dying for your country is sweet and right; he wants people to stop saying it to children — Dulce et Decorum Est; “This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want.” — the Ghost of Christmas Present shows Scrooge two thin, ragged children, named Ignorance and Want (an old word for poverty); a reader who pities them may decide to give money, food or time to help poor children — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look for what the text asks us to do, or for a problem it shows that people could help to solve. · Feel: We feel pity, guilt or hope when a text shows a problem such as poverty or war that we could help to change. · Think: We work out what the writer wants us to change, and ask whether the writer's reason for that change is fair. · Act: We may give to a charity, sign a petition, vote or treat people more kindly after a text shows us a problem.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any moment where a text may lead its audience to act, by asking directly or by showing a problem. 1. What might the audience do, or decide to do, after reading or hearing the text? 2. Which words or details encourage that action, such as “we” or “you”, or a story of someone in need? 3. What reason does the writer give, or suggest, for acting? 4. What does the writer want the audience to feel or understand as they act? Try the questions on the Gettysburg Address, a speech by Abraham Lincoln, President of the United States, given during the American Civil War at a battlefield where many soldiers had died. Lincoln asks his listeners to commit themselves to finishing the work of the soldiers who fought there, so that the nation survives: “It is for us the living, rather, to be dedicated here to the unfinished work”. Lincoln says “us” and “we”, as in “we here highly resolve”, so he includes himself among the people who must do the work. The reason is the dead soldiers' sacrifice: “these dead shall not have died in vain”. Lincoln wants the audience to feel that honouring the dead means carrying on their cause, so that the nation can have “a new birth of freedom”.

**How to create it:** Choose one action you want your reader to take, such as signing a petition, speaking up or helping someone. Tell the reader plainly what that action is. Use “we” or “you” so the reader is part of it. Give one clear reason why the action matters. Ask a friend to say in one sentence what you want them to do; if they cannot, rewrite the request more simply.

### Foot `Ft`

A foot is a small group of syllables that repeats along a line of verse, usually with one strong syllable and the rest soft. A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. An iamb is a foot of two syllables, soft then strong (da-DUM); a trochee is strong then soft (DUM-da). Poets name a line by how many feet it has: five iambs make one line of iambic pentameter, which has ten syllables. A line may keep its foot exactly or break it.

**The concept:** A foot lets a poet build a beat that readers can feel and count. Readers get used to the pattern, so a change stands out. In Macbeth, Macbeth sees what looks like a dagger and asks “Is this a dagger which I see before me”. The line has five feet of soft then strong (is THIS, a DAG, ger WHICH, I SEE, be FORE), where the pattern gives “which” a beat that ordinary speech would leave light, and one extra soft syllable (me). When you write about any line of verse, say which foot repeats, how many times, and what the steady beat, or any break in it, shows.

**Examples:** “The curfew tolls the knell of parting day” — ten syllables in five feet of soft then strong, in a line about an evening bell — Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard; “Peter, Peter, pumpkin-eater” — eight syllables in four feet of strong then soft, so the rhyme sounds like a chant — Peter, Peter, Pumpkin-Eater; “’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house” — twelve syllables in four feet, each with two soft syllables and then a strong one, so the line bounces along — A Visit from St. Nicholas

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen for a small pattern of strong and soft syllables that repeats, and notice where it stops. · Feel: We feel calm or secure while the pattern holds, and uneasy when it breaks, because the rhythm we expected has failed. · Think: We ask what the steady beat, or a break in it, shows about the poem's subject, such as order, control or loss. · Act: We notice the beat in songs, chants and adverts, and ask why a repeating rhythm makes some messages easy to remember.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any foot, one small repeating pattern of strong and soft syllables in a line of verse. A strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Which syllables in the line are strong and which are soft, and which small pattern repeats? 2. How many times does that pattern repeat in the line? 3. Does the line, or the next one, break the pattern anywhere, and if it does, which words does the break land on? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand through the steady beat, or through a break in it? Try the questions on “Whose woods these are I think I know” from Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening by Robert Frost. The strong syllables are “woods”, “are”, “think” and “know”: whose WOODS these ARE I THINK I KNOW. Each strong syllable follows a soft one, so the repeating pattern is soft then strong. The pattern gives “are” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is said lightly. It repeats four times, so the line has four feet. Neither line breaks it: the next line, “His house is in the village though”, keeps the same pattern. The steady beat sounds calm and quiet, which suits a speaker who has stopped alone to watch snow fall on woods. Frost may want the reader to share that quiet.

**How to create it:** Choose the pattern your lines will repeat, such as soft then strong. Decide how many times it repeats in each line. Write the first line, then tap one finger on each strong syllable as you read it aloud. Write the next lines to match. Check each line by marking every syllable strong or soft; if a line breaks the pattern by accident, reword it, and keep a break where the meaning needs one.

**Related:** Metre, Iamb, Trochee, Dactyl, Anapaest, Spondee, Pyrrhic

### Iamb `Ib`

An iamb is a foot of two syllables, soft then strong (da-DUM), and it is the commonest foot in English poetry. A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. Many English words and phrases fall into this pattern, such as today and my friend, so iambic lines sound close to speech. Five iambs in a line make iambic pentameter: five feet, ten syllables. The trochee is the opposite foot, strong then soft (DUM-da).

**The concept:** The iamb lets a poet write verse that sounds like natural speech. Many English phrases already put a strong syllable after a soft one, so a reader can stop noticing the beat. In Romeo and Juliet, Romeo sees Juliet appear at a window above him and says “But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?” (yonder means over there). The line has ten syllables in five iambs, and none of them is broken. When you write about any iambic line, say how regular the beat is, and what any break in it shows.

**Examples:** “If music be the food of love, play on” — ten syllables in five iambs, as Duke Orsino asks his musicians to keep playing; the pattern gives “be” a beat that ordinary speech would leave light, but the line still sounds like easy talk — Twelfth Night; “Is this a dagger which I see before me” — five iambs and one extra soft syllable at the end, as Macbeth speaks aloud to himself; the pattern gives “which” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is said lightly — Macbeth; “Is hung with bloom along the bough” — eight syllables in four iambs, in a line about a cherry tree covered in blossom, so the description sounds calm and even — A Shropshire Lad

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We settle into a beat that sounds like ordinary speech, so we notice the words before we notice the rhythm. · Feel: A beat close to speech and heartbeat feels calm and natural, so a sudden break in it can make us uneasy. · Think: We ask what a break in a steady iambic line shows about the speaker or subject, such as anger, grief or loss of control. · Act: We notice how natural a speaker sounds in speeches and interviews, and ask whether sounding natural makes us trust them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any iamb, a two-syllable foot with a soft syllable then a strong one (da-DUM). Take a line of verse built from them. A strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Mark each syllable of the line soft or strong. Is it soft then strong all the way through? 2. Where does the line differ from that pattern, such as an extra soft syllable or two strong ones side by side, and which words does that land on? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand through the steady beat, or through a break in it? Try the questions on “To be, or not to be, that is the question” from Hamlet, spoken by Prince Hamlet as he thinks aloud about whether to go on living. It is soft then strong five times: to BE, or NOT, to BE, that IS, the QUES. The pattern gives “is” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is said lightly. The only difference is one extra soft syllable at the end, “tion” in “question”. The beat is so close to ordinary speech that a huge question sounds calm and thoughtful, as if Hamlet is reasoning, not panicking. Shakespeare may want the audience to hear a mind at work.

**How to create it:** Write your line so a soft syllable comes first and a strong one second, and repeat that pair for each foot. Choose words whose natural stress falls where you want the beat, such as “to-DAY” or “a-GAIN”. Read the line aloud and tap each strong syllable. Check that it sounds like natural speech; if a word is pushed onto the wrong beat, swap it for another.

**Related:** Foot

### Trochee `To`

A trochee is a foot of two syllables, strong then soft (DUM-da), the opposite of the iamb. A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. The beat falls on the first syllable, so a trochaic line can sound like a chant, a command or a spell. A trochee can also appear on its own inside lines of other feet, where it changes the rhythm for a moment. The iamb is the foot that starts with a soft syllable (da-DUM).

**The concept:** The trochee lets a poet make a line strike on its first syllable, like a command or a chant. Many English phrases start with a soft syllable, so a line that starts with a strong one can sound firm and unusual. In Macbeth, the three witches say together “Fair is foul, and foul is fair”. The line has seven syllables: three feet of strong then soft and a final strong syllable (FAIR is FOUL and FOUL is FAIR), so it sounds like a spell. When you write about any trochaic line, say what the beat makes the speaker sound like, and what any break in it shows.

**Examples:** “Peter, Peter, pumpkin-eater” — eight syllables in four feet of strong then soft, so the rhyme sounds like a chant — Peter, Peter, Pumpkin-Eater; “Jack and Jill went up the hill” — seven syllables, with a strong beat on Jack, Jill, up and hill (JACK and JILL went UP the HILL), so the rhyme starts each beat with force — Jack and Jill; “Should you ask me, whence these stories?” — eight syllables in four feet of strong then soft, as the poem begins like a storyteller starting a tale (whence means where from) — The Song of Hiawatha

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice that each foot begins on a strong syllable, so the lines seem to start with force. · Feel: A beat that begins hard can feel commanding, urgent or magical, so we sense the speaker's power or threat. · Think: We ask what a chant-like or commanding rhythm shows about the speaker, such as power, magic or a hold over others. · Act: We notice chants, slogans and commands in everyday life, and ask why a strong first beat makes them hard to ignore.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any trochee, a two-syllable foot with a strong syllable first and a soft one after it (DUM-da). A strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Mark each syllable of the line strong or soft. Does each foot start on a strong syllable? 2. Does every foot follow that pattern, or does one differ, such as a foot with only a strong syllable, and which words does that land on? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from a beat that starts each foot with a strong syllable, such as being commanded, chanted at or sung to? Try the questions on “Twinkle, twinkle, little star”, a children's song. It runs TWIN-kle TWIN-kle LIT-tle STAR, so each of the first three feet starts on its strong syllable. The last foot is only the single strong syllable “star”, so the line ends on a firm stop. The beat makes the line sound like a song, gentle and easy to sing and remember.

**How to create it:** Choose words that start on a strong syllable, such as “GOLden”, “TIger” or “WINter”, and put one at the start of each foot. Decide where a voice should sound unnatural, such as a spell, a command or a chant, and use a strong-then-soft beat there. Tap each strong syllable as you read the line aloud. Check that every foot starts on a strong syllable; if one starts on a soft syllable by accident, change the word.

**Related:** Foot

### Dactyl `Dc`

A dactyl is a foot of three syllables: one strong, then two soft (DUM-da-da). A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. After the strong beat, the line drops away in two quick syllables, so dactylic lines often sound fast and rolling. A dactylic line often ends on a shorter foot, so not every foot has three syllables. The anapaest is the opposite foot: two soft syllables, then a strong one (da-da-DUM).

**The concept:** The dactyl lets a poet make a line roll forward, because two quick soft syllables follow each strong beat. In The Charge of the Light Brigade, Tennyson writes about soldiers on horses riding into battle: “Half a league, half a league” (a league is about three miles). Each “Half a league” is one dactyl: the beat falls on “Half”, and the rhythm carries “a league” lightly, although in speech “league” is also said with some force. The rhythm can sound like galloping horses. When you write about any dactylic line, say what speed the rhythm gives it, and what that speed shows about the subject.

**Examples:** “This is the forest primeval” — eight syllables: two dactyls and a closing foot of two (THIS is the FOR-est pri-ME-val), so the opening rolls on like a storyteller's voice (primeval means very ancient) — Evangeline; “Merrily, merrily” — six syllables in two dactyls (MER-ri-ly, MER-ri-ly), as the spirit Ariel sings that he will live happily — The Tempest; “Just for a handful of silver he left us” — eleven syllables: three dactyls and a closing foot of two (JUST for a HAND-ful of SIL-ver he LEFT us), as the speaker says a man left his friends for a little money — The Lost Leader

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen for one strong beat followed by two quick soft ones, which makes a line seem to run forward. · Feel: We feel carried along by the speed, which can feel exciting, playful or frightening, depending on the subject. · Think: We ask what the subject has in common with the rushing rhythm, such as a charge, a chase or a fall. · Act: We notice rolling rhythms in songs, chants and adverts, and ask what the speed is persuading us to feel.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any dactyl, a three-syllable foot with one strong syllable then two soft ones (DUM-da-da). A strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Mark each syllable of the line strong or soft. Does each foot start on a strong syllable followed by two soft ones? 2. Does the line change the pattern anywhere, such as ending on a single strong syllable, and which words does that land on? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from the speed of the rhythm, such as hurry or excitement? Try the questions on “Hickory dickory dock”, the first line of a nursery rhyme about a mouse. It runs HICK-o-ry DICK-o-ry DOCK: one strong syllable then two soft ones, twice, so the first two feet follow the pattern. The last foot is the single strong syllable “dock”, so the line ends on a stop. The rhythm is quick and bouncy, which suits the next line, where the mouse ran up the clock. The rhyme seems meant to feel playful, like a small animal scampering.

**How to create it:** Choose words with one strong syllable then two soft ones, such as “MERrily”, “DANgerous” and “CAREfully”. Decide what is rushing, such as a chase, a crowd or a feeling, and write a short line about it using two or three of those words. Read the line aloud and tap each strong syllable. Check that the line hurries; if it does not, look for a word that puts a strong syllable in the wrong place.

**Related:** Foot

### Anapaest `Ap`

An anapaest is a foot of three syllables: two soft, then one strong (da-da-DUM). A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. The two light syllables run up to the strong one, so anapaestic lines often sound quick and bouncing, as in nursery rhymes, limericks and galloping verse. A line of anapaests may start with a shorter foot. The dactyl is the opposite foot: one strong syllable, then two soft (DUM-da-da).

**The concept:** The anapaest lets a poet make a line speed up, because two quick soft syllables run up to each strong beat. In How They Brought the Good News from Ghent to Aix, Robert Browning writes about three riders on a fast ride, and the speaker says “I sprang to the stirrup, and Joris, and he”. After one opening foot of two syllables, the line has three anapaests (to the STIR, rup and JOR, is and HE), so it gallops. When you write about any anapaestic line, say what speed the rhythm gives it, and what that speed shows about the subject.

**Examples:** “’Twas the night before Christmas, when all through the house” — twelve syllables in four anapaests (’twas the NIGHT, be-fore CHRIST, mas when ALL, through the HOUSE), so the opening bounces along — A Visit from St. Nicholas; “And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold” — twelve syllables in four anapaests (and his CO, horts were GLEAM, ing in PUR, ple and GOLD), as the poem pictures the Assyrian army shining in purple and gold (cohorts are groups of soldiers) — The Destruction of Sennacherib; “There was an Old Man with a beard” — eight syllables: one opening foot of two syllables, then two anapaests (there WAS, an old MAN, with a BEARD), so the limerick bounces from its first line; the pattern gives “was” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is light — A Book of Nonsense

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We hear two quick soft syllables run up to each strong beat, so the line seems to speed up. · Feel: We feel energy and excitement, or sometimes panic, because the line hurries and bounces forward. · Think: We ask what the subject has in common with that speed, such as a ride, an attack or a joke. · Act: We notice bouncing rhythms in jingles, rhymes and adverts, and ask why a fast, light beat makes a message easy to remember.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any anapaest, a three-syllable foot with two soft syllables then a strong one (da-da-DUM). A strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Mark each syllable of the line strong or soft. Does each foot have two soft syllables before the strong one? 2. Does the line change the pattern anywhere, such as a shorter first or last foot, and which words does that land on? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from a beat that rises to each strong syllable, such as cheer, speed or anticipation? Try the questions on “In a beautiful pea-green boat” from The Owl and the Pussy-Cat by Edward Lear, a nonsense poem about an owl and a cat who sail away to sea. It runs in a BEAU-ti-ful PEA green BOAT: two soft syllables then a strong one, twice, so the first two feet follow the pattern. The last foot, “green boat”, has only one soft syllable before its strong one, so the line ends a little shorter. The beat rises and bounces like a small boat rocking on the sea, and Lear may want the reader to enjoy a happy, silly journey.

**How to create it:** Choose a moment of rising excitement, such as a ride, a chase or a journey beginning. Build each foot from two soft syllables then a strong one, such as “on the HILL” or “in a RUSH”. Write two or three of those feet in a line. Read it aloud and tap the strong syllables. Check that you tap once for every three syllables; if a foot has a different count, change the words.

**Related:** Foot

### Spondee `Sn`

A spondee is a foot of two syllables that are both strong (DUM-DUM). A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. With no soft syllable between them, both beats land hard, so the line slows down and the reader stays on those two words. Spondees are uncommon in English, and poets often place one inside lines of other feet to add weight or shock. Its opposite is the pyrrhic, a foot with no strong beat at all (da-da).

**The concept:** The spondee lets a poet slow a line and put weight on two words together. Because both syllables are said with force, a reader cannot hurry past them. In Macbeth, Macbeth hears that his wife, Lady Macbeth, is dead, and he says “Out, out, brief candle!” (he is speaking about how short life is). The first two words are both said with force, so the line opens with two heavy beats. When you write about any spondee, say which words it puts together, and what the weight, or the slowing of the line, shows.

**Examples:** “Break, break, break” — three strong words in a row, so any two of them side by side make a spondee, and the line sounds slow and heavy as the speaker calls to the sea — Break, Break, Break; “Rocks, caves, lakes, fens, bogs, dens, and shades of death” — six one-syllable nouns in a row, each said with force, so any two side by side, such as the first two nouns, make a spondee, and the line sounds slow and heavy as the fallen angels cross the land of hell — Paradise Lost; “Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks! Rage! blow!” — “Blow, winds” puts two strong beats together, so the order King Lear gives the storm starts with force — King Lear

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We slow down and press on two strong words together, so each one gets our full attention. · Feel: Heavy beats can feel like grief, anger or shock, because the line will not let us hurry past. · Think: We ask why the writer wanted this weight, and what it shows about the speaker's grief, anger or despair. · Act: We notice when slogans and warnings press hard on several words in a row, and ask what they want us to feel.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any spondee, a two-syllable foot in which both syllables are strong (DUM-DUM). A strong syllable is said with more force. 1. Which two words side by side both take a strong stress when you read the line aloud? 2. How does the double stress change the pace or mood of the lines around it? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from the double stress? Try the questions on “Gas! Gas! Quick, boys!” from Dulce et Decorum Est by Wilfred Owen, a poem about soldiers in the First World War. Both “Gas” and “Gas” are shouted with a strong stress, with no soft syllable between them. The first stanza describes a slow, tired march: “Men marched asleep.” The two heavy beats cut into that, so the poem jolts from weariness to panic. Owen wants the reader to feel the sudden terror of a gas attack, which fits his argument that war is not glorious.

**How to create it:** Choose one word or phrase that deserves a pause, such as a loss, a blow or an order. Place two strong words side by side there, such as “cold stone” or “hard rain”. Surround them with lighter, quicker words so the two heavy ones stand out. Read the line aloud and check that you slow down on the two words; if you do not, swap in words that each carry weight.

**Related:** Foot

### Pyrrhic `Pi`

A pyrrhic is a foot of two soft syllables (da-da), with no strong beat of its own. A strong syllable is said with more force than a soft one. The reader hurries across a pyrrhic, so the line lightens for a moment and the strong syllables around it seem heavier. Some readers hear a faint beat in a pyrrhic, so it is partly a matter of judgement. Its opposite is the spondee, a foot of two strong beats (DUM-DUM).

**The concept:** The pyrrhic lets a poet lighten one place in a line, so the words on either side stand out. It is often made from small words such as “in”, “of”, “to” and “the”, which carry little stress when we speak. In Macbeth, Macbeth says that each tomorrow “Creeps in this petty pace from day to day” (petty means small and unimportant). The small words “in this” are both soft, so the line hurries over them and then slows on “petty pace”. When you write about any pyrrhic, say which small words it uses, and what the light moment, and the strong words around it, show.

**Examples:** “When in disgrace with fortune and men’s eyes” — the small words “tune and” are both soft, so the line hurries and then lands on the strong words “men’s eyes”, as the poet describes feeling unlucky and ashamed — Sonnet 29; “The paths of glory lead but to the grave” — the small words “but to” carry no strong beat, so the line hurries to its final strong word, “grave”, in a line saying that fame ends in death — Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard; “In the forests of the night” — the small words “of the” carry little stress, so the line hurries between “forests” and “night”, in the poem's picture of a tiger in the dark — The Tyger

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We hurry across two small soft words, so the strong words on either side seem to stand out. · Feel: We feel the line lighten and then land harder, as if a thought rushes ahead or a feeling suddenly presses down. · Think: We ask which words the writer wanted to stand out, what those words say about the subject, and why the line lightens before them. · Act: We notice how speakers hurry over small words and press on key ones, and ask what they want us to remember.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any pyrrhic, a foot of two soft syllables with no strong beat (da-da). A foot is one small unit of rhythm in a line, and a strong syllable is said with more force, a soft one more lightly. 1. Which two soft syllables sit together with no strong beat between them? 2. Which strong syllable comes next, and does it stand out more because of the soft syllables before it? 3. What does the writer want the reader to notice or feel because the line is quieter at that point? Try the questions on “Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall”, the first line of a nursery rhyme. Read naturally, it mostly falls strong then soft: HUMP-ty DUMP-ty SAT on a WALL. The two soft syllables are “on a”, between the strong syllables “sat” and “wall”. The next strong syllable is “wall”, the last word of the line, which stands out because the line hurries over “on a” to reach it. The rhyme's writer is unknown, but the effect is that the line quickens and then stops hard on “wall”, ready for the fall in the next line.

**How to create it:** Choose the word you want to stand out in your line. Put two small, light words just before it, such as “of the”, “and a” or “in the”. Make the words on either side of those two light words strong ones. Say the line aloud. Check by asking a friend which word they heard as the strongest; if they do not name your word, change the light words before it.

**Related:** Foot

### Tetrameter `Tm`

A tetrameter is a metre with four feet in each line. A metre is the pattern of beats in a line of verse, and a foot is one repeating group of syllables with one strong syllable. The word comes from Greek: tetra means four. A trimeter has three feet and a pentameter has five. A four-beat line is easy to sing and to remember, so tetrameter is common in ballads (songs that tell a story), hymns and chants.

**The concept:** A tetrameter gives a line four beats, which makes it short enough to say in one breath and easy to remember. Whether the line sounds quick or slow depends on its words and on whether each foot is soft then strong or strong then soft. In Macbeth, the three witches chant “Double, double, toil and trouble”. The line has eight syllables, with a strong beat on dou, dou, toil and trou (DOU-ble DOU-ble TOIL and TROU-ble), so it sounds like a spell. When you write about any tetrameter, say how the four beats move, and what that sound shows about the speaker or subject.

**Examples:** “I wander through each chartered street” — eight syllables in four feet of soft then strong; the pattern gives “through” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is light, so the speaker’s walk through London sounds steady — London; “In Xanadu did Kubla Khan” — eight syllables in four feet of soft then strong, so the opening line about a ruler named Kubla Khan has an even, chant-like beat — Kubla Khan; “Close to the sun in lonely lands” — eight syllables with four strong beats, on close, sun, lone and lands, in a line about an eagle high above the ground — The Eagle

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We follow four beats to the line, so each line is short enough to take in at once. · Feel: Four beats can feel playful, urgent, steady or hypnotic, so we feel the speaker's energy, calm or a spell. · Think: We ask what the four-beat pattern suggests about the subject, such as a march, a chant, a journey or a spell. · Act: We notice four-beat rhythms in songs, chants and slogans, and ask why they are so easy to remember and repeat.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any tetrameter, a line with four feet, so four main beats. A foot is one small repeating pattern of strong and soft syllables, and a strong syllable is said with more force. 1. How many strong beats does the line have? Count them in two lines. 2. Do the four beats sound quick and light, or slow and heavy, and which words make them sound that way? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from the beat? Try the questions on “I wandered lonely as a cloud” from Daffodils by William Wordsworth. “I WAN-dered LONE-ly AS a CLOUD” has four beats, on “wan”, “lone”, “as” and “cloud”. The metre gives “as” a beat, although in ordinary speech it is said lightly. The next line, “That FLOATS on HIGH o'er VALES and HILLS”, has four as well. Here the four beats sound light and song-like, because the words are soft and easy to say. The easy swing matches the daffodils “Fluttering and dancing in the breeze” and the speaker's happiness, so Wordsworth may want the reader to share his joy.

**How to create it:** Choose a subject that suits a short, repeated beat, such as a journey, a chase, a chant or a slow walk. Decide that every line will have four main beats. Write the first line, then tap one finger on each beat as you read it aloud. Write the next lines to match, adding or cutting words. Check that each line gives four taps; where one gives three or five, change it.

**Related:** Metre

### Trimeter `Ri`

A trimeter is a metre with three feet in each line. A metre is the pattern of beats in a line of verse, and a foot is one repeating group of syllables with one strong syllable. The word comes from Greek: tri means three. A trimeter is shorter than a tetrameter (four feet) and a pentameter (five feet), so it can sound short, sharp or breathless. In ballads, a trimeter often follows a longer line.

**The concept:** A trimeter lets a poet end a line sooner than a reader expects, which gives it a clipped, firm sound. A short line also leaves empty space around its words, so each word carries more weight. In The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, an old sailor stops a man on his way to a wedding, and Coleridge writes “And he stoppeth one of three” (stoppeth means stops). It has three strong beats (and he STOP-peth ONE of THREE) and follows a line with four. When you write about any trimeter, say how it differs from the lines around it, and what its shortness shows.

**Examples:** “Half hidden from the eye” — six syllables in three feet of soft then strong, a shorter line that follows a longer one and describes a violet by a mossy stone — She Dwelt among the Untrodden Ways; “Of his bones are coral made” — seven syllables with three strong beats (of his BONES are COR-al MADE), as the spirit Ariel sings that a drowned man's bones have turned to coral — The Tempest; “From yon far country blows” — six syllables in three feet of soft then strong, a shorter line about a wind from a faraway place (yon means over there) — A Shropshire Lad

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice that a line stops sooner than we expected, so the words in it stand out. · Feel: A short line can feel clipped, urgent or final, so we feel a thought shut, or a feeling cut short. · Think: We ask what the writer wanted to compress or end sharply, and how the shortness connects to the poem's subject. · Act: We notice short, firm lines in slogans, warnings and speeches, and ask what they are trying to settle.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any trimeter, a line with three feet, so three main beats. A foot is one small repeating pattern of strong and soft syllables, and a strong syllable is said with more force. 1. How many strong beats does the line have? Count them in each line of a stanza. 2. Does every line keep that count, or does a longer line appear, and where? 3. What does the writer want the reader to feel from short lines like these? Try the questions on “Had he and I but met” from The Man He Killed by Thomas Hardy, in which a soldier thinks about the man he shot. “Had he and I but met” has six syllables and three beats, on the second, fourth and sixth syllables: “he”, “I” and “met”. The next line, “By some old ancient inn”, has three as well. Line three, “We should have sat us down to wet”, has four, while the other lines in the stanza have three. Short lines leave no room for long phrases, so the soldier sounds plain and blunt, like a man speaking his thoughts without decoration. Hardy seems to want the reader to feel the soldier’s plain, unpolished honesty.

**How to create it:** Decide what your poem holds back, such as a hard feeling the speaker cannot finish saying. Write short lines with three main beats each. Read each line aloud and tap one finger on each beat. If a line has more than three taps, remove or replace a word that carries a beat. Check that each line gives three taps; if you keep one longer line on purpose, read it next to the short ones and notice the extra beat.

**Related:** Metre

### Metatheatre `Mh`

Metatheatre is theatre that draws attention to the fact that it is a play. A character may speak straight to the audience, talk about acting, or perform a play inside the play. A chorus, a speaker who comments on the action, may also point out that the stage is only a stage. This reminds the audience that they are watching a performance, not real life.

**The concept:** Metatheatre makes an audience think about how stories are made, and how life can seem like a performance. The ‘meta’ in the name comes from a Greek word meaning ‘beyond’, and here it means a play that is about being a play. When a play admits what it is, the audience cannot forget that it is watching. In Macbeth, Macbeth hears that his wife is dead and says “Life's but a walking shadow; a poor player”, comparing life to an actor on a stage. When you find any metatheatre, say how the work admits it is a performance, why it reminds us we are watching, and what that shows.

**Examples:** “Can this cockpit hold / The vasty fields of France?” — the Chorus, who speaks to the audience, asks whether this small playhouse can hold the huge fields of France, and asks us to imagine them — Henry V; “release me from my bands / With the help of your good hands” — Prospero, at the end of the play, asks the audience to clap, so that they set him free — The Tempest; “If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended” — Puck, a fairy, calls the actors “shadows” and tells the audience to think of the play as a dream — A Midsummer Night's Dream

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the moment a play admits it is a play, and see the stage, actors or audience as part of the story. · Feel: We feel included, and sometimes unsettled, because we are reminded that we are watching and that nothing on the stage is real. · Think: We ask why the writer breaks the illusion, and what the play says about pretending and about the roles people play in life. · Act: We notice when films, news or social media show us a staged version of events, and ask who is performing, and for whom.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any metatheatre, theatre that shows it knows it is a play. 1. How does the work admit it is a performance: a play within the play, a character speaking to the audience, a Prologue or Chorus, or a character talking about acting? 2. Does anyone inside the story watch as an audience, and if so, who and how do they react? 3. What does the admission make the real audience notice about the story or about themselves? 4. What does the writer want the audience to understand? Try the questions on Hamlet. Hamlet arranges for travelling actors to perform a play before King Claudius, because one scene “comes near” the murder of his father. Claudius and the court watch, and Hamlet and his friend Horatio watch Claudius. Claudius stops it by calling “Give me some light: away!” We watch an audience watching a pretend murder, and see that a performance can make a real person give himself away. Shakespeare may want us to see that a play can show a truth people hide, as Hamlet says it will “catch the conscience of the king”.

**How to create it:** Choose the point where you want your audience or reader to stop and notice that a story is being told. Make a character perform a play, a story or a song, or let a narrator speak straight to the reader. Link that performance to something in your plot, so a character reacts to it as if it were real. Check that the moment makes the reader think about your story's real subject; if it is only a trick, change it or cut it.

### Parallelism `Pz`

Parallelism is the repeating of the same sentence shape in a row of phrases, clauses or lines. For example: ‘He was tired, he was hungry, he was lost.’ The matching shape makes the ideas feel linked, so the reader weighs them together. Writers use it to build a rhythm, to add up a list of ideas, or to set ideas against each other. A group of three matching parts is called a tricolon.

**The concept:** Parallelism gives ideas the same shape, so that a reader hears them as one connected group. The repeated shape also creates a rhythm, which can make a speech sound confident and easy to remember. Because the pattern is predictable, a part that breaks it stands out. In Henry V, King Henry tells his soldiers before a battle, “We few, we happy few, we band of brothers”: three matching phrases that each begin with “we”, so that the soldiers sound like one group. When you find any parallelism, say what shape repeats, whether the matching parts build, add up or oppose each other, and whether any part breaks the pattern.

**Examples:** “This other Eden, demi-paradise, / This fortress built by Nature for herself” — John of Gaunt, a dying nobleman, praises England in a long list of phrases that each begin with ‘this’ — Richard II; “Theirs not to make reply, / Theirs not to reason why, / Theirs but to do and die” — each line begins “Theirs”, and the third changes “not” to “but”, so the order to die comes last — The Charge of the Light Brigade; “As Caesar loved me, I weep for him; as he was fortunate, I rejoice at it; as he was valiant, I honour him; but, as he was ambitious, I slew him” — Brutus builds three matching clauses, and the fourth ends in killing — Julius Caesar

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the same sentence shape repeating, and compare the ideas that fill each part. · Feel: We feel the rhythm build into certainty or urgency, because each repeated shape adds weight to the one before. · Think: We work out how the matching parts connect, and what the pattern, or a break in it, shows about the writer's purpose. · Act: We notice when speeches, adverts and slogans repeat one shape to sound convincing, and ask whether the ideas deserve that confidence.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any parallelism, the repeating of one grammatical shape across clauses or lines. 1. Which words or shape repeat in each clause, and how many times? 2. Do the matched items build, add up or oppose each other? 3. Does any item break the pattern, and if it does, what does the break do? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol, Stave 5. Scrooge cries, “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy.” The shape “I am as … as a …” repeats, and then a fourth time with “giddy as a drunken man”. The items build, because each adds another kind of joy. None breaks the pattern, and the sameness makes the feelings sound as if they are tumbling out. Dickens wants the reader to see that Scrooge is changed.

**How to create it:** Choose three or four ideas that belong together, such as the things a character fears. Write each as a clause with the same shape, for example “I fear the dark, I fear the silence, I fear the morning.” Make each clause a little stronger than the one before. Decide whether the last clause should break the pattern to stand out. Check by listing the clauses one under another; if the shapes do not match, change the grammar until they do.

**Related:** Tricolon, Repetition

### Equivocation `Ec`

Equivocation is speech that misleads a listener without telling a lie. The words are true in one sense, but the listener understands them in another. The speaker can then claim to have told the truth. It works because listeners often hear the meaning they expect or hope for.

**The concept:** Equivocation shows a character who hides the truth but can still say ‘I did not lie’. The word comes from Latin words meaning ‘equal’ and ‘voice’, because the same words carry two meanings. In Macbeth, a spirit called up by the witches promises Macbeth that “none of woman born” will harm him. Macduff then reveals that he was cut from his mother's womb, and Macbeth cries that these fiends “palter with us in a double sense”. When you find any equivocation, say what the listener understands, what other meaning the words truly have, and why the speaker needs to hide the truth.

**Examples:** “yet indeed she is my sister; she is the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother” — Abraham had told King Abimelech that his wife Sarah was his sister, which is true only because she is his half-sister — The Bible (Genesis); “Macbeth shall never vanquish'd be until / Great Birnam wood to high Dunsinane hill / Shall come against him” — a spirit called up by the witches says this, and Macbeth takes it to mean he will never be beaten, because a forest cannot move; later the enemy soldiers carry branches cut from the wood — Macbeth; “if he should march against the Persians he should destroy a great empire” — the oracle tells King Croesus this without saying whose empire, and it is his own that falls — The History of Herodotus

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at words that sound simple and true, and notice that they can be read in another way. · Feel: We feel unease and sometimes anger, because a listener is misled by words that were technically honest. · Think: We work out what the speaker is hiding, and why the writer lets the speaker keep the defence of having told the truth. · Act: We notice when promises, adverts and official statements are true in one sense but misleading in another, and ask what has been left out.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any equivocation, speech that misleads without a lie. 1. What does the listener understand the words to mean? 2. In what other sense are the words true, and what small gap lets that sense hide? 3. Why can the speaker not say the truth openly? 4. What does the writer want the audience to understand about the speaker? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet, Act 3 Scene 5. Lady Capulet says she hopes Juliet will be “satisfied” once Romeo is dead. Juliet answers, “Indeed I never shall be satisfied”, and the next line begins “With Romeo till I behold him”. Her mother hears that Juliet wants Romeo dead, because Romeo killed Juliet's cousin Tybalt. The other sense is that Juliet will not be content until she sees Romeo. The gap is the word “dead” between dashes: “With Romeo till I behold him—dead— / Is my poor heart so for a kinsman vex'd”. Her mother joins “dead” to “behold him”. In Juliet's own sense, “dead” starts a new sentence, which says that her heart is dead with sorrow for her cousin. She cannot say so, because she has secretly married Romeo. The writer wants the audience to see Juliet already divided between her family and her husband.

**How to create it:** Choose a secret your character must protect and the person they are speaking to. Write a sentence that the listener will understand one way, but that is true in another way, using a pause, a word with two senses or something left out. Show the listener acting on the wrong meaning. Check that the speaker could defend every word if challenged; if a word is false, change it.

### Apostrophe `Ae`

Apostrophe is when a speaker talks directly to someone or something that cannot answer, as if it could hear. The one spoken to may be a dead or absent person, an animal, an object, a place or an idea. The address often begins with “O” or with the name of the one spoken to. An apostrophe can be a sudden line or two in a play, or it can last a whole poem. Apostrophe in this sense is not the punctuation mark (’) with the same name.

**The concept:** Apostrophe lets a speaker express a strong feeling to someone or something that cannot answer. The word comes from a Greek word meaning ‘a turning away’, because a speaker may turn away from the audience to address someone else. Because no reply can come, the speaker's need to speak at all often shows how strong the feeling is. In Julius Caesar, Antony, Caesar's friend, asks the dead Caesar, “Dost thou lie so low?”, in grief that so great a man has fallen. When you write about any apostrophe, say who or what is addressed, why it cannot answer, and what feeling or need the speaker shows.

**Examples:** “O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being” — the speaker talks to the autumn wind from the poem's first line, as if it were a person who could hear him — Ode to the West Wind; “Stars, hide your fires! / Let not light see my black and deep desires.” — Macbeth, speaking aside after King Duncan names his son Malcolm as heir, tells the stars to hide their light — Macbeth; “Where be your gibes now?” — Hamlet holds the skull of Yorick, a court jester he knew as a child, and asks the dead man where his jokes are now — Hamlet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice a speaker talking directly to someone or something that cannot hear or answer. · Feel: We feel the speaker's strong emotion, such as grief, awe or longing, because they speak aloud to a listener who will never reply. · Think: We work out why the speaker needs this listener, and what that need shows about the writer's subject, such as grief, guilt or wonder. · Act: We notice when people speak aloud to a grave, a photograph or an empty room, and understand the feeling that makes them do so.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any apostrophe, a direct address to someone absent or dead, or to an object or idea, as if it could hear. 1. Who or what is addressed, and why can it not answer? 2. What feeling or need does the speaker show by speaking to it? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the address? Try the questions on “The Tyger” by William Blake. The poem addresses a tiger, which cannot answer, and the poem is made almost entirely of questions to it. The speaker shows awe and fear, and a need to understand how the tiger was made. One of its questions asks, “Did He who made the lamb make thee?” The writer wants the reader to wonder how one maker could create both a gentle lamb and a terrifying tiger.

**How to create it:** Choose a person or thing that cannot answer, such as a dead friend, the sea or a season. Write a line that starts by calling it directly, with “O” or its name. Decide what the speaker wants from it: to plead, blame, question or thank. Add a second line where the speaker admits a feeling they would not say to anyone else. Check that nothing answers; if something does, change the reply into silence.

### Plot Twist `Pt`

A plot twist is a sudden turn in a story that shows the reader the truth is different from what they believed. First the writer leads the reader to believe one thing; then the truth is revealed. A well-made twist often has clues earlier in the story, so the reader can look back and find them. A twist can change a single event or the meaning of the whole story. A weak twist simply surprises, with no clues at all.

**The concept:** A plot twist makes readers look again at everything they have already read. The writer lets the reader build a belief, then overturns it, so the reader goes back over earlier scenes. In Macbeth, the witches' spirits tell Macbeth that no one born of a woman can harm him, so he and the audience think he is safe. Then Macduff says he “was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripp'd”, meaning he was cut out of her before a natural birth. When you write about any plot twist, say what the reader believed before it, what the twist reveals, and which earlier clues, if any, pointed towards it.

**Examples:** “there stood Henry Jekyll!” — Dr Lanyon, Jekyll's old friend, watches the man Hyde drink a potion and change into Dr Jekyll, so the reader learns that they are one person — Jekyll and Hyde; “The marriage cannot go on: I declare the existence of an impediment.” — a lawyer interrupts Jane Eyre's wedding to Mr Rochester, and she and the reader soon learn that Rochester already has a wife — Jane Eyre; “In one long yellow string I wound / Three times her little throat around, / And strangled her.” — the gentle scene between a man and his lover becomes a murder, as the speaker strangles Porphyria with her own hair — Porphyria's Lover

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look back over earlier scenes to find what we missed, once the truth is revealed. · Feel: We feel shock when a belief breaks, then unease that the writer led us so easily to trust what was false. · Think: We ask which clues pointed to the truth, and what the writer wants us to learn about trusting appearances. · Act: We notice when news stories, adverts or people give us only part of the truth, and ask what we are being led to believe.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any plot twist, a turn that overturns what the reader believed. 1. What does the reader believe before the twist? 2. What does the twist reveal? 3. Which earlier details, looking back, pointed towards it? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel through it? Try the questions on Great Expectations by Charles Dickens. Pip, the hero, believes the old, rich Miss Havisham is secretly paying for his life as a gentleman. The twist is that his benefactor is the convict he helped as a boy, Magwitch, who says he has made a gentleman and tells Pip: “you're him!” Looking back, Pip had given that convict food and a file in the opening chapters, and his lawyer, Mr Jaggers, told him the benefactor's name must stay secret. Dickens may want the reader to see Pip's snobbery: Pip describes feeling “abhorrence” for the man who made him a gentleman.

**How to create it:** Decide the truth your reader will discover at the end. Write the early scenes so the reader believes something else. Plant two small clues that point to the truth, each hidden inside another detail. Reveal the truth in one scene where your main character must react. Check each clue: could a reader point to it afterwards and say, “It was there all along”? If not, make it clearer.

**Kinds of Plot Twist** — One surprise told many ways — each a different kind of turn that overturns the reader's expectation yet, looked back on, was fairly set up. Open a card, name the kind, and trace how the set-up made the reversal feel earned.

- **Hidden identity** — A character revealed as someone other than they claimed — the reader re-reads every earlier scene in a new light
  - **An Inspector Calls** — Gerald's flat realisation that the family's inquisitor held no official power at all — the authority they feared, and confessed to, dissolves, throwing every earlier answer into doubt. _(e.g. "That man wasn't a police officer" — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Great Expectations** — Magwitch's boast collapses Pip's belief that Miss Havisham funded his rise, unmasking the branded convict as his true benefactor and his gentility as bought with tainted money. _(e.g. "I've made a gentleman on you!" — Great Expectations)_
  - **Twelfth Night** — Viola's paradox quietly concedes that Cesario is a fiction — the disguised self admitting its own concealment while Illyria reads only the surface before it. _(e.g. "I am not what I am" — Twelfth Night)_
- **The double & split self** — One figure who proves to be two — a hidden second self, twin or mirror
  - **Jekyll and Hyde** — Jekyll's confession fuses the hunted Hyde and the respected doctor into one divided man — a single nature split against itself rather than two separate beings. _(e.g. "man is not truly one, but truly two" — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Frankenstein** — The creature names his cruelty as made, not born, casting himself as the dark reflection of Victor's own neglect rather than a separate monster. _(e.g. "misery made me a fiend" — Frankenstein)_
  - **Blood Brothers** — The superstition binds the separated brothers to one shared doom, the omen marking the twins as two halves of a single fated life. _(e.g. "shoes upon the table" — Blood Brothers)_
- **False death & the return** — A death feigned, mistaken or undone — grief turned inside out
  - **Romeo and Juliet** — The Friar's potion engineers a death that only looks real — the feigned end that, fatally misread, turns a rescue plan into catastrophe. _(e.g. "this distilled liquor drink thou off" — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Much Ado About Nothing** — Hero's staged death, proclaimed on her false epitaph, is the engineered end held in reserve so that slander can be undone and she can return. _(e.g. "Done to death by slanderous tongues" — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — The dead Marley returns fettered by the chain his own indifference forged — the revenant whose warning recolours everything Scrooge assumes about his fate. _(e.g. "I wear the chain I forged in life" — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Reversal of fortune (peripeteia)** — The secure ground gives way — the turn where ascent becomes descent
  - **Macbeth** — The witches' promise that no man born of woman can harm him proves a trap once Macduff's birth is revealed — the very security that undoes him. _(e.g. "none of woman born" — Macbeth)_
  - **Lord of the Flies** — The conch — emblem of order and shared voice — bursts apart, the collapse into savagery made concrete at the instant civilisation finally breaks. _(e.g. "into a thousand white fragments" — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Of Mice and Men** — The refrain of the dream farm, the shared fiction that keeps the men human, is the very tenderness the ending exists to shatter. _(e.g. "live off the fatta the lan'" — Of Mice and Men)_
- **Too-late recognition (anagnorisis)** — The truth arrives only when nothing can be done with it
  - **Othello** — The epithet Othello repeats over his betrayer exposes a misplaced trust whose recognition arrives far too late to be redeemed. _(e.g. "honest Iago" — Othello)_
  - **To Kill a Mockingbird** — The Inspector's creed of shared responsibility lands as the family's dawning guilt — each private cruelty gathered, too late, into one collective reckoning. _(e.g. “his shoulders jerked as if each "guilty" was a separate stab between them” — To Kill a Mockingbird)_
  - **Macbeth** — Macbeth's bleak image of a brief, meaningless candle is his recognition of all he has forfeited, clarity arriving only when nothing can be reclaimed. _(e.g. "Life's but a walking shadow" — Macbeth)_
- **The unreliable reveal** — The telling itself hid the truth — the account, not just the plot, turns
  - **The Curious Incident** — The literal narrator who cannot lie both grounds and limits the account — his exactness withholding the adult meanings the reader must infer past him. _(e.g. "cannot tell lies" — The Curious Incident of the Dog in the Night-Time)_
  - **Jekyll and Hyde** — The neglected door, blistered and distained, is the facade behind which the narrative itself withholds the Jekyll–Hyde connection — concealment built into the mystery. _(e.g. "blistered and distained" — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Great Expectations** — Pip's retrospective admission of shame discloses a narrator judging his own younger self — the older voice disowning a gentility he once mistook for worth. _(e.g. "It is a most miserable thing to feel ashamed of home" — Great Expectations)_
- **The planted payoff (Chekhov's gun)** — An early, seeded detail that returns to spring the turn — set-up paying off
  - **Twelfth Night** — The photograph, withheld and shown to one Birling at a time, is the seeded device whose controlled return steadily tightens the moral pressure. _(e.g. “I left no ring with her” — Twelfth Night)_
  - **Frankenstein** — The creature's early threat, planted and half-forgotten, pays off with devastating precision on the wedding night — the promise the reader was dared to dismiss. _(e.g. "I shall be with you on your wedding-night" — Frankenstein)_
  - **A Christmas Carol** — Scrooge's callous Malthusian line, planted early, returns to indict him when the spirits throw his own words back into his face. _(e.g. "decrease the surplus population" — A Christmas Carol)_
- **The final sting** — A last-moment turn that recolours everything before it
  - **An Inspector Calls** — The Inspector's parting prophecy of catastrophe recolours the whole play at its close, the warning that turns the family's comfort to dread. _(e.g. "fire and blood and anguish" — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Blood Brothers** — The narrator opens with the twins' deaths, so the final gunshot arrives as a fate long foretold — the ending seeded in the beginning. _(e.g. "So, did you hear the story of the Johnstone twins?" — Blood Brothers)_
  - **Lord of the Flies** — Ralph's grief converts rescue into indictment, the closing turn that recolours the boys' salvation as the same darkness, merely scaled up to the adult world. _(e.g. "wept for the end of innocence, the darkness of man's heart" — Lord of the Flies)_

**Related:** Stunning Surprise, Subverted Expectation, The Shadow, Surprise, Peripeteia, Anagnorisis, Unreliable Narrator, Setup & Payoff

### Stakes `Sk`

Stakes are what a character will lose if they fail to get what they want. A loss can be large, such as a life, or small, such as a friend's trust. When the stakes are clear, readers know what is at risk and so care about the outcome. Stakes are not the same as tension: tension is the worry of waiting to see what happens, and stakes are the loss behind that worry.

**The concept:** Stakes make a reader care about what happens, because they show exactly what could be lost. A loss the reader can picture holds attention better than a vague one. In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Present shows the miser Scrooge a poor, sick child, Tiny Tim, and says: “If these shadows remain unaltered by the Future, the child will die.” Now Scrooge's choice to stay mean has a clear cost: a child's life. When you write about any stakes, say what could be lost, how clearly the reader can picture it, and whether the cost grows as the story goes on.
