**Examples:** “Or I'll have your heart and liver out.” — the convict Magwitch threatens Pip, a young boy alone in a graveyard, unless he brings a file and food, so Pip's life is at risk — Great Expectations; “I shall be with you on your wedding-night.” — the creature Victor made warns him of a threat on the night of his marriage, so Victor's life and his hope of happiness are at risk — Frankenstein; “If all else fail, myself have power to die.” — Juliet, ordered by her parents to marry Paris while already secretly married to Romeo, says that if the Friar cannot help her, she can end her own life, so what is at risk is her marriage to Romeo, or her life — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch what the character could lose, and notice each step that brings that loss closer. · Feel: We feel fear and worry for the character, because we can picture what failure would cost them. · Think: We ask why this loss matters so much to the character, and what the writer shows about what people value most. · Act: We ask what is really at risk when someone says a decision is urgent, and whether they have named the loss clearly.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any stakes, what a character stands to lose if they fail. 1. What does the character stand to lose if they fail? 2. How specific is that loss: could you picture exactly what would be lost? 3. Does the cost rise as the story goes on, and if it does, how? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or wonder? Try the questions on The Merchant of Venice. Antonio, a merchant, signs a bond with Shylock, a moneylender, to borrow money for his friend Bassanio. If he cannot repay on time, Shylock may take “an equal pound of your fair flesh”, and his life could be at risk. The loss is very specific: a named sum of three thousand ducats, a deadline of three months and a pound of Antonio's flesh. The cost rises when news comes that his ships are lost: his letter says “my ships have all miscarried”, and the bond is forfeit. Shakespeare may want the audience to fear for Antonio and to wonder whether anyone can save him.

**How to create it:** Decide what your main character will lose if they fail, and choose one specific thing a reader can picture, such as a home, a friend or a place. Show early what it is worth to them, with a detail or a memory. Set a deadline. Make the cost rise by shortening the time or adding a second thing to lose. Check that you can finish this sentence: “If they fail, they lose …”. If not, make it more specific.

**Stakes** — What the protagonist stands to lose or gain — the cost of failure that makes us care

- **Body & Mind**
  - **Survival / Physical** — Life and limb at risk — the threat of injury or death. _(e.g. “Kill the beast! Cut his throat! Spill his blood!” — the chant turns boys into hunters, so life itself is what is on the line — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Psychological / Sanity** — The mind itself endangered — guilt, breakdown, despair. _(e.g. “Out, damned spot! Out, I say!” — Lady Macbeth’s mind gives way, so the danger has moved inside her own head — Macbeth)_
  - **Identity / Self** — The risk of losing who one is, or one's grip on a coherent self. _(e.g. “that man is not truly one, but truly two” — Jekyll’s own account of the split that finally costs him a self — Jekyll and Hyde)_
- **Bonds & Standing**
  - **Relational / Love** — A bond or beloved that may be lost — connection at risk. _(e.g. “My life were better ended by their hate, than death prorogued, wanting of thy love.” — Romeo weighs his life against the love and stakes it — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Reputation / Honour** — Public name and credibility threatened with exposure or shame. _(e.g. “brave Macbeth — well he deserves that name” — the name he begins with, and by the end he is “this dead butcher”, so his reputation was always the thing at risk — Macbeth)_
  - **Belonging / Abandonment** — The danger of being cast out, deserted or left alone. _(e.g. “I was a discord in Gateshead Hall; I was like nobody there” — being unwanted is the danger Jane grows up inside — Jane Eyre)_
- **World & Soul**
  - **Existential / The World** — The survival of a people, a civilisation or the world itself rests on the outcome — stakes at their largest scale. _(e.g. “race of devils” — Victor’s fear that one more creature could put everybody alive in danger — Frankenstein)_
  - **Ideological / Belief** — Rival worldviews collide; what is truly at risk is which set of values will prevail. _(e.g. “We don’t live alone. We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other” — what the play risks is which belief a whole society lives by — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Moral / Integrity** — Principles at risk — the cost of compromising one's conscience. _(e.g. “I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition” — Macbeth names the only reason he has to kill, so his conscience is the price — Macbeth)_
  - **Societal / Political** — The wider order endangered — community or state destabilised. _(e.g. “Bleed, bleed, poor country!” — one murder tips a whole nation into disorder — Macbeth)_
  - **Material / Financial** — Wealth, security or livelihood on the line. _(e.g. “spend as much money as possible” — the club’s own pledge shows Pip’s fortune draining, so his security is what the story puts at risk — Great Expectations)_

**Related:** Protagonist, Tension, Conflict, Inciting Incident, MacGuffin

### Mood `Md`

Mood is the feeling that a piece of writing creates in the reader, such as dread, calm or sadness. A writer builds it from details of setting, weather, light, sound and word choice. Mood is not the same as tone: mood is what the reader feels, and tone is the writer's attitude to the subject. A text can change its mood from one scene to the next.

**The concept:** Mood lets a writer make readers feel something before they understand why. The details of a place can set a feeling before the reader knows what will happen, and that feeling can change how the reader understands what comes next. In Macbeth, the play opens with thunder and lightning, and three witches chant “Hover through the fog and filthy air”. The audience feels unease before any murder has happened. When you write about any mood, name the feeling, say which details of setting, light, sound or word choice build it, and what the writer wants the reader to understand by it.

**Examples:** “the merciless iced east winds that knive us” — the soldiers' pain from the cold wind is described as the cut of a knife, so the reader feels misery and fear, although the poem soon says “nothing happens” — Exposure; “It was on a dreary night of November that I beheld the accomplishment of my toils.” — Victor, who has made a creature, calls the night he brings it to life dreary, so the reader feels gloom and unease before the creature moves — Frankenstein; “Mud-coloured clouds drooped sadly over the muddy streets” — on the evening Miss Morstan, Holmes and Watson set out to meet a stranger, the weather is gloomy, so the reader feels gloom before the meeting — The Sign of Four

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the details of place, weather, light and sound that build a feeling. · Feel: We feel an atmosphere, such as dread or calm, before we know what is happening in the scene. · Think: We ask what the feeling of a place tells us about the people in it, and what the writer wants us to understand. · Act: We notice when films, adverts and shops use music, light and colour to change how we feel, and ask what they want from us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any mood, the feeling that a piece of writing creates in the reader. 1. Which details of setting, weather, light, sound or imagery build the atmosphere? Name two or three. 2. What feeling do those details leave you with, in a word or two? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand by creating that feeling? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde, in the scene where Mr Utterson, a lawyer, rides in a cab through London on the morning after a murder. He is going to find the house of Mr Hyde, the man the police are hunting. The scene is set in fog: “a great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven”. A pall is the cloth laid over a coffin, so the sky seems to cover the city like a funeral cloth. The cab also “crawled from street to street”, which makes the journey slow. The feeling is gloom and unease. Robert Louis Stevenson wants the reader to sense that something shameful is hidden in respectable London, before Hyde's house is even reached.

**How to create it:** Decide the one feeling you want your reader to have. Choose three details of setting, weather, light or sound that point to that feeling. Show those details and leave out the name of the feeling, so do not write that the place was gloomy. Match your sentence length to your feeling: for tension, try short sentences; for calm or sadness, try longer ones. Ask a friend to name the feeling after reading the scene; if the answer differs from yours, change one detail.

**Mood & Atmosphere** — The emotional weather of a text — what the reader is made to feel

- **Tense & Threatening**
  - **Ominous / Foreboding** — A sense that something dark is coming — threat hangs in the air before any harm arrives. _(e.g. “When shall we three meet again / In thunder, lightning, or in rain?” — the weather sets dread before a word of plot arrives — Macbeth)_
  - **Tense / Suspenseful** — Held pressure and uncertainty that keep the reader uneasy and turning the page. _(e.g. “Thou canst not say I did it. Never shake / Thy gory locks at me” — he answers a ghost in a room full of guests, and could give himself away at any second — Macbeth)_
  - **Eerie / Uncanny** — The familiar made strange — reality and the supernatural blur unsettlingly. _(e.g. “I flamed amazement” — a spirit describes setting the ship alight with a fire that burns nothing, so the terror is real and the danger never was — The Tempest)_
  - **Claustrophobic** — A suffocating, closing-in atmosphere with no way out. _(e.g. “Out, damned spot! Out, I say!” — she is shut inside her own guilt, scrubbing at a stain nobody else can see — Macbeth)_
- **Sorrow & Solitude**
  - **Melancholic** — A reflective sadness — sorrow tinged with thought about loss. _(e.g. “We stood by a pond that winter day, / And the sun was white, as though chidden of God” — a cold, still scene holds a love that died long ago — Neutral Tones)_
  - **Desolate / Lonely** — Emptiness and disconnection — the solitary figure in a bare world. _(e.g. “All their eyes are ice, / But nothing happens” — men wait in a frozen, empty landscape where nothing ever arrives — Exposure)_
  - **Sombre** — Grave and subdued, weighted by seriousness or mourning. _(e.g. “And they, since they / Were not the one dead, turned to their affairs” — a death is met in silence, and the silence weighs more than crying would — Out, Out—)_
- **Warmth & Light**
  - **Joyful / Celebratory** — Bright, buoyant feeling — happiness and shared release. _(e.g. “I am as light as a feather, I am as happy as an angel, I am as merry as a schoolboy” — three quick comparisons lift the whole page — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Tender / Romantic** — Soft, intimate feeling of affection or yearning. _(e.g. “If I profane with my unworthiest hand / This holy shrine, the gentle sin is this: / My lips, two blushing pilgrims, ready stand” — he treats her hand as sacred, so the touch is gentle rather than bold — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Serene / Tranquil** — Calm and untroubled — a stillness that reassures. _(e.g. “Dear God! the very houses seem asleep” — even the buildings are resting, so the empty city feels calm rather than lonely — Composed upon Westminster Bridge)_

### Tone `Ta`

Tone is the writer's attitude to the subject, shown through the words the writer chooses. A tone can be warm, cold, amused, angry, sad or mocking. Tone is not the same as mood: tone is the writer's attitude, and mood is what the reader feels. Irony, which means saying one thing while meaning another, is one way to show an attitude without stating it. A text can change its tone from one part to the next.

**The concept:** Tone shows the writer's attitude, and it tells readers how to judge what they are told. Two writers can report the same fact, and one word can show which attitude each has. Pride and Prejudice begins by saying that it is “a truth universally acknowledged” that a rich single man must want a wife. The narrator, who speaks for Jane Austen, pretends everyone agrees, but the story then shows mothers hunting for rich husbands for their daughters, so the tone is gently mocking. When you write about any tone, say what attitude the words show, which words show it, and what the writer wants the reader to think.

**Examples:** “squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching” — the narrator piles up harsh words to describe the miser Scrooge, so the tone towards him is scornful — A Christmas Carol; “lean, long, dusty, dreary and yet somehow lovable” — Mr Utterson, a lawyer, is first described in cold words, but “yet somehow lovable” shows that the narrator feels fond of him — Jekyll and Hyde; “Nothing beside remains. Round the decay / Of that colossal wreck, boundless and bare, / The lone and level sands stretch far away.” — after a king's proud boast, the speaker describes only a broken statue and empty sand, so the poem mocks the king's pride without saying so — Ozymandias

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen for the words that show how the writer feels about the subject. · Feel: We feel the attitude the writer wants us to share, such as scorn, fondness or sympathy, often before we notice why. · Think: We ask what the writer thinks about a person, a society or an idea, and whether the writer means what the words say. · Act: We notice the tone of speeches, news reports and adverts, and ask what attitude they want us to share.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any tone, the writer's attitude to the subject. 1. Which words does the writer choose to describe the subject, and which of them sound warm, cold, mocking or admiring? 2. Does the writer say one thing and mean another, which is called irony, or does the writer mean what the words say? 3. What attitude does the writer want the reader to share? Try the questions on Animal Farm, in its first sentence about Mr Jones, the farmer who owns Manor Farm. Orwell uses plain, flat words, like a report, and one blunt phrase: Mr Jones “was too drunk to remember” to finish shutting up the farm. Orwell means what the words say. The sentence says Jones locked the hen-houses, as a careful farmer would, then shows he could not finish the job. Orwell reports this calmly and does not call Jones careless, but the plain report leaves the reader to judge him. Orwell may want the reader to see Jones as careless and unfit to run the farm.

**How to create it:** Decide your attitude to your subject before you write, for example fond, scornful, amused or sad. Choose words that carry that attitude: write stingy for a scornful tone and thrifty for an approving one. Report one fact in a calm voice, then add one word that shows what you think of it. Ask a friend to name your attitude in a word after reading the passage; if the answer differs from yours, change the strongest word.

**Tone** — The writer's attitude to the subject — the voice behind the words (distinct from mood, which is the reader's feeling)

- **Grave & Distant**
  - **Solemn / Grave** — Weighty, serious treatment with no lightness — the subject handled with full moral seriousness. _(e.g. “If men will not learn that lesson, then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish” — no lightness anywhere; the subject is handled with full moral weight — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Detached / Objective** — Cool emotional distance — a voice observing rather than feeling. _(e.g. “Mr Utterson the lawyer was a man of a rugged countenance that was never lighted by a smile; cold, scanty and embarrassed in discourse” — the man is listed like an inventory, observed rather than felt — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Elegiac** — Mournful and reflective, grieving what has passed. _(e.g. “There is a change — and I am poor” — mourning something already lost, and counting the loss as poverty — A Complaint)_
  - **Resigned / Pessimistic** — Weary acceptance of an inevitable, unhappy outcome. _(e.g. “What's done cannot be undone.” — weary acceptance, with every better ending already closed off — Macbeth)_
- **Sharp & Critical**
  - **Ironic** — A gap between what is said and what is meant — the surface contradicts the truth beneath. _(e.g. “Look like th' innocent flower, / But be the serpent under't” — the surface and the truth beneath it are set against each other in one line — Macbeth)_
  - **Satirical** — Mockery and exaggeration used to expose folly or injustice. _(e.g. “All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others” — the rule is exaggerated until it collapses, and the collapse is the attack — Animal Farm)_
  - **Sardonic** — Grimly cutting — bitter humour edged with contempt. _(e.g. “they'll probably have their bottoms kicked and sent home the long way” — bitter humour with contempt inside it — Explorers or boys messing about?)_
  - **Commanding / Authoritative** — Certain and controlling, speaking in imperatives without hesitation. _(e.g. “leave all the rest to me” — five plain words, no hesitation, and the decision is made — Macbeth)_
- **Warm & Sincere**
  - **Reverent** — Respectful, even awed treatment of the subject. _(e.g. “the voice of a kindly god” — ordinary water treated as something holy — Blessing)_
  - **Playful / Witty** — Light, comic delight in language and situation. _(e.g. “I had rather hear my dog bark at a crow than a man swear he loves me.” — quick, comic exaggeration that invites us to enjoy the fight — Much Ado About Nothing)_
  - **Sincere / Earnest** — Open, heartfelt directness with no irony. _(e.g. “I wanna kiss y', an' put me arms around y'... but I don't know how to tell y'” — plain and open, with no joke to hide behind — Blood Brothers)_

### Want (Goal) vs Need `Wa`

A want is what a character is chasing, such as a crown, a prize or an escape. A need is what the character truly requires, such as love, truth or belonging, and it is often something the character does not yet see. In many stories the want and the need pull against each other, and the story's main change comes when the character must choose between them. In some stories the want and the need are the same.

**The concept:** Want and need let a writer show that people often chase the wrong thing. The want often moves the plot forward, and the need often gives the story its meaning. In Macbeth, Macbeth gets the crown he wanted, but near the end he says he cannot expect “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends”, the things that should come with old age. The reader sees that the crown has not given him what a person needs. When you write about any want and need, say what the character chases, what they truly need, and how chasing the first keeps them from the second.

**Examples:** “Mankind was my business.” — the ghost of Marley, Scrooge's dead partner, says that people and their welfare should have been his business, though he spent his life on his trade — A Christmas Carol; “O Joe, you break my heart!” — Pip, who wanted to be a gentleman and was ashamed of his plain friend Joe, finds Joe nursing him through an illness and begs Joe to be angry with him, so the reader sees how much Pip needs Joe's love — Great Expectations; “I am a free human being with an independent will” — Jane, who loves Mr Rochester, tells him that she is free and will use her own will to leave, so her need to be treated as his equal comes before her wish to stay — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch what the character chases, and notice what the character ignores or loses on the way. · Feel: We feel pity or frustration as the character chases the wrong thing, and relief or sorrow when the truth is seen. · Think: We ask what the character truly needs, and what the writer suggests that people should value most. · Act: We ask what we are chasing, such as grades, money or approval, and whether it would give us what we truly need.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any want and need, the gap between what a main character chases and what they truly need. 1. What does the character say they want, and what do they do to get it? 2. What does the character truly need, without realising it? 3. How does chasing the want keep the character away from the need? 4. When the character finally chooses, what does the writer want the reader to understand? Try the questions on the film Shrek. Shrek is an ogre who lives alone in a swamp. He wants his swamp back, because the ruler Lord Farquaad has sent fairy-tale creatures to live there, so he agrees to rescue Princess Fiona for Farquaad. He needs someone who accepts him, because he lives alone after being judged on his looks. Chasing the swamp leads him to hand Fiona to Farquaad when he wrongly thinks she is insulting him, and then to go home. There he finds he is miserable without her. He chooses Fiona over solitude, and stops her wedding to Farquaad. The film seems to say that being accepted matters more than being left alone.

**How to create it:** Choose something your character says they want, and make it concrete, such as a prize, a place or a win. Decide what the character truly needs, which should pull against the want. Let the character chase the want through the middle of the story, so that each success leaves the need unmet. Near the end, make the character choose between the two. Ask a friend what your character wants and needs; if the answers sound the same, separate them.

**Want vs Need — Goals** — The external goal a character chases (the want) and the internal goal they truly need (the growth) — internal goals after Carol Ryff’s dimensions of psychological well-being

_External Goals — the Want_

- **External Goals** — What the protagonist consciously chases out in the world
  - **Win** — Achieve victory in a competition or conflict. _(e.g. “I ought to be chief... because I’m chapter chorister and head boy” — Jack says the goal out loud: to beat Ralph and lead — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Stop** — Prevent something from happening. _(e.g. “Each of you helped to kill her” — the Inspector’s aim is to stop the family walking away unchanged — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Retrieve** — Get back something that was taken. _(e.g. “Just keep swimming” — the lesson Marlin carries across an ocean while he searches for the son he means to get back — Finding Nemo)_
  - **Escape** — Break free from a situation or place. _(e.g. “I guess it comes down to a simple choice, really. Get busy living or get busy dying.” — Andy makes the escape a decision before it is a tunnel, which is how a goal survives twenty years of digging — The Shawshank Redemption)_
  - **Revenge** — Make someone pay for a wrong. _(e.g. “Either thou or I, or both, must go with him” — Romeo turns grief into a goal: make Tybalt pay — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Deliver** — Complete a mission, or bring something to someone. _(e.g. “I can’t carry it for you … but I can carry you!” — Sam cannot take the burden off Frodo, so he carries the person instead: when the goal is delivery, the help has to fit the goal — The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King)_
  - **Maintain** — Protect what they have from being lost. _(e.g. “To be thus is nothing, / But to be safely thus” — Macbeth already has the crown, so his goal becomes keeping it — Macbeth)_
_Internal Goals — the Need_

- **Internal Goals** — What the protagonist truly needs within (Ryff’s six dimensions of well-being)
  - **Positive Relationships** — Being loved, belonging, connection. _(e.g. “An’ live off the fatta the lan’” — the dream Lennie asks for again and again is really a goal of belonging — Of Mice and Men)_
  - **Self-Acceptance** — A positive evaluation of oneself and one's life. _(e.g. “the animal within me licking the chops of memory” — Jekyll calls his own appetite an animal, which is a man refusing to own a part of himself — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Personal Growth** — Becoming a fuller, more complete person. _(e.g. “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year” — Scrooge sets himself an inner goal rather than an outer one — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Environmental Mastery** — The ability to manage one's life and surroundings effectively. _(e.g. “the rules are the only thing we’ve got” — Ralph’s goal is to make the island manageable by keeping order — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Autonomy** — Independence, self-determination, the freedom to choose. _(e.g. “You mustn’t try to build up a kind of wall between us and that girl” — Sheila chooses her own values over her parents’ — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Purpose** — A clear sense of meaning and direction. _(e.g. “May the Force be with you.” — one line names the cause the characters serve, and a cause is what gives a life direction — Star Wars)_

**Related:** Protagonist, The Ghost / Wound, The Flaw, Ironic Reversal, Character Arc

### Character Arc `Cr`

A character arc is the change in a character between the start of a story and its end. The change can be in what the character believes, wants or does, and it can be for better or for worse. The character with an arc is often the protagonist, the main character. Some characters stay the same from start to end, so they have no arc.

**The concept:** A character arc shows how events, choices and other people can change someone. Readers believe a change more easily when the story shows its cause, such as a loss, a warning or a new love. In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge at first asks “Are there no prisons?” when men collect money for the poor. After three spirits visit him, he sends a turkey to the family of his clerk, Bob Cratchit. When you write about any character arc, compare the character's words and actions at the start and end, say what caused the change, and say what the writer wants readers to learn.

**Examples:** “When I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.” — Benedick, who said at the start that he would stay a bachelor (an unmarried man), hears his friends say that Beatrice loves him, and decides to love her too — Much Ado About Nothing; “By you, I was properly humbled.” — Mr Darcy, a proud rich man, tells Elizabeth Bennet that she taught him a lesson, so he states his own change from pride to humility in words — Pride and Prejudice; “I humbly entreat my Redeemer to give me strength to lead henceforth a purer life than I have done hitherto!” — Mr Rochester, once ready to marry Jane while his first wife was still alive, prays for a better life after losing his sight — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch what the character says and does, looking for signs that they are changing. · Feel: We feel hope when a character changes for the better, and pity or fear when one changes for the worse. · Think: We ask what caused the change, and what the writer is saying about whether people can change. · Act: We notice when someone we know changes, and ask what caused the change.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any character arc, the change in a main character between the start of a story and its end. 1. Who is the character at the opening, and what flaw or want shapes their choices? 2. What pressure forces the character to act differently? 3. What small proofs show the change, such as a reaction the character no longer has, or something they now do or refuse? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the change? Try the questions on Macbeth. At the start Macbeth is a brave soldier, and a captain calls him “brave Macbeth”. Ambition shapes his choices once three witches tell him he will be king. The pressure comes from the witches and from his wife, Lady Macbeth, who urges him to kill King Duncan. Once he is king, he has others killed to keep the throne. The proofs come late. In Act 5 he says “I have almost forgot the taste of fears”, and when he hears that Lady Macbeth is dead, his first reply is short: “She should have died hereafter”, which shows how little he can now feel. Compare Act 2, where, just after killing King Duncan, he says “I am afraid to think what I have done”. The change is from a soldier who is brave in battle but frightened by murder to a man who has almost forgotten what fear feels like. Shakespeare may want the reader to see that each crime can make the next one easier for the person who commits it.

**How to create it:** Decide who your character is at the start, and give them one flaw. Decide how the character will be different at the end. Write three small proofs of the change, such as a reaction the character no longer has or a habit they drop. Place the first proof early and the last at the end. Compare your opening and ending: if the character would react the same way to the same kind of event in both, add another proof of the change.

**Related:** Protagonist, The Flaw, The Ghost / Wound, Self-Revelation, Universal Human Values, Prop, Want (Goal) vs Need

### Ironic Reversal `Iv`

**Also known as:** Situational Irony

An ironic reversal is an event in which a character's own actions bring about the opposite of what they hoped for. It is irony in what happens, not in what is said: the gap is between what the character hopes for and what actually happens. The result is often a loss, but not always: a plan meant to harm someone can end up helping that person instead.

**The concept:** An ironic reversal shows that a character misjudged what their own actions would do. Readers can judge whether the result is deserved: a selfish plan that ends in ruin can feel like justice, while a kind act that ends in disaster can feel cruel. In Jekyll and Hyde, Dr Jekyll makes a drug hoping to free his good side from his evil side. Instead the drug frees only his evil side, Mr Hyde, and in the end Jekyll becomes Hyde without taking it. When you write about any ironic reversal, say what the character hoped for, what their actions brought about, and what the writer wants readers to learn.

**Examples:** “Naught's had, all's spent, / Where our desire is got without content” — Lady Macbeth, now queen, says that the crown Macbeth killed King Duncan to win has brought them no contentment: they hoped it would make them happy, and it has done the opposite — Macbeth; “the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart” — Victor Frankenstein worked for nearly two years to give life to a body, and the moment he succeeds he is filled with horror, not pride — Frankenstein; “I am what you have made me” — Miss Havisham adopted Estella and taught her to show men no mercy, and Estella says this when Miss Havisham calls her cold, so Miss Havisham's own teaching has made Estella cold to her too — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We compare what the character hoped for with what happens, and look for the action that caused the difference. · Feel: We often feel shock and pity when a character's own plan brings them the opposite of what they hoped for. · Think: We ask what the character misjudged, and what the writer is saying about ambition, revenge or pride. · Act: We check our own plans before acting on them, and ask whether they could bring about the opposite of what we want.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any ironic reversal, where a character gets the opposite of what they hoped for. 1. What does the character want, and what do they do to get it? 2. What happens that is the opposite of what they hoped for? 3. Does the reversal feel fair, given the character's own choices? Why? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the reversal? Try the questions on the myth of King Midas, as the Roman poet Ovid tells it in his Metamorphoses. Midas wants gold, and when the god Bacchus, called Dionysus in Greek, offers him any reward, he asks that everything he touches should turn to gold. He gets exactly that, but when he sits down to eat, the food and drink turn to gold as he touches them, so he cannot eat. The wish that was meant to enrich him becomes something he hates, and he begs to be free of it. It feels fair, because Midas chose the reward himself without thinking what touching things would mean. The story may want readers to see that getting what we ask for can cost us the thing we wanted it for.

**How to create it:** Name what your character wants in one noun, such as gold, power or revenge. Write the scene where the character gets the want, and show that it takes away the thing the want was meant to give. Show one earlier choice by the character that causes the reversal. Check that a reader looking back could point to that choice; if not, add a clearer hint earlier.

**Related:** Duality, Dramatic Irony, Irony, Want (Goal) vs Need, The Ghost / Wound

### The Ghost / Wound `Gh`

**Also known as:** The Wound & Shield

A ghost, or wound, is a hurt from a character's past that still shapes what the character does in the present. The hurt may be a loss, a betrayal or a failure. The character often builds a habit or a defence around it, such as anger, pride, coldness or refusing help, and the habit can look like a plain flaw. The hurt may be revealed slowly, or never fully explained.

**The concept:** A ghost helps readers understand why a character acts badly. A flaw can look like cruelty until the writer shows the old hurt behind it. In Frankenstein, Victor brings the creature to life, then abandons it. Alone and shunned, the creature takes revenge on Victor's family and says why: “I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.” Adam was the Bible's first man; a fallen angel was thrown out of heaven. When you write about any ghost, say what the hurt was, how it shapes what the character does, and what the writer wants readers to see.

**Examples:** “The villany you teach me, I will execute” — Shylock, a moneylender whom Antonio has insulted and spat on for being a Jew, says he will copy the cruelty he was taught, so an old hurt drives his wish for revenge — The Merchant of Venice; “I stole her heart away, and put ice in its place.” — Miss Havisham, who was left by her bridegroom on her wedding day, admits that she raised Estella to be cold, meaning to save her from misery like her own — Great Expectations; “you have my full and free forgiveness” — Jane, now a grown woman, says this to her dying aunt, Mrs Reed, who was cruel to her as a child, so Jane faces the old hurt instead of carrying it — Jane Eyre

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look for a past hurt behind the way a character acts now. · Feel: We feel sympathy for a character who seemed cruel or cold, and sadness that an old hurt still controls them. · Think: We ask what the character is protecting themselves from, and what the writer says about how a past hurt shapes people. · Act: We ask what old hurt may lie behind a person's anger or coldness, before we judge them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any ghost, or wound, the old hurt from a character's past that still steers what they do. 1. What hurt happened to the character before the story, or early in it? 2. How does the hurt show in what the character does or refuses to do now? 3. Does the character face the hurt by the end, or still run from it? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the wound? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol by Charles Dickens, with Scrooge, a rich and lonely man, as the main character. As a boy he was left alone at school at Christmas. The Ghost of Christmas Past says “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.” Later Belle, the woman he was to marry, leaves him, saying “Another idol has displaced me”, and the idol is gold. Now the hurt shows in how he lives: he refuses to give to the poor and keeps other people away. He faces it when the Ghost shows him the lonely boy and he sobs. By the end he keeps Christmas, sends a turkey to the Cratchits and joins his nephew's party. Dickens may want the reader to see that Scrooge's meanness comes from a lonely hurt, so we pity him as well as judge him.

**How to create it:** Decide what hurt happened to your character before the story begins. Choose one habit or defence that the hurt causes, such as refusing help or controlling other people. Show that habit in the first scene without explaining where it comes from. Reveal the hurt later, through a memory or another character. Check that an earlier scene makes more sense once the hurt is known; if not, change the habit.

**Related:** The Flaw, Want (Goal) vs Need, Protagonist, Character Arc, Ironic Reversal

### Self-Revelation `Sr`

A self-revelation is the moment a character sees a true and uncomfortable fact about themselves, such as a flaw or a false belief. The character has often avoided that fact before. Something outside, such as a loss, a letter or another person's words, usually forces the character to see it. It is different from a plot twist, which reveals a fact about the story's events, not about the character. What the character does next shows whether the insight changes them.

**The concept:** A self-revelation shows that the biggest change in a story can happen inside a character. Readers can judge it by what the character does next. In Othello, Othello learns that Iago's lies made him kill his innocent wife, Desdemona. He asks people to speak of him as “one that loved not wisely but too well”, which admits that his love lacked good judgement. When you write about any self-revelation, say what the character now sees about themselves, what led them to see it, and what they do next.

**Examples:** “Till this moment, I never knew myself.” — after reading Darcy's letter, Elizabeth Bennet, who has prided herself on judging people well, sees that her vanity made her judge badly — Pride and Prejudice; “I am not the man I was” — after seeing his own neglected grave, Scrooge tells the Spirit that he has changed; when he wakes, he acts on it by sending a turkey to the Cratchits — A Christmas Carol; “I could never, never, undo what I had done.” — after learning that a convict, not Miss Havisham, paid for his new life, Pip sees how badly he has treated his old friend Joe, and knows he cannot undo it — Great Expectations

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the moment a character stops avoiding a truth about themselves, and what forces them to see it. · Feel: We feel pity, relief or admiration as a character faces a truth that has been hard to see. · Think: We ask what the character now understands, and whether what they do next shows that the understanding is real. · Act: We ask what we avoid admitting about ourselves, and what we would have to do to show we have understood it.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any self-revelation, the moment a main character finally understands the truth about themselves. 1. What has the character believed or avoided about themselves up to this point? 2. What leads the character to see the truth? 3. What does the character do next? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through this moment? Try the questions on the film The Lion King. Simba, a young lion, believes his father's death was his fault, because his uncle Scar told him so. He runs away and lives carefree for years, avoiding his duty as the rightful king. Nala, a lioness from his old home, tells him the land is suffering under Scar. Rafiki, an old mandrill who advises the animals, tells Simba to learn from the past instead of running from it. Simba also sees the spirit of his father in the night sky, telling him to take his place as king. Simba stops running from his past, which he shows when he returns and confronts Scar. The film seems to say that facing the past is part of taking responsibility.

**How to create it:** Decide the false belief or flaw your character has held since the start of the story. Show two small signs of it early, such as a place they avoid or a lie they tell. Build outside pressure until the character cannot avoid the truth. Show what the character now sees. Write the next scene so that the character acts differently. Check that the character could not have taken that action on the first page; if they could, change the action to one that depends on what they now understand.

**The Growth Arc — Express, Battle, Overcome** — How to SHOW a character change through action, not narration — three beats (Eric Edson).

- **Three beats of change**
  - **Express** — The character reveals their flaw or wound — we see plainly what holds them back. _(e.g. “If they would rather die, they had better do it, and decrease the surplus population” — the flaw said out loud, with no shame attached to it — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Battle** — They try to face it and fail — the inner struggle shown through a physical action, never a speech. _(e.g. “Spirit, tell me if Tiny Tim will live.” — he asks the question his own words already answered, and cannot face the answer — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Overcome** — Under real pressure they finally act differently — the change earned, not announced. _(e.g. “I’ll send it to Bob Cratchit’s!” — the change proved by something he does, not something he says — A Christmas Carol)_

**Related:** Epiphany, Character Arc, Empathy

### Universal Human Values `Ui`

The six universal human values are wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence. Wisdom means the wish to learn and judge well; humanity means care for other people; temperance means self-control; transcendence means a sense of meaning larger than yourself. In 2005, three psychologists studied the great religions and philosophies of China, India and the West, and found these six values again and again. A reader can use them as a scale: a character may have too little of a value, too much, or a good balance.

**The concept:** The six values let readers measure how a character changes as a person. A character can have too little or too much of a value. In Macbeth, Macbeth says “I dare do all that may become a man; / Who dares do more is none”, meaning that a man who dares too much is no longer a man. He then murders King Duncan, so the play shows courage without humanity. When you write about any character's values, say which of the six they lack or overuse, which one changes most, and what that change says about how the writer thinks a person should live.

**Examples:** “I will keep the law given by God; sanctioned by man.” — Jane, who loves Mr Rochester, decides to leave him because he is already married, so she shows temperance, which is self-control: she keeps to her principles although her feelings urge her to stay — Jane Eyre; “I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year.” — Scrooge, who had no care for other people, promises to keep Christmas all the year, so humanity moves from too little to enough — A Christmas Carol; “I had desired it with an ardour that far exceeded moderation” — Victor Frankenstein says that his wish to learn how to make life was stronger than moderation allows, so a good value, the wish to learn, is shown going out of balance — Frankenstein

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch which value the character lacks or overuses, and which one shifts as the story goes on. · Feel: We feel admiration when a character grows towards balance, and dread or pity when a value goes too far. · Think: We ask what the shift in one value says about how the writer believes a person should live. · Act: We ask which of the six values we ourselves lack or overuse, and what one choice this week could bring more balance.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any story's universal human values, which are wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence. Temperance means self-control, and transcendence means a sense of meaning larger than yourself. 1. At the opening, which of the six values does the main character have too little or too much of, if any? 2. What pressure pushes that value toward balance, or further out of balance? 3. By the end, which value has shifted most? 4. What does that shift show about how the writer thinks a person should live? Try the questions on An Inspector Calls, with Sheila Birling, the daughter of a rich family, as the main character. At the start Sheila has too little humanity: out of jealousy over a dress, she got a shop worker, Eva Smith, sacked. The pressure is the Inspector's questioning, which makes Sheila see what her act did to Eva, who has since died. By the end humanity has shifted most. Sheila feels guilty, and she tells her parents they are “pretending everything's just as it was before”. Priestley seems to want readers to live with care for other people and to accept responsibility when they have harmed someone.

**How to create it:** Choose the one value your character is short of or has too much of, such as courage or justice. Show that value in the first scene through something the character does. Add a pressure that tests it. Show the value shifting in small steps, with a choice at each step. Ask a friend which value changed; if the answer differs from yours, add a clearer step.

**The Six Universal Human Values** — Researchers who studied ideas of goodness in many cultures over about 2,500 years reported six values that many of them have in common. A protagonist is often moving towards these six values. List which ones your character has at the start and which ones they lack. The gap between the two is your theme. Too much of one value can break a character as surely as too little.

- **The six values** — what a character is measured against, at the beginning and at the end
  - **Wisdom and knowledge** — This value includes creativity, curiosity, open-mindedness and love of learning. Curiosity with no limit can make a clever person dangerous. _(e.g. “Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge” — Victor Frankenstein tells Walton to learn from his example how dangerous it is to gain knowledge. His own curiosity had no limit, and it ruined his life. — Frankenstein)_
  - **Courage** — This value includes bravery, persistence, honesty and energy. A person with no fear and no conscience can become a tyrant. _(e.g. “I dare do all that may become a man; / Who dares do more is none.” — Macbeth tells Lady Macbeth that he dares to do whatever suits a man, and that anyone who dares more is no man. Here his courage has a limit set by conscience. Later he drops the limit and becomes a tyrant. — Macbeth)_
  - **Humanity** — This value includes love, kindness and the ability to understand other people. A person who loves without any limits can give up everything and lose themselves. _(e.g. "solitary as an oyster" — The narrator calls Scrooge solitary as an oyster, closed up and shut away. Over the story, Scrooge gets back the kindness he held back. — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **Justice** — This value includes citizenship, fairness and leadership. It is the belief that you owe something to other people. _(e.g. "We are members of one body. We are responsible for each other" — The Inspector tells the Birlings that we are all members of one body and responsible for each other. This is the central message of the whole play. — An Inspector Calls)_
  - **Temperance** — This value includes forgiveness, mercy, humility, care and self-control. It is the ability to hold yourself back from anger, greed or revenge. _(e.g. "the rarer action is in virtue than in vengeance" — Prospero, a magician who has the power to take revenge on his enemies, says that mercy is a rarer and better action than revenge. He chooses to forgive. — The Tempest)_
  - **Transcendence** — This value includes appreciating beauty, gratitude, hope, humour and spirituality. These lift a character above their own worries. _(e.g. "I will honour Christmas in my heart, and try to keep it all the year" — Scrooge promises to honour Christmas in his heart and try to keep it all the year. He feels grateful, and the feeling changes how he lives. — A Christmas Carol)_

**Related:** Theme, Character Arc, Empathy

### The Dilemma `Db`

A dilemma is a hard choice in a story, where a character cannot keep both of two things they value. Choosing one of the two things means giving up the other. The two things can be people, duties, beliefs or hopes.

**The concept:** A dilemma lets a writer show what a character values most, because the character must choose which of two valued things to keep. In Romeo and Juliet, Romeo, Juliet's new husband, has just killed her cousin Tybalt. Juliet first speaks angrily about Romeo. When the Nurse asks if she will speak well of him, Juliet answers, “Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband?” Her choice to defend Romeo shows that she values him more than her cousin. When you find any dilemma, say which two things the character values, which one they keep, and what the writer wants us to understand.

**Examples:** “I will keep the law given by God; sanctioned by man.” — Jane, who loves Mr Rochester, has learned that he is already married; she tells herself she will keep her principles, even though this means losing him — Jane Eyre; “to inflict this curse upon everlasting generations” — Victor Frankenstein promised to make a female companion for the creature he created, but fears that her children could threaten all humankind, and asks whether he has the right to make her — Frankenstein; “’Tis proper I obey him, but not now.” — when her husband Iago orders her to go home, Emilia says it is right to obey him, but she stays and tells the truth that exposes his lies — Othello

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We focus on the moment of choice, and on what the character will lose whichever way they choose. · Feel: We feel tension and sympathy, because the character cares about both things and must give one of them up. · Think: We ask what the character values most, and what the writer is saying about loyalty, duty or love through the choice. · Act: We notice hard choices in real life, such as loyalty against honesty, and ask what a person's choice shows about them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dilemma, a hard choice between two things a character values. 1. Which two things does the character value that cannot both be kept? 2. What would the character lose whichever way they choose? 3. What does the character choose, and how do we know? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand through the choice? Try the questions on Julius Caesar, with Brutus, a Roman nobleman, as the character. Brutus values his friend Caesar, the ruler of Rome, and he values the freedom of Rome. If he spares Caesar, he fears the Romans will become slaves under a king. If he joins the plot against Caesar, he loses his friend. He chooses Rome and joins the plot, and Caesar is killed. Afterwards he tells the crowd: “Not that I loved Caesar less, but that I loved Rome more.” Shakespeare may want the audience to feel what it costs a man of honour to give up someone he loves.

**How to create it:** Choose two things your character values, and make both good, such as loyalty to a friend and duty to a community. Show early in the story why each one matters to the character. Build to the moment when the character cannot keep both. Make the character choose, and show what is lost. Check that neither choice is clearly wrong; if a reader picks one at once, give the other side more weight.

### Epiphany `Ea`

An epiphany is a moment when a character suddenly understands a truth that changes how they see a person, a situation or themselves. It is a change inside the character's mind, not an event in the world. It is often caused by something the character sees, hears, reads or remembers, such as an object, a letter or another person's words. It is close to a self-revelation, a moment when a character learns the truth about themselves, but an epiphany can be about any truth.

**The concept:** An epiphany lets a writer show a change in a character at one exact moment: the character's old belief ends and a new understanding begins. In Macbeth, a spirit that the witches call up tells Macbeth that no man born of a woman can harm him. Then Macduff says he was cut from his mother's womb before the usual time. Macbeth sees that the witches tricked him with words that only seemed to promise safety, and says they “palter with us in a double sense”. When you find any epiphany, say what the character believed before, what they understand now, and what makes them see it.

**Examples:** “Till this moment, I never knew myself.” — Elizabeth Bennet cries this after reading Mr Darcy's letter, which shows her that she judged both him and Mr Wickham wrongly — Pride and Prejudice; “It darted through her, with the speed of an arrow, that Mr. Knightley must marry no one but herself!” — Emma, who has been trying to find a husband for her friend Harriet, realises that she herself wants to marry Mr Knightley, a family friend, when Harriet says she hopes he loves her — Emma; “Et tu, Brute?” — Caesar says this in Latin, meaning ‘And you, Brutus?’, when he sees that his friend Brutus is one of the men stabbing him — Julius Caesar

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch the moment a character suddenly sees a truth, and notice what makes them see it. · Feel: We often share the character's sadness, shame or relief, because their old view of a person or a situation has just been proved wrong. · Think: We ask what the character's new understanding shows about the text's themes, such as pride, trust or love. · Act: We notice when new facts show that we have misjudged a person or a situation, and we change our view.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any epiphany, the moment a character suddenly sees something they had not understood before. 1. What did the character believe before, and what do they now see? 2. What forces the recognition: a failed plan, an object, a memory, or something else? 3. Does the reader know the truth before the character does, and if so, how does that change the moment? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about seeing, or refusing to see, the truth? Try the questions on Othello. Othello, a general, believed that his wife Desdemona had been unfaithful with Cassio, his lieutenant, because Iago, one of his officers, told him so. He now sees that she was faithful and that Iago lied. Emilia, Iago's wife, says she found Desdemona's handkerchief and gave it to Iago, and Cassio explains how he came by it. Their two accounts of the handkerchief force the recognition. Othello then cries “O fool! fool! fool!” Yes, the audience knew the truth first, because Iago explains his plot to us. We watch Othello catch up too late. Othello has already killed Desdemona. Shakespeare shows that Othello learns the truth only when it is too late to repair anything, after he trusted Iago and refused to believe Desdemona.

**How to create it:** Decide what false belief your character holds, and what true thing will replace it. Choose something that forces the truth on them, such as a failed plan, an object or a memory. Write the moment they see it in one short line. Check that the false belief appears earlier in your story; if it does not, add it.

**Related:** Self-Revelation

### Dramatic Through-line `Dr`

A dramatic through-line is the one question that runs through a whole story: will the main character succeed, fail or give up? By the end, the story usually gives an answer. Most scenes move the main character closer to that answer. The answer may be mixed, such as winning one thing but losing another.

**The concept:** A through-line lets a writer link the scenes of a story to one question, so the story feels planned, not like a list of events. In A Christmas Carol, Marley, Scrooge's dead partner, appears as a ghost and says “you have yet a chance and hope of escaping my fate”. This raises the question the story answers: will Scrooge change in time to escape Marley's fate, which is to wander after death in heavy chains as a punishment for a selfish life? When you find any through-line, say what question runs through the story, what answer the writer chooses, and how the scenes lead to it.

**Examples:** “And oh, Aunt Em! I'm so glad to be at home again!” — Dorothy, a girl from Kansas, has spent the story trying to get home from the Land of Oz, and in the book's last words she is home — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz; “honour, love, obedience, troops of friends, / I must not look to have” — near the end, Macbeth, who killed King Duncan to become king, sees that he has the crown but will never have honour, love or friends, so he has both succeeded and failed — Macbeth; “So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone” — David, a young shepherd, offers to fight Goliath, a giant Philistine soldier, and this line answers the question that runs through the story of David and Goliath: can he win? — The Bible (1 Samuel)

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look at how the scenes move the main character towards one answer. · Feel: We feel hope or dread grow stronger as the scenes keep moving towards the same ending. · Think: We ask what the writer is saying about success, failure or giving up, and why this ending, not another, is the answer. · Act: We notice how news stories, speeches and adverts arrange events so that they lead to one chosen ending.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any dramatic through-line, the one question that runs through most scenes: will the main character succeed, fail or give up? 1. Who is the main character, what do they want, and which answer does the writer choose? 2. Does the text signal that answer early, and if it does, in what words? 3. Take two scenes from different parts of the text. How does each push the story towards the same answer? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand once the whole pattern is clear? Try the questions on Romeo and Juliet. Romeo and Juliet, young people from two families that hate each other, want to be together, and they fail: they die. The Prologue, a speech before the play begins, says so at once: “A pair of star-cross’d lovers take their life”. In Act 3 Romeo is banished for killing Tybalt, Juliet's cousin, which separates the lovers. In Act 5 Friar Lawrence's letter to Romeo is never delivered, so Romeo believes Juliet is dead. Both scenes take the lovers further from a happy ending. Shakespeare may want readers to see that the lovers' deaths end the families' hatred, because the Prologue says their deaths “bury their parents’ strife”, where “bury” means end.

**How to create it:** Decide whether your main character will succeed, fail or give up. Write one sentence that states what they want and the answer you have chosen. Add a note to each scene saying how it moves the character towards that answer. Cut or change any scene with no note. Check that your last scene gives the answer you chose; if not, change one of them.

### Leitmotif `Le`

A leitmotif is a kind of motif: an image, sound or phrase that comes back again and again in a text. What makes it a leitmotif is that it belongs to one character, place or idea. Each time it returns, it reminds the reader of that character or idea, even if the name is not used. Its meaning can stay the same or change as the story goes on.

**The concept:** A leitmotif lets a writer announce a character or idea without a name: its return tells the reader who or what is near. The word is German and means a leading or guiding motif; it comes from the study of opera, where a tune returns with one character. In Jane Eyre, Jane hears “a curious laugh; distinct, formal, mirthless” in an empty corridor, and later a laugh outside her bedroom door. Both belong to Bertha, Mr Rochester's wife, whose identity the story hides until Jane's wedding day. When you find any leitmotif, say what it belongs to, what happens each time it returns, and whether its meaning changes.

**Examples:** “Four legs good, two legs bad!” — the sheep chant this slogan again and again; in the last chapter “bad” is replaced by “better”, which shows that the pigs now walk on two legs like men — Animal Farm; “God bless us every one!” — Tiny Tim, the youngest Cratchit child, says this at the family's Christmas dinner, and the narrator ends the book by repeating it: “God bless Us, Every One!” — A Christmas Carol; “What, will these hands ne'er be clean?” — Lady Macbeth asks this while sleepwalking, as if washing her hands; after the murder she had said “A little water clears us of this deed”, so the return shows that water has not cleared her guilt — Macbeth

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch for the sound, image or phrase that keeps returning, and notice who or what it belongs to. · Feel: We feel unease or comfort each time the sign returns, because it tells us that someone or something is near. · Think: We ask why the writer keeps returning to this sign, and what the character or idea it belongs to means for the story's themes. · Act: We notice the slogans and tunes that brands and speakers use again and again, and ask what each wants us to feel.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any leitmotif, an image or phrase that keeps returning and belongs to one character or thing. 1. What image or phrase keeps returning, and who or what is it tied to? 2. Each time it returns, what is happening, and who reacts to it? 3. Does its meaning stay the same, or change between the first return and the last? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand through it? Try the questions on Peter Pan. The sound “tick tick” returns again and again. It belongs to a crocodile that has swallowed a clock and hunts Captain Hook, a pirate. Hook tells Smee, one of his pirates, that he hears the tick and runs away. Later, as Hook is about to make Wendy watch the captured boys walk the plank, a tick stops him, and everyone on the ship hears it. This tick is not the crocodile's, because its clock has run down: Peter Pan is ticking on purpose. At first the tick warns Hook and protects him. At the plank it frightens him, and the pirates clear a way for him to hide. The author, J. M. Barrie, may want us to feel Hook's fear: a frightening pirate is made nervous by a small sound.

**How to create it:** Choose one character and one image or short phrase that belongs to them. Show it the first time in an ordinary moment. Bring it back each time the character meets the same kind of pressure. Change what it means a little each time, for example by placing it in a worse situation. Check that each time the image returns, a reader would think of the same character; if not, change the scene so that it points back to that character.

**Related:** Motif

### Atmosphere `Am`

Atmosphere is the feeling that a place or scene gives off, such as menace, calm or tension. A writer builds it mainly through setting, which is where and when a scene happens, and imagery, which is words that make a picture for the senses. It is close to mood, the feeling the reader has: atmosphere is the feeling of the place itself. It can be built before any character speaks, and it can match the events or clash with them.

**The concept:** Atmosphere lets a writer prepare the reader's feelings before anything happens: a place can seem threatening, calm or sad before any character speaks. It works because weather, light and sound affect readers in books as they do in life. In Frankenstein, Victor, a scientist, brings his creature to life on “a dreary night of November”, with rain tapping on the window and his candle almost burnt out, so the scene feels bleak and fearful before the creature moves. When you write about any atmosphere, say what feeling the place gives off, which details create it, and what the writer wants us to feel.

**Examples:** “a dense drizzly fog lay low upon the great city” — Dr Watson, the narrator, describes a foggy London evening as he rides in a cab with Sherlock Holmes and Miss Morstan to a strange meeting, and says it made him nervous — The Sign of Four; “the cold winter wind had brought with it clouds so sombre, and a rain so penetrating” — Jane, the narrator, describes a day when the weather keeps her indoors, so the book opens on a cold, gloomy feeling — Jane Eyre; “The fog came pouring in at every chink and keyhole” — the fog is so thick that the houses across the court look like ghosts, while Scrooge works in his counting-house — A Christmas Carol

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look closely at the weather, light, sound and smell of a place, because they carry its feeling. · Feel: We feel unease, calm or sadness before anything happens, because the details of the place affect us as real places do. · Think: We ask why the writer wants the place to feel this way, and what that feeling suggests about the people and events in it. · Act: We notice how films, shops and adverts use light, music and colour to make a place feel safe, exciting or tense, and ask why.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any atmosphere, the feeling a place gives off, such as menace or calm. 1. Where and when is the scene set, and what is the weather or light like? 2. Which words make the air feel a certain way, and which senses do they use? 3. Does the atmosphere match what happens in the scene, or clash with it? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel about the place or the people? Try the questions on Jekyll and Hyde. Mr Utterson, a lawyer, rides through the Soho district of London with a police officer at nine in the morning, in the first fog of the season. They are going to find Mr Hyde, who is wanted for a killing. The thick fog makes the morning dark and brown. The words use sight: “a great chocolate-coloured pall lowered over heaven”. A pall is the cloth laid over a coffin. The streets seem “like a district of some city in a nightmare”. The dark, deathly air matches the hunt for a killer. Stevenson makes London feel sick and threatening, so the reader feels dread before reaching Hyde's door.

**How to create it:** Choose the feeling you want the place to give, such as dread or calm. List three details of weather, light, sound or smell that suit that feeling. Describe the place with those details before any character speaks or acts. Try not to name the feeling itself. Check by asking a friend to name the feeling from your description alone; if they cannot, add one more detail.

### Empathy `Ey`

**Also known as:** 48 Ways, Kinds of Empathy

Empathy is feeling with a character, as if from inside, instead of feeling sorry for them from outside. Writers build it by giving a character a clear wish, a hardship they do not deserve, or a brave choice that costs them something. We understand the character; we do not have to approve of them. We usually feel it for the protagonist, the main character, though it can attach to any character, even one who does wrong.

**The concept:** Empathy lets a writer make a reader share a character's feelings from the inside, so the reader understands why the character acts. We can understand a character without approving of them. In Frankenstein, the creature, whom Victor Frankenstein made and then abandoned, becomes violent, but he tells Victor: “I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.” We understand how loneliness and rejection turned him cruel, and we judge Victor's neglect. When you find any moment of empathy, say whose feelings you share, which details of their hardship or wish make you share them, and what the writer wants you to understand about that person.

**Examples:** “I am no bird; and no net ensnares me” — Jane, a poor governess, tells Rochester, her employer, that she is not a trapped bird but a free person with a will of her own, and we share her pride — Jane Eyre; “Life's but a walking shadow” — Macbeth, who has murdered to become king, hears that his wife is dead and calls life a walking shadow, and we understand his empty despair though we do not approve of him — Macbeth; “My only love sprung from my only hate!” — Juliet learns that Romeo, the man she has fallen in love with, is a Montague, her family's enemy, and we feel the pull between her love and her family — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look out through a character's eyes, instead of looking at the character from outside. · Feel: We share a character's hope or pain as if it were ours, even when we do not approve of what they do. · Think: We separate understanding someone from excusing them, and ask what the writer wants us to understand about people who do wrong. · Act: We listen to people who are suffering or have done wrong, and try to understand them before we judge them.

**How to analyse it:** Ask three questions of any moment of empathy, where the reader feels with a character from the inside. 1. Whose feelings does the reader share? 2. Which details of that person's hardship, wish or courage help us understand them? 3. What does the writer want the reader to understand about this person? Try the questions on A Christmas Carol. Scrooge, a miserly old man who hates Christmas, is shown a scene from his boyhood by the Ghost of Christmas Past. We share Scrooge's feelings: he sobs and weeps at the sight. The other boys have gone home for Christmas, and the Ghost says “A solitary child, neglected by his friends, is left there still.” and Dickens shows “a lonely boy was reading near a feeble fire”. Dickens may want us to understand that Scrooge's coldness has a cause: he was once a lonely, forgotten child.

**How to create it:** Choose a character and one thing they want badly. Show that want in a small action early in the story. Give the character a hardship they do not deserve, or a brave choice that costs them something. Describe how it feels to them, using what they see, hear and think. Ask a friend whether they would stay with this character through a bad moment; if not, make the want clearer.

**Kinds of Empathy** — Empathy through the 48 Ways — the reasons a reader comes to feel WITH a character rather than merely sorry for them (Iglesias)

_Empathy & Sympathy_

- **We care about VICTIMS — sympathy**
  - _Injustice & Betrayal_
    - **Unfair Injury & Injustice** — Inflict blatant, undeserved mistreatment so we side with the victim at once.
    - **Betrayal & Deception** — Have someone deceive or betray them, so we feel the wrong done to a worthy character.
    - **Not Believed** — Let a truthful character go unbelieved, so we share their helpless frustration.
    - **Misunderstood** — Have them misjudged while we see their true motive — everyone feels misunderstood.
  - _Isolation & Loss_
    - **Abandonment** — Desert or abandon them by a loved one — a primal trigger of pity.
    - **Exclusion & Rejection** — Shut them out of a group or love; the universal need to belong makes us care.
    - **Loneliness & Neglect** — Isolate or neglect them so we root for the lonely figure.
    - **Undeserved Misfortune** — Visit bad luck or grief they did not deserve.
    - **Suffering Injury** — Have them hurt and needing care.
  - _Inner Wounds_
    - **Mistakes & Regret** — Let them err and then regret it; fallibility makes them human.
    - **Haunted by the Past** — Wound them with a painful backstory they repress.
    - **Vulnerability** — Show a moment of weakness — grief, self-doubt, fear.
    - **Shame** — Expose them to the fear of disconnection that shame brings.
  - _Relatable Humanity_
    - **Familiar Setting** — Place them in an ordinary, recognisable world (home, school, work) so readers see themselves in them.
    - **Familiar Role** — Give an everyday role — pupil, parent, worker — that readers already identify with.
    - **Familiar Flaws & Foibles** — Give small, recognisable weaknesses and awkwardness.
    - **Frustrations** — Show everyday frustrations readers have felt themselves.
    - **A Universal Wish** — Give them a shared human longing: love, acceptance, purpose.
  - _Danger & Struggle_
    - **Jeopardy** — Put them in danger so we worry for them.
    - **Overcoming Fear** — Set them against a primal fear — the unknown, powerlessness, death — and we identify with the struggle.
    - **Handicap & Hardship** — Burden them with disability, poverty, addiction or circumstance — the underdog.
- **We care about HUMANISTIC VIRTUES**
  - _Selflessness & Sacrifice_
    - **Caring at a Cost** — They help others at real cost to themselves.
    - **Risking Life for Others** — They risk or give their life for someone.
    - **Fighting a Just Cause** — They fight selflessly for something larger than themselves.
    - **Nurturing Acts** — Small acts of kindness and care.
  - _Warmth & Tenderness_
    - **Liked by Children** — Children — innocence — like, or are liked by, them.
    - **Patting the Dog** — They like animals, or animals like them.
    - **Loving Others** — They love family, friends and neighbours deeply.
    - **Humanity in Private** — They show their true, gentle self when no one is watching.
  - _Moral Standing_
    - **Integrity** — Show them ethical, loyal, dependable, responsible.
    - **Valued by Others** — Others admire, respect or rely on them.
- **We LIKE DESIRABLE QUALITIES**
  - _Competence & Power_
    - **Skill & Expertise** — Make them brilliant at what they do.
    - **In Touch with Power** — They command real power — over others, to act, to express, or a super-power.
    - **A Glamorous Profession** — Give them an alluring job.
    - **Wit & Cleverness** — They outthink their problems.
  - _Grit & Drive_
    - **Courage** — They find the courage to face their problem.
    - **Persistence** — They keep trying against the odds.
    - **Hard Working** — A tireless capacity for work that drives the story.
    - **Obsession & Passion** — Intense passion or obsession focused on a single goal.
    - **Physicality** — Athletic or physical prowess.
  - _Charm & Likeability_
    - **Funny** — They make us laugh, so we forgive much.
    - **Just Plain Nice** — A plainly good heart.
    - **Attractiveness** — Beauty appeals.
    - **Childlike Wonder** — Innocence or wide-eyed enthusiasm.
    - **Loved by Friends** — Shown already loved, granting us permission to care.
  - _Admirable Character_
    - **A Valued Trait** — They strongly display a prized virtue — loyalty, love, courage.
    - **Misfit / Rebel** — An outsider who flouts authority and is at ease with themselves.
    - **Eyes of the Audience** — We learn only as the hero learns, sharing their viewpoint.

**Related:** Protagonist, Moment of Humanity, Universal Human Values, Self-Revelation

### Chorus `Cb`

A chorus is a voice, or group of voices, outside the main action of a play that comments on it for the audience. In ancient Greek plays it was a group of citizens who spoke and sang together. In later plays it is often one speaker, who may open the play or begin an act. It usually speaks to the audience, not to the characters in the scene.

**The concept:** A chorus lets a writer step outside the story and guide how the audience understands it. The word comes from a Greek word for a group that sang and danced together. Because it stands outside the scene, a chorus can tell the audience what is coming, or ask the audience to imagine what the stage cannot show. In Henry V, the Chorus opens the fourth act by asking the audience to “entertain conjecture of a time”, when two armies wait in the dark. When you find any chorus, say who speaks and for whom, what it tells or asks the audience, and what it wants them to feel or judge.

**Examples:** “A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life” — the Chorus tells the audience in the opening speech that the lovers will die, before the play begins — Romeo and Juliet; “O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend / The brightest heaven of invention” — the Chorus opens the play by asking for inspiration, and asks the audience to imagine a kingdom as the stage — Henry V; “Now old desire doth in his deathbed lie, / And young affection gapes to be his heir” — the Chorus tells the audience before Act 2 that an old love is dying and a new one is ready to take its place — Romeo and Juliet

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We listen to a voice that stands outside the action and speaks to us about it. · Feel: We feel dread or sadness, because the chorus can tell us what is coming before the characters know it. · Think: We work out what the chorus wants us to judge, and what lesson about the characters or their society it points to. · Act: We notice when news reports, commentators and narrators tell us how to feel about events, and ask whether we agree.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any chorus, a voice or group set apart from the action that comments on it for the audience. 1. Who forms the chorus: one voice or a group? 2. Does it stand outside the action, and does it speak to the characters, to the audience, or both? 3. What does it tell or warn the audience that the characters do not know? 4. What does the writer want the audience to think or feel through it? Try the questions on Time in Shakespeare’s The Winter’s Tale, at the start of Act 4. The chorus is one voice: Time, the idea of time acted as a person, and the stage direction reads “Enter Time, the Chorus.” Time stands outside the story and speaks only to the audience, whom he calls “Gentle spectators”. He tells them that sixteen years have passed, and that Perdita, the daughter King Leontes lost, is “now grown in grace”. Leontes, who is grieving so deeply that he shuts himself away, does not know where she is. Shakespeare may want the audience to accept the gap in time, and to see time as a power that brings both joy and terror, as Time says of himself.

**How to create it:** Decide who your chorus is: one voice or a group that speaks for the people watching. Place it outside the scene, speaking to the reader. Give it one thing to say before the main event, such as a warning or the ending. Make it say what your characters do not know. Check that the chorus comments rather than acts; if it changes the plot, give that job to a character.

### The Flaw `Fw`

A flaw is a weakness in a character that shapes how they act now. Often it is a strength taken too far: courage can become recklessness, and loyalty can become blind trust. This makes it hard to give up, because losing the flaw could mean losing the strength. A flaw is different from a past wound, the old hurt that may have caused it: the flaw is what the reader sees in the character's actions.

**The concept:** A flaw lets a writer show that a character's best and worst qualities can be the same quality. A reader can then feel sorrow, not only blame, when the flaw causes harm. In Othello, Iago, Othello's officer, says of him “The Moor is of a free and open nature / That thinks men honest that but seem to be so”. Othello's trusting nature is a strength, and Iago plans to use it to deceive him. When you write about any flaw, say what strength or desire lies behind it, what it costs the character and other people, and what the writer wants us to learn.
