**Examples:** “I, who have prided myself on my discernment!” — Elizabeth Bennet, proud of how well she judges people, cries this after she learns that she judged both Mr Darcy and Mr Wickham wrongly — Pride and Prejudice; “Wisely and slow; they stumble that run fast.” — Friar Lawrence, who has just agreed to marry Romeo and Juliet, warns Romeo, who says he is in “sudden haste”, that people who hurry stumble — Romeo and Juliet; “I will work harder” — Boxer, the strongest horse on Animal Farm, answers every problem with this motto and adds “Napoleon is always right”, so his strength and loyalty lead him to trust Napoleon, the pig who leads the farm, without question — Animal Farm

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We watch how one trait, taken too far, keeps pulling the character towards the same kind of trouble. · Feel: We feel pity and worry, because the character's own admirable quality is what puts them in danger. · Think: We ask what strength lies behind the flaw, and what the writer is saying about pride, trust, ambition or jealousy. · Act: We notice that people we admire can have a quality that harms them when taken too far, and ask what ours might be.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any flaw, the weakness that shapes how a character acts now. 1. What is the character good at, or admired for? 2. What trait causes them trouble now, and is it the same quality as that strength, taken too far? 3. What does the flaw cost the character, or other people? 4. What does the writer want the reader to learn from what the flaw does? Try the questions on Frankenstein. Victor Frankenstein is a gifted, determined young scientist who works until he discovers how to give life to a body. His flaw is ambition, the same drive that made him succeed, with no limit and no care for the result. He warns Walton, an explorer, that the man who “aspires to become greater than his nature will allow” is less happy than one who stays content. When his creation comes alive, Victor runs away from it, the abandoned creature turns against him, and people Victor loves die. Mary Shelley may be warning about ambition without care for the result: in the 1831 edition, Victor tells Walton, “Seek happiness in tranquillity and avoid ambition”.

**How to create it:** Choose one strength you want readers to admire, such as courage, loyalty or cleverness. Show that strength working well early in the story. Show the same quality going too far in a later scene, so that it ignores other people's needs. Then show it causing a problem. Check that a reader could name the strength and the flaw as one trait; if not, make the link clearer.

**Kinds of Flaw** — The flaw is the trait that shapes how a character acts NOW — not the wound that caused it (that is the Ghost). Its richest form is the flip-side of a real strength, which is why giving it up feels like losing themselves. Pick the one that fits your character, then name the strength it is the other face of.

- **Flaws of EXCESS — a strength pushed too far** — the character wants, feels or reaches too much
  - **Ambition / over-reaching** — Drive that will not stop at the place the world has allotted them. The flip-side of courage. _(e.g. "Vaulting ambition, which o'erleaps itself" — Macbeth names the flaw in the very speech where he argues himself out of the murder, and does it anyway — Macbeth)_
  - **Hubris** — Pride that refuses correction, warning or limit — the flaw that cannot be told anything. _(e.g. “Wealth was an inferior object, but what glory would attend the discovery if I could banish disease from the human frame” — the aim is glory, and glory is the thing no warning can reach — Frankenstein)_
  - **Jealousy** — Love turned possessive and suspicious, so devotion becomes surveillance. _(e.g. "the green-eyed monster" — Iago names the very thing he is planting in Othello — Othello)_
  - **Obsession** — One purpose crowding out every other, until the character stops living in the present. _(e.g. “Break their hearts, my pride and hope, break their hearts and have no mercy!” — one purpose repeated, with nothing else left in the life around it — Great Expectations)_
  - **Impulsiveness / haste** — Feeling converted straight into action with no pause for consequence. _(e.g. “Is it e'en so? Then I defy you, stars!” — feeling turned straight into a decision, with no pause to check the news — Romeo and Juliet)_
  - **Greed / miserliness** — Hoarding — money, time, affection — until the hoard replaces the life. _(e.g. "I wear the chain I forged in life" — Marley shows Scrooge the debt a hoarding life runs up — A Christmas Carol)_
- **Flaws of DEFICIT — a strength withheld** — the character will not give, risk or see enough
  - **The walled heart** — Hurt so deeply that they let no one in. The defence is real self-protection, which is exactly why it is so hard to lower — and it reads as coldness from outside while feeling like safety from within. _(e.g. "solitary as an oyster" — Scrooge's isolation is armour built on old losses, and the whole novella is the work of prising it open — A Christmas Carol)_
  - **The heart trained out** — Not hurt into hardness but RAISED into it — taught that feeling is weakness, so warmth was never allowed to form. _(e.g. "I have no heart" — Estella states it plainly, as something done to her rather than chosen — Great Expectations)_
  - **Cowardice / passivity** — Seeing what is right and not doing it — the flaw of the character who could have spoken. _(e.g. “The world, that understandable and lawful world, was slipping away.” — he can see exactly what is being lost and still does not act to hold it — Lord of the Flies)_
  - **Self-deception** — Refusing to look straight at one's own nature, so the truth has to arrive as catastrophe. _(e.g. “the moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde” — the sentence is already untrue when he says it, and he needs it to be true — Jekyll and Hyde)_
  - **Snobbery / class pride** — Valuing rank above people, so status decides who counts as human. _(e.g. “community and all that nonsense” — one dismissive word cancels every duty he owes to people below him — An Inspector Calls)_

**Related:** Protagonist, The Ghost / Wound, Want (Goal) vs Need, Antagonist, Character Arc, Hamartia

### Moment of Humanity `Hn`

A moment of humanity is a small moment that shows a character's human side, such as kindness, love, sadness or wonder. It is usually something short that the character says or does. It builds empathy, which is sharing a character's feelings, often for a character the reader might otherwise dislike or fear. It can come early in a story, or after the reader has seen the character do wrong.

**The concept:** A moment of humanity lets a writer show that a cruel or frightening character has real feelings, so readers can care about them. In Romeo and Juliet, Lord Capulet tells Paris, who wants to marry Juliet, that she is too young: “My child is yet a stranger in the world”. Later he threatens to throw her out of his house for refusing Paris, but this early moment shows that he loves her. When you find any moment of humanity, say what human side it shows, where it comes, and what the writer wants us to understand about the character.

**Examples:** “wept to see his poor forgotten self as he used to be” — Scrooge, a mean old businessman, weeps when the Ghost of Christmas Past shows him the lonely schoolboy he once was — A Christmas Carol; “I gazed with a kind of wonder” — the creature that Victor Frankenstein made tells Victor about his first days alive, and says this about the moon rising above the trees — Frankenstein; “No little children to love me!” — Captain Hook, the pirate who is Peter Pan's enemy, says this to himself on his ship when he is feeling gloomy — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice the small moment when a cruel, frightening or distant character shows a human feeling. · Feel: We feel some sympathy for the character, even if we dislike or fear them, because their feeling is one we share. · Think: We ask what the character is really like, and what the writer is saying about people we judge too quickly. · Act: We look for the human side of difficult people in real life, and do not judge them from one moment.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any moment of humanity, a small beat that makes the reader feel for a character. 1. Which character might the reader dislike or keep at a distance? 2. What small thing do they say or do that shows a human side, such as a joke, a kindness or a fear? 3. Where does it come, and what has the character done just before? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand about the character after this moment? Try the questions on Macbeth. Lady Macbeth, who has pushed her husband Macbeth to kill King Duncan, may seem cold and cruel. She says she would have done the killing herself “Had he not resembled / My father as he slept”. It shows a flash of family feeling. It comes in Act 2 scene 2, as Macbeth returns from the killing, after she has drugged the king's guards and laid out their daggers. Shakespeare may want readers to see that she is not only cold: a human side shows even here.

**How to create it:** Choose a character you want readers to dislike or distrust at first. Give them one small, real moment, such as a kindness, a joke or a worry. Keep it short, a line or two, and make it fit their personality. Do not explain it. Check by asking a friend whether the character seems like a real person after that line; if not, make the detail more specific.

**Related:** Empathy

### Narrative Ellipsis `Ne`

Narrative ellipsis is when a writer leaves out a stretch of the story's time. The writer jumps from one moment to a later one and trusts the reader to imagine what happened in between. One sentence can skip years, and a chapter break can skip a war. It differs from a summary, which tells the skipped time quickly: an ellipsis tells little or nothing of it.

**The concept:** Ellipsis lets a writer decide which parts of a story the reader sees, and so which parts seem most important. The reader fills the gap with their own imagination, and what is left out can matter as much as what is told. In the Bible story of Jacob (Genesis), Jacob works to marry Rachel, and one verse skips seven years: “Jacob served seven years for Rachel; and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her”. When you find any ellipsis, say how much time is skipped, what has changed afterwards, and what the writer wants us to think about what is left out.

**Examples:** “I now pass a space of eight years almost in silence” — Jane, the narrator, skips eight years of her life in one sentence, and adds only a few lines to link what comes before and after — Jane Eyre; “For eleven years, I had not seen Joe nor Biddy with my bodily eyes” — the last chapter opens eleven years after Pip left for the East, as he walks into Joe and Biddy's kitchen; the years between are not shown — Great Expectations; “the years came and went without bringing the careless boy” — years pass in one sentence, and when Wendy next meets Peter Pan she is a married woman — Peter Pan

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We notice where the story skips time, and wonder what happened in the gap we are not shown. · Feel: We feel curiosity or loss, because time has passed without us and the character has changed while we were not looking. · Think: We ask what changed in the gap, and why the writer left it out: what does the writer want us to imagine? · Act: We notice what is left out of news reports, adverts and the stories people tell about themselves, and ask what the gap hides.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any narrative ellipsis, a stretch of story time the writer leaves out. 1. How much time is skipped, and does the text say how much? 2. How does the writer mark the jump: a chapter break, a short sentence or something else? 3. What has changed on the far side of the gap? 4. What does the writer want the reader to think about what was left out? Try the questions on Animal Farm. Years are skipped, but the text gives no number. The jump is marked by a chapter break followed by a short sentence: “Years passed.” On the far side, a time has come when “there was no one who remembered the old days before the Rebellion” except Clover, a horse, Benjamin, a donkey, Moses, a raven, and a number of the pigs. Orwell may want readers to see how easily the past is forgotten when almost nobody remembers it, so that the pigs' version can replace it.

**How to create it:** Choose a stretch of time in your story that does not need to be shown, such as a journey or a long wait. Write the last moment before it and the first moment after it. Mark the jump with a short sentence or a chapter break. Show on the far side of the gap what has changed. Check that a reader can tell what changed without being told; if not, add one detail.

**Related:** Scene vs Summary

### The Sublime `Ub`

The sublime is the mix of awe and fear we feel before something too large or powerful for the mind to understand fully. Awe is wonder mixed with respect. Examples of such things are a mountain, a storm, the sea or the great age of the earth. Writers build the sublime from huge scale, often with one small human figure set beside it. A beautiful scene only delights us; a sublime one also frightens us.

**The concept:** The sublime lets a writer show how small a person, or a person's power, is beside nature or time. In Ozymandias, a traveller describes the broken statue of a king who boasted of his power, and beyond it the desert: “The lone and level sands stretch far away.” The endless sand makes the king look small, and we feel awe at its size and unease that his power has not lasted. When you find any sublime moment, say what is vast, what small person or thing is set beside it, and what the writer wants us to understand or feel about the vast thing.

**Examples:** “a huge peak, black and huge” — Wordsworth remembers rowing a boat he had taken in secret, when a huge black peak seems to rise up and stride after him, and he is frightened — Extract from The Prelude; “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” — God speaks to Job out of a whirlwind and asks questions that show how small human knowledge is beside the making of the world — The Bible (Job); “And ice, mast-high, came floating by, / As green as emerald.” — the Mariner remembers his ship driven into the frozen southern sea, where ice as tall as the mast surrounds it and cracks and roars, so the sight is both beautiful and frightening — The Rime of the Ancient Mariner

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We look up at something far larger than the small human figure standing beneath it. · Feel: We feel awe and fear together, because the vast thing is wonderful to look at and could also destroy us. · Think: We measure human pride and power against nature and time, and ask what the writer wants us to learn about our smallness. · Act: We may treat wild places and natural forces with more care and respect after meeting something far bigger than us.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any sublime moment, one where something too vast to understand fully brings awe and fear together. 1. What is vast, and how does the writing show its size? 2. Which person or thing is set small beside it? 3. Which words give wonder, and which give fear? 4. What does the writer want the reader to understand or feel about the vast thing? Try the questions on Frankenstein. Victor Frankenstein, a young scientist, makes his way into a ravine, a narrow valley, in the Alps. 1. The mountains and precipices, or steep cliffs, are vast, and the word “immense” shows their size. The raging river and the dashing waterfalls add noise and force, and together they make Victor think of “a power mighty as Omnipotence”, meaning unlimited power, usually God's. 2. Victor is the small figure beside them. 3. Wonder comes in the valley's “magnificent and astonishing character”; fear comes in the elements shown “in their most terrific guise”, where “terrific” means terrifying. 4. Mary Shelley may want readers to feel that nature has a power far greater than any person's, even a scientist's.

**How to create it:** Choose something huge, such as a mountain, the sea or the night sky. Set one small human figure inside it. Give two details of its size, such as how far it stretches or how long it has lasted. Add one word of wonder and one word of fear. Ask a friend how the figure feels; if they cannot say, add something the figure sees or does.

### Secondary World `Wb`

A secondary world is an invented world with its own places, history and rules, not our real world. A writer holds it together by consistency: once a rule is set, the story keeps to it. A world that breaks its own rules is hard to believe, while one that keeps them can feel real however strange it is. Some secondary worlds look like ours but change one rule, such as a place where animals talk.

**The concept:** A secondary world lets a writer explore real ideas, such as power or fear, in an invented place with rules the writer sets. Readers believe in the place when the story keeps its rules. In Peter Pan, Barrie sets a rule: when a child says “I don't believe in fairies”, a fairy somewhere falls down dead. Later Tinker Bell, a fairy, says she could get well if children believed in fairies, and when many children clap she lives. When you write about any secondary world, say what rules the writer sets, whether the story keeps them, and what the world lets the writer show.

**Examples:** “DRINK ME” — a label on a bottle that Alice, who has fallen down a rabbit-hole, finds in Wonderland; drinking from it shrinks her, and the story keeps this rule when a cake marked “EAT ME” makes her grow — Alice's Adventures in Wonderland; “a human creature not six inches high” — Gulliver, a ship's surgeon, wakes tied down and sees a person of Lilliput, a land of tiny people, whose size sets the scale for the people and buildings of that land — Gulliver's Travels; “it takes all the running you can do, to keep in the same place” — the Red Queen tells Alice that in her country you must run as fast as you can just to stay where you are — Through the Looking-Glass

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We focus on the rules of an invented place, and notice whether the story keeps to them. · Feel: We feel wonder at how strange the place is, and trust when it keeps its rules. · Think: We ask what real ideas the invented world lets the writer explore, because a made-up place can show them from a distance. · Act: We notice how games, films and adverts build whole worlds with their own rules, and ask what those rules want us to accept.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any secondary world, an invented reality with its own places, history and rules. 1. What has the writer invented: places, peoples, history, or rules for how things work? 2. Choose one rule of the world. Does the story keep to it every time it matters? 3. How does this world differ from ours, and what does the difference let the writer show? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or understand through it? Try the questions on The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum. Baum invented the Land of Oz, with places such as the Emerald City, peoples such as the Munchkins, and four witches, two good and two wicked. One rule is that the Wicked Witch of the West fears water: “the old Witch never touched water, nor ever let water touch her in any way.” The story keeps it. She never comes near Dorothy while Dorothy bathes, and later, when Dorothy is her prisoner, a bucket of water that Dorothy throws over her melts the Witch away. Unlike Kansas, Dorothy's home, Oz has living witches. The Scarecrow, the Tin Woodman and the Lion also talk, and each asks the Wizard for a brain, a heart or courage. This lets Baum ask what those qualities really are. The Wizard tells the Lion “You have plenty of courage, I am sure.” Baum may want readers to feel that people often have the qualities they think they lack.

**How to create it:** Write down three rules of your world, such as what a power costs, who can use it and where it stops. Invent one place and one piece of history that explain those rules. Write scenes that obey every rule, even where breaking one would be easier. Check each scene against your list; if a scene breaks a rule, change the scene or change the rule everywhere.

### Stunning Surprise `Us`

A stunning surprise is a shock that changes what the main character is trying to do. It turns a general wish into one clear job, or destroys the character's plan so that a new one is needed. It often comes near the end of the first act, the first main part of a play, but not always. A plot twist, a sudden reveal that changes what the reader believes, is a stunning surprise only when it also changes what the character must do.

**The concept:** A stunning surprise lets a writer give the main character a new, urgent task, often at the end of the first main part of a story. Without it, the middle of a story can drift, because the character has nothing urgent to do. In Macbeth, Macbeth already hopes to be king. When King Duncan names his son Malcolm as heir, Macbeth sees a clear obstacle and says “That is a step / On which I must fall down, or else o'erleap”. When you find any stunning surprise, say what the character wanted before it, what they must do after it, and what the writer wants us to feel.

**Examples:** “The marriage cannot go on: I declare the existence of an impediment.” — a voice in the church stops Jane's wedding to Mr Rochester, who already has a wife, so her plan to marry him is destroyed — Jane Eyre; “get thee to church a Thursday, / Or never after look me in the face” — Capulet orders Juliet, who is secretly married to Romeo, to marry Paris on Thursday, so she must find a way out and goes to Friar Lawrence for help — Romeo and Juliet; “Kill the Wicked Witch of the West” — Oz, the Wizard, says Dorothy must do this before he will help her go home, so her wish to go home becomes one dangerous job — The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

**Effect on the reader** — Focus: We focus on the shock, and on what it takes from the character or what job it gives them. · Feel: We feel the jolt of the shock, and then worry, because the character's old plan no longer works. · Think: We ask what the character must do now, and what the shock shows about what they truly want and what it will cost. · Act: We notice how sudden news forces people to change their plans, and ask how we would respond.

**How to analyse it:** Ask four questions of any stunning surprise, a shock that changes what the main character is trying to do. 1. What shock happens, and where in the story does it fall? 2. What did the character want before it, and what must they do after it? 3. Does it make the character's want more specific, or destroy their plan and force a new one? 4. What does the writer want the reader to feel or think at this point? Try the questions on Great Expectations. Magwitch, a convict whom Pip helped as a boy, appears in Pip's rooms and says that he, not Miss Havisham, has paid for Pip to become a gentleman. Magwitch's return ends the second of the book's three stages. Before his return, Pip believed Miss Havisham meant him to marry Estella. After it, Pip must hide and protect Magwitch, who could be hanged if caught. The return destroys Pip's plan and gives him one urgent job. Dickens makes the reader feel Pip's shame: Pip thinks he has deserted Joe, the blacksmith who raised him.

**How to create it:** Decide what your character wants at the start of the story. Choose a moment near the end of the first section where something shocking happens. Make the shock take away their plan, or turn a general wish into one specific job. Show the character deciding what to do next. Check that the character now has a task they did not have before; if not, change the shock.

**Stunning Surprise — how the act-ending shock lands** — The beat in detail: what has to be true for the shock to turn the story rather than merely startle.

- **What makes it land**
  - **Happens to the hero alone** — The shock strikes the protagonist, no one else — it is their world that tilts. _(e.g. “This gentleman, Mr. Rochester, has a wife now living... Her name is Bertha Mason.” — the shock is Jane's alone; hers is the life changed in a single sentence — Jane Eyre)_
  - **In a single instant** — Not a slow reveal — one sudden blow that arrives abruptly. _(e.g. “Kapow!” — Queen Mary dies and Elizabeth is handed the crown)_
  - **Truly unexpected** — It must genuinely shock the hero and the reader — completely unforeseen. _(e.g. “Macduff was from his mother's womb / Untimely ripped” — Macbeth and the audience both believed he was safe, yet the wording of the prophecy had allowed this all along — Macbeth)_
  - **Changes everything** — The hero’s old life is over; things can never look the same. A vague goal becomes one burning, specific goal. _(e.g. “I've made a gentleman on you!” — Pip's old life ends in one line: his fortune came from the convict, not from Miss Havisham — Great Expectations)_
  - **The darkest-hour version** — A second Stunning Surprise can destroy the hero’s plan at their lowest point, forcing a total rethink. _(e.g. “Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler” — the writing on the van destroys everything the animals have worked for, at the lowest point of the book — Animal Farm)_

**Related:** Inciting Incident, Surprise, Plot Twist, Turning Point, Subverted Expectation
